title: WebMCPify
pitch: Give any existing website an agent interface — without rebuilding it.
about_excerpt: Give any existing website an agent interface — without rebuilding it. Like Comment Story Updates home demo Inspiration Most websites were built for people clicking around. Agents are bad at that. They guess at buttons, and that’s a terrible idea when money is involved. WebMCP is the right fix: the page exposes real tools. But the site has to add them. Shopify can. Almost nobody else will. I wanted something in between. Paste a URL. Keep the original site. Agents still get tools. What it does Paste a public URL. WebMCPify crawls it, GPT-5.6 writes tools as recipes (click this, fill that — not page JavaScript), we run them on the live site, and a small script registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool . You get an agent-ready URL (Cloudflare proxy, no change to the original site) or a one-line script for you to update it in code. Humans keep the same UI. Agents call named tools. How I built it Playwright crawls the site (this runs on Render). GPT-5.6 writes the tools. We try them on the live site. If one fails, a second model ( gpt-5.6-terra ) tries to fix it. A Cloudflare Worker serves the page and injects the script. Or you drop in a script tag. GPT never writes code that runs in the browser. If a tool would pay, order, delete, or send something, we mark it sensitive and show a confirm dialog. Results stay small so the agent doesn’t get a wall of HTML. What I learned Don’t let the model write page JavaScript. Recipes are boring and that’s the point. They’re easy to check and they can’t eval anything. OpenAI structured outputs hate nested schemas. My first recipe format used a union type per step and the API just rejected it. I flattened the schema and generate started working. ChatGPT only sees tools on the top-level page. A bookmarklet or an iframe doesn’t count. The proxy keeps the shop UI and the tools on one origin, which is what the in-app browser needs. Netlify doesn’t have a real filesystem. Site state lives in Redis. The dashboard is a WebMCP page too. You can ask it to analyze a site and hand back the agent-ready URL. Challenges Sites you don’t own. A script tag is clean, but most sites won’t add one. The Worker proxy injects the same bridge with no deploy on their side. I shipped both. Same origin, or it doesn’t count. Tools have to sit on the top-level document. That’s a proxy problem, not a prompt problem — rewrite HTML, patch fetch/history, keep the UI. Don’t trust the model with money. Pay / order / delete / send is marked sensitive in code and gets an on-page confirm. The agent can still call place_order . A human has to click Confirm. Structured outputs. Nested step types died at the API. One flat step object, unused fields null , and the pipeline runs. What’s next Tighter locators on messy SPAs. Confirm as a hard rule in the interpreter, not only in the recipe. More navigation than fetch / history . Then more of the public web. The web isn’t getting rebuilt. It can still grow an agent interface. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. video_transcript_excerpt: SVGenT stages fictional coding agent sessions and renders them to SVG images and video. With Web and CP, the agent in ChatGPT's browser writes and directs them with you on the real product. The page is open in ChatGPT's built-in browser, the full studio, and on the right, the agent rail reports that the site tools are registered. The first request goes in. The agent reads the authoring guide and writes the script. This wait is sped up. The script lands through load script and the camera comes on. The stage plays it right away. A heading, three bullets, and a code block typed out on the stage. Next, a choice step. Edit message adds three options and picks the developer one. The stage restarts on the new beat and the log on the right shows every call as it happens. The question becomes voice input. The composer shows a capture instead of typing. title: Release Evidence Room
pitch: The agent builds the release evidence case. The human makes the call.
about_excerpt: The agent builds the release evidence case. The human makes the call. Like Comment Story Updates Start here Release Evidence Room — agent review dashboard: Open the release review workspace Checkout QA Sandbox — synthetic shopping test site: Generate response-loss and retry evidence Source code — application, WebMCP tools, and tests: Browse the public GitHub repository Judge walkthrough — exact evaluation sequence: Follow the step-by-step WebMCP guide Inspiration Release decisions are often fragmented across dashboards, test systems, network traces, and chat. A release can report 18 of 18 tests passing while still lacking evidence that a response-loss retry is safe. Scraping screens gives an agent context, but not a stable contract for evidence provenance, bounded access, safe mutation, or human approval. I built Release Evidence Room to turn the review page itself into a typed collaboration surface for the agent and the release owner. What it does Release Evidence Room starts with a public fictional checkout sandbox. The first operation is accepted but its response is lost; retrying the same intent with a new idempotency key creates a second modeled operation. The browser hands that exact synthetic session to the Release Evidence Room. The page exposes five narrow WebMCP tools. An agent can read the release snapshot, query only page-owned sanitized evidence, propose a missing regression test, run an approved verification, and propose a verification-linked READY or HOLD decision. The human must approve the test before verification can run, and only the human can confirm the final release decision. The approved verifier supports an exact targeted replay and a deterministic seeded monkey run. In the intentionally risky fixture, both reproduce two modeled side effects and support a HOLD recommendation. This demonstrates a release risk; it does not claim that a real customer was charged twice. How I built it The application is a two-route React and TypeScript project built with Vite. The Release Evidence Room registers exactly five imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_release_snapshot , query_network_evidence , propose_test_case , run_approved_verification , and propose_release_decision . Every tool has a strict JSON schema with additionalProperties: false and a separate runtime parser. The UI and the tool handlers use the same pure release-domain transitions. Versioned localStorage adapters validate both structure and cross-field consistency before restoring a checkout session or release state. State-changing calls require the current expectedStateVersion and a reusable clientRequestId . Stale calls fail with state_conflict , while exact retries replay their original result without creating duplicate work. Verification runs only inside a deterministic page-owned sandbox and cannot fetch a URL, execute arbitrary code, access a live payment system, approve a proposal, deploy a release, or confirm the final decision. Vitest covers the state machine, evidence handoff, domain rules, persistence, components, verifier, and WebMCP handlers. Playwright covers the complete checkout-to-HOLD path. The application is deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making the agent useful without giving it release authority. Approval and final confirmation therefore are not merely prompt instructions: no WebMCP tool exists for either action. A second challenge was demonstrating a realistic retry risk without exposing company data, raw packets, credentials, customer details, or a real payment backend. I solved this with a deterministic fictional checkout model and opaque, page-owned evidence references. The third challenge was making agent retries and concurrent-looking state changes safe. Optimistic state versions reject stale mutations, idempotent request IDs prevent duplicate proposals and verification runs, and deterministic seeds make bounded monkey verification reproducible. Accomplishments that I am proud of The public application completes a two-route checkout-to-release workflow without requiring an account, card, credential, backend, or real payment. It exposes exactly five bounded WebMCP tools and keeps human approval and the final release decision outside the agent interface. A clean native run in ChatGPT's in-app browser completed the checkout handoff, tool discovery, approval guard, targeted replay, seeded monkey verification, idempotent replay, stale-state rejection, READY guard, human-confirmed HOLD, and reload persistence. The repository reports 88 passing automated tests. Its production build, Playwright integration path, and high-severity dependency audit also pass. All submitted evidence is fictional, synthetic, and privacy-safe. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable as a narrow domain contract rather than a collection of automated buttons. Page-owned tools can give an agent reliable structured context while keeping data access and actions smaller than the full UI. I also learned that schemas alone are not enough: runtime validation, optimistic concurrency, idempotent retries, deterministic verification, and visible attribution are all necessary for trustworthy agent workflows. Human-in-the-loop safety is strongest when sensitive authority is absent from the tool surface, not merely discouraged in a prompt. What's next Next I would add adapters for other sanitized, page-owned evidence formats while continuing to prohibit raw traffic fetching and arbitrary code execution. I would also add portable evidence bundles, authenticated multi-reviewer workflows with serialized writes, and more deterministic verification strategies for retry and workflow risks. Human approval and final release confirmation would remain explicit boundaries. title: AquaEye
pitch: Agentic water safety system that connects live industrial sensors, PLC control, and WebMCP tools for intelligent monitoring and safe pump decisions.
about_excerpt: Agentic water safety system that connects live industrial sensors, PLC control, and WebMCP tools for intelligent monitoring and safe pump decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP tools Siemens_TIA_Portal_PLC_Program AquaEye dashboard Sensors + PLC + Raspberry Pi Inspiration## Inspiration Water safety systems often generate large amounts of sensor data, but operators still need to interpret those signals and interact with industrial control systems manually. We wanted to explore how an AI agent could work with a real physical system while keeping industrial safety logic in control. This led to AquaEye — an intelligent water safety system combining real-time water sensing, Siemens PLC control, Raspberry Pi edge computing, and WebMCP-based AI-agent interaction. What AquaEye Does AquaEye monitors water conditions using pH, turbidity, and flow sensors connected to a Siemens PLC. The system architecture consists of: Industrial sensors for real-time water monitoring Siemens PLC for industrial control and safety logic Raspberry Pi as the edge-computing layer Python backend communicating with the PLC using Snap7 Web dashboard for human monitoring WebMCP tools that allow AI agents to interact with AquaEye through the browser The backend converts the physical sensor signals into structured information and evaluates the water condition against configured safety limits. WebMCP Integration WebMCP is the key interface between AquaEye and AI agents. AquaEye exposes five tools: get_water_status — retrieves the current water measurements and system condition. analyze_water_safety — analyzes the current water parameters and returns a safety decision. get_system_status — provides the overall system state. start_pump — provides controlled pump-start interaction. stop_pump — provides controlled pump-stop interaction. This allows an AI agent to discover AquaEye's capabilities and interact with live system information through the browser instead of relying only on a traditional dashboard. Human + Agent Collaboration The dashboard is designed for the human operator, while WebMCP provides an interface for AI-agent interaction. The human can visually monitor the physical system and dashboard, while an AI agent can request structured system information and analyze the current water-safety condition. Importantly, the AI interaction does not replace the industrial safety layer. The PLC and programmed safety logic remain responsible for the physical control system. How It Was Built The physical sensors are connected to the Siemens PLC. The Raspberry Pi communicates with the PLC using Snap7 and runs the AquaEye backend. The Flask backend exposes the system data through APIs. The web frontend presents the live information to the operator. WebMCP is implemented directly in the frontend using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each registered tool connects an agent request to the corresponding AquaEye backend capability. Challenges One of the main challenges was connecting the browser-based WebMCP layer to a real industrial PLC system. We had to integrate PLC communication, Raspberry Pi networking, the Python backend, the web dashboard, and WebMCP while maintaining a clear separation between AI interaction and physical safety control. Another challenge was making the system work with live industrial data rather than a simulated software-only environment. What I Learned This project demonstrated how WebMCP can become an interface between AI agents and real-world systems. I learned how to combine industrial automation, PLC communication, edge computing, web technologies, and agent-facing tools into one architecture. The project also showed that AI-agent interaction can be added on top of an existing industrial control architecture without removing the deterministic safety logic that protects the physical system. What's Next The next stage for AquaEye is to expand the system with additional water-quality parameters, richer historical analysis, predictive monitoring, and more intelligent agent workflows. The long-term goal is to develop AquaEye into a platform where AI agents can assist operators in monitoring, diagnosing, and managing industrial water systems while maintaining appropriate industrial safety boundaries. title: Lobby — a concierge for humans and their agents
pitch: Lobby gives any business an AI concierge on its website. With WebMCP, the embed also exposes the concierge as structured tools — whatever a guest can do, a visiting agent can do too.
about_excerpt: Lobby gives any business an AI concierge on its website. With WebMCP, the embed also exposes the concierge as structured tools — whatever a guest can do, a visiting agent can do too. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every business answers the same questions all day — "are you open?", "how do I book?", "do you do private events?". Lobby started as an answer to that: a concierge any business can put on its website that actually knows the business and speaks with its guests. But guests are changing. More and more of them don't browse — they send their agent. A person asks ChatGPT or Claude to "find me a tennis lesson in Miami on Thursday," and the agent goes out to the web to figure it out by scraping pages and guessing at UIs. The businesses we serve are exactly the ones agents struggle with most: small, local, with information living in a conversation rather than structured markup. Our thesis from day one: the concierge should be one gate with two doors — one for humans, one for their agents. WebMCP is the missing piece that makes the second door real. What it does Lobby gives any business an AI concierge at lobby.host/c/<business> and as an embeddable widget on the business's own site (text + voice). With WebMCP, every page that carries a Lobby concierge now also registers structured tools for visiting agents: ask_concierge — ask the business's concierge anything a guest could ask; the reply comes from the same knowledge and logic the human-facing chat uses get_business_info — structured facts: hours, location, services, pricing, policies list_offerings — what the business offers, as data an agent can compare across businesses The point is symmetry: whatever a guest can do through the concierge, a visiting agent can do through the tools — same backend, same knowledge, same conversation engine. A human browsing with their agent can let the agent pre-ask the boring questions, then take over the conversation themselves in the same widget. One integration, many businesses: because the tools live in the Lobby embed, every business that installs Lobby becomes agent-accessible without writing a line of code. How we built it WebMCP layer (new, built during the challenge): an open-source script that ships with the Lobby widget and registers the tools via navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext.registerTool() . Tool schemas are generated from the concierge's public API, so any concierge slug works. Concierge platform (pre-existing): NestJS + PostgreSQL backend on Railway, Next.js frontend on Vercel, SSE streaming for replies, OpenAI for voice (TTS/STT). In line with the challenge rules on pre-existing work: the Lobby platform predates the challenge; everything WebMCP — the tool layer, its repo, and the demo integration — was built during the submission period, and the repo README documents the boundary between the two. Challenges we ran into Designing tools that are useful to an agent without letting it bypass the business's own boundaries — the tools expose exactly what the human-facing concierge exposes, nothing more. Making one tool surface work for both "agent browsing alongside a human" and "agent acting for an absent human" — the shared-session UX took the most iteration. Testing across ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled, which behave differently enough to matter. What's next Bookings and transactions: the next set of tools lets an agent not just ask, but do — check availability and book, through the same permissioned gate. Lobby becomes the way a small business plugs into the agentic web without rebuilding anything. title: Seedy Research
pitch: We make un-agentable archives agentable.
about_excerpt: We make un-agentable archives agentable. Like Comment Story Updates An agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser calls discover_research The agent calls build_research_path and the human's Research Path updates in place. Every supported claim resolves to a real page in a real NCCE volume. Verifiable, not generated — click through and read the Thai original. Inspiration Every AI agent shipping today can search the web. None of them can read Thailand's research output. Thailand's National Convention on Civil Engineering has run for decades. The proceedings exist as PDFs. Mixed encodings, no text layer on older scans, no cross-volume search, no API. To an agent, this archive does not exist. So a graduate student surveying prior work does it the 2005 way: download a volume, Ctrl-F, guess Thai keyword variants, repeat. Then their advisor asks "has anyone already done this?" and nobody can answer with confidence. Point a general-purpose agent at it and you get the worst possible failure mode: a citation that looks right. A fake page number inside a real volume survives review. It gets published. That's the wedge. Not "search is bad." The archive has no interface an agent can hold onto, and the substitute agents invent is dangerous. Three things made now the moment to build it: Agents got good enough to be trusted with research tasks — and therefore dangerous enough that unverifiable citations became a liability, not a quirk. WebMCP made the browser a distribution channel for tools. Before this, an agent-facing corpus meant getting into someone's MCP config. Now it means shipping a URL you can send to a professor. Retrieval got cheap enough to run at national scale. Our full stack runs under \$10/month. Archives held by underfunded institutions only get digitized if the running cost rounds to zero. ## What it does Seedy Research is a research workspace over an indexed Thai corpus — CE Project archives and NCCE Proceedings vol. 25, 26, and 29 — that exposes itself to any agent in the page. Surface What it does Agent-callable Explore Thai-first discovery; local = page-cited evidence, global = links only ✅ Chat Cited answers, paragraph-level retrieval ✅ Workspace Shared state: saved passages, comparisons, candidate gap ✅ read + write Research Path Evidence → connection → gap → testable next study ✅ Share & export Session URL, JSON export of the full evidence trail ✅ Every surface is agent-callable. That's deliberate. A workspace the agent can't write to is a workspace the human maintains alone. What people and agents can now do together that was hard or impossible before: Ask across 941 Thai PDFs and get a page you can open. The agent calls a tool, the passage renders with volume and page, and the human clicks through to the Thai original. Cross-language research without losing the source. The corpus is Thai. The agent reasons and answers in English while every citation still points at the Thai page. Co-author a gap statement. Human sets direction, agent fills evidence into the shared workspace, human prunes. Every line traceable. Hand off a session, not a transcript. JSON export or session URL — the next person, or the next agent, resumes with the same evidence set. ## How we built it We built the server-side MCP version first. It was the wrong product. A server-side MCP server hands an agent a database. It returns a string: "NCCE vol. 26, p. 412 reports a 14% reduction." The researcher then has two options — trust it, or go find volume 26 themselves. Neither one is research. WebMCP hands the agent the application . The agent calls our tool, the passage renders in the human's Evidence panel at that page in the original Thai, and then the tool returns to the agent. Verification stops being a task and becomes a glance. Same retrieval engine, completely different product. The tool layer. Next.js 15 on Vercel. Tools register client-side from a provider that mounts on session init. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_evidence", description: "Search the indexed Thai research corpus and return paragraph-level passages " + "with exact volume and page citations. Use for any claim that needs citing. " + "Do NOT use to find papers outside the indexed corpus — use " + "discover_related_research for that.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" }, collection: { enum: ["all", "ce_project", "ncce"] }, max_passages: { type: "integer", minimum: 1, maximum: 20 } }, required: ["query"] }, execute: async ({ query, collection = "all", max_passages = 6 }) => { const passages = await retrieve({ query, collection, max_passages }); setEvidencePanel(passages); // the human sees it first return { content: [{ type: "text", text: formatWithCitations(passages) }] }; } }); Two contracts hold the design together: Render before return. execute writes app state, then returns to the agent. One line of ordering separates a shared session from a remote control. We did not wrap our API. We shipped the verbs a researcher uses. Closed domains are enums, so agents produce a valid call on the first attempt instead of probing. Tool What it does for the agent search_evidence Page-cited paragraph retrieval over the local corpus answer_with_citations Cited answer through the bounded-context planner open_source_page Opens a document at a specific page for the human discover_related_research Metadata-only global discovery — no quotable field save_to_workspace Writes a passage into shared state list_workspace Reads back current shared state build_research_path Evidence → connection → gap → next study set_collection_filter Scopes the session to a collection export_session Full evidence trail as JSON Under the tool boundary. ChatGPT / Chrome agent │ document.modelContext.registerTool() ▼ Next.js 15 (Vercel) ── WebMCP tool layer ──► app state (Evidence, Workspace) │ ▼ FastAPI ── Bounded Agentic Context ──► planner → dedup → context budget │ → citation formatting ▼ Supabase pgvector — 49,965 chunks, page provenance preserved end to end The Bounded Agentic Context layer is our real engineering asset. A planner decides retrieval depth, deduplicates overlapping chunks, manages a context budget, and formats citations before anything reaches a model. The agent makes one call and gets clean, budgeted, citation-formatted results. All the expensive judgment lives inside the tool where we can guarantee it, instead of hoping the calling agent gets it right — and every future agent client inherits that for free. Collection PDFs Chunks CE Project Database 67 4,520 NCCE Database 874 45,445 Total 941 49,965 Auth, rate limiting, timeout control. Under \$10/month. Trust boundary and user control. Exposing tools means letting something else act inside a logged-in session, so we treated that as a product decision: Reads are free; writes are visible. Retrieval is frictionless. Anything that mutates shared state renders immediately and is reversible in one click. Nobody has to audit a log to learn what happened. No tool escalates scope. No generic fetch , no run_query , no arbitrary endpoint. Closed argument spaces, enums where the domain is closed. The surface an agent sees is exactly the surface we intend. Tools register with the session, not the origin. They mount after session init and unmount with the surfaces backing them. Nothing destructive is exposed. The worst outcome of a confused agent is a workspace with extra passages in it. Export is explicit. export_session returns to the human's session; it transmits nowhere. That posture is the precondition for institutional adoption. A university will not put its archive behind an agent that can delete things. When things go wrong. A demo that only shows the happy path isn't a product: Ambiguous requests get a question, not a guess. Scope-ambiguous queries return zero passages with an explicit note instead of weak matches. Agents route correctly on retry. Empty results are a real answer. "Nothing in the indexed corpus supports this" is returned as such. For a gap-finding tool, absence is the product. Budget overruns degrade rather than fail. Cap and deduplicate, never truncate mid-passage. Fewer complete citations, not more broken ones. Timeouts return partial evidence with a flag, so slow retrieval still yields something citable rather than an error the agent narrates as fact. ## Challenges we ran into Thai PDFs are hostile. Mixed encodings, no text layer on older scans, heading structure that shifts between NCCE volumes. Keeping page numbers alive through chunking, so a citation is actually clickable , was harder than retrieval itself. Page fidelity across the tool boundary. Volume and page must survive pgvector → planner → JSON tool result → UI panel. Any layer that drops that metadata breaks the only promise we make. Most retrieval systems lose citability here, and we had to rebuild our chunker to stop doing the same. Context budget versus completeness. Twenty passages makes an agent confident and wrong. We cap, ded

title: Jobbbler
pitch: A job site any WebMCP agent can operate end to end - find, compare, keep watching, apply - with the person in control.
about_excerpt: A job site any WebMCP agent can operate end to end - find, compare, keep watching, apply - with the person in control. Like Comment Story Updates A job site that serves people through its pages and agents through its tools. The site announces 29 actions; any WebMCP client discovers them on every page, with nothing to install. One request becomes one typed call: search_jobs runs and the page follows with the filters the agent set. Quiet reads leave the page still; open_job_details moves it. Every call stays visible to the person. Three roles compared on the facts the site returns, in a single call. Saved once. The review waits for the person's decision; then the server keeps checking after the tab closes. An agent-prepared application: read-only while it works, with the exact review of what would be sent. The web is getting its agent interface Websites were built for people: a page to read, buttons to click, forms to fill. An agent can drive that interface too, the way a person would, but it is slow, brittle and blind to what the site actually offers. That is why agentic APIs appeared: MCP gave agents proper, typed tools. It came with a catch. Every service needed its own server, every person needed to install and configure it, and an agent only knew about the handful of services someone had wired up in advance. WebMCP closes that gap. The website itself publishes its tools, right on the page, and any WebMCP-capable client discovers them the moment it arrives: ChatGPT's built-in browser today, Chrome with WebMCP, external agent clients that speak the protocol. No setup, no separate server, no integration to maintain. An agent moving through the web meets, on every site that adopts it, an interface made for agents: typed actions with clear inputs and results, instead of a screen to interpret. That is a different web. Call it headless: the same site serves people through its pages and agents through its tools, from one place, with one set of rules. Three things follow: Agents get a native interface to the web. Actions, not pixels. Reliable enough to hand real work to. It scales like the web does. One protocol; every site that adopts it extends every agent at once, with nothing to install. Delegation becomes possible. A person states an outcome, the agent operates the site, and the site keeps the person in the loop exactly where it matters. Jobbbler is what that looks like on one concrete, everyday task. One sentence, a whole job search Looking for a Product Designer position, remote, $90k+. Compare options, pick the top 2, and apply. Schedule for daily updates (every morning). My CV is attached. Said to a person, that is a week of open tabs. Said to an assistant on Jobbbler, it becomes a sequence of site actions: Find. The assistant asks Jobbbler which filters it accepts, then runs one search: product designer, remote, $90k and up. The results page follows along: URL, filters and matches update in front of you. Compare. It opens the strongest roles and compares them on the facts the site returns: compensation, location, seniority, why each one matches. Apply, with control. It prepares two applications on its own: your request to apply is the authority to prepare. It proposes answers that stay marked as its own and requests one exact review of what would be sent. The page turns read-only while it works. Nothing leaves until you decide, in your client. Keep watching. It asks Jobbbler to monitor the search. The site states what it will check, how often, where the updates go and how to stop. You approve once. Then the tab can close: Jobbbler's server does the morning check, and the next time you ask, you hear only what changed. Every step is a real tool call, visible in the Agent activity panel on the page. That panel is for people watching (you, or a judge); the agent never needs it. Two kinds of tools, on purpose Some site actions should be silent, others should be seen. Jobbbler separates them: Quiet tools return structured facts and leave your page alone: search, read a role, compare, check what changed. The assistant can do most of the work without disturbing what you are looking at. Follow tools move the real page: open a role, show the results, open the comparison. Say "show me" and the site follows the agent, so you can watch instead of trusting. The assistant picks the tool. The person can always see what was done. Where control lives Discovery is automatic, but tool access is not authority. Two things always need the person: an email destination, and the final submission of the exact application to its recipient. Each is a request-bound decision: the site issues an expiring request, the client presents it, the person decides, and the server checks that the decision matches the exact request it issued. Consent can be withdrawn in one call. This is the part that makes delegation worth trusting, and it is the part most agent demos skip. Why this is bigger than jobs Nothing in this design is specific to job search. A shop, a clinic's booking page, a documentation site: any data-rich website can publish its actions the same way and become operable by the assistant a person already uses. Jobbbler is one worked example, end to end, of a web that works for people and their agents at the same time. Under the hood 29 WebMCP tools registered directly in the page, the same set on every route. Private or stage-specific tools answer with the next safe step instead of pretending to succeed. One command layer, two adapters: the visible interface and the tools share the same server commands, so the page and the agent never disagree. Honest continuation: WebMCP lives while the page is open; durable monitoring runs on Jobbbler's server with a leased worker. No second model behind the site: understanding and drafting stay with the person's client; Jobbbler supplies typed data, deterministic search, workflow state and enforced authority. TypeScript monorepo: Next.js, domain packages, SQLite for local runs and PostgreSQL (Supabase) in production, Resend-compatible email, a small design system. Production runs at jobbbler.com under the Chrome WebMCP origin trial and is verified with unit, contract and browser suites plus real tool runs in ChatGPT Desktop's browser. Try it Open jobbbler.com in a WebMCP-capable client, open Agent activity → Tools to see what the site offers, then say: Looking for a Product Designer position, remote, $90k+. Compare options, pick the top 2, and apply. Schedule for daily updates (every morning). My CV is attached. Or take it one step at a time: "Find remote senior platform roles in Europe, top three and why." "Show me the second one." "Keep watching this search, email me only what changes." "Prepare my application for the first role and show me exactly what would be sent." title: GraphContract
pitch: Design agent behavior together—before it becomes code.
about_excerpt: Design agent behavior together—before it becomes code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent workflows are usually reviewed after they have already become code, prompts, and framework-specific configuration. At that point, important decisions such as branching, tool use, approval gates, parallel work, retries, and failure paths are scattered across files and difficult to understand as one system. I built GraphContract because I wanted humans and coding agents to agree on agent behavior before implementation—not debug that agreement afterward. What it does GraphContract is a human-governed planning layer for agent systems. It gives a person and a coding agent a shared visual canvas where they can design, review, revise, and freeze an agent workflow as a structured contract. A user can start from a blank canvas or a reusable workflow pattern. A coding agent reads the currently accepted graph through WebMCP and proposes a structured revision. GraphContract renders that candidate separately, shows what was added, changed, or removed, and keeps the accepted graph locked until the human decides what happens next. The human can inspect the proposal, request changes, approve it, or reject it. Once the contract is accepted, GraphContract derives deterministic branch scenarios, lets the user inspect each route on the canvas, freezes the reviewed contract, and exports implementation handoff artifacts. The canvas supports typed Start, Task, Agent, Tool, Human, Merge, End, and Subgraph structures; normal, conditional, command, fallback, bounded-loop, and dynamic Send ×N routing; human-in-the-loop gates; sensitive-effect policies; deterministic scenarios; and a read-only runtime projection. How WebMCP powers the collaboration GraphContract deliberately exposes exactly three browser-native WebMCP tools: get_graph reads the accepted contract, its revision identity, validation state, and outstanding human feedback. propose_graph_changes submits typed operations against a known revision and produces a review-only candidate. get_branch_scenarios reads the deterministic paths derived from the accepted graph. The small tool surface is intentional. The agent can inspect and propose, but it cannot approve, reject, freeze, unfreeze, answer human gates, control runtime execution, or download artifacts. Those actions remain visible and human-owned in the interface. This is where WebMCP adds real value. A graph has stable identities, topology, validation rules, revisions, and authority boundaries. Asking an agent to infer those from screenshots or cursor coordinates would be fragile. WebMCP lets the agent work with the graph as structured data while the website remains the source of truth and the place where consequential decisions are made. How I built it The application is built with React, TypeScript, React Flow, Zustand, and Zod. React Flow powers the canvas, Zustand manages the local workspace and proposal lifecycle, and Zod enforces schema and migration boundaries. The public application is deployed on Netlify with a custom domain. I also created a portable GraphContract skill published from the website. A browser-capable coding agent can discover the skill, learn the inspect → propose → review → revise → freeze → handoff lifecycle, and then use the three WebMCP tools consistently. Codex helped throughout the project: researching real agent patterns, shaping the domain model, implementing the canvas and proposal workflow, debugging browser behavior, and building the test library. I used Vitest and Testing Library for domain and component contracts, plus Playwright journeys that exercise the real page-registered WebMCP tools in a cold browser. Challenges I faced The hardest part was not drawing nodes. It was keeping the experience truthful under human–agent collaboration. I needed one accepted graph and a separate proposal candidate; atomic validation without silently repairing agent input; deterministic scenarios that remain bounded around loops and dynamic parallelism; and runtime observations that never become editable design truth. I also had to keep the interface understandable while representing nested subgraphs, human gates, Merge reducers, Send ×N workers, and multiple routing modes. Accomplishments I am proud of A complete human–agent planning lifecycle instead of a single tool-call demo. Structured proposals that never mutate accepted state before human approval. Clear visual diffs with request-changes, approval, and rejection flows. First-class human approval gates, sensitive effects, conditional routing, fallback paths, bounded loops, nested structures, Send ×N, and Merge. Deterministic scenario review and downloadable graph, scenario, and Python path-test handoffs. A reusable agent skill and a deliberately narrow WebMCP authority boundary. What I learned The best human–agent interfaces do not simply maximize agent authority. They make authority legible. WebMCP is especially powerful when it exposes the smallest structured surface an agent needs while leaving validation, review, and consequential actions visible to the person. I also learned that a visual graph can be more than documentation. With stable identities, typed edges, revision checks, scenarios, and explicit approval state, it can become a negotiated contract between human intent and agent implementation. What's next Next I want to generate framework-specific implementations from frozen contracts, add repository-linked contract diffs in CI, accept trusted runtime events so live execution can be highlighted against the frozen graph, and expand the library with more source-backed agent patterns. title: OpsRelay
pitch: Human guided incident recovery where AI agents investigate disruptions, compare recovery options, and execute approved plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Human guided incident recovery where AI agents investigate disruptions, compare recovery options, and execute approved plans through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Opsrelay Inspiration I wanted to build something where an AI agent actually does useful work inside a real application, not just answer questions or chat. I started thinking about manufacturing and operations because one small problem can turn into a much bigger one very quickly. A supplier being late can affect stock, production, customer orders and money all at the same time. That is where the idea for OpsRelay came from. What it does OpsRelay is a manufacturing incident recovery dashboard. For the demo I created a scenario where a supplier is 48 hours late delivering Aluminium 6061 Sheet. That delay causes a material shortage, affects production, puts three customer orders at risk and exposes R423,000 in revenue. The user can give the AI agent one request and the agent can use the WebMCP tools in OpsRelay to work through the problem. It can: check the current incident find the orders that are at risk check available inventory search for other suppliers compare the supplier options create a recovery plan send that plan for approval execute it once a human has approved it check the final recovery status The main idea is that the user does not have to manually jump between every part of the system just to investigate one incident. Why WebMCP WebMCP is basically the part that makes the whole idea work. Instead of the agent trying to understand the website by looking at buttons and text on the screen, OpsRelay gives it proper tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools connect to the same data and state that the user sees in the dashboard. So the agent is not just telling the user what it thinks should happen. It can actually use the application to investigate the incident and work through the recovery process. Humans + agents I did not want the agent to have full control over everything. The agent can investigate the problem, compare options and create a recovery plan, but it cannot approve its own plan. The approval has to be done by a human in the dashboard. Only after that approval can the agent execute the recovery plan. I liked this setup because the AI can do a lot of the repetitive work, but the important decision still stays with the person using the system. How I built it OpsRelay is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS and is deployed on Vercel. I registered nine WebMCP tools: get_current_incident get_inventory get_at_risk_orders search_supplier_options compare_supplier_options simulate_recovery_plan request_recovery_approval execute_recovery_plan get_recovery_status The demo uses browser-local data and a fixed incident scenario so it can be reset and tested again without needing an external database or real supplier system. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was deciding what the AI should be allowed to do by itself and what should still require a person. I also had to make sure that when the agent used a WebMCP tool, the result matched what was happening in the dashboard. Another challenge was getting the full workflow working from beginning to end instead of just making a few separate tools that worked on their own. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The biggest thing for me is that the full workflow actually works. The agent can start with a supplier incident, investigate what is affected, compare recovery options, create a plan, send it for human approval and then execute the approved plan. I am also happy with the human approval part because the agent cannot simply approve and execute its own actions. What I learned Before building this I did not really understand how useful WebMCP could be. I originally thought of AI inside websites mostly as chatbots or assistants. Building OpsRelay showed me that the website itself can expose tools to an outside agent, while still keeping the normal interface for the person using it. That opened up a completely different way of thinking about how people and AI agents can use the same application together. What's next for OpsRelay The current project is a simulated manufacturing incident, but the same idea could work with real operational systems. The next step would be connecting it to live inventory, supplier, order and production data instead of the demo state. I would also like to add more incident types, such as machine breakdowns, sudden demand changes and other supply chain problems. title: pact
pitch: Gives agents only the exact authority needed for one approved transaction, with stale-state protection, verification, auditability, and receipts.
about_excerpt: Gives agents only the exact authority needed for one approved transaction, with stale-state protection, verification, auditability, and receipts. Like Comment Story Updates PACT PACT is a transaction and authority protocol for AI agents performing consequential actions inside web applications. Most agent systems give an AI broad access to application tools and rely on instructions such as “only change these resources” or “do not touch billing.” PACT treats that model as insufficient for high-impact operations. Instead, PACT turns every consequential task into an explicitly scoped transaction. The workflow is: Intent → semantic preview → exact-plan approval → scoped authority → commit → canonical verification → receipt. Before any mutation occurs, PACT determines the exact effects required by the task. The human sees precisely what will change and what will not change. Approval is bound to the specific plan, its hash, and the canonical state on which it was created. If the underlying state changes after approval, the plan becomes stale and commit authority disappears. The agent must re-plan and obtain approval for the new state instead of silently executing an outdated operation. PACT includes protections for stale state, duplicate commits, idempotency, version conflicts, approval expiry, negative invariants, post-condition verification, audit integrity, rollback conditions, and transaction recovery. Its key WebMCP contribution is that agent capability is not equivalent to permanent administrative access. Mutation capabilities can appear only after an exact transaction has been approved and disappear when the authorization is no longer valid. The reference implementation demonstrates this through operations such as contractor offboarding, ownership transfer, access revocation, and protected resources such as billing or deletion. The broader thesis is that agents should not receive permanent authority. They should receive narrowly scoped, temporary, verifiable authority for a specific approved transaction. title: FloorPlan
pitch: An agent-native floor-planning workspace where humans and AI design the same live plan together.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native floor-planning workspace where humans and AI design the same live plan together.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was exploring WebMCP and trying to find a use case where it does more than just help an agent fill a form or click around a website.
Floor planning felt like a good fit because it is very visual. A person can easily drag rooms, doors, windows and furniture, but an agent would normally have to understand the editor UI and perform a lot of small browser actions.
The idea was to let the person use the floor-plan editor normally, while giving the agent higher-level actions for working on the same plan. 

 What it does 

 FloorPlan is a simple floor-plan editor that both a person and an AI agent can use.
A person can create and edit a plan manually by moving rooms, doors, windows, furniture and outdoor areas.
Through WebMCP, the agent can read the current plan and perform larger actions such as creating a new layout from requirements, optimizing an existing plan, or generating another variation.
One of the main demos is asking:
 I have 1,800 sq ft. I need 3 bedrooms, a maid room, storage, laundry, a closed kitchen, garden and parking. 
The agent creates another floor plan below the one the user already made. The user can then ask for another variation, edit the generated plan manually, and ask the agent to continue from those edits. 

 How we built it 

 I built the app with React, TypeScript, Vite and Zustand.
The important part is that the UI and the WebMCP tools use the same floor-plan state. If the user moves something manually, the agent sees that updated state. If the agent changes the plan, the same editor updates immediately.
I registered tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(). 

 Some of the main tools are: 

 
 get_floorplan_state 
 create_floorplan_from_requirements 
 generate_floorplan_variations 
 optimize_floorplan 
 replace_floorplan 
 add_architectural_element
I tried to keep the tools focused on floor-planning actions instead of browser actions. For example, the agent can ask the app to create a floor plan from requirements instead of trying to click the Room button and drag each room itself. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was deciding what should be a WebMCP tool.
At first it was tempting to expose lots of small actions such as moving individual objects. But that starts to look like another version of browser automation.
The more useful approach was to expose actions that match what the user actually wants, such as creating a complete plan or generating another layout with different priorities.
I also had to make sure that manual edits and agent edits stayed in sync, so both now go through the same shared state. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are especially proud that WebMCP is not just an additional feature in FloorPlan; it fundamentally changes how the application can be used.
A human can manually design a floor plan, and an agent can immediately understand and continue from that exact state.
The agent can generate a complete floor plan from requirements such as: 

 
 1,800 sq ft available area 
 3 bedrooms 
 maid room 
 laundry room 
 storage room 
 closed kitchen 
 garden 
 car parking
It can then generate multiple alternatives with different priorities such as larger living space, better bedroom privacy or more efficient circulation.
The human can modify any generated option and the agent can continue working from those changes. 
 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most powerful when websites expose domain outcomes instead of UI controls.
For FloorPlan, useful agent actions are: 

 
 create an efficient three-bedroom floor plan 
 optimize a layout for daylight 
 generate a privacy-first alternative 
 add a window to the master bedroom
rather than: 
 click the Room button 
 drag an object 
 move something 100 pixels
We also learned that genuine human-agent collaboration depends on shared state. The experience becomes much more natural when the person and agent are editing the exact same artifact. 
 

 What's next for FloorPlan 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 more advanced geometry and constraint solving 
 irregular plot shapes 
 multiple floors 
 richer room-adjacency optimization 
 side-by-side plan comparison 
 undo/redo 
 saved projects 
 PDF and image export 
 accessibility analysis 
 daylight analysis 
 optional 3D visualization 
 configurable building-code rules
FloorPlan is currently intended as a conceptual planning tool rather than construction documentation.

title: ProdPermit
pitch: Agents investigate incidents through WebMCP where humans approve the exact recovery before execution
about_excerpt: Agents investigate incidents through WebMCP where humans approve the exact recovery before execution Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Home Screen WebMCP Tools Audit Logs Project name ProdPermit Inspiration AI agents can investigate production incidents faster than a person moving between dashboards, logs, release history, and diagnostics. However, giving an agent permanent production access creates a serious risk. ProdPermit explores a safer model: the agent investigates and prepares an exact recovery, while a person retains authority over execution. What it does ProdPermit presents a simulated checkout incident caused by release_284 . The release changed database authentication to password , while the database still requires scram-sha-256 . The website exposes six initial WebMCP tools: inspect_incident compare_releases query_logs run_diagnostic prepare_recovery verify_recovery The agent uses these tools to identify the authentication mismatch and prepare a rollback to the healthy release_283 . Preparing the plan does not change production. ProdPermit displays the target release, supporting evidence, expiry, risk, and SHA-256 fingerprint for human review. Only after the person clicks Approve exact plan does the browser register execute_approved_recovery . The temporary tool can execute only that approved plan. It disappears after execution, rejection, revocation, reset, or expiry. After execution, checkout returns to a healthy state: Error rate falls from 18.7% to 0.2% P95 latency falls from 1,420 ms to 176 ms Database status changes to DB_CONNECTION_OK The audit timeline records preparation, approval, execution, and verification Why WebMCP WebMCP gives the agent typed, purpose-built operations instead of forcing it to scrape labels or guess which buttons to click. More importantly, the website can change the available tools when authority changes. The agent can investigate immediately, but execution does not exist until a person approves one exact recovery. This creates a clear partnership: the agent gathers evidence and recommends an action, while the human controls the production decision. How we built it The Next.js and React frontend registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Zod validates data at the browser boundary. A Rust and Axum backend owns the recovery rules, authorization checks, session state, expiry, replay protection, and plan fingerprints. SQLite stores isolated demo sessions, evidence, plans, recovery results, and audit events. Vercel hosts the frontend. Cloudflare Tunnel connects the public application to the loopback-only Rust service. Tailscale Funnel provides a fallback route. Challenges The hardest part was making human approval a real authorization boundary instead of a cosmetic confirmation button. The backend must reject unapproved, modified, stale, expired, replayed, and cross-session plans. Execution, telemetry changes, diagnostic results, and audit records must also commit atomically. We also handled browser registration behavior, session revocation, persistent recovery state, tunnel reliability, and end-to-end WebMCP testing. What we learned WebMCP works best when websites expose meaningful domain operations rather than generic interface controls. We also learned that dangerous capabilities do not need to exist permanently. A website can register a narrow tool only when the server confirms that the human has granted temporary authority. What's next ProdPermit currently demonstrates one deterministic checkout incident. The next version could support multiple services, recovery actions, organization roles, approval policies, and real deployment providers.
