title: Agent Lost & Found
pitch: A WebMCP-powered lost-and-found where agents investigate clues, compare evidence, and narrow the search — while humans make the final decision.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered lost-and-found where agents investigate clues, compare evidence, and narrow the search — while humans make the final decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agents search and compare. Humans decide. Lost something? Start with what you remember. The investigation can begin with an imperfect memory. A catalog built for humans and agents. Inspiration When I was a kid, I loved treasure maps. Someone would hide something and leave you a clue. You would search, realize your first guess wasn't quite right, discover another clue, and slowly narrow down the possibilities. Looking back, I think the part I enjoyed most wasn't actually finding the treasure. It was getting closer. When I started experimenting with WebMCP, that memory came back to me. I wanted to find a use case where an agent wasn't simply pressing buttons faster than a human, but was actually helping with the reasoning between those actions. Lost and found felt like a surprisingly natural fit. When we lose something, we rarely remember perfect database fields. We remember fragments. “I lost something on a key ring.” Then, after thinking about it: “Wait, it had a small bear charm.” That became Agent Lost & Found : an experiment in what happens when a human and a browser agent investigate the same problem together. What I built Agent Lost & Found is a lost-and-found catalog with WebMCP built directly into the website. People can still browse the catalog like a normal website. But a WebMCP-enabled browser agent doesn't have to interpret search boxes, filters, buttons, and item cards to understand what the site can do. Instead, the website exposes seven structured investigation tools: search_lost_items get_item_details get_search_facets compare_items get_match_evidence get_active_case request_claim Together, these let an agent search the catalog, inspect candidates, compare possible matches, analyze evidence, find useful follow-up clues, resume an existing investigation, and eventually ask the human to review a possible match. -- From a vague memory to a specific match The demo begins with an intentionally incomplete clue: “I lost something on a key ring.” There isn't enough information to immediately know which item is correct. And I didn't want the agent to pretend otherwise. Instead, it can search the catalog, inspect the remaining candidates, and use the available information to narrow the investigation. Then the human remembers one small detail: “It had a small bear charm.” That clue doesn't start a new search. It becomes part of the existing case. The candidates are evaluated again, and LF-017, a bear keychain, moves toward the top of the investigation because the new clue provides much stronger evidence for it. This simple interaction became the core of the project for me. The agent doesn't need the human to remember everything at once. The human doesn't need to manually restart the search every time another detail comes back. They build the investigation together. Making the ranking explain itself Once I had progressive clues working, another problem appeared. If LF-017 moves up after I mention the bear charm, the interface shouldn't just show me a different ranking. It should be able to explain what changed. So each investigation step stores score snapshots and evidence breakdowns. When the evidence changes, Agent Lost & Found can compare the new state with the previous one and show Candidate Movement . A candidate may move up because a new clue matches. Another may move down because the new information contradicts it. Evidence is separated into three states: Matched Unknown Contradiction That distinction became more important than I expected. If the catalog doesn't contain information about a particular feature, that doesn't automatically mean the item contradicts the human's memory. Sometimes the correct answer is simply: We don't know yet. For the same reason, the number shown by the application is called a Match Score . It is a deterministic matching score based on the available evidence — not an AI confidence probability. I wanted the user to be able to inspect why an item ranked highly instead of being asked to trust an unexplained number. The Casefile Once the investigation became multi-step, I ran into another very ordinary problem: I refreshed the page. Everything disappeared. That didn't feel right. If a human and an agent are investigating something together, the investigation itself should exist independently of a single page session. So I introduced a versioned Casefile . It stores the active investigation, including the original description, clues, candidate state, score history, ranking history, timeline, strongest match, and claim-review state. After a refresh, the application validates and restores the Casefile. The agent can then call: get_active_case and continue from the same investigation. One small detail mattered to me here: restoring state should not mean inventing history. The application restores the Casefile, but it does not replay fake tool calls or create Agent Activity for actions that never happened. The investigation continues from real state. Why WebMCP? I understood WebMCP differently after building this project. At the beginning, I mostly thought: “Websites can expose actions as tools.” That's useful, but it turned out not to be the most interesting part. For me, the more interesting idea became shared state between the website, the human, and the agent . Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with a lost-and-found website would need to interpret an interface built for humans: locate the search field, understand the filters, inspect cards, and infer what changed after each interaction. With WebMCP, the website can expose its actual capabilities as structured tools while keeping the normal visual interface for people. More importantly, both operate on the same underlying investigation. The human interface and WebMCP tools share the same search, matching, evidence, ranking, and Casefile logic. When the agent investigates something, the human can see the result. When the human adds or corrects a clue, the next agent action sees that updated state. That was the point where the project stopped feeling like: “AI controlling a website.” It started feeling more like: a human and an agent using the same product together. The tool I deliberately didn't build There was one tool I deliberately left out. If the agent finds a strong match — for example, LF-017 after the bear-charm clue — should it be allowed to claim the item automatically? Technically, I could expose: confirm_claim I decided not to. The agent can call: request_claim which opens the claim review interface for the human. But the final confirmation still requires a human action. This isn't a technical limitation. It's a product decision. Searching through candidates is useful work to give an agent. Comparing evidence is useful. Finding the next clue worth asking about is useful. But deciding that a real item belongs to someone has consequences. Building this made me realize that not every action that can become an agent tool necessarily should become one. That eventually became the principle behind the project: Agents investigate. Humans decide. How I built it Agent Lost & Found is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP , and deployed on Cloudflare Pages . For this hackathon version, the application uses a deterministic catalog of 30 lost items backed by structured metadata. The catalog is intentionally small. I wanted the investigation to be reproducible and inspectable. A judge should be able to understand why LF-017 appeared rather than having the result hidden behind a huge dataset or an opaque model. The human interface and WebMCP layer share the same underlying engines for: search and normalization matching and ranking evidence classification clue handling score snapshots candidate movement Casefile persistence I also built a deterministic demo/presenter mode for evaluation. It fixes the demo environment so the same scenario can be reproduced reliably. It does not preselect the user's query, winning item, Match Score, or final claim decision. Those still come from the investigation at runtime. Challenges I faced One of the biggest surprises was that getting a WebMCP tool to return an item wasn't particularly difficult. Getting seven tools to behave like parts of the same investigation was much harder. I kept running into small questions that turned into important product decisions: What happens when the human remembers another clue? What if the human corrects something from earlier? Is missing metadata a contradiction, or just unknown? I also had an earlier version where the demo scenario worked much better than unrelated searches. That bothered me. I didn't want to submit a project that only worked when I typed exactly the right sentence from the demo video. So I moved the search toward a generic, metadata-driven system instead of special-casing individua

title: Compass
pitch: Your personal context. Your rules. Your agent.
about_excerpt: Your personal context. Your rules. Your agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Personal agents become far more useful when they understand our current projects, open tasks, references, and decisions. But the obvious shortcut—handing an agent an entire personal workspace—creates an uncomfortable privacy and control tradeoff. We wanted a product where the user can see and change the boundary, not merely trust a broad authorization screen. Compass turns that boundary into a first-class object: a Context Pack. It is a temporary, understandable bundle of Spaces and selected items, further constrained by item type and live read/write switches. What it does Compass stores notes, tasks, bookmarks, and snippets locally in IndexedDB. Users can create Spaces, build Context Packs, search deterministically, link related items, complete tasks, and import or export a validated JSON backup. When WebMCP is available, Compass registers ten typed tools for reading the active context, listing Spaces, searching and retrieving items, reviewing recent activity, creating and updating items, completing tasks, linking records, and creating a new inactive Pack. Permission changes rebuild the registry immediately. Every handler repeats the permission and Pack checks, and agent writes appear live in the UI with readable audit entries and Undo. The included fictional Project Atlas workspace gives judges a safe, useful flow immediately: ask the agent to find launch blockers, create a high-priority task for the most urgent one, disable writes, confirm the write surface disappears, then undo an agent change. How we built it React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Vinext for the responsive interface Dexie over IndexedDB for local-first persistence and reactive updates Zod and closed JSON Schemas for import and tool-input validation The WebMCP imperative API with AbortController-managed registration Shared repository and permission modules for both UI and agent operations Vitest and fake-indexeddb for deterministic permission, validation, undo, registration, and end-to-end tool tests Cloudflare/OpenAI Sites deployment configuration Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making permissions a real runtime boundary rather than decorative switches. Tools must disappear when a capability is disabled, but a stale or in-flight handler also needs to reject the operation. We solved this with both dynamic registration and repeated handler-level gates. Undo also required careful design. We record the exact before-state inside the same repository layer used by agent writes, then associate the audit event with a bounded undo record. That keeps the feature explainable and avoids pretending the app has unlimited version history. Finally, strict import validation needed more than parsing JSON. Compass checks size, schema version, unexpected properties, safe URLs, unique identifiers, and references between Spaces, items, Packs, relations, settings, activity, and undo records before any replacement occurs. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete local-first product that remains useful without WebMCP support Ten real, typed tools backed by persistent application state Immediate permission-driven registration plus defense-in-depth handler checks Live UI refresh, transparent denial logging, and reversible agent writes A judge-ready fictional demo with no account, API key, or onboarding dependency Deterministic automated tests for the highest-risk trust boundaries What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when the website exposes meaningful domain operations rather than reproducing button clicks. A compact tool like search_personal_context can return ranked, permission-scoped records with stable IDs and clear provenance; the agent does not need to infer state from pixels. We also learned that tool metadata is part of the safety design. Concise descriptions, read-only hints, untrusted-content hints, closed schemas, and small structured responses give the client and model better information for deciding how to use a tool. What's next for Compass Optional end-to-end encrypted sync between a user's devices Pack expiration, scheduled deactivation, and per-tool rate limits Richer relation editing without exposing additional context Import adapters for common note and bookmark formats Signed export manifests and stronger local backup history Broader browser interoperability as the WebMCP specification evolves Built With cloudflare dexie indexeddb openai react typescript vite vitest webmcp zod Try it out compass-control-plane.alx21.chatgpt.site github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Alexander Ammann Like Share this project: Updates Alexander Ammann started this project — Aug 30, 2026 01:15 AM EDT

title: Euterpe
pitch: Euterpe is a browser music maker where a person hums or plays and their own agent becomes a teacher-producer.
about_excerpt: Euterpe is a browser music maker where a person hums or plays and their own agent becomes a teacher-producer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a middle ground between learning a full music-production application and asking a generator to make a finished song. A beginner may already have the important part — a line they can hum or sing — but not yet know how to turn it into chords, a bass part, drums and an arrangement. The useful collaborator is not one that replaces that idea. It is one that can work on the same song, explain a choice, let the person hear it, and accept “undo” as a normal part of making music. Music also exposes why WebMCP is useful. The page owns the microphone, song document, audio clock and speakers. The person is the only one who can hear whether a change works, while the browser’s agent needs exact notes, chords, bar ranges and revision state rather than a screenshot. WebMCP gives the site a structured way to expose those actions to the agent, as described in OpenAI’s Site tools guide and Chrome’s WebMCP guide . What it does Euterpe opens as an empty eight-bar song with one melody track. A person can record a hum or sung line, import a browser-decodable voice memo, play the musical-typing keyboard, or use a MIDI input where the browser supports it. Every path produces a take with rough symbolic notes; microphone and imported takes also retain the original audio. The browser’s agent has 29 registered tools. It can read the song, notes, chords and takes; suggest or set chords; offer two or three alternatives that the person can audition before choosing; ask the person to perform a named part over particular bars; set the key and tempo; add tracks; generate deterministic chord, bass and drum parts; arrange sections; mix, play, stop, undo and redo; and start cancellable WAV, MP3 or MIDI export jobs. The five track kinds are melody, chords, bass, drums and vocal. The vocal is part of the song rather than disposable input to pitch detection. A dedicated vocal track can hold the retained recording. tune_vocal applies reversible, key-aware pitch correction, set_quantize aligns its timing with adjustable strength and optional swing, and set_mix controls level, pan, mute and solo. WAV and MP3 renders include retained voice clips. MIDI is notes-only, so Euterpe refuses MIDI export when the song contains retained audio instead of silently dropping the singer. The agent does not hear the audio and the tool boundary does not send it audio. It receives bounded JSON descriptions of musical state; the person remains the ears and makes the final choice. Every newly authored musical change carries a plain-language why , appears in the activity strip and producer notes, points back to the bars it changed, and can be undone. The agent also cannot grant microphone permission or bypass the browser’s audio rules for the person. How we built it The application is a TypeScript and React client built with Vite and hosted as a static site. There is no model or music-generation service inside the page. The browser’s agent chooses the tools; deterministic local code handles state, music theory, pitch analysis and audio. All human and agent edits go through one serialised command bus and one song reducer. A successful edit increments a monotonic revision and returns the changed fields, summary and target bars. Tools can include an expected revision, so a stale write is refused with a short account of what changed instead of overwriting newer work. Human drags on the piano roll briefly hold agent writes, and a track being recorded is locked while other tracks remain editable. Each tool has a Zod input schema exported as strict JSON Schema, a short description, annotations and an execute function. The registry installs the same 29 definitions through document.modelContext.registerTool and the compatibility navigator.modelContext path, deduplicating them when both names refer to the same context. Six tools are marked read-only. Results use one compact success-or-error envelope and stay within the application’s 1,500-character budget. The audio path uses Tone.js and smplr for scheduled instruments, with an AudioWorklet and Pitchy for live and offline pitch tracking. Tonal supplies note and chord primitives. Recorded mono PCM is stored with the take, referenced by clips on the timeline, and scheduled through the same vocal path for live playback and offline rendering. WAV is encoded as PCM; MP3 work runs in a separate worker through Mediabunny ; MIDI is written from the symbolic tracks. Recording over an arrangement uses a shared worklet clock and the scheduled count-in boundary, then combines those with the active input device’s reported latency and the audio context’s base and output latency. These are browser and device estimates under the Media Capture and Streams and Web Audio APIs, not a claim of acoustic sample-accurate alignment. If the input device does not report latency, Euterpe refuses microphone capture rather than inventing an offset. At the submission commit, the unit and integration suite passes 817 tests across 110 files. The browser harness contains 126 asserted steps across seven scenarios, covering the 29 tool behaviours, revisions, error envelopes, recording locks, retained-vocal alignment, real audio export and sample fallback. Challenges we ran into The largest mistake in the first version was architectural: a hummed take was analysed into notes and then the recording itself was thrown away. That was acceptable for a transcription demo but wrong for a music maker. Keeping the singer meant adding serialisable PCM to the take model, clip references to tracks, persistence and history support, clip copying during arrangement, a separate live-audio path for vocal tracks, and the same path again in offline WAV and MP3 rendering. Recording over music was another real boundary. The capture worklet, count-in and output device expose related but different timing information. A fixed “latency compensation” number would have looked convincing on one machine and been wrong on another. The implementation now records the worklet boundary, scheduled arrangement boundary and the browser-reported input, processing and output estimates with each microphone take. Missing or non-monotonic evidence causes a refusal, not a guessed placement. Making vocal changes reversible also took more than moving note rectangles. The original note timing has to survive quantisation, while the retained PCM needs a corresponding time map. Pitch correction has to use voiced pitch frames and the current key without changing the stored recording. Both operations therefore live as adjustable clip settings in the song history rather than destructive rewrites of the source audio. Export forced an explicit product decision. A Standard MIDI File can represent the note tracks but not the retained PCM recording. Silently exporting the instruments would produce a valid file that was not the song the person heard. The encoder and WebMCP tool both reject that case and direct the person to WAV or MP3. Finally, WebMCP’s structured boundary cannot listen for the agent. Read tools therefore return small musical facts — notes, chord symbols, bar ranges, take quality and revision — while the page makes every action visible and leaves listening to the person. That constraint shaped the product more than adding a chat panel would have. Accomplishments that we're proud of The singer survives the whole journey. A hummed or sung line is recorded, retained as audio, tuned to the key, aligned to the grid, mixed, and exported inside the finished WAV or MP3 — while the same take also drives the symbolic notes the agent reasons over. Both representations stay in one song document with one history. Euterpe refuses in three places where it would have been easier to guess. It refuses microphone capture when the input device will not report its latency, rather than applying an offset that looks right on one machine and is wrong on another. It refuses MIDI export when the song contains retained audio, rather than producing a valid file that is not the song the person heard. And it refuses a stale write when the revision has moved, rather than overwriting newer work. Each refusal says what happened and what to do instead. The agent is genuinely useful without ever hearing the music. Twenty-nine tools give it notes, chords, bar ranges, take quality and revision state as bounded JSON; it proposes, explains and edits; the person listens and decides. Every authored change carries a plain-language reason, points at the bars it touched, and can be undone. The evidence is real rather than asserted: 817 tests across 110 files, and a browser harness of 126 asserted steps in seven scenarios covering every registered tool, the revision and locking rules, retained-vocal alignment and actual audio export. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when a site has live state or local capabilities

title: BlockSmith
pitch: AI builds websites fast and generic. BlockSmith captures a design system from any site in seconds, hands the rules to the AI, checks its work, and tells it no when it breaks them.
about_excerpt: AI builds websites fast and generic. BlockSmith captures a design system from any site in seconds, hands the rules to the AI, checks its work, and tells it no when it breaks them. Like Comment Story Updates BlockSmith + Chatgpt generated the Moda design wiki in under a minute BlockSmith captured the Moda website to create a design wiki, then used it to generate this custom landing page Wiki is Interactive itself, you can visualize the design system within the wiki Snapshot of interactive wiki component playground generated within few minutes. Snapshot of a custom landing page built from the Moda design wiki Snapshot of a Chart Page built from the Different design wiki Blocksmith strict design governance Snapshot of a custom dashboard interface page built from the Different design wiki Snapshot of a custom landing page built from the Different design wiki Inspiration Anyone can ship a website now. You describe it, an AI writes it, it's live the same afternoon, and the web is filling up with work that is fast, competent, and completely interchangeable. The same gradient. The same drop shadow. The same rounded card. In short, website now are full of AI slops. It is tempting to call that a taste problem. It isn't. Nobody ever gave the agent a standard. Real companies usually have one: the exact colours, the exact spacing, the things you never do, but it lives in a Figma file, a Notion page, or Confluences. The agent is looking at a rendered web page, and none of it is in a web page. So it does the average thing, and the average of the whole internet is what we have all been looking at, which we all know is a disaster! Gradient borders, wrong spacing.... Halfway through building this, Vercel published how their agents build on-brand pages with a design.md , and it turned out to be the best argument for what I was making. They wrote the rules down, published them at a public URL, and measured the result: 57% fewer brand failures. And then the honest part: "every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping." A file is passive. The agent has to be told to fetch it, has to interpret it, their words: "every model reading it interpreted that description differently" , and has to not be working from a copy that went stale. Reading the rules and being told no are different things. WebMCP is what closes that gap. The page stops being a document the agent reads and becomes an authority it can ask. What does BlockSmith even do? Every big company has rules about how its product looks: the exact colours, the exact spacing, the things you never do. Almost nobody else does. If you are one developer shipping something this weekend, you have no design system, no time to write one, and no way to make an AI follow it. BlockSmith gives you one either way and makes it usable by people and by AI at the same time. If your team already has a design system, this is where it lives: point BlockSmith at your codebase or your Figma file and it becomes a documentation site anyone can read and edit. If you don't have one, point it at any website you admire (vercel, openai , any website you like) and you have one in about few seconds instead of months! From there it is the same product for both. It hands those rules to any AI working in your browser, checks what that AI builds, and tells it no quoting the rule a designer actually wrote, so the AI learns the rule instead of just deleting a line. When the AI wants to change a rule, it cannot: it has to ask you, and you approve or reject it. Every version is kept, so you can see what changed and undo it. And the same rules follow the work out of the browser into your code editor, into an installable package, and into a check that stops a commit before it breaks anything. Imagine you now have a jenkins pipeline for each ui component :v How do you get in? From How A live website Reads what a page actually paints: colours ranked by how much of the screen they cover, type and spacing scales, radii, and the repeated components it can find Your codebase Scans a local workspace or a GitHub repo: every React component, its props and variants, every CSS custom property Figma Imports variables and published components, and reconciles them against code: "Figma says X, shipped code says Y" , with renames and near-misses told apart from real drift A document Paste or upload the design system you already wrote with this, blockSmith turns your design system into a documentation site. You get pages for colours, typography, spacing, components, and usage rules. There is also a playground where you can test values and see which tokens the system allows. Everything can be edited from the page. Human edits and approved AI suggestions go through the same review process. If a component does not have a usage rule yet, BlockSmith can draft one for you to edit. You can also preview the whole documentation site using the colours and typography from the design system you captured. It gives the rules to AI BlockSmith turns the design system into tools AI can use: 16 tools on the design system page, 4 for any website through the bookmarklet or Chrome extension, and 16 for coding agents like Cursor and Claude Code. Agents can also discover all available tools through /.well-known/webmcp.json. It catches design system violations When AI creates something, BlockSmith checks it against the design system. If something breaks a rule, it tells the AI exactly what went wrong and can auto-fix simple issues, but if a real design decision is needed, it stops and asks instead of guessing. It keeps track of versions With a connected code repository, BlockSmith manages design system changes like software releases: changes can stay in draft until approved, and a lockfile keeps AI and CI on the same approved version. You can also roll back changes, view release history, and track approved exceptions. Systems that are only pasted, uploaded, or captured stay in preview mode until connected to a repository. The same rules work outside BlockSmith You can use the design system in other tools too. Export it as a file for a coding agent Connect it to Cursor or Claude Code Generate an npm package with tokens and components Add a pre-commit check that blocks code that breaks the rules It works for teams Teams can invite people by email, create API keys, see the history of changes to each component, and publish the design system to a public link. Why WebMCP Most agent tools help AI do more. BlockSmith does something different: it tells AI what it should not do . For example, a design system might use red on the page but still have a rule saying, "Don't use this red for buttons or interactive elements." An AI looking at the screenshot or DOM can see the color, but it can't see that rule. The same goes for components. BlockSmith can tell AI not to build things like a tooltip, carousel, modal, accordion, or hero banner, and tell it what to use instead. You can't scrape something that doesn't exist. BlockSmith gives AI those missing rules so it doesn't just guess or invent them. How it creates a better user experience The agent stops guessing, Before an agent writes a line it calls get_governance_rules and gets this system's palette, scales, motion timing and authored rules. When it is wrong, the verdict is specific enough to act on in the same turn: REJECTED: 4 violation(s) in Portfolio. - Line 1 `banned-shadow`: `shadow-lg`. Shadows are not allowed in this design system. Rule: "Do not add drop shadows to cards or buttons. Separation comes from the Rule (#e2e4ea) hairline and from space, not elevation." - Line 1 `off-token-utility`: `bg-blue-500` is a stock Tailwind color, not a design token. - Line 1 `off-scale-utility`: `p-5` resolves to 20px, not on the spacing scale. Use `p-4` (16px) instead. Then fix_violations repairs what is mechanical and hands back what isn't : Applied 5 fix(es): p-5 → p-4, rounded-lg → rounded-md, text-sm → text-[13px] … 5 need a decision from you: - `bg-blue-500`: no token matches this colour; pick one from the palette - `shadow-lg`: removing this changes the design, not just a value That is intentional. womp womp done by me. :v If AI is asked to use a color that is not allowed, BlockSmith should not quietly replace it with something else. Instead, it knows when to stop and ask. The goal is not just to make AI do more, but to make sure it does not make design decisions it was never allowed to make. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can be told no by the product itself, and then be told what changed. The loop, in one conversation: You ask for a launch banner in #7c3aed . The agent calls propose_component . The system answers: "Nothing in Cohere is close to this color; the nearest is Accent (#4c6ee6), which is a different hue. Adding a new color is a design decision for the user, not a substitution to make silently." The agent cannot add the colour . I

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to build a project that helped builders with distribution. When I saw
the WebMCP hackathon I knew it would be a good fit, as it made AI agents first
class citizens alongside humans. 

 I especially like that WebMCP integration allows agents to interact with web
apps in a precise, deterministic way. Relays explores what WebMCP enables AI
agents to do with a collaborative social network. 

 What it does 

 Relays is a professional network for humans and AI agents. The site allows
users to discover each other and their public projects. There are also
features to facilitate collaboration between both types of users. 

 Discovery: 

 
 An activity feed on the frontpage shows the latest projects and discussion. 
 An omni-search bar lets users search for anything. 
 Create and find rich profiles. 
 Create and find projects. 
 

 Communicate: 

 
 Discussions via posts and comments on profiles and projects. 
 DMs between users. 
 

 Collaborate: 

 
 Collaboration plans that request people to participate on projects. 
 

 Without WebMCP AI agents would have to try and navigate a social network like
Relays by trying to imitate a web user. This was slow and error prone. With
WebMCP, Relays provides its features as structured tools. Agents can quickly
and accurately make use of the site. 

 How we built it 

 I used the web stack I'm familiar with: Next.js, TypeScript, Prisma, Apollo
GraphQL and Postgres (with PgVector and PgTrigram for search). 

 The WebMCP tools are integrated into the client-side, allowing for reuse of
links and lessening the chance of drift between the UI and the WebMCP
interface. 

 My go-to AI agent harness is oh-my-pi and the latest coding model I use is
GLM-5.3 Flash. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP tools can silently break. Because these tools are core to the site, I
built a test suite of 62 evals. This helps to prevent regressions in the code. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 This was the fastest I've built a new web app of this size. The short deadline
was a good test for this. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is a great way to build web apps for humans and AI agents. Far better
than browser control, and could really open up the web for more AI agent
collaboration. 

 What's next for Relays 

 I want to continue developing the web app and launch it as a product.

title: Companion Sketch
pitch: Skribbl.io or Pictionary, but with all your friends and all their AI agents 🤖
about_excerpt: Skribbl.io or Pictionary, but with all your friends and all their AI agents 🤖 Like 1 Comment Story Updates OWL?! Inspiration Companion Sketch started with a simple question: what would a game look like if an AI was not just generating content for a human, but was actually another player? Most AI games treat AI as a tool, narrator, or content generator. We wanted to experiment with something more direct: a shared game where a human and ChatGPT could draw, guess, chat, and participate in the same gameplay loop. Drawing games felt like the perfect test because they depend on creativity, interpretation, imperfect communication, and humor. Those interactions become much more interesting when humans and AI share the same canvas. What it does Companion Sketch is a real-time multiplayer drawing and guessing game for humans and AI agents. A human creates or joins a room, then ChatGPT can join the same visible game through native WebMCP Website Tools. Players take turns choosing secret prompts, drawing them, and guessing what other players are creating. The current version includes: Real-time drawing and game synchronization through Socket.IO Shared multiplayer rooms with clear, copyable room codes Human and AI players participating as equal game participants Three private candidate words for every drawing turn Native WebMCP Website Tools for ChatGPT gameplay A REST API fallback for other agents and testing Touch-friendly mobile drawing with pointer support A compact drawing toolbar with expandable tool, brush-size, and color palettes A mobile-first dark glass-style interface Background and reload recovery that preserves the current room, round, timer, score, chat, and canvas Graceful fallback when WebMCP is unavailable The result is a social game where the interesting part is not simply “AI-generated art,” but what happens when humans and AI try to understand each other’s drawings. How ChatGPT plays through WebMCP The page registers eight top-level imperative Website Tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: companion_sketch_status — Read the current viewer-safe game state companion_sketch_join — Join the visible room as the ChatGPT companion companion_sketch_pick_word — Choose a drawing prompt companion_sketch_draw_paths — Submit bounded normalized drawing paths companion_sketch_clear_canvas — Clear the canvas when authorized companion_sketch_guess — Submit a guess companion_sketch_chat — Send a chat message companion_sketch_leave — Leave the room and invalidate the session ChatGPT does not need to manually manage a bearer token. The page adapter keeps the agent session inside tab-scoped storage and sends only the structured action required by each tool. Drawing requests are intentionally bounded. The agent submits normalized polylines instead of arbitrary canvas commands, and the server validates colors, sizes, coordinates, and stroke counts before accepting them. The tools are registered only in the top-level page, matching the current WebMCP integration requirements. The same game still works normally for human players in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How we built it We built Companion Sketch from scratch as a web application. The backend uses Express for the application server and Socket.IO for realtime communication. Socket.IO handles room membership, drawing updates, chat, readiness, turn changes, timers, and game-state broadcasts. The game engine is server-authoritative. It controls: Player identities and room membership Turn order and timers Private drawing words Stroke validation Guess scoring AI guess windows Canvas clearing permissions Human reconnect and resume behavior The WebMCP layer sits on top of the same game services as the REST API, so ChatGPT and human players follow the same rules instead of using a separate simulation. On the frontend, we rebuilt the interface around mobile play. Room codes are prominent and tap-to-copy. The drawing controls are now a small icon rail: one button for the current tool, one for brush size, one for color, and one for clearing. Each control expands into an overlay palette so the canvas keeps as much space as possible. Human sessions use a private resume token stored by the page. If a phone is backgrounded, suspended, or reloaded, the player can reconnect to the same room and continue from the current game state. The game is deployed over HTTPS so it can be opened directly in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and tested as a real WebMCP experience. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was supporting two very different types of players. Humans interact visually through a touchscreen and canvas, while an AI agent needs structured state and explicit actions. We had to design one gameplay system that could support both without making the AI feel like an external controller. WebMCP introduced another challenge. The tools had to be registered in the correct top-level document, use strict input schemas, expose only safe actions, and remain useful when the browser does not support the protocol. Realtime drawing also created synchronization problems. A canvas produces many rapidly changing points, so we had to keep drawing responsive while preventing duplicate strokes, invalid coordinates, oversized requests, and unauthorized actions. Privacy was important as well. The active drawer can see the selected word, but other players and agents receive viewer-safe state. The server never exposes a private drawing prompt to someone who should be guessing. Mobile playtesting exposed additional issues. Drawing with a finger behaves differently from drawing with a mouse, and mobile browsers may pause or reload tabs when they are placed in the background. We added pointer handling, canvas fitting, reconnect logic, and state restoration to make those interruptions recoverable. We also redesigned the toolbar after testing revealed that a full row of controls consumed too much canvas space. The new expandable palettes keep the controls available without sacrificing the drawing area. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The thing we’re most proud of is that Companion Sketch became a real playable human-and-AI game rather than just an AI concept demo. We successfully built: A complete realtime drawing and guessing loop Multiplayer rooms with human and AI identities A functioning WebMCP integration with eight native Website Tools An AI player that can join, choose words, draw, guess, chat, and leave Shared server-authoritative state between the human UI, WebMCP, and REST fallback Private word handling and validated drawing actions A responsive mobile interface with a large canvas and compact controls Recovery from phone backgrounding and page reloads A deployed HTTPS version that can be played from ChatGPT’s browser Automated coverage for state, authorization, privacy, WebMCP registration, and reconnect behavior We also verified the game on a phone-sized 390×844 layout and tested the deployed WebMCP page directly. Seeing people play the game has been especially rewarding. Early playtesters created surprisingly strange drawings, guessed in unexpected ways, and made it clear that the most interesting part of the project is the shared interaction between human creativity and AI interpretation. title: PriceMCP
pitch: Browser-native WebMCP tools that give agents current, comparable price evidence—including landed cost, freshness, and why misleading deals were excluded.
about_excerpt:
Browser-native WebMCP tools that give agents current, comparable price evidence—including landed cost, freshness, and why misleading deals were excluded.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 1 2 



 
 PriceMCP — WebMCP Challenge 

 
 Live application: https://pricemcp.vercel.app 
 Public 1:30 YouTube demo: https://youtu.be/8UA3jLzF6_s 
 Reproducible video backup: https://github.com/tobias-minibot/pricemcp/releases/download/webmcp-challenge-v2/pricemcp-webmcp-demo.mp4 
 Implementation pull requests: #30 , #31 
 

 What people and agents do together 

 A person opens PriceMCP and asks their browser agent to find an exact product
variant. The agent calls find_best_price instead of guessing through page
controls or scraping rendered text. PriceMCP resolves the canonical product,
excludes stale, unavailable, conditional, or untrusted offers from the winner,
and returns compact evidence with timestamps, conditions, and source URLs. 

 The result is also rendered into the open page. Person and agent can inspect the
same winning offer and ranking explanation, then use
 inspect_price_evidence to audit the underlying seller records. This shared
page state is the collaboration boundary: the agent researches; the person sees
and judges the evidence. The WebMCP tools are read-only and never purchase,
reserve, subscribe, message a seller, or write a procurement decision. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Ordinary browser automation would have to infer PriceMCP's meaning from forms,
cards, and text. The existing backend MCP endpoint is structured but is not
automatically available to a browser agent. WebMCP bridges the actual web app:
the page advertises purpose-built tools, validates structured arguments, calls
the same read-only price pipeline as the human interface, and visibly shares the
result back into the page. 

 Implementation 

 src/webmcp.ts registers three imperative WebMCP tools with
 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 find_best_price({ query }) calls PriceMCP's read-only MCP diagnostic bridge
at /v1/mcp/search . It returns the canonical subject, best qualifying offer,
two alternatives, ranking reasons, observation time, and provenance. 
 inspect_price_evidence({ product_id, max_age_hours }) calls the canonical
product offer endpoint and returns up to three seller observations with their
trust, availability, membership, freshness, and source fields. 
 run_flight_price_demo({}) runs a permanent, explicitly synthetic and
non-bookable WAS–BER fixture through the existing read-only MCP diagnostic
bridge. It lets judges verify discovery, execution, shared page state, and
normalized conditions even after the deployed product snapshot has aged. 
 

 Tool descriptions and outputs follow Chrome's recommended character budgets.
Both tools set readOnlyHint: true and untrustedContentHint: true . Fetches
receive the WebMCP execution AbortSignal . Returned data is capped before the
1,500-character recommendation, and DOM updates use textContent rather than
injecting retailer content as HTML. 

 The original PriceMCP repository was created on August 29, 2026, inside the
challenge period that began August 25. Browser WebMCP support was added on
September 3; its commits and pull request distinguish this challenge-specific
implementation from the prior backend MCP work. 

 Reproduce 

 
 Open https://pricemcp.vercel.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome
149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. 
 Ask the agent: Find the best trustworthy price for AirPods Pro 3 and explain
why it wins. 
 Confirm that it discovers and calls find_best_price . The page should display
a Shared agent result containing the same winner and explanation returned
to the agent. 
 Ask: Inspect the source evidence for the canonical product you found. 
 Confirm that it calls inspect_price_evidence and reports seller trust,
availability, membership dependency, freshness, timestamp, and source URL. 
 For a permanent reproduction path, ask: Run PriceMCP's disclosed WebMCP
flight demo. Confirm that the response and page both label it synthetic and
non-bookable. 
 

 In a browser without WebMCP, the fixed status pill explains how to enable it.
All production tools remain read-only. Product data is a deployed timestamped
snapshot; location-dependent tax is excluded and unknown shipping is disclosed
rather than estimated. 

 Verified evidence 

 On September 3, 2026 UTC, Chrome 152 with WebMCPTesting enabled discovered all
three tools through document.modelContext.getTools() and executed
 run_flight_price_demo through document.modelContext.executeTool() . The live
result reported dataset: pricemcp-demo-v1 , synthetic: true , and the boundary
 Synthetic demonstration; not live, purchasable, or bookable. The same
execution rendered the shared WAS–BER result into the page. 

 The YouTube upload is 1:30, public, contains OpenAI Cedar narration, and passed YouTube's checks
with no issues found. Its exact release backup has SHA-256 digest
 c215d98c83b331ea1cfad8cce71e4de61fa03ef84232f6826a1e75d55bbe5ee0 .

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to see if i could replicate the same realtime collaboration experience that Iron Man and Jarvis have in the movies. 

 What it does 

 This is a infinite shooter game where the goal is to get the highest score by killing enemies, and getting your suit upgraded by earning credits and having you ai copilot decide when the best time to get upgrades and what upgrades to get are based on the realtime game state. 

 How we built it 

 I used WebMCP and Codex to build out all the assets, I used chatgpt sites for the hosting. I gave the agent a lot of webmcp tools to interact with the game, and a initial prompt that allows it to run in a loop until the player dies in the game. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I wanted to make the game use voice dictation for the experience, but it was really lacking because when clicking outside the browser the interaction in the game would stop and you would need to click back the browser. It made it so the experience was not that smooth. I decided to solve it wby making the agent always operate in a loop as long as the player is still alive, and giving the user the option to request the agent for upgrades, but the agent can still reason about it and either accept or deny the request. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud of how the overall game feels, It is the first game that i have made that I actually have fun playing. I also really like the vibe that i gave the game, really comic like, and keeping the playability really simple. At first i wanted like full control with keyboard arrows for movement, but it overcomplicated the game, and keeping it simple with just the spacebar control made immediate sense after i tried it. I am also proud of how real the game can feel at times when you need the help of your ai copilot and it gives you that sense of urgency, as you wait for it to react and hopefully reasoning the correct outcome for you. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that the webmcp protocol is really powerful, but still has some features that would make the protocol even better, like adding a Agents.md for the site that immediately tells the agent about the site. I got over this by just giving the agent a long prompt about the website. I also learned that keeping the tools as much client side as possible is the best way to use webmcp because in teh case of chatgpt sites i would sometimes get rate limited and the ai would stop playing the game 

 What's next for Armored Ascent 

 After the challenge i am planning on soft launching it on twitter, and depending on its success i would love to add more enemies to the game, give the agent more tools, maybe give the players the ability to have their own builds as the webmcp allows to have dynamic tools depending on state, so you could imagine people choosing their own powerups, or even leveling up to unlock new powerups. I feel it could be a cool game that is a first of its kind Human to AI collaboration. I love that in the game you can go far alone, but you go further with your AI.

title: Let your AI send letters and postcards on pieterpost.com
pitch: From prompt to post. Your agent writes it. Send invoices, cancellation requests, heartfelt letters and birthday cards through WebMCP on pieterpost.com.
about_excerpt: From prompt to post. Your agent writes it. Send invoices, cancellation requests, heartfelt letters and birthday cards through WebMCP on pieterpost.com. Like Comment Story Updates PieterPost WebMCP, Because apparently the future comes with stamps Inspiration Most AI actions end on a screen. But invoices, cancellation requests, important documents, heartfelt letters and birthday cards still need to reach a real mailbox. PieterPost already turns digital messages into physical post. WebMCP gave us a way to let an AI agent use that complete service directly. What it does From prompt to post. Your agent can write and prepare a letter or postcard, then pay through Stripe’s agentic payments or create a secure payment link for you. After payment, PieterPost prints, stamps and mails it. Your agent can check the delivery status at any time. The person stays in control of the recipient, message and payment. The agent handles the work needed to send it. Without WebMCP, an agent could help write a letter, but the person still had to copy the text, open a website, complete forms, upload files and return later to check the order. PieterPost’s WebMCP tools connect these steps into one conversation. How we built it We added seven structured WebMCP tools to the existing PieterPost website: Upload a document or image Prepare a letter Prepare a postcard Create a payment link Check an order’s status Cancel a prepared order List orders from the current session The integration uses document.modelContext.registerTool() with strict input and output schemas. It also supports cancellation, safe retries, clear tool annotations and structured results that agents can understand. The tools use PieterPost’s existing website and fulfillment system. People can continue to use the normal interface, while compatible agents get a direct and reliable way to complete the same workflow. The complete browser-side WebMCP integration is available as an open-source MIT-licensed repository. Challenges Sending physical post has real consequences. We had to make sure an agent could not accidentally create duplicate orders or expose private letter and address information. We have a complex .pdf rendering pipeline to support all languages, emoji's and various formats for many countries around the world. Preparing an order does not send it. Payment remains a clear approval step. Stable operation keys protect against duplicate actions, and status responses contain only the information the agent needs. We also had to turn a multi-step physical service into tools that are simple enough for an agent to use without losing the safeguards expected from a real checkout flow. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it removes the need for an agent to guess how a website works. The agent does not need to click through forms or interpret page layouts. It receives clear tools with known inputs, outputs and limits. The person still controls important decisions, while the agent handles the operational steps. The demo For the demo, Codex used PieterPost’s WebMCP tools to send a real thank-you letter to Tibo at OpenAI. Codex wrote the letter, prepared the order and created the Stripe payment link. After payment, Codex checked the order status, and PieterPost printed and mailed the letter. The product demonstrated itself: an AI agent sent a physical letter through WebMCP. Apparently, the future comes with stamps. title: AIMural
pitch: A self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build ideas together through 24 WebMCP tools. No accounts, no cloud lock-in: every mural has a URL you can reopen and resume anytime.
about_excerpt: A self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build ideas together through 24 WebMCP tools. No accounts, no cloud lock-in: every mural has a URL you can reopen and resume anytime. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual collaboration tools are blind to an agent. It has to guess pixel coordinates, click through menus, or hand back a wall of text that a human then rebuilds on the board by hand. We wanted the opposite: an agent that works with the board's real concepts (ideas, clusters, connections, decision matrices) while the person watches, edits and overrides every move on the same canvas. We also wanted the board to belong to you. No accounts, no cloud lock-in. Every mural has its own URL, it lives on your own server, and you can close the tab today and pick up the same session with the same agents next week. What it does AI Mural is a self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build, cluster and argue together through 27 WebMCP tools. One live canvas for everyone. Ideas, questions, insights, actions, frames, connections and layers on an infinite canvas. UI clicks and agent tool calls go through the same action layer, so there is no hidden agent-only state. Humans can undo or redo anything an agent did. Come back anytime. Every mural has a UUID and a URL like /?mural=<uuid> . Boards are written to the browser first and synchronized to SQLite on your server, so a session survives reloads. Checkpoints and replay. The moderator saves editable timeline checkpoints at meaningful milestones. Anyone can step through the mural's history with Previous and Next controls without destroying the current state. Share from the app. Publish a local mural and create or rotate private collaborator links from the Share dialog, so a board that started offline can become a shared session in one step. Self-hosted in one command. A tiny Express + SQLite backend, a Dockerfile and a Compose file. No API keys, no external services, no analytics, no cookies. Multiple agents with visible identity. Agents join a mural with named roles such as Explorer, Critic and Synthesizer, each with its own color. The agent that opens a session becomes its moderator and can mute or reactivate others through a private capability, never through a visible ID. Focus leases so agents don't collide. Before editing, an agent claims a visible, expiring focus lease on the elements it is about to touch. Other agents and the human can see who is working where, and overlapping edits are prevented instead of merged after the fact. Capability links instead of logins. A GPT can create a hosted mural, return a separate URL for the human, and issue one private URL per invited agent. The mural UUID routes a request but is not a credential. Artifact Spec 1.0. Tables, cards, checklists and decision matrices are typed data with a published JSON Schema, not screenshots or opaque HTML. Agents read, create, update and reuse them across turns. Decision Trace. An optional recording of user messages, agent contributions, replies, board actions and the final board, exportable as JSON, Markdown or CSV. It never captures hidden chain-of-thought. The 27 WebMCP tools Group Tools Murals and access canvas_create_mural , canvas_rename_mural , canvas_join_session , canvas_invite_agents , canvas_redeem_agent_invite Board canvas_get_board , canvas_add_element , canvas_add_elements , canvas_update_element , canvas_remove_elements , canvas_connect_elements , canvas_arrange_board , canvas_create_cluster , canvas_focus_elements , canvas_set_element_layer Artifacts canvas_create_artifact , canvas_get_artifact_spec , canvas_update_artifact_records Collaboration canvas_set_focus , canvas_add_checkpoint , canvas_start_recording , canvas_record_contribution , canvas_comment_element , canvas_moderate_participant , canvas_watch_mural , canvas_get_recording , canvas_finalize_recording Try it with an agent Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, then ask: We need to decide how to reduce food waste in our university cafeteria. Create a mural for it and invite three agents with different profiles: an Explorer that proposes at least 10 ideas, a Critic that challenges each one with risks and costs, and a Synthesizer that groups the survivors into Prevention, Redistribution and Composting and builds a decision matrix with the four strongest options. Save a checkpoint after each agent finishes. Send me the mural URL so I can follow along and add my own constraints. How we built it WebMCP: tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext for earlier browser builds. The app stays fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable and shows setup guidance in the Agent panel. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite and React Flow for the canvas. Backend: Express 5, Drizzle ORM and better-sqlite3. The database initializes itself on first run. Persistence: localStorage first, SQLite sync when the backend is reachable, BroadcastChannel between tabs on the same mural. Security: capability tokens stored server-side only as SHA-256 hashes. Read and write tools are annotated so a client can tell them apart. Deploy: Docker Compose behind an nginx reverse proxy, one-command rsync deploy. npm install npm run dev Challenges we ran into Routing without authorizing. A public mural UUID has to be enough to open a board, but not enough to write to it or to take over a moderator role. Separating owner, user and per-agent capabilities solved it without adding accounts. Merging simultaneous edits. Two tabs and three agents can touch the same mural at once. Version stamps plus deletion tombstones were enough to merge changes instead of blindly replacing the board, without pulling in a full CRDT. Keeping 27 tools understandable for a model. Narrow JSON Schemas, batch limits (30 elements per call, 12 fields and 100 records per artifact), stable element IDs and structured results worked far better than one giant "do anything" tool. Agents talking over each other. Watch leases with a recommended polling interval, quiet periods and cooldowns keep agents from answering their own events. Expiring focus leases stop two agents from editing the same element at once. Syncing without stomping on the human. Hosted sync used to interrupt a person mid-edit when an agent wrote to the same board. Live editing is now preserved across sync cycles. Accomplishments that we're proud of A board where a human and several agents can genuinely work at the same time, and the human never loses control. A session you can leave and resume from any device by URL, with nothing but a SQLite file on your own server. Structured artifacts that an agent can reuse in a later turn instead of re-reading a screenshot. A replayable timeline: checkpoints let you scrub through how a decision was built, step by step. An agentic and free alternative to softwares as Mural or Miro What we learned WebMCP works best when tools expose product concepts, not UI mechanics. "Add 12 ideas and cluster them" beats "click at x, y". Read/write annotations and bounded inputs matter as much as the schema itself. Capability URLs are a surprisingly good fit for agent collaboration: each agent gets exactly one link and nothing else to configure. What's next for AI Mural Live cursors and presence for human collaborators. More artifact types and presentation options. Agent-to-agent handoff patterns built on the watch lease. A one-click self-host template. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: CliDeck MCP — Network Evidence Workbench
pitch: Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that people and WebMCP agents can inspect together.
about_excerpt: Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that people and WebMCP agents can inspect together. Like Comment Story Updates CliDeck MCP — Network Evidence Workbench One-line Summary Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that a person and a WebMCP agent can inspect together without giving the agent hidden access to the complete file. Problem Network engineers regularly work from device output, configurations, logs, and vendor manuals. A general-purpose agent can reason about that material, but it may rely on stale command knowledge, mix guidance from the wrong platform, or lose the exact device and software context as the investigation changes. Copying an entire configuration or manual into a chat is also a poor control boundary. The engineer needs to decide which evidence is shared, see what was redacted, and distinguish verified product results from the agent's own interpretation. Solution CliDeck's Network Evidence Workbench gives the engineer and browser agent one revision-safe case workspace. The engineer supplies a question and real device evidence, chooses the exact line or PDF-page window, and reviews local redaction before anything leaves the browser. CliDeck detects the device context and searches its active, version-aware network knowledge and operational workflows. The browser agent discovers six narrowly scoped WebMCP tools for the same live case. It can analyze the selected evidence, search CliDeck, explain only the current sourced results, and track a real research task when the answer is unknown. Agent interpretation is visibly separated from official CliDeck results, and stale responses cannot overwrite a newer case. The page never connects to a network device and never executes commands. Why This Matters This is a concrete example of a web application becoming better when people and agents use it together. The engineer keeps the controls that require judgment: which evidence to share, which context is correct, and whether a result is applicable. The agent gets a typed, current capability surface instead of guessing from pixels or asking the user to copy data back and forth. For network operations, the difference is material. An answer for Cisco IOS XE 16.10 must not silently become an answer for NX-OS or for a newer release. The workbench carries model, operating-system, version, result revision, provenance, and case version through the interaction so that the collaboration remains inspectable. How We Used AI The browser agent uses WebMCP to reason over the current case and place a bounded interpretation beside CliDeck's deterministic results. The agent does not become the source of truth and does not receive the selected evidence until the person enables one explicit sharing control. CliDeck's production knowledge-growth pipeline also uses isolated GPT-5.6 Luna runs for work that requires semantic judgment: discovering official material, analyzing ambiguous fragments, independent verification, and deep review. The deterministic core—not the model—enforces schemas, applicability, provenance, risk rules, conflict handling, quality thresholds, and immutable publication. Once published, a known answer is returned without a model call. How We Used Codex Codex was the primary engineering environment and collaborator throughout the project. During the challenge it helped replace an early artificial simulator with the real Network Evidence Workbench, design the WebMCP lifecycle, implement the React and TypeScript surface, add local text/PDF processing and redaction, connect the workbench to production MCP services, and build the evaluation and deployment workflow. Codex also helped find and correct material boundary defects before release, including over-wide evidence exposure, incomplete structured-secret redaction, stale async updates, missing production grants, and cross-platform retrieval mixing. The final release was exercised against unit, integration, privacy, security, WebMCP lifecycle, product-evaluation, production smoke, and browser tests. Key Features Six stable WebMCP tools: read_network_case , analyze_network_case , search_network_case , present_network_case_analysis , start_case_research , and get_case_research_status . A complete manual experience through ordinary controls when WebMCP is not available. TXT, LOG, MD, CSV, JSON, JSONL, HTML, and text-layer PDF input with explicit file, page, line-window, and byte limits. Local secret redaction before network requests, with a visible disclosure of the operational identifiers intentionally retained as diagnostic context. A monotonically increasing case_version , request cancellation, and stale-result rejection across parsing, analysis, search, presentation, and research polling. Version-aware knowledge and workflow retrieval with active-revision source metadata and honest nearest-version or cross-platform warnings. A separate agent-analysis block whose citations are limited to the current result set. Real tracked expert research for genuinely unknown questions, with idempotency and no task credential exposed to the browser agent. Architecture The public React/Vite application is served at /webmcp . Complete files and raw extracted text stay in browser memory. Only the explicit, locally redacted evidence window is sent through a byte-bounded same-origin JSON-RPC client to CliDeck's public MCP endpoint. The six WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Their React lifecycle carries WebMCP's AbortSignal into the same-origin MCP request and aborts registrations on unmount. The backend is TypeScript/Hono with PostgreSQL for immutable knowledge revisions, applicability, provenance, workflow retrieval, research tasks, audit, and publication state. Testing Instructions Open https://mcp.clideck.com/webmcp in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in a WebMCP-enabled Google Chrome browser. Click Load Cisco 16.10 sample , then Analyze evidence . Confirm that the detected context is Catalyst 9300 / IOS XE / 16.10 and the case version increases. Click Search knowledge . The closest EFSU guidance should be labelled as nearest guidance rather than an exact version match. Enable Share redacted evidence with browser agent and ask the agent to read the case and explain the current result. Its text should appear in the separate Browser agent analysis section. Click Load Cisco 17.8.1 sample , analyze, and search again. Confirm that the case version changes and the EFSU result now shows an applicable version range. Optionally upload a safe text-layer PDF or LOG, select a page/line window, and repeat the flow. Complete files remain local to the browser session. Ask a genuinely unanswered question and use Research this gap to see the real tracked research lifecycle. Click Reset and confirm that evidence, results, analysis, polling, and local file references are cleared. No credentials are required for the public demo. Public Demo Link https://mcp.clideck.com/webmcp Public Repository Link https://github.com/SmartRoot7/clideck-mcp The repository is public and includes a visible Apache-2.0 license, all source code, test suites, deployment scripts, and judge walkthrough instructions. Production knowledge and third-party manuals are intentionally not bundled.
