title: Lantern
pitch: Your AI agent builds the lesson as a playable game, not a quiz. Lantern uses WebMCP to turn learner actions into visible evidence of understanding.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent builds the lesson as a playable game, not a quiz. Lantern uses WebMCP to turn learner actions into visible evidence of understanding. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most learning software is fixed before the learner opens it. Teachers, parents, and trainers must search through existing courses and accept content that may not fit the learner, skill, context, or preferred way of learning. AI can generate explanations and quizzes, but learning should involve more than reading generated text or selecting answers. We wanted learners to explore, experiment, make mistakes, revise their thinking, and demonstrate understanding through play. That idea became Lantern : a WebMCP-powered canvas where browser agents turn natural-language learning goals into playable games. What it does A user describes the learner, skill, and desired world in ordinary language. For example: Create an ecosystem game for a six-year-old where the learner restores a pond, meadow, and woodland by experimenting with sunlight, water, food, and shelter. The user gives this brief to a WebMCP-compatible browser agent. The agent then: Inspects Lantern’s capabilities and safety limits. Creates or resumes a game draft. Writes the complete HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Opens the game in a safe playtest. Checks validation errors, runtime diagnostics, and learning evidence. Improves the game and requests human review. The result is a functioning browser game rather than a description, code snippet, or dressed-up quiz. While the learner plays, Lantern records evidence such as predictions, attempts, observations, corrections, hint usage, and demonstrated mastery. Agent-created games receive dedicated pages and remain saved in the browser. How we built it Lantern was built through close human–agent collaboration. I provided the product direction, learning use cases, design feedback, safety requirements, and decisions about the final experience. OpenAI Codex handled most of the implementation —building the interface, defining the WebMCP tools, creating the isolated game runtime, implementing browser persistence and evidence reporting, debugging interactions, testing the application, removing legacy code, and preparing the project for submission. The resulting application uses Vinext, React, TypeScript, WebMCP, sandboxed srcDoc iframes, Canvas 2D/WebGL, and browser local storage . Lantern registers eight tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_game_canvas_capabilities list_saved_game_drafts resume_game_draft create_game_draft set_game_source preview_game get_game_runtime_diagnostics request_game_review These tools allow an agent to inspect the canvas, create or resume drafts, write game source, open playtests, diagnose problems, and request human review. Generated games communicate with Lantern through two small host APIs: lantern.evidence() reports predictions, experiments, attempts, observations, corrections, and other learning signals. lantern.complete() reports mastery and triggers host-controlled completion feedback. This development process reflected Lantern’s central idea: a human supplies the intent and judgment, while an agent handles the technical work required to turn that intent into a functioning product. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was giving agents enough creative freedom to build ambitious games without giving generated code unrestricted access to the browser. Games run inside isolated iframes with a strict Content Security Policy. External scripts, network requests, storage APIs, nested frames, and hidden navigation are blocked. Lantern also validates generated source and rejects unsafe APIs, oversized payloads, dynamic evaluation, and obvious unbounded loops. Another challenge was designing tools that agents could use reliably. A single “generate game” action would hide too much state and make failures difficult to diagnose. We created a structured workflow with explicit capabilities, drafts, revisions, previews, diagnostics, persistence, and review. We also had to make gameplay educationally meaningful. A score alone reveals very little about understanding, so Lantern captures how a learner predicts, experiments, uses hints, corrects mistakes, and revises their thinking. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Lantern produces real interactive games rather than descriptions or generated quizzes. A browser agent can discover Lantern’s tools, create a structured project, program the complete game, inspect errors, revise its work, and open the playable result through WebMCP. We also built: Persistent browser-local game drafts Dedicated pages for agent-created games Safe, isolated game execution Source and runtime validation Revision and idempotency protection Human review boundaries Learning-evidence reporting Host-controlled mastery celebrations Five example games covering mathematics, literacy, spatial reasoning, ecosystems, and computational thinking Most importantly, Lantern demonstrates a complete human–agent workflow: the human describes the desired outcome, the agent builds it, and the resulting experience can be played and evaluated immediately. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a website exposes meaningful product capabilities instead of adding a chatbot beside fixed content. Agents perform better when they can inspect constraints before acting, observe the consequences of their changes, diagnose failures, and resume from structured state. We also learned that browser-local persistence can support surprisingly capable agent workflows without requiring a backend service. Most importantly, generative education becomes much more compelling when the output is something learners can manipulate—not simply something they consume. What's next for Lantern We plan to add reusable 3D components, richer physics and shader tools, teacher-defined assessment rubrics, accessibility presets, collaborative learning worlds, and portable game packages. We also want agents to adapt existing games from teacher feedback and learner evidence while keeping educators in control of review and publishing. Our long-term goal is to let anyone describe what someone needs to learn and collaborate with an agent to build a safe, memorable world for learning it. title: Kopilotti Sales — Kopilotti WebMCP Challenge build
pitch: A 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot—where an agent can research and prepare, but only a human can approve deterministic price evaluation and its auditable receipt.
about_excerpt: A 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot—where an agent can research and prepare, but only a human can approve deterministic price evaluation and its auditable receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Kopilotti WebMCP turns a fictional car storefront into a 24/7 digital sales channel—not a chatbot. Car shopping is repetitive enough for an agent, but consequential enough that a human must stay in control of the commercial outcome. WebMCP is a strong fit because the page exposes the safe parts of the journey—search, comparison, condition review, draft preparation, and approved evaluation—as explicit, schema-constrained tools. The agent calls those capabilities directly instead of scraping the page or guessing at controls. Every action updates the same visible workspace and activity log the person can inspect, which makes the experience clearer, more reliable, and easier to correct. Together, the person and agent can move a sales conversation forward outside dealership opening hours. The agent can find vehicles, compare factual fields, retrieve condition facts, and prepare a €90,000 non-binding discussion draft independently. It cannot cross the consequential boundary by itself: approval for deterministic evaluation is a page-native human action that is never registered as a tool. A scripted .click() has no effect. After approval, a fixed public policy evaluates €90,000 against the fictional €95,000 asking price as exactly 9,473 basis points, returns COUNTER at €92,150, and resists an agent policy-override attempt. The resulting JSON receipt records the policy and approval evidence with binding: false and transmittedToDealer: false. The implementation uses five narrowly scoped WebMCP tools—search_vehicles, compare_vehicles, get_vehicle_condition, prepare_price_discussion, and evaluate_price_discussion—over fictional in-memory inventory. WebMCP and manual controls call the same application functions, while the activity log labels the real invocation source as webmcp, manual, or human-ui. When a browser does not expose WebMCP, a persistent readiness banner immediately offers the complete, honestly labeled manual path rather than presenting the application as broken. Inspiration Car shopping is a useful test case for agentic browsing: the research is repetitive, the facts are structured and the commercial consequences matter. A useful agent should accelerate the research without silently gaining authority to negotiate, contact a dealer or create a transaction. Kopilotti WebMCP explores that boundary. The browser agent gets explicit, schema-constrained tools. Every result appears in the same workspace the person sees, and the final commercial action remains outside the agent's authority. What it does The demo registers five WebMCP tools: search_vehicles filters and sorts a fictional six-vehicle inventory. compare_vehicles returns a factual side-by-side comparison without choosing a winner. get_vehicle_condition selects a vehicle and displays its versioned condition facts. prepare_price_discussion creates a pending, local and non-binding discussion draft. evaluate_price_discussion evaluates only the exact draft that received page-native human approval and creates a machine-checkable receipt. Approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. The page also contains a numbered manual fallback for browsers that do not expose WebMCP; it uses the same application functions and labels each invocation honestly as manual. How we built it The project is a dependency-free static web app using semantic HTML, modern CSS and JavaScript modules. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and include bounded JSON Schemas, descriptive titles, explicit annotations and abort-signal handling. Tool execution calls small, independently tested domain functions and then updates the visible UI. A page-native approval gate binds the human action to the current draft context. The public demo policy produces deterministic ACCEPT, COUNTER or ESCALATE results and an in-memory JSON receipt. There are no production APIs, external data sources, customer records or hidden production pricing rules. Why WebMCP matters here Visual automation would have to infer search controls, card layouts and state transitions. WebMCP gives the agent stable named capabilities with typed inputs and clear safety boundaries. The user can watch the same workspace change after each tool call, making the process observable and correctable. Safety and responsible design All vehicle data is fictional. No tool accepts personal data. Search and comparison are explicitly read-only. Preparing a price discussion creates only pending local UI state. No tool can grant human approval, set or override policy, submit an offer, contact a dealer or create a transaction. Evaluation runs only after page-native human approval and produces a non-binding, unsent demo receipt. The repository contains no proprietary Kopilotti Sales decision logic or production data. Challenges The main design challenge was making price evaluation genuinely useful without allowing the agent to authorize itself. The solution was a reversible drafting step, a page-native approval action that is absent from the tool manifest, context-bound validation and a deterministic receipt. What we learned Agent-native design is not just adding an API to a page. The tool contract, the visible UI and the authority model must agree. A narrow tool with an honest description can be more useful than a broad tool that leaves the user uncertain about what the agent actually did. What's next Test the tool contracts against additional WebMCP-capable agents. Expand manual assistive-technology and cross-browser regression coverage. Explore dealer-approved, explicitly confirmed handoffs without giving the model pricing authority. Built with WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Node.js test runner AI-assisted development disclosure Development was AI-assisted with OpenAI Codex. Product scope, trust-boundary decisions, verification and submission remain human-directed. This open challenge build is separate from the private production Kopilotti Sales engine and contains none of its source code, data or private pricing rules. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: StealthLab
pitch: A global, community-contributed library of verified, traceable capabilities that AI agents can discover, adapt and execute to make ANY project work faster, cheaper and more reliable.
about_excerpt:
A global, community-contributed library of verified, traceable capabilities that AI agents can discover, adapt and execute to make ANY project work faster, cheaper and more reliable.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI is changing the way we work, but every agent still largely works alone. 

 A useful workflow discovered by one agent is often lost in its context window. A clever solution buried in a GitHub repository remains invisible to other agents. A procedure that worked yesterday has to be rediscovered tomorrow. 

 We believe this is a fundamental limitation of the current AI stack. 

 What happens when procedural knowledge becomes global and shareable? 

 Instead of every agent learning independently, successful ways of doing things could accumulate into a shared layer of intelligence, where agents don't just share information, but share how to act . 

 That is the idea behind StealthLab. 

 What it does 

 StealthLab is building a living procedural memory for AI agents . 

 It turns knowledge and experience from sources, repositories, and agent executions into structured, reusable capabilities: 

 Claims → Procedures → Tasks → Implementations 

 But we don't want to stop at retrieval. 

 A procedure can be executed, verified, and connected to evidence: 

 Source → Claim → Procedure → Task Graph → Implementation → Execution → Verification → Evidence 

 This lets an agent move from: 

 
 “Here is some information that might help.” 
 

 to: 

 
 “Here is a way of solving the problem, here is how it can be executed, and here is evidence that it works.” 
 

 StealthLab exposes this knowledge through MCP so agents can directly search for procedures, inspect evidence, compare solutions, and eventually discover the best verified way to accomplish a task. 

 How we built it 

 We built StealthLab as a structured knowledge and execution layer rather than another document store. 

 The system separates: 

 Claims — what the system believes
 Procedures — reusable ways of acting
 Tasks — reusable capabilities
 Implementations — how those capabilities are actually executed
 Executions — what really happened
 Verification — whether the result satisfied the goal
 Evidence — why the result should be trusted 

 Underneath this is a PostgreSQL-backed substrate, FastAPI services, a React/TypeScript interface, semantic retrieval, execution graphs, and an MCP interface for agents. 

 We also built a claim graph that makes the system's understanding inspectable rather than hidden inside a model. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest problem is that retrieval alone does not create reliable intelligence . 

 Finding a relevant document is easy. Knowing whether its procedure applies to a particular problem is harder. Executing that procedure safely is harder still. And determining whether it actually worked is harder again. 

 LLMs also introduce their own failure modes: hallucinated tool results, unreliable actions, context degradation, and overconfident answers. 

 This forced us to separate knowledge from execution and confidence from evidence. 

 A procedure shouldn't become trusted simply because a model generated it. It should become trusted because it can be tested and supported by evidence. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built the beginnings of a system where what one agent learns can become reusable knowledge for other agents . 

 During the submission period, we expanded the procedural-memory substrate, built structured ingestion into claims, procedures and tasks, added semantic retrieval, connected procedures to executable implementations, added execution and verification paths, built the claim-graph interface, and exposed the system through MCP. 

 Most importantly, we started closing the loop between knowledge and reality: 

 knowledge → action → execution → verification → evidence → better knowledge 

 That is a fundamentally different direction from simply putting more documents into a context window. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the missing layer in agent infrastructure may not be another bigger model or another larger context window. 

 It may be shared procedural memory . 

 Agents already generate enormous amounts of useful knowledge while solving problems. The challenge is turning that transient experience into something structured, reusable, attributable, and trustworthy. 

 We also learned that memory without verification can compound mistakes just as easily as it can compound knowledge. 

 So the system needs to remember not only what worked , but why we believe it worked, where it came from, when it applies, and what happened when it was actually executed . 

 What's next for StealthLab 

 We are building toward a world where agents don't have to repeatedly rediscover the same solutions. 

 The next step is making StealthLab's knowledge layer increasingly intelligent: learning how to traverse the graph, combine procedures, choose between implementations, personalize retrieval, and use execution history to improve which solutions it recommends. 

 Over time, we want deterministic tools and specialized implementations to replace fragile LLM steps wherever possible. 

 The end goal is a shared procedural layer for AI: 

 one agent discovers a better way → StealthLab verifies it → the knowledge becomes available to everyone. 

 That is how we think global procedural memory can change the way we all use AI.

title: Seating Repair
pitch: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A surprising number of everyday operational problems are really placement problems in disguise. You have a set of people, tasks, items, vehicles, or events, a limited number of places or resources, and a collection of rules that determine what can go where. We see this everywhere. Guests need to be assigned to tables. Patients need beds. Employees need shifts. Classes need rooms. Aircraft need gates. Jobs need machines. Inventory needs storage locations. In every case, the basic question is the same: how do you put the right thing in the right place while respecting all the constraints around it? Creating the first plan is only part of the challenge. The harder part often comes later, when reality changes after the plan has already been accepted. A guest suddenly needs an accessible table. Two people can no longer sit together. A VIP needs a specific position. A resource becomes unavailable. A manager makes a last-minute decision that should not be undone. At that point, the goal is not to throw everything away and optimize from scratch. It is to repair the existing plan while preserving as much of what already works as possible. Traditional optimization systems are good at solving structured problems, but people do not usually describe operational changes as formal constraints. They say things like "keep these two apart", "do not move this person", or "this group needs to stay together". An AI agent can help translate that kind of natural-language intent into structured constraints, but there is another problem: the agent may be working from an older version of the plan while a person is still editing the live page. That creates a very real failure mode. A person can make an important manual change, and the agent can later overwrite it simply because it is still acting on stale state. We wanted to explore a collaboration model where that cannot happen silently. We chose seating because it makes the larger idea easy to see. A guest represents an entity that needs to be assigned. A table represents a limited-capacity resource. "Together" and "apart" rules behave like clustering constraints. Accessibility and fixed-table rules represent eligibility and placement requirements. A locked guest represents a human decision that the agent is not allowed to override. Seating Repair is our way of exploring how WebMCP can bring these pieces together: natural-language agency, deterministic constraint solving, live application state, and direct human control, all operating on the same shared planning surface. What it does Seating Repair is a WebMCP application for solving and repairing constrained placement problems while a person and an agent are both working on the same live plan. The demo uses 12 fictional guests and three tables because that makes the idea easy to understand at a glance. But underneath the seating interface, the application is dealing with a more general planning problem: limited-capacity resources, people who must stay together or apart, fixed placements, eligibility requirements such as accessibility, decisions that a human has explicitly locked, and the need to keep as much of the existing plan unchanged as possible. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can read the exact current state of the board, understand the active constraints, add new hard constraints from a person's request, repair the plan, and then validate the result. The goal is not simply to press an "optimize" button and generate a completely new seating arrangement. In a real planning workflow, many existing decisions are already correct and should stay that way. A useful repair needs to preserve what still works, respect every hard constraint, treat human-locked placements as authoritative, change only what is necessary, and verify that the final result is actually valid. This becomes especially important when a person and an agent are working at the same time. If the agent reads the board and a person then moves or locks a guest, the agent is no longer allowed to write using the old version of the plan. That stale write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. The agent has to read the page again and continue from the decision the person actually made instead of silently overwriting it. In the demo, this is easy to see: a person can move Grandma Rose to a different table and lock her there. The agent can then add another constraint, repair the remaining conflicts, and validate the board while leaving Grandma Rose exactly where the person placed her. Seating is the domain we chose to demonstrate the idea, but it is not the limit of the underlying pattern. The same kind of constrained allocation and repair appears in restaurant and event operations, protocol seating, workforce scheduling, room and resource allocation, patient-to-bed assignment, airport gate reassignment, and many other situations where a working plan has to adapt as constraints and human decisions change. The current build is intentionally focused on demonstrating that shared coordination model clearly. It is not meant to pretend that one seating demo is already a complete product for every one of those industries. Instead, it shows the core interaction pattern: an AI agent can help repair a constrained plan, while the live application remains the source of truth and human decisions remain in control. How we built it We built Seating Repair as a lightweight TypeScript app with Vite. Everything runs in the browser, with no backend and no separate database for the agent. The seating board that the person sees is the same state the WebMCP tools work with. We kept the WebMCP side intentionally simple and exposed only four tools. One reads the current seating state, one adds hard constraints, one repairs the plan, and one validates the result. That was enough to cover the full interaction we wanted to demonstrate without turning the project into a large collection of overlapping tools. We also did not want the language model itself to be responsible for deciding whether a seating plan is correct. The agent can understand a request such as "keep these two apart" or "do not move this guest", but the actual planning is handled by deterministic application code. The repair logic runs in the browser and searches for an arrangement that satisfies all of the current constraints. It checks table capacity, together and apart rules, fixed-table requirements, accessibility, and human locks. When there is more than one valid solution, it prefers one that changes as little of the current plan as possible. Human edits are treated as first-class state changes. A person can move a guest manually and lock that placement. Once a guest is locked, the agent cannot move them during a repair. There is no hidden tool option that lets the agent ignore the lock; the person has to unlock that guest first. One of the main things we wanted to get right was what happens when the human changes the board while the agent is working. Every change to the seating plan increments a revision number. When the agent tries to change the plan, it has to provide the revision it previously read. If the board has changed since then, the write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. That means the agent cannot quietly apply an old plan over a newer human decision. It has to read the current board again and continue from there. Repairs are also atomic. The solver works on a snapshot first and only updates the live board after it has found a complete valid solution. If the constraints cannot be satisfied, the current plan stays as it was instead of being left in a partially changed state. The manual UI and the WebMCP tools share the same store, validation logic, and constraint model. We wanted there to be one source of truth rather than one version of the plan for the person and another version for the agent. For the demo, state is stored in browser localStorage, which keeps the project self-contained. We also added tests for the behaviors we considered most important: constraint validation, deterministic repairs, minimum-change solutions, human locks, unsatisfiable plans, stale revisions, invalid tool input, and WebMCP tool execution. The overall design is fairly simple on purpose: the agent handles natural-language intent, WebMCP gives it structured access to the live application, and normal deterministic code is still responsible for enforcing the rules and deciding whether the final plan is valid. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not the seating solver itself. It was deciding how a person and an agent should safely work on the same plan without one silently undoing the other. At first, it is tempting to treat the agent like a normal automation flow: read the state, calculate a better arrangement, and write the result back. That works until the person changes something in the meantime. Once we started testing that interaction

title: Paper Trail
pitch: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted.
about_excerpt: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every big life event arrives with a hidden invoice: not money, but paperwork . A birth triggers 15–40 separate actions scattered across the Social Security Administration, the health insurer, and the employer's HR portal — each with its own login, its own forms, its own deadlines (add a dependent within 30 days or wait for open enrollment), and its own ways of spelling the same name. Humans have always been the integration glue between these portals: re-typing identical data, making format mistakes, missing windows. When we read the WebMCP spec, one sentence rewired how we think: websites can hand agents structured capabilities instead of forcing them to screenshot pixels. The paperwork layer is the biggest unclaimed prize for that idea — so we built the app we wished existed: say it once, and the whole bundle gets done, with the human still sovereign. What it does Type one sentence — "We had a baby girl on June 3rd at General Hospital." One interview , no forms: the hub derives the facts and materializes an action bundle across three independent portals, with deadline math computed live (DOB June 3 + 30 days → insurer window closes July 3). Each portal owns a tool surface : walking into a page dynamically registers its tools and walking away unregisters them ( AbortController ). The agent only ever sees the tools for the page it's on. Drafts fill from one canonical profile — and a reconciliation engine catches cross-portal conflicts (the hospital's "Okafor-Reyes, Amara" vs. the profile's "Amara Okafor-Reyes"; "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03"), explains them in plain language, and standardizes only on the human's say-so. Nothing files without a human click. Every write tool is a two-call gate: the first call opens an on-page dialog showing every field about to be filed; the second call executes only if the human actually approved — enforced in code, not in a prompt. Replay a confirmation id → unknown_confirmation_id . Let the agent approve itself → human_approval_missing . File twice → already_submitted . Everything ends in a receipt ledger : payload digest → confirmation number → timestamp → human-approval flag. The showpiece : pt_cascade_update . The family moves mid-flow; one call re-derives the whole situation — deadlines recomputed, every pending draft re-filled across all three portals — while filed actions stay untouched, because receipts preserve what was actually submitted. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static SPA — classic scripts, no framework, no backend, deployable anywhere (it even runs from file:// ). mcp.js — the WebMCP layer: registerTool with readOnlyHint annotations, per-portal AbortSignal lifecycles, and a guarded executor (activity-rail logging, ~1.5K output budgets, throws → typed errors agents can self-correct from). portals.js — three fictional portals (SSA, Meridian Health, employer HR) with schemas, strict in-code validation whose errors are written for the agent, the two-call ConfirmGate , and the reconciliation engine. hub.js — the one-sentence interview resolver and the hub tool surface ( pt_start_life_event_interview , pt_get_action_bundle , pt_reconcile_field_conflicts , pt_get_receipt_ledger , pt_cascade_update ). store.js / bundle.js — canonical profile, dependency-aware bundle, deadline math, event-sourced receipts — plus a store subscription so the page the human is watching re-renders live when the agent mutates state through the protocol. 26 tools across 4 surfaces; 13 annotated read-only; 3 gated writes. A /diag.html page probes the runtime (API presence, live registration, getTools() visibility, abort lifecycle) — 11/11 checks pass in Chrome 150 with #enable-webmcp-testing . Challenges we ran into The runtime diverges from the spec text. In the real Chrome build, modelContext.registerTool() returns undefined , not a Promise — our .then() chain silently died at boot. We caught it only by testing against the actual enabled runtime, and now handle both styles. That bug alone justified building a diagnostics page. Tool identity is page-scoped. Re-entering a portal risks a synchronous Duplicate tool name throw; abort-then-re-register had to be proven clean (it is — verified via getTools() ). The "shared live app" requirement is real work. When the agent conducts the interview through the protocol, the human's screen must react — we wired store-driven re-rendering so the bundle materializes on screen as the tool call lands. Timezones and dates. "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03" needed part-wise date comparison, not toISOString() gymnastics that silently shift days across UTC offsets. Making the gate genuinely binding. The tempting shortcut is a confirm dialog the agent can talk its way past. We made approval a server-side-of-the-page fact: the finalize call checks the human's actual click in code, and we proved the negative paths on camera. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full judge experience runs through the runtime's own executeTool : interview → surface swap → gated filing (pending → human approval → submitted) → reconciliation → cascade → ledger. Not a scripted path — the protocol path. Receipts as evidence : every filing carries a payload digest and confirmation number; the ledger reads like an audit trail, because that's what it is. Honest degradation : without a WebMCP runtime the chip says so, the human buttons drive the same code paths, and the app still demonstrates every flow. A dark, full-height activity rail that narrates every tool call — the human and the agent visibly share one live artifact. What we learned Protocol depth is a design material, not a checkbox. Dynamic surfaces, annotations, and elicitation-shaped gates changed the architecture, not just the API calls. Human-in-the-loop belongs in code. A prompt saying "ask first" is a suggestion; a gate that physically cannot finalize without the human's click is a guarantee. Test in the real judging environment early. The single most dangerous bug we fixed was invisible in every browser except the one with the flag enabled. Agents need agent-legible errors : strict in-code validation with messages written for self-correction turns failures into progress. What's next for Paper Trail Move and bereavement event packs — the bundle engine takes new event types without architecture changes. Native requestUserInteraction elicitation as a progressive enhancement of the two-call gate. An accessibility operator mode — the same tool surfaces are a better substrate than the visual DOM; narration and pacing ride the protocol for free. Handoff export — the remaining human-only actions (notary visits, in-person verifications) as a calendar file, because a good agent knows what it can't do. title: HOUSELIGHTS
pitch: HOUSELIGHTS turns seat maps into 14 WebMCP tools, letting AI find and hold the best seats while people see every action and retain final purchase authority.
about_excerpt: HOUSELIGHTS turns seat maps into 14 WebMCP tools, letting AI find and hold the best seats while people see every action and retain final purchase authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Buying theater tickets should be a perfect job for an AI assistant: compare hundreds of seats, balance price against view quality, and keep adjacent seats together. In practice, agents see most seat maps as pixels. They must guess where to click, and the person cannot easily understand or correct what the agent is doing. HOUSELIGHTS asks: what if the box office exposed its real structure to the agent while the person stayed in control? What it does HOUSELIGHTS is a shared live-theater box office for a person and an AI agent. Through 14 WebMCP tools, an agent can search performances, inspect every seat's availability and price, compare sightline, acoustic, and value scores, recommend adjacent seats, and place time-limited holds. Those actions immediately appear on the same seat map the person is viewing. Agent-held seats pulse amber with a visible countdown. The person can inspect, veto, release, or move them into the cart before completing checkout. The agent provides machine-speed comparison across the whole house. The person keeps taste, context, and final purchase authority. How we built it HOUSELIGHTS uses vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS with one shared in-memory AppStore . Human interactions and agent tools mutate the same store, preventing the UI and agent from developing separate versions of the box office. The top-level page registers 14 imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Every tool has a JSON Schema contract and returns structured data rather than forcing the agent to scrape the DOM. Core tools include: get_seat_map for structured availability, pricing, and seat-quality data recommend_seats for budget-aware adjacent-seat ranking hold_seats for visible, expiring reservations get_board_state for shared human-agent context announce_to_user for visual and screen-reader announcements undo_last_action for reversing agent-authored changes checkout for requesting—but not completing—human confirmation The checkout form is deliberately not exposed as an agent tool. Its confirmation token is bound to the exact cart snapshot, and only a trusted human submission can create the order. The app is deployed on Cloudflare Pages and includes a fallback registry so the same tool handlers can be tested in browsers without WebMCP enabled. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making collaboration visible rather than merely functional. A successful tool call is not enough if the person cannot see what changed. We connected every hold, cart update, announcement, and expiration to the live seat map and activity feed. The second challenge was defining the purchase boundary. The agent needs enough authority to be useful, but it must not silently complete a transaction. We therefore separated requesting checkout from confirming checkout and bound confirmation to the reviewed cart. We also had to handle expiring holds, conflicting seat requests, stale confirmations, undo ownership, performance switching, and accessibility without letting human and agent state diverge. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes an application's real domain model—not when it recreates screen clicking with different syntax. We also learned that accessibility and agent usability reinforce each other. HOUSELIGHTS uses a real ARIA grid, keyboard navigation, live-region announcements, reduced-motion support, and state indicators that do not rely on color alone. The same explicit structure that helps assistive technology also gives agents a safer and more understandable interface. What's next HOUSELIGHTS is currently a client-side interactive simulation. A production version would connect the tool surface to authoritative inventory, atomic server-side seat locks, persistent sessions, idempotent checkout, and a real payment provider. The larger idea extends beyond ticketing: agents should handle structured comparison and reversible preparation while people retain informed authority over consequential actions. The project taught me how to design agent tools around a real domain model while keeping consequential actions visible, reversible, and under human control. title: Happy Coffee: The Agent-Native Data Developer Portal
pitch: Turning a data portal into an agent-native workspace: agents explore, query, test, and stage data products through WebMCP while developers see every result, lineage, and run in real time.
about_excerpt: Turning a data portal into an agent-native workspace: agents explore, query, test, and stage data products through WebMCP while developers see every result, lineage, and run in real time. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Dataset details Costs Development Quality checks Home page Sources Inspiration Data developers spend too much time moving between catalog pages, lineage graphs, SQL editors, quality dashboards, and pipeline runs. This project shows what changes when an agent can use a data developer portal directly - not by guessing from the UI, but through explicit WebMCP tools. Happy Coffee is built around the idea that the agent does the routine development work while people can see, understand, and control the outcome. What it does Happy Coffee is an agent-native data developer portal powered by WebMCP. It gives AI agents structured tools to understand and operate the portal without relying on screenshots, DOM scraping, or UI automation. An agent can: discover the portal’s capabilities and safeguards; search datasets, sources, quality checks, pipeline runs, logs, lineage, and costs; inspect schemas and preview bounded samples of data; open a browser-local DuckDB workspace and write or run SQL; create temporary derived tables and data-quality checks; prepare a table for publication with metadata, field descriptions, transformations, schedule, and attached quality checks. At the same time, the portal gives people visual feedback for every meaningful step. They can inspect the source data, review the SQL, see result grids, follow lineage, understand quality-check failures, and observe mocked staging runs. On critical decisions, such as publishing a table to production, the agent is not doing it automatically. A human must intentionally review and approve it. How we built it Happy Coffee is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. The development experience runs on DuckDB-Wasm inside the browser. Generated catalog data is loaded into the happy_coffee schema, while temporary derived data is created in a local workspace schema. This means the SQL experience is immediate, portable, and does not require a server-side database. The portal registers structured tools through document.modelContext , and each tool returns a versioned contract with stable IDs, bounded data previews, navigation context, and explicit safeguards. This lets an agent reason about the portal as an application—not as a collection of pixels. The app is deployed on Cloudflare Pages. Every merge to main produces a new production deployment, and pull requests receive preview deployments. It was tempting to expose one more tool that would publish a table automatically, for example. Instead, we made publishing a deliberate boundary. The agent can do all preparatory work, but it cannot cross the final line without a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a portal that an agent can understand through structured capabilities rather than visual inference. We made the human-agent experience observable: the agent acts, while the portal explains and visualizes the work. We designed a complete development arc—from catalog discovery to SQL, quality checks, publishing preparation, and mocked execution. We added data-integrity guarantees specifically because agent workflows need trustworthy relationships, not merely realistic-looking data. We kept DuckDB-Wasm local to the browser, making the SQL workspace fast, private, and easy to deploy. We established a meaningful safety boundary: agents can prepare a publishable table, but people retain the final publishing decision. What we learned We learned that agent-native UX is not about adding a chat box to an existing product. The real work is deciding what an agent should know, what it should be able to change, what context it needs to make safe decisions, and how the human can verify the result without reading a wall of tool output. We also learned that visual feedback is not a fallback for agents - it is the collaboration layer for people. Sample rows, lineage graphs, quality cards, result tables, and run logs turn invisible agent actions into something a developer can inspect, challenge, and trust. Finally, we learned that safe autonomy is a design advantage. The human publish step does not weaken the agent experience; it makes the experience credible. What's next for Happy Coffee: The Agent-Native Data Developer Portal Next, we want to make the collaboration model even richer: reusable agent workflows for common data-development tasks; visual explanations for query plans and quality-check failures; richer staging and production simulation; shared ephemeral workspaces for team review; better ways to compare an agent’s proposed data product against existing catalog assets. title: VERROCCHIO
pitch: A WebMCP workshop that preserves missing proof, the next action, and human checkpoints for interrupted solo builders.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workshop that preserves missing proof, the next action, and human checkpoints for interrupted solo builders. Like Comment Story Updates What VERROCCHIO does VERROCCHIO is a WebMCP workshop for time-constrained solo builders whose projects are repeatedly interrupted. It keeps the next action, missing proof, active work, and human checkpoints together so an AI can help without turning an unverified claim into “done.” The browser exposes four bounded, state-aware WebMCP tools: inspect_workshop reads the live mission, missing proof (MANCA), active work, and the next bounded action. call_fermo stops when evidence, scope, safety, or intent is ambiguous. propose_workshop_draft validates and returns an unsigned plan that waits for human FIRMA. return_work_result records a structured CLAIMED result without marking its evidence verified. Human-only actions—FIRMA approval, evidence verification, resume, publication, and final submission—are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A person and an agent must act on the same live project state. With ordinary DOM automation, an agent has to rediscover controls and infer whether visible text is a claim, approval, or proof. WebMCP gives the page an explicit contract and exposes only the transitions the agent is allowed to perform at that moment. The result is not simply fewer clicks. It is a clearer division of responsibility: the agent can inspect, draft, stop, and return bounded work; the human retains purpose, approval, evidence judgment, publication, and submission. Better experience for interrupted solo work A solo builder working around a full-time job carries coordination that a conventional team would normally distribute: rules, next actions, interruption recovery, evidence review, and stops before irreversible actions. VERROCCHIO makes that coordination visible and resumable. The core flow is: MANCA → unsigned plan → human FIRMA → bounded work → CLAIMED → human VERIFIED or CHANGES_REQUESTED After an interruption, the builder can reopen the workshop and see what is still missing, what is active, and exactly where human attention is required. What people and agents can now do together The agent works directly with structured browser state instead of guessing from screenshots or page text. It can propose the smallest valid next plan, detect ambiguity, and return a result with checks, evidence references, and remaining risk. The human can adopt or reject that plan and verify the claim without surrendering the decisions that matter. Implementation VERROCCHIO is a React and Vite application with browser-local persistence. Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool ; their availability changes with workshop phase. Every mutation requires the state version returned by inspection and an idempotency key. Stale state is rejected, identical retries reuse the existing receipt, and conflicting reuse fails. The current ChatGPT or Codex host supplies reasoning, so the app does not require its own OpenAI API key. Evidence Public live app: https://verrocchio-workshop.honabochi.chatgpt.site/ Public source and MIT license: https://github.com/honabochi/verrocchio-public Frozen release: webmcp-submission-2026-09-03 at revision 439161e Automated test suite: 121 passing tests Hosted evaluation: seven fixed natural-language cases plus two DOM baselines Demo: a 70-second public YouTube video with audio The WebMCP-versus-DOM evaluation showed fewer actions for the tested stop and unsigned-plan paths (2 versus 3, and 2 versus 4). Recorded elapsed time was not faster, so no speed claim is made. Existing-project disclosure The July 19 baseline 91315a1 already contained the local workshop, MANCA proof gates, work packets, and human FIRMA/FERMO controls. Beginning with challenge-period commit 0176211 on August 27, the project added the four native WebMCP tools, state-aware availability, versioned and idempotent mutations, unsigned plans, CLAIMED results that cannot close proof, evaluation receipts, and the hosted judge path. Comparison: https://github.com/honabochi/verrocchio-public/compare/91315a120059cae3b9eb68566c81d5c8d87fd903...webmcp-submission-2026-09-03 Known limitations Persistence is browser-local rather than synchronized across devices. Human-only controls are a workflow boundary, not actor authentication. The keyless path depends on a WebMCP-capable host. title: FLINT AgentGate
pitch: FLINT AgentGate gives enterprises a verified agent identity registry, a screened MCP tool registry, and real-time gateway controls for authorization, monitoring, and revocation.
about_excerpt: FLINT AgentGate gives enterprises a verified agent identity registry, a screened MCP tool registry, and real-time gateway controls for authorization, monitoring, and revocation. Like Comment Story Updates FLINT AgentGate Dynamic Agent Fleet Observation and Command/Control (C2) Precise Version Assessment Agent/Tool Identity Registry and Passport Semantic Identity Registry Versioned Authority Gateway Allow and Block Signed and Exportable Machine Readable Evidence High Risk Tool Blocked FLINT AgentGate Community Inspiration WebMCP gives agents a direct way to discover and use browser capabilities. That improves the experience over asking an agent to interpret a visual interface, but enterprises still need to answer four questions before a capability becomes available: Which agent is acting? Who authorized it? Which exact tool version may it use? Why was this request allowed or blocked? FLINT AgentGate began with a simple requirement from a CISO colleague: an agent should receive a tool only when its current identity, principal authority, approved tool version, and request context agree. We built AgentGate Community as a public reference implementation that builders can clone, inspect, and challenge without an account or API key. It also reports what it can observe. Connected surfaces, attribution confidence, and known blind spots stay visible throughout the demo. What it does AgentGate connects tool assessment, agent identity, semantic authority, runtime policy, and signed evidence in one browser session. Assess one exact tool version. A builder submits publisher metadata, capabilities, destinations, data classes, behavior annotations, JSON Schema, and tool instructions. A bounded deterministic scanner checks the declaration for prompt injection, destructive behavior, excessive access, ambiguous schemas, unrestricted outbound access, missing controls, and toxic combinations. AgentGate computes a canonical SHA-256 artifact digest without fetching or executing the submitted tool. Issue a Community Tool Passport. A passing artifact receives a locally signed credential bound to its exact version, digest, and assessment. The credential uses an ephemeral ECDSA P-256 key and is labeled community-self-attested . It proves local payload integrity for the demo. It is not a FLINT Stamp or a claim that FLINT verified the publisher. Bind identity and semantic authority. The Identity Registry keeps 4 records separate: CAN: What the agent build claims it can do. MAY: What the named principal authorizes. TOOL: What the assessed tool version permits. MAY NOW: The narrow assignment that survives the current intersection. Govern the capability through WebMCP. AgentGate feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and registers only a currently eligible capability. Browsers without native WebMCP receive a labeled operator fallback that calls the same Trust Provider and policy evaluator. Every invocation rechecks identity, passport integrity, assignment, action, resource, destination, data class, side effects, purpose, expiry, and revocation. Produce signed decision evidence. An aligned request returns ALLOW . Purpose drift, stale authority, revocation, or another policy failure returns BLOCK . Each decision produces a signed, version-bound record with a plain-language reason, technical reason codes, policy fingerprints, and copy or JSON download controls. The overview adds a moving fleet visualization. Operators can inspect an agent's identity state, tool, scope, and mandate while viewing coverage only for named, connected demo surfaces. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns authorized capability into a structured agent experience. A human operator defines the agent, principal, mandate, and permitted resources. The agent discovers only the tool that survives those controls. The Gateway evaluates the request before execution, and the operator receives evidence tied to the exact versions that governed the decision. This creates a workflow that was difficult to maintain with visual automation or static tool configuration. The human sets authority in one place. The agent receives a machine-readable capability instead of guessing through a UI. The security team can reconstruct what happened without correlating unrelated logs. WebMCP provides the capability surface. AgentGate makes exposure conditional based on current authorization. How we built it AgentGate Community is a browser-session React and TypeScript application built with Vite. Zod validates versioned agentgate.v0 contracts at each boundary. JSON Schema describes tool inputs. The Web Crypto API generates ephemeral ECDSA P-256 keys and verifies signed credentials. Canonical serialization produces stable SHA-256 artifact and policy fingerprints. A replaceable ScannerAdapter normalizes deterministic findings into a stable assessment contract. A separate TrustProvider owns assessment, credential issuance, identity resolution, assignment, runtime decisions, revocation, and evidence. This keeps the public contracts stable if an organization later replaces the local provider with a managed trust service. The native WebMCP adapter and visible browser fallback call the same evaluator. Identity, authority, tool version, and assignment are resolved again at invocation time instead of being trusted from an earlier screen transition. We studied the public Snyk Agent Scan and Visa Vulnerability Agentic Harness projects for risk categories, staged evidence, and deterministic gates. Their code is not vendored into this repository. OpenAI Codex served as an engineering and product partner. We used it to challenge the authorization model, trace policy paths, implement the React and TypeScript application, write tests, run security and novice-usability reviews, improve the documentation, and produce the demo assets. The application does not use an LLM to override authorization decisions. Challenges Keeping the assurance boundary honest A local signature can reveal later changes, but it cannot establish organizational trust. We encoded that distinction in the credential schema, verification result, interface copy, tests, and README. Preventing capability from becoming permission Builder declarations are untrusted inputs. Agent capability, principal authority, tool semantics, and assignment remain separate versioned records. Directional subset checks reject an assignment that expands an upstream envelope. Adding semantic intent safely Purpose drift needs more than exact string matching. AgentGate allows semantic analysis to escalate a deterministic ALLOW to REVIEW or BLOCK. It cannot convert a deterministic denial into ALLOW, and a provider error fails closed. Supporting an emerging browser standard Native WebMCP availability varies by client. The product identifies the active surface and preserves one policy path across native registration and the operator fallback. Making agent identity understandable The model is advanced, so we tested the workflow as a novice. We added a guided safe path, prefilled examples, prerequisite states, plain-language verdicts, a glossary, a How it works view, transient fleet inspectors, and visible next actions. What we learned Conditional tool exposure should be an output of authorization. Every authority-bearing record needs an issuer, version, status, validity window, and relationship to the evidence used at decision time. We also learned that explicit limits improve security evidence. Named observation surfaces and visible blind spots give an operator something concrete to evaluate. The final lesson was about user experience. A correct policy decision still needs a readable explanation, a portable record, and a clear next action. Accomplishments AgentGate demonstrates the complete path from exact-version assessment through Tool Passport issuance, identity registration, semantic authority, assignment, conditional WebMCP exposure, ALLOW, signed evidence, mandate-drift BLOCK, authority revision, revocation, and risky-tool rejection. The repository is MIT licensed and runs without a FLINT account, database, scanner credential, or production signing key. The release gate passes its source scan, TypeScript validation, production build, dependency audit with 0 production vulnerabilities, and 57 automated tests covering contracts, scanner failures, signature tampering, authority expansion, stale assignments, semantic drift, browser fallback behavior, evidence integrity, and revocation. What's next AgentGate Community will remain the cloneable reference implementation. FLINT Command will provide managed organizational identity, FLINT-controlled Stamp issuance, continuous discovery and reassessment, centralized monitoring, evidence retention, enterprise policy administration, response controls, and network intelligence. The public contracts and deterministic enforcement mechanics give builders an integration path while managed trust remains an enterprise service. Try FLINT AgentGate View the pub

title: Giffium
pitch: Giffium is a tool to generate animated code snippets that highlight the diff between two different snippets. The goal is to generate sharable GIFs and/or MP4s in a similar vein to Carbon or Ray.so.
about_excerpt: Giffium is a tool to generate animated code snippets that highlight the diff between two different snippets. The goal is to generate sharable GIFs and/or MP4s in a similar vein to Carbon or Ray.so. Like Comment Story Updates The Giffium Home Page GIF The result of generating a GIF Inspiration Giffium takes its inspiration from tools like carbon.now.sh and ray.so. The goal is to make socially sharable diffs instead of static code snippets. Adding WebMCP support seemed like a good idea to give agents access to its functionality without having to build a CLI tool from scratch. What it does Giffium takes in 2 code snippets and animates them to and from each other using shiki-magic-move. The result is captured into a set of frames that we build a GIF from. There is the option to create an MP4 file as well for smoother animation compared to a GIF. The WebMCP tool allows the agent to generate a gif of a diff. It also exposes a separate tool to modify the styling such as font, font size, syntax highlighting theme, and background color. How wIbuilt it Giffium was originally built for the SolidJS hackathon 2024 before AI was as capable as it is now. So it was hand-coded. It won that year of the hackathon. The core functionality is due to shiki-magic-move by antfu. However, we still needed to build out the entire configuration layer as well as the building of the GIF and MP4 files. The WebMCP support was fairly simple to add for the WebMCP challenge after using OpenSpec to explore the WebMCP spec and documentation. Challenges we ran into Capturing shiki-magic-move is not as simple as expected. This is because it is animating raw DOM elements. So, we needed to use RequestAnimationFrame to capture the HTML contents into an off-screen canvas and capture that into individual frames. Some other challenges involve font space and element offsets. The fonts are loaded in from Google Fonts and the WebMCP tool for generating the GIF was not giving the font enough time to download which broke the layout and spacing of elements. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Adding MP4 support using ffmpeg-wasm was a fun experiment that turned out well. The trickiest part was making sure we didn't blow up the bundle size by including it by default. Giving the user the option to download it and handling that process was a good UX problem to solve. What I learned Implementing WebMCP is much more straight-forward than a full proper MCP server and testing is as simple as asking ChatGPT Desktop to validate all of the tools. What's next for Giffium It might be nice to implement some loop metadata configuration since the GIF spec supports assigning X amount of loops and stopping at the end, as an example. This will be tricky since the library being used is modern-gif which doesn't have support for loop metadata, yet. I might also consider packaging the tool's functionality into a CLI.  Project Story 

 I was searching for a car on a local second-hand marketplace, and tbh, it is kind of an awful experience. 

 There are overwhelmingly many filters, but somehow they are still not the right ones. I kept wishing I could just filter and sort listings using my own custom criteria. Something like: 

 s c o r e = 0.5 × m i l e a g e + 0.3 × p r i c e + 0.2 × y e a r 

 Or really anything else I care about at that particular moment. 

 Reading listing descriptions is also tiresome. It requires a surprising amount of focus and attention, especially when you have dozens of tabs open. Comparing cars isn't easy either. And then, once you finally have a shortlist, you still need to message sellers, ask the same questions, negotiate, keep track of replies, etc. 

 While struggling through all of that, I saw an ad about the WebMCP hackathon which felt completely unrelated at the moment. 

 At first I didn't really understand what WebMCP was or how it worked. But when I looked through the examples, it clicked, and I was basically like: "Hell, I wish marketplaces had that" 

 And here I am with this project. 

 I built Relay as a second-hand marketplace where the website stays a normal website, but an external agent can actually work with it: search and read listings, create completely custom filters and rankings, compare items, save them into collections, message sellers, and make offers. 

 One of the interesting challenges was making the agent feel like part of the marketplace rather than some separate chatbot bolted onto it. The agent works with the same interface the user sees, and its actions are reflected back in the UI. Building that also made me understand WebMCP much better. Before the hackathon it felt pretty abstract; after actually using it, the idea of giving agents structured access to normal websites suddenly feels very natural. 

 Anyway, thanks for organizing this! It was really fun to build and experiment with.

title: ShopMate — Agent-Native Shopping with WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native e-commerce experience where AI agents discover products, compare options, check stock, and manage carts through browser-native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native e-commerce experience where AI agents discover products, compare options, check stock, and manage carts through browser-native WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration## Inspiration 

 Traditional e-commerce websites are designed primarily for humans. Users have to search through pages, apply filters, compare products, check availability, and manually manage their carts. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: 

 What if an AI agent could interact with an e-commerce website through structured, browser-native tools instead of relying on brittle UI automation? 

 That question led us to build ShopMate , an agent-native shopping experience powered by WebMCP. 

 What we built 

 ShopMate exposes the core capabilities of an e-commerce application as WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . 

 The application currently exposes 10 tools : 

 
 search_products 
 filter_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 check_stock 
 calculate_cart_total 
 add_to_cart 
 remove_from_cart 
 update_cart 
 build_bundle 
 

 Read-only operations can be performed autonomously, while state-changing operations require human approval. 

 This creates a human-in-the-loop shopping experience where an agent can perform useful work while the user remains in control of consequential actions. 

 For example, an agent can: 

 
 Search for laptops. 
 Filter them by price, brand, category, or stock. 
 Retrieve detailed specifications. 
 Compare multiple products. 
 Check inventory. 
 Ask the user for approval. 
 Add the selected product to the cart. 
 Calculate the resulting cart total. 
 

 How we built it 

 ShopMate was built with: 

 
 Next.js 16 
 React 19 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 React Context for application state 
 Browser-native WebMCP APIs through document.modelContext 
 

 A major part of the implementation was making WebMCP registration reliable inside React's rendering lifecycle. 

 We designed the registration system to be idempotent so that React re-renders and Strict Mode do not create duplicate tool registrations. 

 We also added a diagnostics and activity system so that WebMCP availability, registered tools, tool changes, and agent activity can be observed directly inside the application. 

 Challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was that WebMCP registration interacts with the React lifecycle in ways that are easy to get wrong. 

 Our initial browser implementation encountered a Maximum update depth exceeded error. The underlying problem was not duplicate WebMCP registration itself, but the interaction between registration, diagnostics state updates, effects, and event listeners. 

 We investigated the lifecycle, added dedicated React lifecycle tests, and fixed the ownership of the WebMCP toolchange listener. We also eliminated a race involving the approval state reference. 

 Another interesting issue was the browser-generated toolchange event during initial registration. Since the browser emits a tool-change event for each registered tool, registering 10 tools produced unnecessary activity-panel noise. We kept the listener but suppressed those expected initialization events and retained logging for genuine post-registration tool changes. 

 What we learned 

 This project taught us that making an application "agent-compatible" is more than exposing a list of functions. 

 The tools need: 

 
 Clear schemas and descriptions. 
 Predictable inputs and outputs. 
 Safe boundaries around state-changing actions. 
 Idempotent registration. 
 Correct lifecycle management. 
 Human approval for consequential actions. 
 Observability so developers can understand what the agent is doing. 
 

 We also learned how important it is to test both the tool layer and the actual React/browser lifecycle. Our standalone WebMCP tests passed while the real browser initially exposed a lifecycle issue, which led us to add dedicated React and Strict Mode tests. 

 Final result 

 ShopMate now exposes all 10 intended WebMCP tools, supports human approval for cart mutations, and has automated tests covering registration, discovery, execution, approval, diagnostics, Strict Mode behavior, and listener lifecycle. 

 The project demonstrates how existing web applications can evolve from interfaces that humans click into interfaces that AI agents can understand and operate through structured browser-native capabilities .
