title: AgentCut : WebMCP Image & Video Editor
pitch: AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that lets AI agents edit real creative projects through WebMCP - from text and styling to keyframes, motion, and rendered video export.
about_excerpt: AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that lets AI agents edit real creative projects through WebMCP - from text and styling to keyframes, motion, and rendered video export. Like Comment Story Updates AgentCut Home Page Codex WebMCP Chrome WebMcp Inspiration I have basic video editing skills things like splitting clips, adding text, and simple transitions but more advanced editing such as keyframes, motion, and text animation always felt overwhelming. When I learned about WebMCP, I saw an opportunity to change that. Instead of learning every advanced control myself, I could build an editor that exposes those capabilities as structured tools and let an AI agent use them for me. That became the idea behind AgentCut: a lightweight image and video editor where I can describe the result I want, and the agent can use advanced editing features like keyframes, animation, typography, and motion through WebMCP. In practice, it helped me go from using only basic editing tools to creating edits that previously felt like “pro-level” work. What it does AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that can be controlled manually or by an external AI agent through WebMCP. The editor supports things like: image adjustments and aspect ratios multiple text layers and curated fonts video trimming and reframing text timing text animation with keyframes video pan and zoom keyframes undo and redo rendered image and video export The difference is that these editing capabilities are also exposed as structured WebMCP tools, so an agent can inspect the project and perform edits from natural-language instructions. How we built it AgentCut is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, HTML Canvas, MediaRecorder, and browser media APIs. The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same project state. This means an edit made by the agent immediately appears in the editor and can still be changed manually. AgentCut exposes 29 WebMCP tools covering image editing, video editing, text, keyframes, project inspection, undo/redo, and export. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making agent edits reliable rather than just automating clicks. For example, when an agent changes only the font or size of one text layer, every other property needs to remain untouched. Smooth keyframe playback was another challenge. Early animation felt choppy, so the preview was changed to use frame-synchronized video timing. Video export was also difficult. AgentCut originally downloaded only the source file, but it now renders the actual edited composition and exports the result as MP4 or WebM depending on browser support. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am most proud that AgentCut lets someone like me use editing features that previously felt too advanced. In my demo, I could simply ask the agent to create a travel title, animate only one text layer, add a cinematic push-in, and change the aspect ratio. The agent translated those requests into structured edits and keyframes. The project now has: 29 WebMCP tools independent text layers fonts and styling text and video keyframes smooth animation real rendered video export 97 automated tests covering the editor and WebMCP workflows What we learned The biggest lesson was that giving an AI access to a webpage is not the same as giving it access to the product. WebMCP lets a website expose meaningful capabilities directly to an agent. Instead of trying to visually find and click controls, the agent can work with structured project state and editing actions. I also learned that this can make advanced software much more approachable. The user can focus on describing the result instead of learning every control first. What's next for AgentCut Next I would expand AgentCut with more advanced creative capabilities while keeping the same agent-first approach. Possible additions include: easing and richer animation controls transitions audio editing more typography controls reusable styles and presets multi-clip compositions The goal is to keep the editor simple for humans while exposing increasingly powerful creative tools to AI agents through WebMCP. title: CoRep
pitch: CoRep is a local-first training log that publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools. Your AI coach doesn't advise from outside the app — it operates the same plan you do. Every change signed.
about_excerpt: CoRep is a local-first training log that publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools. Your AI coach doesn't advise from outside the app — it operates the same plan you do. Every change signed. Like Comment Story Updates CoRep You and your AI agent build the plan together! plan page Edit Logging an exercise Timer Badges! Mobile view Every change is logged Mobile friendly Bring it to the gym Skip or add time at any time The gap I already had an AI fitness coach. It worked like everyone's does: I'd describe my training week to a chat window, it would give me thoughtful advice, and then I would switch to a different app and type that advice in by hand. The advice was good. The arrangement was absurd. My coach could reason about my knee but couldn't see that I'd already dropped the weight on Tuesday. I was the integration layer — a human clipboard between two systems that both wanted the same data. I'd actually tried to fix this before. The app CoRep grew out of had an MCP server bolted onto its Python backend, so my coach could read the database and write to it. It helped, and it also taught me why it wasn't enough: the agent was talking to my database , not to my app . It could change a number, but it couldn't put that number in front of me. I'd find out what it had done later, if I happened to look. WebMCP inverts that, and the inversion is the whole project. What it does CoRep is a training log with no server and no account — every user's data lives in their own browser. It publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools , so an agent on the page operates the same application you do. Not a copy of your plan. Not a screenshot. When the agent raises a weight, it calls the same function your own tap on "Edit" calls, against the same data, and you watch the result land. Three things fall out of that, and they're the parts I'd point a judge at: Every change is signed Writes record who made them and why. The plan view shows both parties in one timeline: Coach 10→15 lbs · shoulders felt strong, small bump You 15→25 lbs · Edited in the plan editor Neither of us is the source of truth. This is the single feature I'd keep if I had to throw the rest away. It's what makes it safe to let an agent act rather than only suggest — you can always see what it did, why it thought so, and overrule it. The nice accident: the app I forked already had an edited_by field and a per-field edit history, built for that old server-side coach. I'd designed the substrate for this without knowing it. Turning it into a shared, two-party document was mostly a matter of letting the second party in. The agent moves the interface, not just the data Four tools exist purely to drive the UI: fitness_navigate , fitness_start_session , fitness_open_plan_editor , fitness_highlight_exercise . So when the agent changes an exercise, the app switches to the plan tab, scrolls to that exercise, and flashes it. When you say you're ready to train, it opens the guided session flow and you're looking at set one. The agent can say "this one" and have you actually be looking at the thing. fitness_open_plan_editor is my favourite of the four because it runs the other direction: it's the agent handing the decision back , opening a blank editor instead of making a choice that isn't its to make. Destructive actions stop and ask delete_plan , delete_exercise and delete_workout don't delete anything. They park the tool call and render a confirmation card in the app showing exactly what's about to go. You tap; the agent is told what you chose. Declining is a normal outcome it handles, and an unanswered prompt counts as "no" after a minute. I built this in the app's own UI rather than leaning on the spec's requestUserInteraction() , partly because that surface is still in flux, and partly because doing it myself meant the confirmation could name the specific plan and its phase count instead of being a generic browser prompt. Why WebMCP is the right primitive here Coaching is a case where an agent and a person genuinely need to co-own one artifact. A training plan is a living document. It changes because your knee hurt on Tuesday, because the gym was out of 25s, because a set that was brutal last month is easy now. Some of those edits you want to make yourself in three seconds. Some you want to talk through. Both kinds have to land in the same place or the plan stops being true. Every other arrangement I tried forces a choice: either the agent owns the plan and you file requests with it, or you own the plan and the agent narrates from outside. WebMCP is the first primitive that let me refuse the choice. What's newly possible: not "an AI that writes you a workout" — that's been available for years and it isn't interesting. It's a plan with two editors and one history , where the reasoning behind every change is attached to the change and visible to both parties. That's a different relationship, and it's one the browser had no way to express until tools could live in the page. How I built it Vite + React + TypeScript + CSS Modules. No backend, no state library, no router. Dependencies: React, Lucide icons, and the WebMCP polyfill. Porting a backend into the browser The original was FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + SQLite. Making it multi-user meant making it zero -user: no server at all, one versioned JSON document in localStorage . The domain layer ported over almost mechanically, because it had been written framework-free — rules.py , badges.py and service.py became rules.ts , badges.ts and store.ts . The Python test suite came with it. src/lib/__tests__/ holds 33 tests carried over from pytest, and having a known-green oracle was worth more than the time it cost, because of this: Python's date.weekday() is Monday=0. JavaScript's getDay() is Sunday=0. The schedule lookup tables were indexed the Python way. Get this wrong and every streak, completion rate and calendar cell silently shifts by one day — nothing crashes, the numbers are just quietly false. The ported tests caught it on the first run. I'd have shipped it otherwise. One choke point makes everything live The load-bearing decision: db.write() is the only way anything in the app changes, and it notifies subscribers. Every data hook subscribes. That's the entire mechanism behind the demo. An agent calls log_workout , and the streak, the calendar, the stat tiles and the badge wall all update instantly — no polling, no refresh, and no separate code path for agent-driven changes. Agent writes and human writes are indistinguishable to the UI, which is exactly the property I wanted. Registering 31 tools Worth passing on to anyone else building this: register your tools in parallel. My first version awaited each registerTool() in a loop. It took several seconds to get through the set, because the implementation flushes the tool list between calls. An agent connecting during that window would see a partial toolset — some tools present, some missing, no error anywhere. I only noticed because I queried getTools() while debugging and got 11 back instead of 31. Promise.allSettled over the whole array lets the flushes coalesce. Same 31 tools, 3 milliseconds . I also hit the spec moving underneath me: the W3C draft relocated the getter from Navigator to Document in May 2026. The app reads whichever exists: const mc = document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext Tool descriptions are written for an agent audience, not a changelog. They state units (pounds, centimetres, seconds), name which tool to call first to get an id, and give judgement guidance — update_exercise asks for a reason phrased for the user , because that text is what shows up next to their exercise. The hardest constraint was the one nobody grades directly I decided early that CoRep had to be completely usable with no agent connected. The agent should be an amplifier, never a dependency. This turned out to be the biggest chunk of work in the whole project, for a reason I didn't see coming: in the original app, plans could only be created by the AI. Plan creation existed solely as an MCP tool. There was no UI for it, because there had never needed to be one — I was the only user and I had the coach. So "works without an agent" meant building the feature an agent-only app never needed: a full manual plan editor. Phases, exercises, reordering, weekday scheduling, the lot. I'm glad the constraint forced it. An app that collapses when the agent disconnects isn't demonstrating collaboration, it's demonstrating dependence. And the editor made the attribution feature real — before it, every edit in the history said "Coach", and there was nothing to contrast against. The agent indicator says all this out loud, too. With no WebMCP available it reads: "WebMCP is not available in this browser, so no agent can connect. Everything in the app still works." title: Brief — Research with your agent
pitch: Brief is a shared evidence board for you and ChatGPT — WebMCP tools add claims, sources, and contradiction flags on the same live brief, so research becomes co-presence instead of a chat dump.
about_excerpt:
Brief is a shared evidence board for you and ChatGPT — WebMCP tools add claims, sources, and contradiction flags on the same live brief, so research becomes co-presence instead of a chat dump.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Chat is a terrible place to hold research. Claims, sources, and caveats scroll away into mush. We wanted a board where a person and ChatGPT could see the same brief — not a summary pasted back into the thread, but a living evidence map they edit together. 

 WebMCP makes that possible: the site exposes tools to add claims, link sources, flag contradictions, and export, on the page you’re already looking at. 

 What it does 

 Brief is an agent-native evidence board: 

 
 Set a research question and title 
 Add claims with stance (supports / neutral / disputes) and confidence 
 Attach sources with snippets and link them to claims 
 Flag contradictions and pin notes 
 Summarize and export the brief 
 Use a full human UI or ChatGPT via WebMCP tools on the same Zustand store 
 Inspect tools + activity feed; run ?demo=1 for the happy path 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite + React + TypeScript SPA ( base: '/brief-webmcp/' ) 
 Zustand shared store for UI and WebMCP execute handlers 
 18 site tools with readOnlyHint on reads; clear_board / export_brief as side effects 
 Feature-detect document.modelContext → navigator.modelContext (top-level page) 
 MIT, static GitHub Pages deploy — Built with Codex 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping agent writes and human edits in lockstep; marking consequential tools correctly; designing a board that’s scannable in a <3 minute demo without becoming a toy. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A third WebMCP submission in a new lane (research, not shopping or canvas): claim→source→flag loops, summarize/export, and a judge-friendly tools panel. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP’s superpower is co-presence. Research needs shared structure more than another chat answer — Brief treats the agent as a colleague on the board, not a ghostwriter in the sidebar. 

 What's next for Brief — Research with your agent 

 Real source fetch/preview, citation styles, multiplayer presence, and deeper ChatGPT desktop testing.

about_excerpt: Hide-and-seek vs a real AI agent. You see everything, it senses almost nothing, but rewrites its own hunting code mid-chase. Survive 3 minutes. And mind a clever model as it may uncover hidden depths. Like Comment Story Updates Start screen The game board Oh noes! The agent got to you The agent rewriting its own hunter code Inspiration I wanted a game where an AI agent plays against you in real time, not turn-based. The challenge is that some agents are fast, some are slow. My fix was to have the seeker run on a built-in bot. The agent wins by rewriting that bot's code during the match using tools exposed via WebMCP. A simple model can let the bot do the work. A smart model writes better and better versions, making intelligence win, not speed. There might also be secrets in this game, revealed only by high model intelligence ;) For the look, I wanted a dark 2D world made of light, where you, the hider, is a light too. What it does You hide, the agent seeks. You see everything, but the agent only gets small sensor readings once per second and decides where to walk. Everything you do costs energy, makes noise, or leaves scent. The goal is to survive three minutes! How we built it Plain js with no dependencies with real 2D raytracing on canvas. The engine holds all the rules, and both the human and the agent play through it. The agent gets the full rulebook through a WebMCP tool, so there is nothing to paste into a prompt. Sound is generated with ElevenLabs. Challenges I ran into The agent should be a blind player, but still get enough information to improve itself. Every mechanic had to fit into small sensor readings, but without bloating the context too much. Too fast or slow agents. Actions cost points and senses tick once per second. Speed buys nothing, better code buys everything. Untrusted code. The agent's bot code runs in a tiny, safe API with hard limits, and every new version is shown on screen. What I learned Don't give an agent a joystick, but instead a body and a reason to rewrite itself.  Centre Remix is a single-page leasing board for Harbour Place, a fictional shopping centre in Millers Reach, NSW. Australian centres already run near full occupancy, so the real job is remix (who should replace whom), not filling empty shops. 

 WebMCP is the fit because the agent should act on the same board the leasing manager is staring at, not a chatbot bolted onto a brochure. title: SupplyMesh
pitch: A map-first WebMCP operations console where agents analyze logistics disruptions, humans retain authority over critical decisions, and every executed recovery is independently verified.
about_excerpt: A map-first WebMCP operations console where agents analyze logistics disruptions, humans retain authority over critical decisions, and every executed recovery is independently verified. Like Comment Story Updates Close-Up view of a truck SupplyMesh on Codex SupplyMesh: Recover the network. Protect the driver. Prove every decision. Inspiration Supply chains do not fail in neat database rows. They fail in the physical world: a truck approaches a low bridge, a road closes, severe weather reaches an active corridor, or a delivery schedule starts competing with a driver’s rest window. Most fleet dashboards can show that something is wrong, but resolving the disruption still requires a dispatcher to manually inspect vehicles, routes, cargo, timing constraints, and safety policies across multiple systems. We built SupplyMesh around a simple idea: An AI agent should help recover the operation without turning the driver into another variable to optimize. Driver rest, vehicle clearance, cargo continuity, and road safety are not soft scores that can be traded away for a faster ETA—they are hard operational boundaries. The agent analyzes the situation and prepares a response, but a human dispatcher retains absolute authority over critical changes. Our first prototype was closer to a conventional fleet dashboard with a small set of read-only tools. It worked, but it did not demonstrate why WebMCP was necessary. We redesigned the project around a complete disruption-recovery workflow that both the human and the agent could understand through the exact same visible application state. What it does The main scenario begins before Unit 211 leaves Toledo. Its assigned route contains a 3.90 m clearance restriction. The vehicle itself is 3.80 m high, but the operator requires an additional 0.20 m safety buffer: 3.80 m vehicle height + 0.20 m operator safety buffer = 4.00 m required clearance Result: 4.00 m required > 3.90 m available (Route rejected) Through WebMCP, the agent inspects the authoritative vehicle, route, cargo, incident, and timing state. It compares the current route with a verified alternative, checks the driver’s remaining operating window, preserves cargo assignments, and stages a recovery plan. What the agent cannot do There is no approval tool. The agent cannot weaken the safety buffer, ignore the rest window, or authorize its own proposal. It can only request human review. When the dispatcher approves the exact plan in the visible interface, SupplyMesh binds that approval to the plan fingerprint and the current scenario revision. Only then does recovery_plan_execute appear dynamically as an available WebMCP capability. Once authorized, the agent can: Execute the exact approved route change. Verify the resulting state independently. Confirm that the clearance policy, rest window, and cargo continuity still pass. Prove that the route was changed only once. Produce a stable, auditable receipt. If the vehicle, route, constraints, or scenario revision change after approval, the authorization invalidates immediately and the execution capability disappears. SupplyMesh also includes a driver-first rest opportunity planner. Instead of treating spare delivery time as extra productivity, it identifies opportunities to give the driver more rest while remaining within delivery tolerance. The agent compares available options, but only a human can schedule or remove the stop. How we built it SupplyMesh is built with: Frontend & Core: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Bun State Management: Zustand for shared application state Mapping & Visualization: Leaflet (operational map) and Three.js (close-range volumetric vehicles) Testing & Verification: Playwright and Vitest for browser and domain validation Agent Integration: Native WebMCP tools The visible UI and the WebMCP tools share the exact same domain operations. This prevents the agent from modifying a hidden copy of the state that disagrees with what the dispatcher sees. The recovery tool surface adapts to the workflow: tools for comparing or staging a plan are available early, while execution capabilities only mount after valid human approval. Deprecated or completed capabilities are torn down using isolated AbortSignal lifecycles. The road network uses 15 checked-in OpenRouteService routes containing 45,577 verified coordinates. Routing is not computed at runtime, and no routing API keys are exposed to the browser. For live context, SupplyMesh integrates Open-Meteo and the public DGT DATEX II traffic feed without paid API keys. Both live feeds are strictly advisory: they inform the operator and agent, but cannot mutate routes, approvals, or safety constraints automatically. Challenges we faced The core challenge was not connecting an AI model to a map, but making every layer of the workflow operationally truthful: State Synchronization: The original alternative route began in Toledo while the vehicle was displayed partway through another route. We fixed this by introducing a deterministic pre-dispatch snapshot where Unit 211 remains at the origin. Spatial Integrity: We ensured clearance calculations, incident markers, exclusion zones, proposed routes, and final audit receipts all referenced the exact same physical coordinates. Enforcing Human Authority: Approval had to be cryptographically and logically bound to a plan fingerprint and scenario revision. Stale or modified plans fail closed by design, and re-executing cannot trigger duplicate route mutations or receipts. Hybrid 2D/3D Rendering: Synchronizing Leaflet coordinates with a shared Three.js canvas required maintaining vehicle progress between perspective changes, aligning truck headings with route bearings, and scaling weather overlays correctly with zoom levels. External Resilience: Public traffic and weather APIs fail intermittently. The live data layer degrades gracefully, keeping the deterministic recovery scenario functional even when external providers go down. What we learned Context over Quantity: The value of WebMCP lies not in the volume of exposed tools, but in providing precise, state-scoped capabilities that map directly to what the human operator sees. Enforceable Human-in-the-Loop: "Human-in-the-loop" should be an architectural constraint, not just a policy. In SupplyMesh, unauthorized execution is structurally impossible because the tool does not exist until approval is granted. Deterministic Trust: Reproducible clocks, versioned routes, explicit scenario revisions, and immutable receipts are what separate an operational enterprise tool from an unpredictable demo. People-First Optimization: Operational efficiency does not have to come at the driver's expense. SupplyMesh treats safety buffers and mandatory rest windows as non-negotiable constraints, not variables to optimize away. What’s next SupplyMesh currently demonstrates a deeply verified single-incident recovery scenario. Next steps include: Dynamic route recalculation and multi-region support. Direct TMS (Transportation Management System) integrations. Multi-vehicle coordinated recovery planning. The goal is not to replace dispatchers, but to give them a shared operational workspace where complex logistics disruptions can be inspected, authorized, and resolved transparently alongside AI agents. title: Lattice Perps
pitch: A safety-first WebMCP trading cockpit for Hyperliquid: agents propose bounded paper trades, humans control authority, and every action is policy-checked with transparent receipts.
about_excerpt:
A safety-first WebMCP trading cockpit for Hyperliquid: agents propose bounded paper trades, humans control authority, and every action is policy-checked with transparent receipts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Web agents can operate a web page, but actions that change state still need to be understandable, inspectable, and safe. 

 We wanted to explore what an agent-native trading interface could feel like without asking anyone to connect a wallet, approve a signer, or risk real funds. Lattice Perps is our answer: a browser-local paper-trading experience where a human and a browser agent can use the same interface, the same account, and the same visible evidence. 

 The project is inspired by Hyperliquid perpetual markets, but this public showcase intentionally stops at deterministic local simulation. 

 What it does 

 Lattice Perps is a paper trading flight recorder for WebMCP. 

 The app starts with one browser-local paper account containing $100,000 of simulated USD and four fixed markets: 

 
 BTC 
 ETH 
 SOL 
 HYPE 
 

 A human can place market or limit orders from the visible interface. Market orders fill at the displayed simulated mark price. Limit orders rest locally and can be cancelled by their local order ID. 

 A browser agent can perform the same paper-trading actions through six WebMCP tools: 

 
 paper_get_markets 
 paper_get_portfolio 
 paper_get_open_orders 
 paper_get_activity 
 paper_place_order 
 paper_cancel_order 
 

 Every human action, system event, and WebMCP call is written to the visible Agent Tape . The portfolio panel updates from the same underlying account state, showing equity, available balance, margin used, realised PnL, unrealised PnL, positions, open orders, and fills. 

 The key idea is simple: 

 
 One local account. One shared state. Two ways to interact. 
 

 You can trade from the page or ask your browser agent: 

 
 Buy 0.05 BTC at market, then show my paper portfolio. 
 

 The result is visible in the Agent Tape and reflected in the portfolio immediately. 

 How we built it 

 The app is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. 

 The human interface and WebMCP tools share one LocalTradingStore . This prevents the UI and agent surface from developing separate balances, positions, orders, or activity histories. 

 The store provides: 

 
 deterministic simulated markets and mark prices 
 market and limit order handling 
 position netting and PnL calculations 
 simulated fees and margin checks 
 local order cancellation 
 browser persistence through localStorage when available 
 an in-memory fallback when browser storage is unavailable 
 a visible activity history for human and WebMCP actions 
 

 WebMCP registration is feature-detected through the browser's document.modelContext surface. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human trading interface still works. Tool inputs use explicit schemas and reject unexpected fields so the agent surface remains narrow and predictable. 

 The project also includes automated tests for the local trading store, WebMCP tool definitions, and the rendered paper-trading interface. 

 Safety by design 

 This showcase deliberately has: 

 
 no wallet connection 
 no exchange connection 
 no network order submission 
 no real funds 
 no private keys 
 no deposits or withdrawals 
 no production trading capability 
 

 WebMCP is treated as an invocation layer, not an authentication or authorization mechanism. The public demo is designed to make the interaction model visible without pretending that a browser tool registration is equivalent to trading authority. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest part was making the human and agent paths genuinely share state. A separate “agent balance” or fake tool response would have made the demo look convincing while hiding the real interaction model. Instead, both paths call the same store and produce the same portfolio projections and activity records. 

 Another challenge was making the demo useful even when the browser does not support WebMCP. The interface therefore remains complete on its own, while WebMCP enhances it when the browser exposes the API. 

 Finally, we had to make the boundaries clear. A trading demo can easily imply that a real exchange, wallet, or signer is involved. The local simulation, explicit labels, and Agent Tape are designed to keep the demo honest. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that agent-native interfaces benefit from visible evidence, not just successful tool calls. A tool invocation is much easier to understand when the user can see its source, timestamp, status, and effect on the shared account. 

 We also learned that deterministic simulation is valuable for WebMCP development. It makes the experience reproducible, easy to reset, and safe to demonstrate while the browser API and authority model are still evolving. 

 What's next 

 A future version could connect this interaction model to a separately approved testnet account behind explicit human authority, policy checks, and post-action reconciliation. 

 For this submission, we intentionally keep the public experience local, deterministic, and risk-free.

title: TaskFlow
pitch: Get help. Hire a Tasker. Or let an agent book the same site.
about_excerpt:
Get help. Hire a Tasker. Or let an agent book the same site.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Websites are still built as if only humans will use them: click, search, filter, compare, book. Agents can already drive that UI, but they do it by guessing at buttons. WebMCP flips that. A page can expose the same capabilities as tools — document.modelContext.registerTool , getTools , executeTool — so an agent uses the site the way a developer would use an API, while a person still uses the normal interface. 

 TaskRabbit is the perfect test of that idea. A move-in is never one listing. It is furniture assembly, cleaning, and TV mounting, coordinated under a budget, with a human still in the loop before anything is booked. We wanted a marketplace that looks like a real service site and behaves like an MCP server in the browser. 

 What it does 

 TaskFlow is a dual-use TaskRabbit-style marketplace. 

 For people: browse services, compare Taskers, and book from a profile — search, listings, hourly rates, availability, confirm. 

 For agents: the same pages register WebMCP tools ( searchServices , findTaskers , getTaskerAvailability , getTaskerPricing , createTaskRequest , scheduleTask , …). An in-page agent dock takes an outcome like “I just moved in. Make my home ready tonight. I have a $250 budget.” It discovers those tools, builds a plan (Marcus $85, Sarah $95, David $60 = $240), and waits for approval before it schedules. 

 Both paths write to the same booking store. My Tasks shows You booked next to Booked by agent . One website, two clients, one set of capabilities. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js App Router , TypeScript, Tailwind, and shadcn/ui — no backend, no real payments, no live TaskRabbit API. 
 A shared marketplace layer ( search , findTaskers , pricing, create/schedule). Human buttons call those functions. WebMCP execute callbacks wrap the same functions. 
 A spec-faithful document.modelContext polyfill so the demo runs in current browsers, using the official WebMCP shape if the native API exists. 
 A deterministic planner (no LLM) so the killer demo is reliable, with staged delays so the tool activity is visible. 
 A TaskRabbit-like light marketplace plus a dark agent dock that keeps Show WebMCP on screen for judges. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is still a draft. Most browsers do not ship document.modelContext , so we had to match the spec closely without pretending the API is everywhere. 

 The harder product problem was not building another chatbot. The original instinct was an AI-only command center. That hid the point. WebMCP only lands if the human site is real and the agent uses that site’s tools — not a parallel fake API. 

 Shared state was picky too: a full navigation wiped in-memory bookings until we persisted them and tagged each row by source ( human | agent ). Tool registration also had to survive hot reload without double-registering names. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A 2–3 minute demo where you book Marcus as a person, then let the agent plan a $240 move-in, and both appear on My Tasks . 
 Judges can see WebMCP: live getTools / executeTool calls, not a hidden prompt. 
 Human-in-the-loop: the agent never books until Approve & Schedule . 
 One implementation for both audiences — not two products glued together. 
 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native websites are not “add a chat sidebar.” They are capability design : the same operations must be safe, named, and schema’d for a model and obvious in a UI for a person. 

 We also learned why the spec cares about annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ) and approval. Tool descriptions are easy to trust too much. Keeping consequential actions behind a human confirm is the product, not a footer. 

 What's next for TaskFlow 

 
 Native WebMCP in a supporting browser, dropping the polyfill on that path. 
 Declarative tools from real forms, as the spec’s declarative section lands. 
 A real LLM planner behind the same tools, with the deterministic demo kept as a fixture. 
 Richer trust UX: show which origin registered a tool, and treat tool output as untrusted when the hint says so. 
 

 TaskFlow’s bet is simple: the next marketplace is designed for both hands and agents.

 Inspiration 

 I had the idea for Nambut long before this hackathon. I wanted to build a personal card that gave users more freedom to design and express themselves. However, after seeing similar ideas like Linktree, I put the project aside because I wasn't sure if it would solve a real problem. 

 When I discovered WebMCP and saw how AI agents could directly interact with tools provided by a website, I became interested in the idea again. I decided to bring Nambut back and explore how AI could help users create and customize their cards. 

 The name Nambut is a play on the Thai word "นามบัตร" (Nam-bat), which means a business card or a card containing your personal information. 

 What it does 

 Nambut is a flexible personal card builder where users can create, customize, and share their own cards. 

 Users can freely arrange elements, customize colors, rotate elements, apply effects such as glass blur and shadows, and choose from templates. 

 With WebMCP, AI agents can also interact directly with the editor using tools such as add_element , move_element , and delete_element . 

 How we built it 

 Nambut is a web-based visual editor with WebMCP integrated into its core functionality. 

 We exposed the editor's main actions as structured tools so that AI agents can understand and interact with the application directly, while keeping the normal UI available for human users. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I had never built an application like this before, and this was also my first time seriously working with AI agents. 

 I had to learn how AI agents work and how to expose the tools I built in a way that an AI could understand and use correctly. 

 Learning about WebMCP and this new way of connecting AI with web applications was challenging, but it also gave me a lot more motivation to learn and build. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud that I was able to bring an idea I had been thinking about for a long time back to life. 

 More importantly, I managed to finish it within the hackathon deadline and turn it into something that actually works. 

 What we learned 

 This project gave me my first real experience with AI agents and taught me that websites can provide AI with structured capabilities instead of simply being interfaces that AI has to navigate. 

 It also showed me how new technologies like WebMCP can change the way we think about building web applications. 

 What's next for Nambut 

 If Nambut proves that there is real potential, I want to add more tools and significantly improve the UX/UI. 

 I also want to make Nambut a way for more people to discover WebMCP and experience how AI can be used more effectively when it can directly interact with the tools of an application.

title: VirtuLab
pitch: A practical learning platform where humans and AI agents experiment together.
about_excerpt: A practical learning platform where humans and AI agents experiment together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration There's a specific kind of frustration that comes from studying physics from a textbook and still not feeling why a 45° launch angle maximises range. Or sitting through a chemistry lecture with no intuition for what actually happens when you change concentration. Practical subjects are meant to be practised but for most students, the lab is a field trip, not a daily workspace. That gap bothered me. Online simulations exist, but they're mostly isolated demos you tweak a slider, something animates, and that's it. There's no structure underneath. No way for anything outside the page to understand what's happening in the workspace. That second part is what crystallised when I read about WebMCP. Traditional AI assistants sit beside an educational tool. They answer questions about it, but they can't see it, interact with it, or work inside it. They're stuck outside the glass. The student describes the experiment; the assistant guesses a response. There's no ground truth shared between them. WebMCP is the first real path to changing that. A standard where the application explicitly exposes what it knows and what it can do so an AI agent doesn't have to guess at the UI, doesn't have to scrape the screen, doesn't have to simulate mouse clicks. The workspace speaks to it directly, in structured terms it can reason about. That's what I built VirtuLab around. Not "add AI to a simulator." Build a practical learning platform where the workspace itself is the interface between the student and the agent and where both participants are working with the exact same state. What It Does VirtuLab is an agent-native practical learning platform with four workspaces. Every workspace is a real simulation environment. Every workspace exposes structured WebMCP tools. The human and the AI agent work inside the same state not parallel versions of it. The Four Workspaces Physics Lab — Explore 14 interactive experiments across mechanics, motion, waves, energy, gravity, and orbital dynamics. Students can experiment with projectile motion, pendulums, spring systems, collisions, energy conservation, wave interference, free fall, the Doppler effect, buoyancy, thermal expansion, gravitational orbits, circular motion, Newton's laws, and friction. The simulations are built from real physics calculations and generate measurable results such as distance, velocity, time, height, force, and energy. These results are also available as structured data, allowing AI agents to understand and reason about what happens inside the experiment. Chemistry Lab — 14 deterministic reactions with a rules engine. Mixing HCl and NaOH produces pH 7 with +6°C temperature rise. Zinc in copper sulfate displaces copper with a colour change. Phenolphthalein turns pink in NaOH, colourless when HCl is added. Nothing is random, nothing is pre-scripted the outcomes emerge from rules that the agent can predict and reason about. Mechanical Workshop — Gear trains, bridge trusses under load, levers, pulleys, inclined planes, hydraulic presses, torsional stress analysis, vibration damping, four-bar linkages, cam mechanisms, and flywheels. Structural tests run real stress calculations per beam element. Gear ratios are algebraic. Painting Studio — A full canvas editor: pencil, marker, spray, eraser, freehand spline, line, rectangle, circle, triangle, flood fill, eyedropper. Multi-layer system with visibility, opacity control, and rename. Symmetry mode, zoom, grid overlay, full undo/redo history, PNG export. The WebMCP tools here are designed for creative collaboration the agent can inspect the canvas, understand what layers and colors exist, configure the brush, and place spatial composition guides without touching the student's artwork without explicit approval. The WebMCP Architecture Every workspace registers its tools automatically when a student navigates to it. When they leave, the AbortController signal fires and tools deregister cleanly. The pattern is consistent across all four workspaces: inspect → understand → act → retrieve → validate . 6 universal tools (all workspaces): Tool Type Purpose get_workspace_state Read Full structured state — experiment, parameters, status, challenge get_current_challenge Read Objective, constraints, success conditions, progress % get_available_items Read Substances / tools / parameters / components depending on workspace run_simulation Action Trigger the simulation engine validate_workspace Read Check build/results against challenge criteria perform_workspace_action Action Controlled action with validated inputs 6 Physics-specific tools: Tool Type Purpose list_physics_experiments Read Discover all 14 experiments with formulas and parameter names get_experiment_info Read Full parameter spec: names, units, valid ranges load_experiment Action Switch experiment, returns new defaults immediately get_experiment_state Read Current params, all measurements with units, observations set_experiment_parameters Action Validated parameter update with instant recalculation run_physics_simulation Action Launch animation, return updated measurements validate_physics_challenge Read Per-condition breakdown: met / not met / completion % 6 Painting-specific tools: Tool Type Purpose get_canvas_state Read Layers, stroke count, color usage analysis, challenge, brush state get_available_tools_and_colors Read All 11 tools with descriptions + 32-color hex palette configure_brush Action Set tool, color, size, opacity, hardness, smoothing manage_layers Action Add, remove, rename, show/hide, set opacity highlight_canvas_region Action Draw a dashed composition guide on canvas; clearable validate_painting_challenge Read Progress %, color variety check, layer usage analysis Plus 3 Chemistry tools ( get_lab_state , mix_supported_substances , get_experiment_observations ) and 3 Mechanical tools ( get_mechanism_state , calculate_gear_system , test_structure ). Human Control Is Architecture, Not Policy Every tool that changes state — set_experiment_parameters , load_experiment , run_physics_simulation , configure_brush , manage_layers , mix_supported_substances — is gated by a real-time approval system. Before the tool executor runs, the call is intercepted, a pending approval entry is created in the Zustand store, and execution suspends. A toast appears in the UI with the proposed action and the full argument payload. The student clicks Apply or Reject . Only then does the tool execute or return { success: false, error: { code: 'REJECTED' } } to the agent. This isn't a checkbox. It's a Promise -based suspension of an in-flight tool call. The agent waits. The human decides. That's the correct relationship. Simultaneously, the Agent Activity Panel embedded directly in the workspace layout shows every tool call in real time: name, arguments summary, result, timestamp. The student always knows exactly what the agent did and what it returned. How I Built It — and Why It Had to Be This Way Without WebMCP, an AI assistant helping a student with this workspace would have two choices: describe what it thinks the workspace looks like (based on whatever the student pastes into the chat), or try to automate the browser through fragile UI scraping. Neither option gives the agent access to the actual simulation state — the real parameters, the real measurements, the real challenge progress. With WebMCP, the workspace exposes exactly what it knows. The agent calls get_experiment_state and receives the current launch angle, the last measured range in metres, the challenge completion percentage, and the observations from the simulation engine. It calls set_experiment_parameters and the physics store updates immediately — the same store that drives the 3D viewport, the measurements panel, and the challenge progress bar. There is one source of truth. The agent and the student are looking at exactly the same thing. That's not incremental improvement. That's a fundamentally different kind of interaction — and it only exists because WebMCP was treated as a core architectural concern from day one, not an add-on at the end. Stack: React + TypeScript + Vite, Zustand for state management, Three.js + React Three Fiber for 3D, WebMCP Imperative API ( document.modelContext.registerTool() ), Supabase for optional persistence, Netlify for deployment. I designed the WebMCP layer before building the UI. Every Zustand store function that matters has a corresponding tool. Every tool description answers three questions: what does it do, when should the agent call it, does it modify anything. The difference in agent behaviour between vague and precise descriptions is immediately visible "Gets data" is useless; a description that names the returned fields and explains when to call the tool changes how reliably an agent selects it. title: Boardspeak - See the tools your agent can use (in a game!)
pitch: An AI agent has 2 bad options for using a website: screenshot and guess or a separate MCP server. WebMCP is the 3rd way: the page itself tells you what you can do. Boardspeak is that, as a board game
about_excerpt: An AI agent has 2 bad options for using a website: screenshot and guess or a separate MCP server. WebMCP is the 3rd way: the page itself tells you what you can do. Boardspeak is that, as a board game Like Comment Story Updates agent plays boardspeak codex agent tools agent call trace Inspiration Today, an AI agent has 2 bad options for using websites: 1) it can take screenshots and guess or 2) the website owner can build a separate “MCP server” that the AI talks to instead of the website. WebMCP is a third way: the web page itself says, in plain JS, “here are the things you can do here and here’s exactly how” - that’s super powerful, especially if we imagine a future where AI does more for us. The specification names improving accessibility through agents as an explicit goal, and I wanted to test that goal on something pretty complex. A board game is the hardest thing I could think of in time for this challenge - the state is entirely visual, legality changes every single turn, and both players have to be looking at the same board state or it's not a game. What it does Boardspeak plays Breakthrough (Dan Troyka, 2000). 8x8, pawns only and pretty simple rules - get your pawn to the other side of the board, you can only go forward (diagonals+straight), and you can eat enemy pawns diagonally. In our scenario, White plays by mouse (a person, or the built-in bot if you're alone) and Black plays by talking or typing to the agent. The page publishes the live board to the agent as 9 WebMCP tools. Ask "what's on the board?" or "what's threatening my left flank?" and the answer comes from the game itself, not from a screenshot. Say "advance the pawn on e7" and the piece moves on the shared board state. Tools appear and disappear with the position. play_capture exists only while a capture is available. list_threats exists only while a pawn is one step from its goal rank. suggest_move exists only on the human's turn, and play_move only on the agent's. An agent that inspects this page mid-game sees a different set of tools than it saw 30 seconds ago, and that set is always exactly what is legal right now. An agent steering a game is not the new part; 2 players and an agent sharing one adversarial board, with the schema as the rulebook, is, and that's the really cool thing that WebMCP enables. Every agent call is logged on the page with its arguments and its result, so both players can see what happened without opening DevTools. The game is fully playable by mouse, in any browser, with no agent and no API key. In Chrome, Black can even play by voice with no agent at all: an on-page mic takes moves like "a7 to a6" and matches them against the same legal-move list, and saying "options" reads the legal moves out loud....but to play by talking to an agent you'll need ChatGPT's or Codex's built-in browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag! How I built it The idea: legality isn't checked inside the tool. The tool only offers legal moves in the first place. For example, play_move 's input schema is regenerated every turn to enumerate exactly the legal moves, so a schema-respecting client can't even form an illegal move. The schema is the contract so a client that ignores it meets the engine, which refuses anything outside of those rules and tells the agent why. I built this on Next.js 15 on Vercel. The game keeps no state on any server and there is no database; the only server code is the optional narration route (works without a key). One bridge component registers each tool on document.modelContext through GoogleChromeLabs' use-webmcp-tool hook, each with its own AbortController - a turn change aborts the old registration and registers the new one. The piece I am most happy about is the commit barrier. No mutating tool call resolves until React has committed the new board and the new tool surface, so that the agent's next getTools already reflects the move it just made and there is no moment where the screen and the agent can even disagree. Tool calls are serialized through a queue so 2 calls cannot interleave mid-turn. readOnlyHint is set on every read tool. Mutating tools return the full board text so the agent can verify what happened rather than assume. resign_game and start_new_game wait on an in-page confirmation. The page draws its own "are you sure?" dialog and waits for a real click, because the protocol does not have a built-in way to ask the human yet. Challenges I ran into WebMCP can't edit a tool after it's registered, and it refuses a second tool with the same name. So every turn the page has to remove the old move tool before adding the new one, in exactly that order, or it crashes mid-game. I wrote a test that plays 20 moves plus a full game reset against a fake browser that throws the moment any tool name repeats, and it finishes with zero errors. The other hard part was resisting the urge to make the agent the star. Every time I gave it a more powerful tool, the game got worse. suggest_move exists because the version where the agent could move the human's pieces was not fun to play against. Two limits I kept instead of hiding. The size check on tool responses runs before the board updates for the two move tools only; the others check after, which is fine today because their responses are small, but it is not the same guarantee. And the "are you sure?" step is a dialog my page draws itself, because the protocol does not have a built-in one yet. I would rather say that than pretend it does. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 9 tools that come and go with the position, so an illegal move is not even a choice the agent can make 82 unit tests, 9 full browser tests from a clean install, and 5 of 5 WebMCP eval cases A perfect 100 Lighthouse accessibility score on mobile and desktop, with the report in the repo Fully playable by mouse in any browser, no agent, no flag, no API key A live panel showing the agent's current tools, and you can watch it change as you play 2 people and an agent on one board, and the board + agent are fully aligned What I learned The list of tools a page offers does not have to be fixed. Publishing exactly what is legal right now, and nothing else, is the most useful thing a page can tell an agent. And it goes way past games: forms, wizards, checkout flows, anything with steps and rules. The harder lesson: the interesting question in building for agents is not what to expose. It is what to withhold, and when. What's next for Boardspeak Both colors by voice, with two agents sharing one board. More games behind the same engine contract. And a getTools -driven spectator mode, where a third agent can watch without being able to touch anything. title: DraftSmith powered by Excalidraw
pitch: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!!
about_excerpt: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!! Like Comment Story Updates Title End Draftsmith (powered by Excalidraw) Live: https://nice-field-0f080db0f.7.azurestaticapps.net Inspiration Every architecture conversation we've had starts on a whiteboard and ends with someone taking a photo of it. If you actually want to keep the diagram, somebody has to sit down and redraw it, and that's the point where you stop thinking about the system and start nudging boxes around to fit one extra service in. We'd already tried the usual escapes. Mermaid and similar tools hand you a rendered picture; change one word and the layout reshuffles under you, and you can't just grab a box and move it. Image models produce something diagram-shaped that can't be edited at all. Agents that drive a canvas by clicking are guessing coordinates off screenshots, and the results look like it. Two things made us think this was worth a weekend. The first is that Excalidraw already stores the right thing. A scene is real data: elements, and arrows that stay bound to the shapes they connect. If an agent could write that scene directly, you'd get a diagram you can keep working in instead of a picture of one. The second is WebMCP. Normally the backend owns the tool list and one bespoke agent loop calls it. WebMCP flips that around: the page declares what it can do, and any agent the browser trusts can discover and call those tools. We wanted to see whether that actually holds up on something hard, and a canvas is about as hard as it gets - it's stateful, it's spatial, and it's basically opaque to an agent that can only click. Somewhere in there we also decided that a diagram handed over with no commentary isn't much use. So the agent should be able to explain what it drew, not just draw it. What it does Draftsmith is Excalidraw with an agent living inside it. Describe a system, get a diagram. "Draw a 3-tier architecture with a load balancer, two app servers and a database" comes back laid out in one turn: ranked into tiers, ordered to reduce arrow crossings, with long arrows routed around whatever sits between their endpoints. Arrows use Excalidraw's native binding, so they snap to shape edges and follow the boxes when you drag them. Nothing about it is an export - you can keep editing by hand, or keep asking. Talk to it while it draws. Voice mode runs hands-free over a single socket. It listens continuously, answers out loud, asks follow-up questions when your request is vague, and pushes back if the design looks off. You can talk over it to cut it off. When a question needs actual thought ("40M events a day, Postgres is melting - shard, CQRS, or a queue?") it says "let me think about that for a second" out loud and hands that one turn to a stronger model, rather than running the whole conversation slowly for the handful of turns that need it. Point at things. Select shapes on the canvas and they show up as pills above the composer, the same way you'd select code before asking your editor about it. "Make this blue" restyles that box and nothing else. "Connect these" binds them in the order listed. No guessing from labels. Ask to be taught. "Walk me through this" starts a spoken walkthrough with a Tutor cursor tracing the canvas, moving to each element as it's explained and panning off-screen ones into view. The finished lesson goes into the chat history, so a follow-up like "why is there a load balancer?" already has it as context. Teaching is a tool rather than a UI mode, which means "draw a 3-tier architecture and then explain it to me" draws it, binds it and teaches it in a single turn. The canvas is a WebMCP tool provider. Eight tools ( get_scene , create_diagram , add_shape , add_text , bind_arrow , set_style , remove_element , teach_diagram ) are declared to the browser, so an agent that knows nothing about our code can still drive the canvas. The panel header shows WebMCP · native · 8 tools or · shim · , and clicking the badge opens the live manifest. That was partly so we could debug it without devtools, and partly so a demo can't quietly imply native support it doesn't have. How we built it It's a fork of Excalidraw with the agent added, but we didn't vendor upstream. setup.sh clones a pinned Excalidraw commit and copies our files in. The repo stays at roughly the 6k lines that are actually ours, and our diff stays readable. The browser owns the tool definitions. app/ai-agent/webmcp/descriptors.ts is the only source of truth for the tool surface, and it lives in the browser because that's where WebMCP expects it - the page is the provider, so the declarations belong next to the code that runs them. The backend gets the list with every request. It carries its own copy, but that's a clearly labelled fallback for clients too old to send one. Our own agents are WebMCP clients. The sidebar and the voice agent both go through callTool exactly like a third party would. This was deliberate. If we'd registered the tools and then kept calling the canvas directly, the published path would have been exercised by nobody and would have rotted within days. As it stands, if the WebMCP surface breaks, the product breaks with it, and we find out immediately. The model does semantics, code does geometry. create_diagram takes an entire graph, and app/ai-agent/layout.ts runs a layered (Sugiyama) pipeline over it: break cycles, assign layers, insert dummy nodes so a long edge reserves a corridor in each layer it crosses, order within layers to cut crossings, then assign coordinates. Those dummy corridors turn into real bend points on the arrow, and since Excalidraw keeps bend points on a bound arrow, the routing survives without losing the bindings. Spatial invariants live in the tool layer. add_shape finds a non-overlapping position before it creates anything, searching outward on a grid, and reports back where the box actually ended up. Colour is assigned per layer instead of per box, so a tier comes out consistent without the model having to think about it. House style - rounded corners, hachure fill, label colour matched to the border - is set in code, so it holds regardless of what the model asks for. Voice is one socket, speech to speech. Mic audio goes up; spoken audio and tool calls come back down, over the Azure OpenAI Realtime API. One model hears audio and replies with both audio and function calls on the same stream, so there's no STT → LLM → TTS chain to keep in sync. The server proxies the socket instead of minting a client token. That keeps the key out of the browser, and because only the server sends session.update , a tampered client can't swap the instructions or widen the tool list. It can talk and listen, and that's it. The lesson is data, not prose. The scene goes to the backend, which runs a teaching prompt with one forced tool call that returns { intro, segments: [{ elementIds, narration }], closing } . Since every chunk of narration names the elements it's about, the frontend can point the cursor at exactly those elements for exactly as long as that chunk is playing. We treat the output as untrusted: schema-checked, then every element id verified against the real scene, with invented ids dropped and a lesson about nothing real rejected outright. Narration uses the browser's own speechSynthesis , so it needs no key and no audio leaves the machine. The tracing cursor isn't custom drawing either - "Tutor" is a synthetic entry in Excalidraw's collaborators map, the same code that renders a teammate's pointer, so it pans and zooms with the scene for free. No server-side session state. Each POST /api/chat is one model turn. It returns either final text or the tool calls to run; the browser runs them against the live editor and posts again. The server is a pure function of the history it's given, so it restarts cleanly, scales without stickiness, and holds the only copy of the credentials. Azure OpenAI and Anthropic sit behind one interface and are selectable per request. It's deployed as two halves on Azure, because they need different things. The editor is a static bundle on Static Web Apps. The backend has to hold a WebSocket open for the length of a voice session, which rules out serverless. Challenges we ran into Arrows went straight through the boxes. The bindings were fine - correct element ids on both ends - but the geometry wasn't, and it took a while to see why. Excalidraw derives an arrow's fixedPoint from the endpoint you seed it with: [(px - box.x) / box.width, …] . Seed an arrow centre to centre and you've recorded [0.5, 0.5] , which literally means "anchor at the centre of this shape." Seeding between the two outlines gives you bottom-centre and top-centre instead. While fixing that we hit a second one: Excalidraw computes default points as element.width || 100 , so a perfectly vertical arrow h

title: CarCare WebMCP
pitch: An AI-powered vehicle maintenance assistant that uses WebMCP to let agents read maintenance history, track services, and identify upcoming maintenance directly through the web app.
about_excerpt:
An AI-powered vehicle maintenance assistant that uses WebMCP to let agents read maintenance history, track services, and identify upcoming maintenance directly through the web app.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Vehicle maintenance information is often scattered across receipts, notes, and service records. It can be difficult for drivers to remember what was serviced and what maintenance is coming next. 

 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make a normal vehicle maintenance website more useful by allowing an AI agent to understand and interact with the application directly. 

 What it does 

 CarCare MCP is a vehicle maintenance dashboard that keeps track of a vehicle and its maintenance history. 

 Users can view completed services, record new maintenance, and see when upcoming maintenance is due based on mileage. 

 The application exposes its functionality to AI agents through WebMCP tools. These tools allow an agent to: 

 
 Get vehicle information 
 Read maintenance history 
 Add maintenance records 
 Calculate upcoming maintenance 
 

 For example, instead of manually filling out a form, a user can tell an AI agent that an oil change was completed at a certain mileage, and the agent can use the WebMCP tool to add that information to the application. 

 How I built it 

 I built CarCare MCP as a lightweight web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 Maintenance data is stored in the browser using localStorage. The application calculates upcoming maintenance based on the latest service mileage and predefined service intervals. 

 I then integrated WebMCP using the Model Context API and registered tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes a description, input schema, and an execute function that connects the AI agent to the same application logic used by the web interface. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel, and the source code is available on GitHub. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the main challenges was understanding how a traditional web application should expose its functionality to an AI agent. 

 Instead of having an agent rely on clicking buttons or interpreting the visual interface, I needed to think about the application's actions as structured tools with clear descriptions and input schemas. 

 I also had to test the experimental WebMCP implementation and verify that the browser correctly registered and exposed the tools. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand the difference between building a website only for humans and building one that can also be understood and operated by AI agents. 

 WebMCP allows the application itself to describe the actions an agent can perform. This can make agent interactions more structured and reliable than depending entirely on visual browser automation. 

 What's next for CarCare MCP 

 Future versions could support multiple vehicles, customizable maintenance schedules, cloud synchronization, service receipts, and more detailed maintenance recommendations. 

 The same WebMCP approach could also allow an AI agent to manage a driver's complete maintenance workflow across multiple vehicles.

title: DOMHamster
pitch: A human-in-the-loop AI dispatcher that helps coordinate volunteers without taking control away from the coordinator.
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop AI dispatcher that helps coordinate volunteers without taking control away from the coordinator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are getting better at using websites, but many of them still have to guess what a page means from buttons, labels, and layout. That is usually fine for simple tasks. It becomes a problem when the agent is working with schedules, approvals, private information, or decisions that a person has already made. I wanted to explore a workflow where the agent could still do useful work, but where important decisions stayed clearly under human control. That idea became DOMHamster , a volunteer-dispatch demo built around WebMCP. What DOMHamster does DOMHamster helps coordinate a fictional, non-emergency volunteer operation with eight requests and five available volunteers. The agent can use WebMCP tools to: Read the current requests, volunteers, assignments, and audit history Create a complete assignment draft Check whether the draft is valid Repair scheduling conflicts Prepare a specific draft version for human review Commit the plan after the coordinator approves it Request one contact record when it is actually needed Review a sanitized history of important actions The agent does not have permission to do everything. It cannot approve its own draft, override a locked human decision, reset the application, or freely access every contact record. Those actions remain controlled by the person using the interface. How the demo works The agent starts by reading the current coordination data and creating a full assignment draft. The coordinator then changes request R-105 from volunteer V-01 to V-03 at 1:00 p.m. and locks that choice. This creates a scheduling conflict with R-106 . Instead of replacing the coordinator's decision, DOMHamster blocks approval and explains what went wrong. The agent is then asked to repair the plan while preserving the locked assignment. The repair keeps R-105 exactly as the coordinator selected it and moves only the conflicting request to another available volunteer. Once the draft is valid again, the agent prepares that exact version for review. The coordinator must approve it through the interface before the agent receives permission to commit it. The commit can only be used once. After the plan is committed, the commit capability disappears, and a repeated attempt is rejected. Contact information is also restricted. The agent can request the contact for one specific assignment only after the plan has been committed. The audit history records that contact access happened, but it does not copy the sensitive contact value into the log. Finally, the coordinator can reset the scenario and return it to the original READY state. How I built it I built DOMHamster as a state-driven web application and exposed its agent capabilities through the native document.modelContext WebMCP interface. The project includes 12 structured WebMCP tools. Each tool has: A clear purpose Structured inputs and outputs State requirements Predictable error responses A JSON Schema contract The available tools change depending on the current application state. For example, the commit tool is not available before human approval. Contact access is not available before the plan is committed. After a successful commit, the commit tool is removed so it cannot be used twice. I also tied approvals and mutations to the current draft version. This prevents an approval from being reused after the underlying plan has changed. I tested the tools with the ChatGPT browser extension , as well as Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. I also used Playwright and the Chrome DevTools Protocol to test tool registration, state changes, invalid actions, and replay protection. The application was built with TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, and deployed with Netlify. I used Remotion and FFmpeg to create and edit the project video. Challenges I faced The hardest part was keeping the WebMCP tool surface synchronized with the actual application state. A tool may be valid in one state but unsafe or meaningless in another. I had to make sure tools appeared and disappeared at the correct time, and that invalid or outdated actions failed in a clear and predictable way. Other challenges included: Preventing a stale draft from being committed Preserving human-locked assignments during an agent repair Making approval apply to one exact draft version Keeping commit authorization short-lived and single-use Rejecting repeated or out-of-order actions safely Restricting contact access until after commitment Recording useful audit events without exposing contact information Resetting the full scenario back to the same starting state for repeated testing Creating the demo video was also more difficult than expected. I had to keep the narration, subtitles, screen states, and timings aligned while still making the workflow understandable to someone seeing the project for the first time. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving an agent more tools does not automatically create a better experience. What matters is giving it the right tool at the right moment. Tool availability can work as part of the permission model. Instead of exposing every action all the time and relying only on written instructions, the application can remove capabilities that are not currently allowed. I also learned that approval is much safer when it is tied to a specific version. A general “yes” is ambiguous if the draft changes afterward. Approving an exact visible version creates a much clearer connection between what the person reviewed and what the agent is allowed to execute. Most importantly, the human-agent experience feels more trustworthy when the agent handles the repetitive coordination work, while important decisions remain visible and controlled through the interface. What's next The next step would be to test DOMHamster with more agent clients and expand the scheduling rules beyond the current deterministic scenario. I would also like to add server-backed authentication and authorization, improve accessibility, and explore how the same approval pattern could work in other coordination tools where agents need to act without silently taking control away from people. title: Aria Grande
pitch: Aria Grande gives AI browsers the context to make every website easier to explore, understand, and use—for everyone. It scales from clients to all websites.
about_excerpt:
Aria Grande gives AI browsers the context to make every website easier to explore, understand, and use—for everyone. It scales from clients to all websites.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Main view 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Main view 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Main view 
 
 1 2 



 
 Aria Grande 

 Inspiration 

 The web is designed primarily for people who can visually scan pages, interpret layouts, and manually move between controls. That makes finding, understanding, and acting on information slower and more difficult for many people, especially people who use assistive technology. AI-assisted browsers can help, but they are often limited to the current page and must infer a website's structure and intent from an interface built for sighted users. 

 I wanted to give websites a simple, interoperable way to share the context they already know with an AI-assisted browser—without making every site adopt one product or requiring users to give up a usable experience on sites that have not yet implemented the standard. 

 This is a practical solution, as it is designed to start small with only client side support that works on any website and scale and improve user experience as websites adopt the proposed system. 

 I believe a simple system can change lives of people with disabilities, by making the web easy to find and browse. 

 What it does 

 Aria Grande is an accessibility-focused interoperability system for AI-assisted browsing, built on WebMCP. It defines seven common browsing activities as consistent WebMCP tools: 

 
 Read 
 Summarise 
 Search 
 Ask 
 Frontpage 
 Explore 
 Login 
 

 Websites can implement whichever actions are useful to them. For example, a site can provide authoritative source material for a summary, return structured search results, answer a question using its own context, or expose a simplified navigation hierarchy. AI-assisted browser clients implement every action along with a local fallback, so the browsing experience remains functional on any website. 

 How I built it 

 I designed a compact action vocabulary and mapped each behaviour to a stable ariag-* WebMCP tool name. For each action, I specified the expected client behaviour, a model prompt, and a fallback strategy. This makes the boundary clear: websites can contribute richer, authoritative information, while clients retain responsibility for a dependable experience. 

 I also built example implementations: a browser extension that acts as an Aria Grande client and a government-website example that demonstrates website-side support. The specification treats website responses as untrusted source data, instructing clients to preserve user intent, validate navigation targets, and avoid inventing answers or claiming actions that did not happen. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The central challenge was balancing a useful standard with a realistic adoption path. A broad protocol would be hard for websites and browser clients to implement; a narrow one would not cover the activities people actually need. I focused on the small set of actions that recur across websites and made every website endpoint optional. 

 Another challenge was ensuring graceful degradation. An AI browser cannot assume a site supports Aria Grande or that a returned result is complete. I therefore defined concrete fallback behaviour for every action, from extracting readable document content to finding visible search and login controls. Security and trust were equally important: tool output may contain instructions, navigation targets must be validated, and secrets must not be passed to the model or tool unless the user intentionally provides them. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I created a practical contract between websites and AI-assisted browsers that improves accessibility without replacing the web. Its seven actions cover the core journey from understanding a page to searching, asking questions, exploring a site, and signing in. 

 I am especially proud that the system makes room for both early adopters and the existing web. Sites may add support incrementally, while clients still provide local fallbacks everywhere. The client guidance also makes safety a first-class part of the design rather than an afterthought. 

 What I learned 

 Accessibility for AI-assisted browsing is not only about extracting text. Useful assistance requires structure, authoritative context, clear navigation, and honest handling of uncertainty. I also learned that interoperability works best when responsibilities are explicit: websites describe what they know, clients protect user intent and perform reliable fallbacks, and users stay in control of consequential actions. 

 What's next for Aria Grande 

 Next, I want to validate the action set with more real websites and AI-assisted browser clients, refine the response formats through interoperability testing, and expand the examples and implementation guidance. I also plan to explore stronger conventions for structured results, navigation validation, and authentication handoffs—while keeping the protocol small, optional for websites, and dependable for users.
