title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . pitch: Turn receipts into intelligent assets with WebMCP-powered warranty tracking and claims, while keeping every important action under human control.
about_excerpt:
Turn receipts into intelligent assets with WebMCP-powered warranty tracking and claims, while keeping every important action under human control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 LifeReceipt — Your Purchases, Remembered 

 The Idea 

 We’ve all been there — you buy something expensive, keep the receipt somewhere “safe,” and then completely forget about it until you actually need it. 

 A warranty expires, a receipt is difficult to find, or you realize too late that you could have made a claim. 

 That made us think: what if our receipts could actually remember things for us? 

 That’s where LifeReceipt came from. 

 What We Built 

 LifeReceipt is a purchase vault that turns ordinary receipts into useful, intelligent assets. 

 Instead of simply storing receipts, it keeps track of purchases, warranty deadlines, receipt details, and potential claims. More importantly, we made these capabilities accessible to AI agents through WebMCP . 

 An agent can search for a purchase, check its warranty, find the receipt, and prepare a claim without the user having to manually navigate through everything. 

 For example, a user can ask: 

 
 “Find my Sony headphones, check if they’re still under warranty, retrieve the receipt, and prepare a claim if eligible.” 
 

 LifeReceipt can handle the investigation and preparation — but it stops before submitting the claim . 

 The user has to explicitly approve the action. 

 That human approval step was an important part of our design because we don't want an agent making consequential decisions completely on its own. 

 How We Built It 

 We built LifeReceipt as a React + Vite web application and created a WebMCP layer that exposes the application's capabilities as agent tools. 

 We implemented 9 tools covering purchase search, warranty checking, receipt retrieval, claim preparation, approval, submission, and claim status. 

 The UI was designed to make the whole process visible. Users can explore their purchases through the Purchase Vault, see upcoming warranty expirations through Warranty Radar, and follow the agent's actions through the Agent Activity Log. 

 What We Learned 

 The biggest thing we learned was that building for agents is different from building a normal website. 

 We had to think about what an agent should be allowed to do , what information it needs, and where a human should take over. 

 WebMCP made us think of the website as more than just pages and buttons. Each useful capability can become something an agent can discover and use. 

 Challenges 

 Getting the WebMCP integration and the normal website experience to work together reliably was one of our biggest challenges. 

 We also faced deployment issues with Netlify, including SPA routing and JavaScript MIME types. Fixing those issues taught us that a project isn't finished when it works locally — it also needs to work reliably in the real environment where people and agents will use it. 

 Why LifeReceipt? 

 We don't want LifeReceipt to be another place where receipts go to be forgotten. 

 We want it to be a place where your purchases stay useful long after you buy them — with an agent handling the boring work and a human staying in control of the important decisions.

title: AgentBadge — WebMCP Agent-Native Compliance Platform
pitch: First agent-native compliance platform powered by WebMCP. 6 imperative tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. 145+ readiness rules, on-chain agent passports on Hedera. Browser-mediated tool calls.
about_excerpt:
First agent-native compliance platform powered by WebMCP. 6 imperative tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. 145+ readiness rules, on-chain agent passports on Hedera. Browser-mediated tool calls.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP vs Traditional API vs MCP: zero keys, zero servers, zero setup. Browser mediates all agent tool calls natively. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 AgentBadge: 6 imperative WebMCP tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. Browser-native agent compliance on Hedera. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent visits agentbadge.xyz, discovers 6 tools via /.well-known/webmcp.json, calls them directly through the browser. No setup. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP vs Traditional API vs MCP: zero keys, zero servers, zero setup. Browser mediates all agent tool calls natively. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 AgentBadge: 6 imperative WebMCP tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. Browser-native agent compliance on Hedera. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent visits agentbadge.xyz, discovers 6 tools via /.well-known/webmcp.json, calls them directly through the browser. No setup. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP vs Traditional API vs MCP: zero keys, zero servers, zero setup. Browser mediates all agent tool calls natively. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents today face a fundamental integration problem. To use any web service, an agent must: read API docs, obtain API keys, install SDKs, configure authentication, and manage secrets. This is the API key bottleneck — every integration requires human setup. 

 Meanwhile, MCP (Model Context Protocol) emerged as a standard for exposing tools to LLMs, but it still requires running a separate MCP server, configuring transport (stdio/SSE), and managing permissions server-side. Agents without MCP clients are left out. 

 We asked: what if agents could discover and use tools directly from the browser — no keys, no servers, no setup? WebMCP answers this by making the browser the mediator. AgentBadge is our answer to "what does an agent-native web look like?" 

 What it does 

 AgentBadge is the first agent-native compliance platform powered by WebMCP . It exposes: 

 
 6 imperative tools via navigator.modelContext.provideContext() :

 
 agent-readiness-scan — scans any URL for 145+ AI readiness checks across 18 categories 
 badge-generate — generates compliance badge SVG 
 passport-issue — mints on-chain NFT passport on Hedera 
 passport-verify — verifies agent identity by token ID or DID (Hedera + EVM) 
 get-compliance-score — quick compliance score (0-100, grade A-F) 
 search-rules — searches 145+ compliance rules by keyword 
 
 1 declarative form — HTML form-based scan submission for declarative agents 
 Automatic discovery via /.well-known/webmcp.json — agents find tools without reading docs 
 Browser-mediated security — per-tool trust levels (trusted/untrusted, readOnly/write), no API keys 
 145+ readiness rules across 18 categories — the most comprehensive AI agent readiness scanner 
 

 How we built it 

 WebMCP Layer 

 
 Discovery endpoint: GET /.well-known/webmcp.json returns a manifest with tool namespaces, endpoints, and descriptors 
 Tool registration: Inline <script> on every page calls navigator.modelContext.provideContext() with 6 tool definitions (input schemas + execute functions) 
 Trust levels: Each tool declares readOnly / write + trusted / untrusted — the browser enforces per-tool access 
 

 Scanner (145+ rules, 18 categories) 

 
 41 parallel HTTP fetchers — robots.txt, sitemap, llms.txt, OpenAPI, WebMCP manifest, WebMCP runtime, content negotiation, payment protocols, identity/DID, bot auth, SEO/AEO, accessibility, and more 
 WebMCP-specific rules: AB-050 (manifest found), AB-051 (form annotations), AB-069 (browser-side tools), AB-102 (descriptor validation), AB-103 (runtime probe), AB-115 (tool schema), AB-116 (content negotiation) 
 Ed25519-signed reports with SHA-256 integrity hashes 
 

 Blockchain Layer 

 
 Hedera HTS — non-transferable NFT passports ($0.001/tx, 3-5s finality, no smart contracts) 
 HCS — immutable audit trail + agent directory (consensus-ordered, timestamped) 
 Mirror Node — free REST API for reads, no indexer needed 
 DID support: did:hcs:{tokenId}:{serial} (Hedera) and did:eip155:{chainId}:passport:{nftAddress}:{tokenId} (EVM) 
 

 Tech Stack 

 
 Runtime: Bun + Hono (TypeScript-native, server-side rendering) 
 Frontend: HTMX fragments — no React, no build step 
 Blockchain: Hedera Testnet (HTS + HCS + HBAR) 
 Metadata: IPFS via nft.storage (immutable JSON, CID = content hash) 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP Spec Readiness 

 WebMCP is an emerging spec — browsers haven't shipped navigator.modelContext yet. We built the full integration (tool registration, discovery endpoint, schemas) so it's spec-ready today : all endpoints work as standard HTTP APIs, and will work natively via WebMCP when browsers implement it. 

 Scanner Complexity 

 145+ rules across 18 categories with 41 parallel fetchers is complex to orchestrate. We built a parallel fetcher architecture with SSRF protection, content-type validation, and timeout handling. Each fetcher returns structured data that feeds into the rule engine. 

 Browser-Mediated Trust 

 Designing per-tool trust levels ( trusted / untrusted , readOnly / write ) that the browser can enforce required careful thinking about the threat model. Untrusted tools ( agent-readiness-scan , get-compliance-score ) are safe for any agent to call. Trusted tools ( passport-issue , passport-verify ) require browser mediation. 

 Cross-Chain Identity 

 Supporting both Hedera ( did:hcs: ) and EVM ( did:eip155: ) DIDs required abstracting the verification layer. The same passport-verify tool handles both formats, resolving to on-chain NFT ownership checks via the appropriate chain's API. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 First WebMCP-native compliance platform — not a wrapper around an existing API, but built from the ground up for browser-mediated agent tool discovery 
 145+ scanner rules across 18 categories — the most comprehensive AI agent readiness framework, covering discovery, documentation, actionability, payments, identity, infrastructure, SEO/AEO, accessibility, and WebMCP itself 
 7 WebMCP-specific scanner rules — AgentBadge scans itself and other sites for WebMCP compliance (manifest, runtime, form annotations, tool schemas, content negotiation) 
 Zero API keys architecture — agents discover and use tools without any authentication setup 
 Cross-chain DID support — Hedera and EVM identity in one tool 
 Spec-ready today — full WebMCP integration that works as HTTP APIs now and natively when browsers ship navigator.modelContext 
 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP is the right abstraction — agents shouldn't need to read API docs or manage keys. Browser-mediated tool discovery is fundamentally better than the API key model. 
 Scanner-first approach works — before exposing tools, check if a site is agent-ready. 145+ rules across 18 categories gives a comprehensive readiness picture. 
 Declarative + imperative is the right combo — some agents prefer tool calls, others prefer HTML forms. Supporting both covers all agent types. 
 Trust levels are essential — not all tools should be callable by any agent. The trusted / untrusted split lets the browser enforce access without authentication. 
 

 What's next for AgentBadge 

 
 Browser-native WebMCP — when Chrome ships navigator.modelContext , AgentBadge tools will work natively without any changes to our code 
 More imperative tools — expand beyond 6 tools to cover marketplace tasks, A2A messaging, and agent directory search 
 WebMCP compliance certification — a badge program for sites that pass all 7 WebMCP scanner rules 
 Agent passport tiers via WebMCP — let agents upgrade their on-chain tier through browser-mediated tool calls 
 Cross-browser testing — validate WebMCP integration across Chrome, Firefox, Safari as implementations ship 
 Community rule contributions — open the 145+ rule framework for community-submitted readiness checks

about_excerpt:
The idea is simple: stop searching and start connecting
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration
Research tools help people find information, while chat tools help people ask questions. However, neither makes it easy to see how ideas, evidence, notes, and decisions connect. 

 We were inspired to build MindLink as a shared thinking space for humans and AI. The goal is simple: 

 Stop searching. Start connecting. 

 We wanted to create a tool that helps users understand research papers in simple language, challenge assumptions, discover relationships, and turn information into better decisions. 

 What it does
MindLink transforms thinking and research into an interactive visual canvas. 

 Users can: 

 Explore questions with AI-generated thoughts.
Compare optimistic and pessimistic perspectives.
Explore multiple future paths.
Search real research papers through OpenAlex.
Add papers, notes, Markdown files, paper files, and images.
Convert research into claims, evidence, methods, risks, gaps, contradictions, and questions.
Connect related thoughts with animated neural links.
Explain selected ideas in simple language.
Build a research story map.
Listen to an audio brief.
Generate images for thoughts.
Ask different AI roles for perspectives, including Investor, Mentor, Domain Expert, Future You, and Devil’s Advocate.
Zoom, move, edit, pin, and delete thoughts.
Lock decisions after reviewing possible outcomes.
Interact with the canvas through WebMCP tools.
MindLink does not just store information. It maps understanding. 

 How we built it
MindLink was built with: 

 Next.js
React
TypeScript
Tailwind CSS
Zustand
Groq AI
OpenAlex
WebMCP
Lucide React
FFmpeg for demo media creation
The application uses a visual canvas where every thought is represented as a node. Nodes contain metadata such as type, source, trust level, author, and relationships. 

 The Research Desk provides a focused workspace for finding papers, adding user context, explaining ideas, creating story maps, and generating audio briefs. 

 We used OpenAlex to retrieve real academic papers from the web. Research results are added to the canvas with source links and confidence indicators so users can distinguish evidence from interpretation. 

 WebMCP exposes MindLink actions to compatible AI agents, including starting a session, adding thoughts, expanding ideas, challenging assumptions, reading the canvas state, locking decisions, and finding research papers. 

 Challenges we ran into
One major challenge was designing a canvas that remained useful as more thoughts and connections appeared. We needed to make relationships visible without overwhelming the user. 

 We also had to handle uncertainty responsibly. AI-generated research explanations can sound confident even when evidence is weak, so we added source labels, trust levels, and clear distinctions between evidence, interpretation, risks, and open questions. 

 Another challenge was combining multiple interaction types in one workspace: research search, file input, visual mapping, audio, images, AI roles, decision-making, and WebMCP. We focused on keeping the canvas as the central experience while moving research tools into a collapsible sidebar. 

 Finally, we had to make the demo reliable even when an AI API was unavailable. We added fallback responses so the core research experience could still be demonstrated. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are proud that MindLink turns a research question into a connected visual experience instead of another chat transcript. 

 Our key accomplishments include: 

 Building a working human + AI thinking canvas.
Adding real research paper retrieval through OpenAlex.
Creating a dedicated Research Desk workspace.
Adding animated neural links between ideas.
Supporting paper explanations with evidence-oriented node types.
Adding audio briefs and visual story mapping.
Adding WebMCP tools for AI-agent interaction.
Preserving human control through editing, challenging, source inspection, and decision confirmation.
Creating a polished hackathon demo with narrated video and visual documentation.
What we learned
We learned that useful AI products are not only about generating better answers. They are also about helping users understand where an answer came from, how reliable it is, and what should happen next. 

 We learned that visual structure can make complex research easier to understand. Separating a paper into questions, methods, claims, evidence, limitations, contradictions, and gaps gives users a more useful mental model than a single summary. 

 We also learned that human control is essential. The best experience is not AI making decisions alone, but AI helping people see possibilities, challenge assumptions, and make more informed decisions. 

 What's next for MindLink
Next, we plan to make MindLink a complete personal research memory system. 

 Planned improvements include: 

 Full PDF text extraction and document parsing.
OCR for scanned papers and research images.
Persistent research libraries beyond browser storage.
Semantic search across personal notes and papers.
Automatic citation and reference graph generation.
More advanced paper diagrams and concept maps.
Better source passage and page-level citations.
Multi-paper contradiction and consensus detection.
Personalized research podcasts with multiple AI voices.
Story-based video generation from research maps.
Zotero, Obsidian, and Markdown export.
Collaborative research workspaces.
The long-term vision is for MindLink to become a living map of a person’s knowledge: a place where papers, ideas, questions, evidence, and decisions continuously connect and grow.

title: Meridian Voyager
pitch: A car configurator where the agent and the human edit the same build. Nine WebMCP tools let it explain every constraint and solve for the cheapest valid car.
about_excerpt: A car configurator where the agent and the human edit the same build. Nine WebMCP tools let it explain every constraint and solve for the cheapest valid car. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Car configurators are one of the most frustrating interfaces on the web, and it isn't because they're badly designed. It's because the options genuinely interact. The tow package needs all-wheel drive. Sport suspension drops the ride height below legal hitch clearance. The 21-inch wheels are locked to trims you may not want to pay for. Every real configurator has a hidden constraint graph, and the only tool it gives you for exploring it is clicking and backtracking. So when someone asks the question they actually care about — "what's the cheapest build with all-wheel drive and a tow hitch that still comes in under fifty thousand?" — the interface has no answer. You brute-force it by hand. That's a constraint-satisfaction problem behind a UI that can't express one. It seemed like exactly the shape of problem WebMCP exists to solve. What it does Meridian Voyager is a car configurator where an agent and a human edit the same build. Not a chat widget stapled to a product page — the page registers nine tools on document.modelContext, and the agent reads and writes the exact state the human is looking at. You can click paint colours yourself and the agent sees your choice on its next read. You can ask the agent for the cheapest build meeting your constraints, and the car on screen changes while you watch. An activity log labels every change You or Agent, so the collaboration is legible rather than magical. The centrepiece is find_cheapest_build. It enumerates the full option space against every compatibility rule and returns an exact cheapest answer, which the agent can then apply in one call. That's the question the UI could never answer. The other half is that constraints get explained, not just enforced. Every rule carries a human-readable reason, and tool responses hand those sentences back: ▎ "The Tow Package needs the front motor for low-speed traction under load, so it requires Dual Motor AWD or Performance AWD." A blocked set_option teaches the agent something instead of erroring. It can then offer a real trade-off — "I can add the hitch if we move you to Dual Motor AWD, which is $5,000 more and costs 12 miles of range" — which is exactly the conversation a good salesperson has and a form never can. How we built it React and Vite, with the domain deliberately separated from the tool layer: src/domain/catalog.ts — the option catalog as pure data src/domain/rules.ts — the constraint engine, pricing, and the exact cheapest-build solver src/store.ts — the single shared configuration src/webmcp/register.ts — the nine document.modelContext tools src/components/CarView.tsx — layered SVG that reacts to paint, wheels, and ride height The catalog and the rules are plain data, so adding an option or a constraint never means touching tool code. The tools describe the catalog to the agent from the same source the UI renders from, which is what keeps the two views honest. The nine tools: get_configuration, list_available_options, check_compatibility, get_price_breakdown, find_cheapest_build, set_option, remove_option, apply_build, reset_build. One store, two writers. The click handlers and the tool implementations both go through store.ts. There's no separate agent-facing model to drift out of sync — that's the whole reason the demo reads as collaboration rather than automation. Read and write get different trust. Read-only tools are marked readOnlyHint, so an agent can explore the entire option space and price out alternatives freely, and only needs the user's confidence when it's about to change the build. Native first. The app waits for a native document.modelContext and uses it directly on Chrome 149+. Only when the browser hasn't shipped the API does it load @mcp-b/global, a polyfill of the same W3C spec, so anyone evaluating it on another browser still gets the full experience. A badge in the header shows which one is active. Challenges we ran into Getting the tool responses right mattered more than getting the tools right. The first version returned bare success and failure, and an agent driving it would just retry the same blocked option. Moving every constraint's rationale into the response — and adding a hint pointing at find_cheapest_build — changed the agent from something that poked at the form into something that reasoned about trade-offs. The solver also had to be exact rather than greedy. A greedy walk produces a plausible build that isn't actually the cheapest, and a wrong confident answer is worse than no answer. The option space is small enough to enumerate honestly, so it does. Detecting the native API was subtler than expected. Registering against the polyfill because document.modelContext hadn't appeared yet silently downgrades a native browser, so the app waits for the host's implementation before falling back. Accomplishments that we're proud of scripts/verify.mjs drives the app through the tool layer in headless Chromium — the same path an agent takes — and asserts the page moves with it. Nineteen checks, all passing, covering tool registration, constraint enforcement, the solver (including a deliberately impossible request it must refuse), agent writes reaching the UI, and human clicks becoming visible to the agent. What we learned WebMCP's real leverage isn't letting an agent click things faster. It's that a page can expose the reasoning behind its own interface — the constraints, the trade-offs, the search space — which is precisely the part a visual UI throws away. The tow-hitch rule exists in every real configurator; WebMCP is the first time the page can explain it rather than just enforce it. What's next for Meridian Voyager Multi-vehicle comparison, financing as a tool so the agent can optimise on monthly payment rather than sticker price, and tightening the transport's allowedOrigins from the demo's permissive setting to a real allowlist. title: At Attin
pitch: Banking you can ask for — with authority you can see.
about_excerpt: Banking you can ask for — with authority you can see. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Banking still makes people translate a simple goal into menus, forms, account rules, and unfamiliar terminology. That friction hits older adults and first-time users hardest, but everyone feels it when a task becomes stressful or complex. We wanted AI to remove the translation work without removing the person’s authority. What it does At Attin is a complete single-user fictional-money bank: accounts, activity, payees, transfers, scheduled and recurring payments, cards and controls, savings goals, budgets, reports, notifications, disputes, trusted contacts, accessibility settings, and manual forms. Its in-site assistant is powered by Featherless and moonshotai/Kimi-K3 . A user asks for a banking outcome in plain language. The model selects one of 56 imperative WebMCP tools, while four visible form tools support browser-native agent interaction. The bank validates the request, prepares an exact preview, applies financial invariants, shows every consequence, and waits for a person. No agent request executes automatically. Every protected read and every mutation requires fresh visible confirmation. Higher-consequence actions require both YES and a new arithmetic challenge. Authorizations expire after 90 seconds, are single-use, bind to the exact preview and state version, and cannot be replayed. All money is fictional ATC, stored device-locally, with no cash value and no real payment rails. How we built it React, TypeScript, Vite, and React Router Browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool() One shared 56-operation descriptor layer for compatible browser agents and the in-site agent Featherless server proxy with Kimi K3; the provider key never reaches the browser App-owned prepare → confirm → commit coordination with cancellation, expiry, stale-state, and replay protection Integer minor-unit money, atomic writes, versioned local persistence, recovery, and append-only local agent audit OpenAI Codex, HyperFrames, Remotion, Kokoro TTS, Suno, and OpenAI Sites Why WebMCP matters At Attin does not add a deterministic intent parser. The model reasons; WebMCP publishes the bank’s real capabilities; the application owns authorization and execution. The same descriptors and confirmation boundary serve the embedded assistant and compatible browser agents. Challenges The hardest part was ensuring preparation could not leak protected data, and that registration, cancellation, retries, legacy persistence, linked savings reservations, balance floors, and dispute evidence all remained fail-closed. We built explicit invariants, version-bound authorization, single-pending-request coordination, and focused regression tests. Accomplishments 56 imperative tools and 4 visible form surfaces Confirmation for every agent read and change Step-up confirmation for critical actions A complete banking surface instead of a narrow proof-of-concept A working Featherless/Kimi K3 assistant with no direct bank-state access 141 automated tests plus lint, build, and Sites-worker verification High-contrast, low-cognitive-load UX with large text, keyboard focus, and reduced motion What we learned Trust improves when proposal, authorization, and execution are visibly separate. WebMCP gives models semantic access to application capabilities without forcing the application to surrender its policy boundary. What’s next Multi-user identity, passkeys, caregiver and small-business policy packs, privacy-preserving audit export, localization, and broader WebMCP conformance testing. Real-money connectivity remains out of scope until external security review. Try it Live app: https://at-attin.astronebulae.chatgpt.site ATC is fictional, device-local, and has no cash value. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Labmate
pitch: An AI lab where your tutor watches the experiment, not the chat. The agent proposes evidence, the learner stays in control — bidirectional tutoring on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI lab where your tutor watches the experiment, not the chat. The agent proposes evidence, the learner stays in control — bidirectional tutoring on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When we entered the WebMCP Challenge, our honest goal was to check what we could do with it. The showcase examples were mostly agents filling shopping carts and forms — useful, but one-directional: the agent acts, the page obeys. Meanwhile, every AI tutor we knew worked beside an educational tool, never inside it. The learner plays with a simulation, then manually types what happened into a chat; the model reasons from a stale summary and, worst of all, happily does the thinking the student was supposed to do. That combination suggested a question: what if the tutor lived inside the lab page itself — reading the same live bench, proposing evidence, but structurally unable to take over the scientific method? A tutor that is bidirectional: the agent sees what the learner actually did, and the learner sees and approves everything the agent actually proposes. LabMate is our answer. What it does LabMate is a 15-minute high-school physics inquiry around one LED circuit, following the scientific method: Predict → Design → Evidence → Reflect . The learner states a prediction ("if resistance decreases, the LED gets brighter because current increases") and locks it. The hypothesis and the final conclusion are learner-owned : visible to the agent, writable by no tool. Through WebMCP, the agent sees the exact live bench — voltages, saved trials, the current stage, model limits, and the page's revision number. It proposes one fair experiment at a time. The proposal appears as a preview card and touches nothing until the learner approves, edits, or rejects it. The demo's climax is a confound challenge: the learner changes the voltage from 5 V to 9 V after the agent last looked. The agent's now-outdated proposal is rejected atomically ( stale_revision ), because it was written against a world it never observed. The agent re-inspects, spots the second variable, and proposes a revised trial that restores a valid controlled comparison. Once a controlled pair exists, the page compares trials and reports the valid pairs. The learner — not the agent — answers four reflection prompts (what changed, what stayed constant, what the measurements show, whether the prediction was supported) and locks the conclusion. Under the hood, the simulation is a conceptual teaching model: $I = V/R$, $P = V \times I$, LED brightness bands keyed to current, and six trial slots — of which the agent may fill at most four, so one slot is always reserved for the learner. Every accepted mutation increments a shared revision and records a Human/Agent receipt, so the collaboration is auditable. And when document.modelContext is unavailable, the status chip flips to LAB READY and the whole lab still works in a regular browser. How we built it The app is a static front end: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Tailwind CSS with shadcn-derived controls. No database, no login, no OpenAI API calls, and deliberately no custom chat surface. Everything — human clicks and agent tool calls — flows through one revision-safe command layer: gates → validation → revision + 1 → a single atomic state update → a receipt. The agent's three Site tools are thin views over those same commands: inspect_experiment() — the only read-only tool; returns the full experiment snapshot. propose_trial(...) — the approval gate; creates a visible preview card, not evidence. compare_trials(...) — surfaces controlled pairs. Two discipline points we refused to compromise on: every tool schema rejects extra fields ( additionalProperties: false ), and actor is never accepted from the model — the registration adapter pins it to agent . Failures are structured codes ( hypothesis_required , approval_required , student_slot_reserved , stale_revision , trial_limit_reached …), never prose, so the agent can actually replan from them. For quality: 26 Vitest unit/contract tests and 3 Playwright flows, including a document.modelContext shim that lets us test the full agent loop headlessly — plus a live run in ChatGPT's desktop browser. typecheck , test , test:e2e , build , and lint are all green. Challenges we ran into Trust by construction. The hardest question wasn't "how does the agent help" but "how do we guarantee it can't write the conclusion?" Our answer is structural: learner-owned fields exist in the page state but in no tool schema. There is nothing for the model to call. Two authors, one page. Human and agent mutate the same state concurrently. Optimistic concurrency ( expected_revision ) makes stale writes fail atomically — but making that rejection legible , so the agent understands "the world changed, look again," took real schema and prompt design. A deterministic demo with a probabilistic actor. Our centerpiece moment depends on the model doing the right thing on stage. We shaped the tools (one-proposal-at-a-time, structured errors) and the demo prompts so the inspect → propose → human-intervenes → stale-rejection → replan loop happens reliably. Testing without ChatGPT. CI can't drive the desktop app, so we mirrored document.modelContext in a Playwright shim and contract-tested the adapter against it. Honest scope. The simulation is a conceptual teaching model: overloaded is a teaching warning above 20 mA, not a real component rating, and forward voltage, tolerance, and temperature are intentionally omitted. The page always says so. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop runs live in ChatGPT's built-in browser: agent proposes → learner approves → human changes the world → stale proposal rejected → agent re-plans → learner concludes, with a receipt for every step. The agent is useful because it is constrained: one proposal at a time, a trial quota that always leaves the learner a slot, and zero silent writes. The lab never depends on the agent: in a plain browser, the pedagogy stays intact. The quality gate is green end-to-end: 26 unit/contract tests, 3 e2e flows, typecheck, build, lint. What we learned Treating the page as the source of truth turns tool design into contract design . Structured error codes beat chat prose for agent replanning. Human–agent experience is mostly a state machine: who may write what, when, and what happens when the world changes under the agent. Getting that machine right is the product. Strictness is what makes trust possible: additionalProperties: false and a pinned actor are the difference between learner control as an aspiration and as an invariant. "The agent may only propose" felt restrictive at first — it turned out to be the feature. It kept the experiments fair and kept the student thinking. What's next for LabMate More missions on the same Predict → Design → Evidence → Reflect skeleton — optics, kinematics, reaction rates — with teacher-authored content. A classroom view so teachers can see receipts, common confounds, and where students get stuck. Extracting the pattern : learner-owned fields, approval gates, revision-safe commands, and agent quotas generalize beyond this lab, and we want to package them for other "human-owned page, agent coach" sites built on WebMCP. title: Rota: the agent proposes, you approve
pitch: Fourteen staff, seven days, one agent that does the hard part and then hands it back. It can propose the whole week. Only you can approve it.
about_excerpt: Fourteen staff, seven days, one agent that does the hard part and then hands it back. It can propose the whole week. Only you can approve it. Like Comment Story Updates Next week's rota as you find it: 73% covered, fifteen unfilled slots, and one rule breach that nobody has spotted. The agent calls the page's own rule engine and rings the two shifts it means: nine hours' rest where eleven are required. Fourteen proposed assignments render as dashed cards on the shifts they affect. Nothing has been applied to the rota yet. The consent surface. Every edit is a checkbox, with before and after coverage, breaches and cost, plus what approval would leave unfixed. Every registered tool with its JSON Schema, runnable by hand. The badge shows whether WebMCP is native here or the bundled polyfill. Every tool call recorded: arguments, result, timing, whether it was read-only, the edits it staged, and who called it. Exportable as JSON. Hours against contract, and who is carrying the weekends and the closes. Managers get this wrong by hand, and staff notice. Wage cost by day and by person against a GBP 5,000 weekly budget, with overtime priced at 1.5x. The agent reads this before proposing. The same week in dark appearance. Light and dark are both first-class, and the theme follows your system by default. Inspiration I didn't want to build another "AI does your admin" demo. They're easy to make and they all feel the same, because the interesting part gets skipped. An agent doing a job for you is only half a product. The other half is how you check it. Shift rotas turned out to be a good place to ask that question. A rota isn't really a spreadsheet, it's a promise to fourteen people about their week. Get it wrong and someone's childcare falls through. So it's exactly the kind of work you'd happily hand to a machine, and exactly the kind you'd never let a machine send out on its own. That gave me one rule I stuck to for the whole build: the agent gets no tool that commits anything. Everything else followed from that. What it does Rota is a shift scheduler for a small café. Fourteen staff, seven days, and an agent that works the rota with you rather than taking it off your hands. When you open it, next week is about three quarters done. Fifteen slots are still empty, and there's one problem buried in it: Marco closes on Wednesday at half nine and opens again on Thursday at half six. Nine hours between shifts. The law wants eleven. Neither shift looks wrong on its own, which is why this kind of mistake survives a proofread. Ask it to finish the rota and it makes about five tool calls. It reads the gaps, runs the solver, and stages fourteen assignments that add £1,384 to the wage bill. Then it stops and tells you the fifteenth slot can't be filled at all: Liam is seventeen so the curfew rules him out, and nobody else left is a certified shift lead. Nothing on the calendar has moved. The fourteen proposals sit on top of the shifts they'd affect as dashed cards, and a drawer lists them one per line with a checkbox each. It shows you what approving would do to coverage, to your rule breaches, and to the cost. Take twelve of them and drop two if you like. Then there's publishing, which is the one action that actually tells fourteen people when they're working. I made that a declarative WebMCP form and left toolautosubmit off it. Per the spec, that means an agent can fill the form in and then has to stop. The browser puts focus on the submit button and waits for a person. So the agent writes the note to staff, picks who gets notified, ticks the confirmation box, and cannot press send. A few other things that come out of building it this way: When it can't do something it tells you why and quotes the rule. "Everyone available is over their consecutive-day limit and Tom is the only other keyholder" is useful. "I couldn't find cover" isn't. Every tool call is logged with its arguments, what came back, how long it took, and who made it. You can export the lot as JSON and answer "why is Nadia on Friday night" properly. Undo works across approvals, because every edit carries a forward and a backward patch. No signup and no API key to try it. How we built it TypeScript, React and Vite. No backend, no database, nothing phoning home. The roster never leaves your tab, which is what makes doing this client side an honest choice instead of a shortcut. Four reasons it's WebMCP and not an MCP server, roughly in the order they mattered to me: The state is in the tab. The roster, the rules and the solver all run in the browser. A server would have to mirror the manager's working state, and half of that state is a proposal nobody has agreed to yet. I didn't want the model reasoning about employment law. It never does. It calls validate_schedule and repeats what the page's own engine said. When assign_staff refuses, the refusal is a fact you can act on: "Liam Doyle is not certified as Baker." The agent needs to be able to point at things. When it says Thursday is the problem it calls highlight and puts a ring round the two shifts on your screen. Nothing running on a server can do that. Some tools should only exist sometimes. Select a shift and two more appear, scoped to it. Stage a proposal and revise_proposal shows up. Deselect and they're withdrawn. Every one of those changes fires toolchange . A static tool list on a server can't manage this, because a server has no idea what you're looking at. Under that there are three layers. The rules engine is plain TypeScript with no React and no DOM near it, because it's the part that has to be correct. Fifteen rules, split between the statutory and contractual ones and the softer ones about fairness, cost and preference. Ranking candidates works by simulating and re-validating. To score someone for a shift I copy the roster, add the assignment, and run the real validator over the copy. It's not the fastest approach, but it means the ranking can never disagree with the rules, and that was worth more to me than the speed. The solver is most-constrained-first, then two passes of local search. It's a heuristic and I'm not pretending otherwise. It won't always find the best answer, but it never returns an illegal rota and it's quick enough to run inside a tool call. Both agent modes go through getTools() and executeTool() . The in-page agent holds no references to its own tool functions on purpose, so my own UI is exercising the same path an outside agent would take. There's also a polyfill for document.modelContext , so the whole thing works in any browser today. If you open it somewhere with real WebMCP the app notices and stands aside. Challenges we ran into The demo data was the hardest part, which I did not expect. My first version of the broken week had 31 rule breaches and 65% coverage, and it just read as sloppy rather than realistic. Worse, I'd written more shifts than the staff had contracted hours to cover, so the solver couldn't finish no matter how good it was and filled nothing at all. Getting to a week that looks like a real half-finished rota, is genuinely fixable, and still leaves one slot that honestly can't be filled took several rounds of counting capacity against demand, role by role. The edit model took two attempts. Applying patches straight meant two assignments to the same shift clobbered each other, so now each patch is rebased against the roster as it stands at the moment the edit lands. And then there was the bug that nearly sank it. The "roster as proposed" value was being rebuilt every time it was read, and it's used as a state selector that compares by reference. So staging anything at all set off an infinite render loop, which tore down React and quietly unregistered all 32 tools. The app looked fine until the first time the agent tried to change something. Accomplishments that we're proud of That the constraint held. There are 36 tools and not one of them can commit, approve or publish. It would have been easy to add a commit tool for convenience halfway through and I didn't. The correctness work is tested rather than claimed. 28 checks on the engine with no browser involved, 33 in a real browser, and 35 that click through the suggested prompts the way a judge would. They assert properties I actually care about: that anyone the ranker calls eligible really is eligible when you re-validate, that the solver never increases the number of hard breaches, that the cheap objective is never more expensive than the balanced one, that absence cover never backfills with the person who's absent, and that the publish form fills but refuses to submit. And the polyfill, because it means anyone can open the URL and use every tool without an origin trial, an API key or a signup. What we learned Three things I got wrong first, all of which changed the code more than any prompt tuning did. I had tools returning JSON.  Inspiration 

 The Nostr and Lightning Network communities overlap heavily, but there's no easy way to bridge the two — to search a Lightning node and see who's behind it on Nostr, or to look up a Nostr identity and see their node's standing on the network. We wanted to build a tool the wider Nostr community could actually use, and one that's genuinely built for the agent-native web this hackathon is exploring — not just a human-facing dashboard, but a site AI agents can query and act on directly. 

 What it does 

 Lightning Network Explorer lets you: 

 
 Search Lightning nodes by pubkey or alias, with capacity, channel count, and network scoring pulled from Amboss 
 View detailed node stats on a per-node basis 
 See network-wide stats — total nodes, channels, and capacity 
 Match a Nostr identity (npub or NIP-05) to its associated Lightning address and node data, resolved live against our own relay (wss://hasky.chat) 
 

 With WebMCP support, an AI agent can call these same lookups directly — searching a node, pulling network stats, or resolving a Nostr identity's Lightning presence — without needing a human to click through the UI first. 

 How we built it 

 Built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind. Node and network data comes from the Amboss GraphQL API; Nostr profile resolution runs against our own relay at wss://hasky.chat. WebMCP tools are registered via document.modelContext.register(), exposing node search, node detail, and network stats directly to agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting clean fallback behavior for malformed or unknown pubkeys (Amboss returns a GraphQL error rather than a clean "not found," which we had to handle gracefully), and designing the Nostr × Lightning matcher so it degrades sensibly when no match is found rather than treating that as an error state. 

 What's next 

 Deeper zap/wallet interactions via Alby Hub and NWC, historical trend charts for network growth, and expanding node scoring with more data sources.

title: HopeSong.ai
pitch: A WebMCP-powered spiritual companion that turns moments of fear, weariness, and uncertainty into personalized journeys of Scripture, prayer, and hope.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered spiritual companion that turns moments of fear, weariness, and uncertainty into personalized journeys of Scripture, prayer, and hope.

 findBibleVerse — Bahasa Indonesia Demo 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 HopeSong.ai began with a simple question: what if AI could recognize a moment of fear, weariness, or uncertainty and help someone find a meaningful path toward hope? 

 When people feel overwhelmed, they may not know what to search for or where to begin. I wanted to create an experience that starts with the human need itself and connects that moment with Scripture, reflection, prayer, and a simple next step. 

 What it does 

 HopeSong.ai is a WebMCP-powered spiritual companion built around a journey from fear to peace and hope. 

 The website introduces users to songs, prayer, Scripture, and hope-centered experiences. Through WebMCP, HopeSong.ai also exposes structured capabilities that an AI agent can discover and use directly. 

 The current implementation provides two WebMCP tools: 

 findBibleVerse — finds a relevant Bible verse based on the user's topic, emotion, or spiritual need. It supports Bahasa Indonesia, English, Chinese, Korean, and Spanish. 

 findHopeJourney — creates a guided journey consisting of Scripture, Reflection, Prayer, a simple Next Step, and Hope. It currently supports English and Bahasa Indonesia. 

 For example, when someone expresses, "I am afraid and uncertain about my future," the agent can use findHopeJourney to return a structured experience designed around that need. 

 How I built it 

 HopeSong.ai is built with React and Vite and deployed as a live web application. 

 I integrated WebMCP using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , allowing the browser to expose HopeSong.ai's capabilities as structured tools instead of leaving them only as visual website interactions. 

 Both tools are read-only and use defined input schemas for topic and language. The implementation can be inspected in the public source code, and the live demo allows the WebMCP tools to be discovered and executed in a supported browser environment. 

 Human + AI collaboration 

 The human brings the need. 

 The AI interprets the context and discovers the appropriate WebMCP capability. 

 HopeSong.ai provides the structured experience behind it. 

 This creates a different interaction from simply browsing pages or searching through content. The user does not need to know which page, verse, or resource to look for first. Their need becomes the starting point for the interaction. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was moving from a traditional website experience to capabilities that an AI agent could discover and execute reliably. 

 I also worked through browser and origin requirements while testing the emerging WebMCP implementation, validated tool discovery with document.modelContext.getTools() , and tested tool execution directly on the production origin. 

 Another challenge was deciding how much functionality to expose. Rather than adding many shallow tools, I focused on two complementary capabilities that demonstrate a clear progression from finding relevant Scripture to creating a more complete Hope Journey. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that HopeSong.ai evolved from a content experience into a working WebMCP-enabled application. 

 The project now exposes two discoverable tools, supports multilingual Scripture discovery, and demonstrates a complete Hope Journey from an emotional need to Scripture, reflection, prayer, a practical next step, and hope. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP is not only a technical addition to the project. It changes how an AI agent can interact with HopeSong.ai's purpose. 

 What I learned 

 Building HopeSong.ai helped me understand the difference between designing only for human navigation and designing capabilities that can also be understood and used by AI agents. 

 I learned how structured tool definitions, clear input schemas, and focused outputs can turn an existing web experience into something agents can interact with more meaningfully. 

 What's next for HopeSong.ai 

 The current project is intentionally focused on proving the core WebMCP experience. 

 Future versions could expand the Hope Journey with more languages, additional hope-centered resources, deeper personalization, and connections between songs, Scripture, prayer, and the user's ongoing journey. 

 The long-term vision is simple: 

 Find Hope. Find Your Song.

title: JiuTuanZhuo 揪團桌
pitch: Group ordering, agent-native
about_excerpt: Group ordering, agent-native Like Comment Story Updates JiuTuanZhuo home — open a table in one tap. Share link generated after opening a table. Only people with the link can join. Ask Claude in Chrome to order combo vermicelli and sausage for Joe. The agent starts reading the page's WebMCP tools. The agent calls submit_order on the page. Joe's order appears instantly, tagged "Agent order," with no clicks on the UI. Host Elsa orders manually through the UI. The table now shows 2 people, 4 items, NT$220. Human and agent orders sit side by side. Host Elsa orders manually through the UI. The table now shows 2 people, 4 items, NT$220. Human and agent orders sit side by side. The host closes the table. Status flips to Closed and sent to the store; each share is locked. Inspiration Office group orders in Taiwan are rarely voluntary. Someone gets picked to ask everyone what they want, and that person has often never run a group order before. After a wall of "+1" messages in the LINE group, figuring out who ordered what, who changed their mind, and who hasn't paid lands entirely on them. JiuTuanZhuo was built for that person: open a table, drop the link, let the system handle the rest. What it does The official website of 油庫口蚵仔麵線 (Youkukou Oyster Vermicelli) now has a built-in "open a table" feature. The host gets a private link; only people with the link can order. Everyone orders from their own phone, every view syncs in realtime, and the host always sees the current combined order. Tables are fully isolated: three companies can each open a table at the same time without their orders mixing. Humans order through the UI; agents order through WebMCP tools declared on the same page. How we built it Lovable (React) + Supabase (anonymous auth, RLS, RPCs, realtime). The frontend is an interface, not a boundary: pricing, item validation, and permissions are all enforced in Postgres RPCs under RLS, so agents and humans go through the same rules. The page declares three WebMCP tools: get_table_status : marked readOnlyHint , returns structured JSON, with user-entered fields wrapped as user_content so they are treated as data, not instructions add_order : writes require an on-page human confirmation before execution close_table : registered only in the host's session; other participants' agents never see this tool All tools unregister when the table closes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part came first: breaking "+1 in a LINE group" into three actions (open, order, close) and deciding which rules belong in the database layer rather than the frontend. The second was environment setup: getting Chrome to actually call the WebMCP tools on the page took a fair amount of configuration and debugging. The third was pinning down where the latency actually lives. Measured on the page, tool execution is in the millisecond range: read tools return frontend state directly in 0.1–0.3 ms; write tools take 498 ms on the first call and settle at 66–72 ms after that. End to end, one order still takes about a minute. The gap sits entirely in the browser-side agent's tool discovery and reasoning; the page implementation itself is not the bottleneck. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is a 40-year-old street-food institution, and the second-generation owner built the system herself with AI vibe coding, so that customers' agents can place orders directly. Planning, architecture, and deployment were all done in-house, with no outside software vendor and no engineering team. The shop is the test bed: what gets built one day is in front of real customers the next. What we learned When the goal is clear enough, AI can build it. Writing code is not the barrier; knowing whose problem you are solving is. What's next for JiuTuanZhuo 揪團桌 First, reshape the flow around how people in Taiwan actually buy: separate pickup and delivery after an order comes in, and print tickets straight to an IoT kitchen printer. Then, service by service, connect Google Maps scooter-distance calculation, payment, the Lalamove delivery fleet, and e-invoicing, until every step from order to handoff is linked. JiuTuanZhuo is the entry point. From here we build inward, one piece at a time, into a full internal operating system for the shop that agents can run directly, ending with the POS itself. Ordering, ticketing, payment, fulfillment, and invoicing on one shared data layer is what a real closed loop looks like. title: Islanding — Restore Critical Power W/o Energizing the Fault
pitch: A human sets safety priorities; an AI agent explores restoration plans; the page enforces exact approval before a synthetic switch is touched.
about_excerpt: A human sets safety priorities; an AI agent explores restoration plans; the page enforces exact approval before a synthetic switch is touched. Like Comment Story Updates Storm outage overview: feeder F1 faulted, 55% battery reserve, and nine WebMCP tools ready. The agent compares plans: the 18% reserve option is blocked and the 27% reserve option is valid. Human approval is bound to the exact switching sequence and held privately in the page. Receipt R-104 confirms one execution: hospital, shelter, and water restored with 26% reserve. Inspiration A grid diagram is readable to an operator but dangerously ambiguous to a general browser agent. The same switch icon can hide a fault interlock, transient state, capacity limit, and sequence dependency. Clicking the right-looking SVG control is not the same as understanding whether a plan is safe. We wanted to show WebMCP at its strongest: not as a faster form filler, but as the semantic control plane for a live professional digital twin. The human should contribute priorities and consent. The agent should contribute rapid constrained exploration. The page should remain the authority for rules, state, and consequences. What it does Islanding opens on a seeded storm outage. Feeder F1 is faulted; hospital and shelter are critical; battery reserve must stay above 25%. An agent uses nine page-hosted WebMCP tools to read exact incident state and topology, simulate two deterministic switching plans, compare their derived trade-offs, and put the best into visible preview. The operator then marks the water pump critical in the normal UI. That page edit increments the state version, invalidates the old draft, and revokes any approval. The agent sees a structured stale_state , re-reads the human choice, and computes a revised plan. The agent can prepare the exact sequence but cannot approve it. A normal page button creates a short-lived internal grant bound to the current draft hash and version. The grant never enters model context. Only then can the agent execute the synthetic sequence once. Retrying the same idempotency key returns the original receipt, not a second execution. The topology visibly restores hospital, shelter, and water pump while the fault stays isolated. The receipt records human approval, exact draft hash, operations, before/after state versions, and final reserve. How we used WebMCP The top-level document registers nine imperative tools through document.modelContext , with the deprecated navigator.modelContext only as a compatibility fallback: semantic reads: incident state and topology; compute: plan simulation and comparison; reversible collaboration: draft preview and current-state validation; trust boundary: exact preparation, page-held human authorization, idempotent execution; evidence: attributable execution receipt. Every registerTool is awaited inside try / catch , has a JSON Schema and explicit description, and is tied to an AbortController lifecycle. Inputs are validated again at runtime so malformed, extra, stale, and unsafe requests receive corrective structured errors before mutation. Each execute callback accepts the browser's independent cancellation signal. Calls that complete a domain operation write to the visible activity ledger, and simulations create candidates, so none is incorrectly marked read-only. Tool inputs never supply safety outcomes; the deterministic page engine derives them. Most importantly, the tools update the same visible UI a human uses. WebMCP does not create a hidden agent-only workflow. How it improves the user experience Without WebMCP, an agent must interpret SVG positions and click tiny controls while guessing at hidden constraints. With WebMCP, it can say exactly which stable operation it wants to simulate and receive exact consequences. The operator sees both alternatives, the winning preview, the stale-state correction after their own edit, and the final receipt. The result is faster than manual trial-and-error, more legible than autonomous clicking, and safer than giving the model a generic “execute” control. A new human-agent capability Islanding demonstrates co-operation on live shared state. The human is not reduced to writing the perfect prompt, and the agent is not reduced to driving the mouse. The person expresses contextual judgment through the interface and explicitly authorizes one exact consequence. The agent performs repetitive search, comparison, validation, and documentation. The website arbitrates both. That pattern can extend to infrastructure training, industrial digital twins, maintenance planning, emergency exercises, and other domains where consequential actions need semantic context and visible consent. How we built it The project deliberately has no framework, build step, backend, account, credentials, or live data. HTML and CSS render an accessible responsive command center. Three JavaScript modules provide a versioned domain engine, WebMCP contracts/registration, and UI wiring. A Node static server runs it locally. The mocked engine includes topology, priorities, deterministic candidate metrics, fault isolation, reserve rules, draft hashes, stale-state detection, 60-second page-held grants, approval revocation, idempotency, and receipts. Node's built-in test runner exercises the complete workflow and uses a fake modelContext to verify all registrations, schemas, annotations, lifecycle cleanup, and cancellation behavior. Challenges we ran into The hardest design decision was consent. An imperative WebMCP execute callback should not pretend it can securely ask the model for human approval, nor should a secret token be handed back to the model. We split preparation from execution and made authorization an ordinary visible page action. The execution tool can only ask the page whether its private grant matches the exact draft and current version. We also kept “simulation” honest. A tempting higher-coverage plan violates reserve; an unsafe S3 close energizes the fault; changing human priorities invalidates the previous plan. These are business-engine results, not claims generated by the agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is indispensable to the experience rather than bolted on. Human and agent paths use the same domain engine and visible state. The golden demo contains a genuine collaboration beat, a trust beat, and an attributable receipt. Unsafe, stale, unapproved, expired, and duplicate paths fail closed. The entire project remains tiny, deterministic, dependency-free, and easy for judges to run. What we learned Semantic tools are only part of agent readiness. A useful site also needs explicit versions, composable state transitions, corrective errors, visible effects, and a clear boundary between what the model can request and what the human must authorize. WebMCP turns the page from a picture an agent operates into a participant in the interaction. The most compelling agent experiences come from designing that shared contract alongside the human workflow. What's next Next steps would add a real optimization solver behind the same interface, multiple training incidents, richer electrical constraints, immutable exported evidence, and authenticated instructor/operator roles. Any real infrastructure integration would require an entirely separate safety, security, regulatory, and operational program; this prototype intentionally makes no such claim. Agents/clients tested Deterministic fake ModelContext harness: passed registration and execution contract tests. Standard human browser path: locally testable without WebMCP . OpenAI Codex desktop in-app Browser with native site tools: passed on the public deployment on 2026-09-02 . Exactly nine tools were discovered; successful calls included incident/topology reads, two simulations, comparison, and visible draft preview. AI tools used OpenAI Codex for research synthesis, implementation, tests, documentation, and submission preparation. webmcp skill from webmaxru/web-ai-agent-skills for current API, compatibility, lifecycle, and validation guidance. Known Limitations Deterministic synthetic training prototype, not a power-flow solver or operational grid-control system. No live utility data, equipment connection, backend, authentication, or persistence; page state disappears on reload. Human approval proves a local page action, not authenticated identity or cryptographic authorization. The visible activity ledger is demo evidence, not an immutable audit log. Native WebMCP support depends on the client/browser. The prior recorded native run and today's automated tests are distinct forms of evidence. Benefits such as faster exploration are design goals illustrated by the demo, not measured comparative performance claims.
