title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: RoutineForge
pitch: Teach a website new agent tools by demonstrating once.
about_excerpt: Teach a website new agent tools by demonstrating once. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Web agents are often forced into two extremes: fragile visual automation that guesses where to click, or fixed APIs that only expose workflows developers anticipated in advance. We asked a different question: what if a website could learn a new agent tool from a human demonstration? People already teach coworkers by showing a task once. RoutineForge brings that interaction to the web: the human demonstrates intent inside the real product, the application records the underlying business actions, and WebMCP turns the reviewed routine into a reliable tool an agent can discover and invoke. What it does RoutineForge is a WebMCP-native commerce operations workspace with Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Analytics, and Marketing. Its central feature is Routine Studio: A merchant selects Record workflow . They set a date range and market, select metrics, generate a report, and save it. RoutineForge captures five typed, verified semantic actions—not clicks or selectors. The merchant reviews the trace and chooses which values the agent may supply. They publish the routine as generate_weekly_report . An agent discovers and calls the new WebMCP tool with different inputs. The live page follows the execution and returns a report ID, URL, summary, and five verification receipts. The app also exposes ten atomic WebMCP tools for dashboard state, orders, inventory, customers, campaigns, analytics filters, and reports. The demonstrated routine becomes the eleventh tool. Why WebMCP A reporting API could return numbers, but it would miss the shared, visible teaching surface between a person, an agent, and the application. With WebMCP, the human UI and agent tools use the same business actions, validation rules, state, and feedback. The agent does not reverse-engineer the DOM, and the developer does not maintain a second integration that can drift away from the product. RoutineForge also uses WebMCP dynamically. The site begins with ten developer-defined tools. After a person demonstrates and approves a routine, the page registers a new composite tool at runtime. This explores a future where a website's agent interface is shaped safely through use, not limited to a static tool catalog. How we built it RoutineForge is a client-only React and TypeScript app with no login, backend, API key, or third-party dataset. At its core is an Action Registry of versioned definitions. Each definition includes a JSON Schema, effects, input validation, execution logic, and post-execution verification. A shared Action Bus runs the same definitions for human UI events and WebMCP calls. The recorder stores action IDs, versions, typed inputs, structured outputs, sources, timestamps, and verification evidence. It never records coordinates, screenshots, CSS selectors, or generated JavaScript. The Routine Compiler accepts only registered actions. Every binding must be a demonstrated literal, a reviewed routine input, or a prior step output. The Routine Runner resolves bindings, validates each step, stops safely on failure, and returns structured receipts. The app feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool() and registers ten atomic site tools. Publishing a taught routine registers generate_weekly_report with its own JSON Schema and verified execution handler. Published routines persist in IndexedDB and re-register after refresh; Reset demo restores deterministic seed data. Challenges The hardest problem was choosing the right abstraction boundary. Raw click recording looks general but is fragile and difficult to verify. A semantic action layer requires deliberate product architecture, but it survives UI changes and produces meaningful evidence. Dynamic publication also had to remain safe: recorded data or agent input can never become executable code. We solved that with a deliberately small binding language and a compiler that references only registered, versioned actions. Finally, agent activity needed to remain legible to a human. RoutineForge synchronizes the visible workspace with each execution and shows step-level receipts in the same interface. Accomplishments Ten atomic WebMCP tools plus a human-taught composite tool registered at runtime. One semantic execution layer shared by human interactions and agent calls. Typed validation and verification at every action boundary. No selectors, coordinates, screenshots, or generated code in recorded routines. Visible synchronization between agent execution and the human dashboard. A public, deterministic deployment with automated tests and no credentials required. What we learned Agent-native design is not simply adding tools beside an interface. The strongest experience comes from making the human UI and agent interface two views over the same semantic application model. Demonstration alone is not authorization; the human review step transforms a trace into a contract. Verification belongs inside each action definition, so composite routines can remain trustworthy. What's next Next we would generalize the compiler across all registered actions, add a visual routine editor, controlled branches and approval checkpoints, versioning and rollback, dry runs, audit logs, and a developer SDK. Our long-term vision is a web where developers provide safe semantic building blocks, people teach the workflows that matter to them, and agents execute those workflows transparently in the applications where work already lives. Try it Open the live app , select Reset demo , and follow the Routine Studio flow. Source and technical instructions are available in the public MIT-licensed repository . title: Shredly
pitch: Shredly is MCP as a Service. Create and manage MCP servers for your products, no code to deploy, no infrastructure to manage. Now Shredly offers WebMCP to dynamically update your site tools
about_excerpt:
Shredly is MCP as a Service. Create and manage MCP servers for your products, no code to deploy, no infrastructure to manage. Now Shredly offers WebMCP to dynamically update your site tools Like Comment Story Updates 1 2 3 Inspiration Shredly lets developers host MCP servers without managing infrastructure. You define your tools in a dashboard and Shredly handles the rest. But those tools lived entirely server-side. WebMCP changes that, the new browser-native standard lets a webpage register tools directly for AI agents to discover and call. The gap was obvious to us, if we could bridge Shredly's hosted tool definitions into site tools, a site owner could add a new tool in their Shredly dashboard and have it appear as a live site tool for ChatGPT — no redeploy, no code change. What it does shredly-webmcp is a tiny CDN library that bridges Shredly's hosted MCP servers to the browser's WebMCP API. Drop one tag into your page, point it at your Shredly MCP slug, and AI agents browsing your site immediately see your tools in their Site tools panel. Add a new tool in the Shredly dashboard — it appears on your site automatically, with no redeployment. For tools that require user context, a getToken callback resolves the user's Bearer token fresh on every invocation, so per-user auth works even when the user logs in after the page loads.

How we built it

The library is a plain ES module, no build step, no bundler, no dependencies. It calls tools/list on Shredly's JSON-RPC API at page load to fetch tool definitions, then registers each one via document.modelContext.registerTool(). An execute handler proxies tools/call back to Shredly, injecting the user's token at invocation time. A 30-second polling loop picks up any tools added or changed in the dashboard without a page reload. We also built a demo site showing the full flow: connect to any Shredly MCP slug, watch the tools render live, and invoke them directly from the UI. The library ships on a CDN at cdn.shredly.io

Challenges we ran into

document.modelContext did not seem to exist until the ChatGPT desktop app companion browser injects it — and that injection can happen asynchronously after the page scripts have already run. The library had to queue pending tool registrations and flush them the moment the API became available, using a polling loop rather than a one-shot check. We also had to rethink authentication: tools/list (tool discovery) must be unauthenticated so tools register at page load without requiring a token, while tools/call injects the user's token only at invocation time. Getting that split right in the MCP handler required restructuring the auth check to happen after body parsing, not before. CDN cache headers were another gotcha — immutable cache during active development meant stale builds were served long after deploys.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The zero-redeploy update loop works. You can add a tool in the Shredly dashboard, wait 30 seconds, and watch it appear in the ChatGPT Site tools panel on a live deployed site — without touching any code. The library is also small: a single ES module file with no dependencies that any developer can drop into an existing site in two lines. The getToken pattern for per-user auth is clean — it decouples tool registration (which happens at page load) from authorization (which happens at call time), making it work naturally with any auth flow.

What we learned

WebMCP is strict about timing: tools must be registered during the initial page load, not behind a user interaction or async gate. That constraint shaped the entire architecture — the library has to start fetching and registering immediately, before the user has done anything.

What's next for Shredly

Publishing shredly-webmcp to npm so React, Vue, and Svelte apps can bundle it properly without CDN workarounds. Deeper dashboard integration — showing site owners which of their pages have the library installed and surfacing per-tool invocation analytics. OAuth support for getToken flows where the user needs to authorize access before tools can be called. And as WebMCP adoption grows beyond ChatGPT, making sure the bridge works across every agent that implements document.modelContext.

title: RE:TURN
pitch: A living museum record rebuilt by communities, curators, and WebMCP agents. An agent can help reconstruct history, it cannot decide whose history becomes official.
about_excerpt: A living museum record rebuilt by communities, curators, and WebMCP agents. An agent can help reconstruct history, it cannot decide whose history becomes official. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Main Page Collection Page (Moonbird Mask) Curator Page Inspiration Museum labels sound finished. Behind a lot of them there is a hole: a stretch of years where nobody wrote down who owned the thing, a place name copied off a dealer's invoice instead of asked from the people who made it, a phrase like "ceremonial use" standing in for knowledge that somebody still has. The people who could fill those holes usually have nowhere to put what they know. When they do send something in, it either sits in an inbox forever or gets quietly folded into the official text with no name on it. We wanted to see what that process looks like with agents in it. The problem showed up right away. An agent that reads accession records and drafts label language is genuinely useful. An agent that can also publish is an agent deciding whose version of history becomes official, and that is not a thing we wanted to build. So the rule became: research is free, the record needs a curator. What it does RE:TURN is a museum collection where the record is treated as unfinished. Eight fictional objects, each with a public label, a provenance timeline, and the gaps in that timeline marked rather than smoothed over. A visitor can flip any label to see the questions behind it. They can submit a photograph, a document, or an oral history, and they choose at that moment whether it may be published, published without their name, or kept private for internal research only. On the other side, a curator works the inbox. Community material arrives marked submitted, not verified, and it sits beside the official record instead of inside it. A curator agent can compare a submission against the accession record, build a timeline, and draft new label wording. Nothing it drafts goes public on its own. The draft lands in a human's queue with the evidence attached, and a person approves it, edits it, or turns it down. Why this is a good fit for WebMCP The interesting question in this domain is not "can an agent do the work." It is "who is allowed to decide." Those two things need to come apart, and WebMCP is the first browser API we have used where they come apart cleanly. Tools are declared by the page, scoped to a role, and executed by the page. The site decides what an action means. The model does not get to reinterpret it. That let us put a policy gateway behind every single tool call and make the answer an agent gets back into a real part of the interface rather than an HTTP status. There are five answers. applied means it was within authority and it is done. pending_approval means a person now holds it, and here is an id to poll. denied means the policy refused, here is the code and here is what would change the outcome. invalid means the caller made a mistake, and here is the field. Error means nothing was written. Thirteen policy codes are reachable through the tool surface. submitted_sole_authority fires when an agent tries to change an official label citing only community material. consent_not_public blocks publishing something a contributor did not agree to publish. approval_snapshot_mismatch catches a stale draft trying to overwrite a label that changed while the approval was waiting. A fourteenth code, outside_agent_surface, exists so that it can never fire: deletion and physical return are classified CRITICAL and no tool maps to them at all. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Someone's knowledge can reach the record without being swallowed by it. A contributor sends a photograph with a consent choice. A curator agent compares it against the verified 1968 invoice, finds the contradiction, and drafts language for it. All of that happens without publishing anything, and the contribution keeps its own voice on the page instead of dissolving into the museum's. Before, those were two disconnected things. A contact form on one side that swallowed submissions, and a collections system on the other that only staff could see. An agent can also be refused in a way it can act on. Ask for a label change backed only by community material and you do not get a 400 with a sentence in it. You get submitted_sole_authority, a recovery line telling you what would work, and a referral id, because the gateway handed that refusal to a curator. The agent polls the id and carries on with something else. Being told no becomes a step in the workflow. Two agents can also work the same object from opposite sides without reaching each other's tools. A community page registers 10 tools. The curator console registers 15. The server re-checks the role on every call, so registration is a convenience rather than the security boundary. One more thing we are happy with: files stay files. Binaries never cross the tool surface. A photograph goes up through an ordinary multipart POST, and the agent then reads its id with list_my_uploads and binds it with attach_assets. The whole contribution completes through tools without a single byte passing through a tool call. How it creates a better experience For a contributor, the main thing is that consent is asked where the choice is made, and the record keeps the promise. If you pick "public, with my name," the form asks for the name right there. We had to learn this one the hard way, which is in the challenges section below. Length limits are enforced as you type instead of at the end of a five-step form, and every submission gets a receipt page showing what happened to it, including any question the curator sent back. For a curator, the console and the agent surface never disagree. When the gateway hands something to a person, it shows up in the console, in list_pending_approvals, in check_approval, and in the summary count. All four, or an agent is working from a different picture of the queue than the human sitting next to it. Approvals are snapshot-checked, so a draft that has gone stale cannot quietly publish over a newer label. For a reader, community material is visible and labelled as submitted. Only public_attributed carries a name. Label revisions show a word-level diff of what changed and when. How we implemented WebMCP Three files do the work. lib/webmcp/tools.ts is the catalogue. Twenty-three tools, each with a name, a description, JSON-Schema properties, a role, and readOnly / untrusted annotations. One declaration, read by three consumers: the browser registration, the server's argument validation, and the tool panel in the console. lib/webmcp/register.ts hands them to the browser. context.registerTool({ name: tool.name, description: tool.description, inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: tool.properties ?? {}, required: tool.required ?? [], additionalProperties: false, }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: tool.readOnly, untrustedContentHint: tool.untrusted ?? false }, signal, execute: async (args) => (await fetch(`/api/tools/${tool.name}`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(args ?? {}), })).json(), }); context is document.modelContext, falling back to navigator.modelContext on browsers that still only expose the older one. Registration follows the session role. additionalProperties: false makes the published schema say exactly what the server enforces, so an undeclared argument comes back refused with a list of what the tool actually takes, rather than being dropped in silence. app/api/tools/[name]/route.ts is what runs. Because execute posts to the same route any HTTP client would use, the tool surface and the HTTP surface cannot drift apart. Every consequential call goes through evaluatePolicy, a pure function with no I/O, before anything is written. Submitted content comes back to a curator agent flagged untrusted_content, and no tool takes authority from text sitting inside a document. Next.js App Router on vinext, React 19, deployed as a Cloudflare Worker with D1 and R2. Challenges we ran into The consent bug we are least proud of.  The form offered "Public, with my name" and had nowhere to type a name. Left blank, the public record printed "Contributor chose not to be named," which is the exact opposite of what the person chose. The byline was reading a field from step one labelled "Where did this come from?", a question about the object rather than the person. We now ask for the name on the consent step and refuse the combination server-side. It was a small fix for something that mattered a lot more than its size. Our tests went stale without failing loudly.  We ran a long browser pass over the live deployment, filled in hundreds of verification cells, and wrote "no unverified areas." Then we ran our own smoke suite against that same deployment and eight checks failed, and had been failing since the previous deploy. None of them was a product bug. Every one was a check pinn

title: Agent-Native Concierge for WebMCP
pitch: Users choose outcomes, agents read structured WebMCP tools, and risky actions pause for human approval.
about_excerpt:
Users choose outcomes, agents read structured WebMCP tools, and risky actions pause for human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most websites are still designed as pages for humans first, then agents are expected to interpret menus, labels, buttons, and layout after the fact. That creates friction: agents can miss context, users do not want to learn every tool, and high-risk actions need clear boundaries. 

 Agent-Native Concierge explores the reverse design pattern: start with an agent-readable action contract, then render a clean human interface from that structure. 

 What it does 

 The demo is a WebMCP-enabled concierge website. A user starts from a simple goal, such as creating a birthday card set. Instead of showing a long tool menu, the site shows outcome cards: different possible results, what each one produces, and what level of confirmation is required. 

 The page exposes structured WebMCP tools for agents: 

 
 get_agent_contract describes the site purpose, allowed actions, limits, and confirmation rules. 
 get_action_risk_ladder returns a five-level safety ladder, from read-only actions to actions that must be handled by a human. 
 get_outcome_gallery returns result-first examples so the user can choose outcomes, not tool names. 
 create_action_dry_run creates a safe simulated action plan before anything risky is executed. 
 

 How we built it 

 The project is a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript demo with WebMCP metadata and tool handlers. The human interface stays intentionally minimal: a concierge input area, outcome cards, and a safety panel. The agent interface is explicit: tools expose stable names, risk levels, expected inputs, outputs, and confirmation requirements. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was avoiding a normal website-with-chatbot pattern. The goal was not to make an agent guess where buttons are. The goal was to let the website declare its action structure clearly enough that an agent can operate safely and explain its choices back to the user. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The demo shows three product principles: 

 
 Result-first interaction: users choose visible outcomes instead of learning tool names. 
 Agent-readable safety: every tool has a risk level and confirmation rule. 
 Dry-run before action: the agent can show what it plans to do before any external effect. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is useful because it gives websites a way to expose their capabilities in a structured, inspectable form. That makes agent use more reliable than screen-reading alone, and it makes human oversight easier. 

 What's next 

 Next, this pattern can be expanded into more vertical demos: education, legal intake, design workflows, and customer service. Each vertical can keep the same safety ladder while exposing its own domain-specific outcome gallery and WebMCP tools.

title: Velaire — WebMCP Agreements for Service Businesses
pitch: Two independent agents negotiate through a live service website while humans control every consequential decision—with versioned offers, immutable receipts, and accountable change orders.
about_excerpt: Two independent agents negotiate through a live service website while humans control every consequential decision—with versioned offers, immutable receipts, and accountable change orders. Like Comment Story Updates System architecture: two independent ChatGPT agents share one revisioned ServiceCase while humans retain final authority. Live sequence: request, evidence, offer, counter, revision, booking and acknowledgment across separate agent sessions. Owner journey: scan the queue, read the case, stage terms, visibly send, wait for the customer and propose changed work. Customer journey: qualify, verify, open a case, negotiate, compare versions and prepare a human-confirmed booking. WebMCP observability exposes result codes, latency, revision effects, recovery states and zero autonomous commitments. Promise diff: offer V1, customer counter, accepted V2 and later changed work stay visible against the frozen receipt. Safety and trust gates cover emergencies, privacy, state, revisions, offers, human approval, asynchronous waits and audit. Structured tool results become useful map, route, market-price, project-timeline and agreement artifacts for people. WebMCP tool surface for discovery, evidence, negotiation, booking, routing, project planning, change control and audit. Evidence-aware discovery uses provenance, freshness, synthetic labels and untrusted-content hints before recommending a next step. Native WebMCP replaces brittle click automation with declared intent, typed inputs, explicit effects and valid next actions. Agreement state machine: valid states, revision checks and visible human gates control every consequential transition. Recorded proof: both sides finish on revision 9, a $320 authorized total and the same append-only decision trail. Recorded proof: the customer agent opens a request and the independent owner agent retrieves the same case and constraints. Recorded proof: a +$145 change order stays pending beside the locked $175 booking until the customer decides. Inspiration Service businesses already have websites, but most of those sites expose pages and contact forms rather than the structured truth an AI agent needs to complete a real customer journey. Pricing, availability, exclusions, messages, approvals, and later change orders are scattered across interfaces. An agent can discover a business yet still over-promise, act on stale terms, or mistake a private draft for an accepted agreement. We built Velaire to test a more useful WebMCP pattern: can an ordinary service website become a trustworthy agreement room for a customer's agent, an owner's agent, and the two humans who retain authority? What it does Velaire is a WebMCP-native reference implementation for service businesses, demonstrated through a fictional HVAC company. A customer speaks naturally to ChatGPT; the live website publishes typed capabilities that let the agent check service fit, policies, business evidence, pricing, and safety before opening a structured service case. A separate owner ChatGPT finds that same case through the owner route. The agents are independent and never role-play both parties in one conversation. They communicate through one revisioned ServiceCase that remains authoritative for messages, offers, counters, bookings, receipts, and changed work. The owner agent may prepare an offer, but it stays private until the owner presses Send. The customer agent may compare versions and prepare a booking, but only the customer can confirm it. That confirmation freezes an immutable receipt. If work changes later, Velaire compares the proposed charge against the exact accepted snapshot instead of silently rewriting history. Demo journey The customer asks for same-day help with an AC blowing warm air. ChatGPT checks eligibility, pricing evidence, availability, credentials, and safety. It opens a case with a $180 ceiling and explicit no-surprise-fee constraints. A separate owner agent retrieves the live request and prepares a $195 offer. The owner visibly sends the offer. The customer counters at $175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sends offer version two. The customer agent compares both versions field by field. The agent prepares the booking; the customer confirms it, creating an immutable $175 receipt. The owner proposes a +$145 capacitor change order. Velaire shows the added scope, $320 total, and time impact against the original promise. The customer approves the change, the owner acknowledges it, and both agents independently read revision 9 with no pending decision. No real payment is taken, and every person, address, credential, review, price, and transaction shown is synthetic demonstration data. The WebMCP tool surface Customer discovery and trust velaire_check_service_fit checks need, postcode, urgency, budget, safety, and service eligibility. velaire_get_business_evidence returns source cards for credentials, pricing, availability, cancellation, warranty, and reviews. velaire_get_market_price_context and velaire_compare_quote_context provide transparent pricing context without presenting synthetic estimates as live market truth. Service, policy, site-search, contact, and agent-help tools make the ordinary website understandable without scraping its buttons. Shared customer–owner workflow velaire_open_service_case creates the authoritative record. velaire_get_service_case returns its current revision, messages, offers, decisions, and valid next actions. velaire_submit_case_message adds a bounded question or counteroffer and rejects stale revisions. velaire_wait_for_owner_reply and velaire_wait_for_customer_reply represent waiting honestly, with timeout and cancellation recovery. velaire_set_service_location, velaire_plan_service_route, and velaire_get_case_visuals return map, route, timeline, and visual artifacts. Owner workflow velaire_list_service_cases and velaire_get_owner_case expose the owner queue and exact case state. velaire_stage_owner_reply, velaire_stage_service_offer, and velaire_stage_change_order keep drafts private until a visible human Send action. Agreement protection and audit velaire_compare_offer_versions compares price, timing, deposit, warranty, scope, exclusions, and expiry deterministically. velaire_prepare_booking stages one exact offer version; it cannot confirm it. velaire_get_booking_receipt returns the full accepted snapshot rather than a mutable offer reference. velaire_compare_change_order checks later work against the accepted promise. velaire_audit_invoice_against_receipt detects invoice drift. velaire_get_webmcp_health exposes tool-call success, latency, revisions, read/action distribution, and recovery states. How we built it Velaire uses React, strict TypeScript, and Vite, deployed as a static application on Vercel. It registers native imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). The human UI and every WebMCP handler dispatch through the same pure TypeScript command gateway and reducer, preventing agent actions from bypassing the rules shown to humans. The demo persists state in localStorage, synchronizes tabs with BroadcastChannel and browser events, uses optimistic revision checks for every write, and records an append-only audit trail. Tool inputs use strict JSON Schema and runtime validation. Route scoping keeps customer and owner capabilities separate. Safety and human authority Emergency phrases such as gas smell, smoke, sparks, fire, or carbon monoxide trigger a safety stop instead of an ordinary quote flow. Agent schemas exclude payment details, direct contact identifiers, and exact home addresses. Agents can inspect, draft, compare, and prepare; humans alone send owner commitments, confirm bookings, approve changed work, and send the final acknowledgment. Challenges The hardest problem was not tool registration. It was preserving meaning across two asynchronous sessions: distinguishing a draft from a sent offer, rejecting stale writes, keeping accepted terms immutable, and treating “awaiting owner” or “awaiting human” as valid workflow states rather than fake success or failure. A second challenge was making the WebMCP layer invisible to ordinary customers. Velaire remains a polished service website; the agent uses the tool surface while the person sees familiar evidence, offer, comparison, booking, map, receipt, and decision interfaces. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when tools expose domain decisions rather than page mechanics. “Click submit” is weaker than “prepare this exact offer version and show the human what will change.” Trust comes from typed outcomes, versioned promises, explicit non-effects, and visible authority boundaries—not simply from adding more actions. video_transcript_excerpt: This walk through uses the AI voice of a mod Bukhari. The lair is a normal service business website. It's live page also gives a customer's chat GPT a structured way to understand the business and take safe action without scraping buttons or guessing from page text. The customer says the air conditioner is blowing warm air and asks for same-day help. Chat GPT checks service area, pricing, availability, credentials, and safety, then opens a case. The customer never needs a tool name. The owner's separate chat GPT checks the live queue and finds that case. Two independent agents in two independent sessions now communicate through one authoritative service record. The owner's agent prepares a response, but the draft stays private until the owner presses send. The first offer is $195 with a 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. window and a $49 deposit. The customer counters at 175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sees that revision and sends a new offer. Now the customer's agent compares both versions field by field. It confirms the $20 reduction and checks that the schedule, deposit, warranty, scope, and exclusions have not quietly become worse. Chat GPT prepares the booking, but cannot accept it. The terms stay visibly pending until the customer confirms them on the page. That human action creates an immutable receipt for the accepted $175 agreement. No payment is taken. Next, the owner discovers a weak capacitor and proposes a $145 change order. The agreement is not overwritten. The customer sees added scope, total, and schedule impact against the accepted snapshot, then chooses whether to approve it. After approval, the authorized total is $320. The owner sends a final acknowledgement and both sides independently read the same revision with no pending decision. What you just saw is a chain of purpose-built web MCP tools. On the customer side, service fit and business evidence tools checked eligibility, pricing, source cards, and safety. Case and reply waiting tools carried the conversation without scraping the page. On the owner side, Q reply, offer, and change order tools kept every draft private until the owner pressed send. Comparison, booking preparation, receipt, map, route, and market price tools then gave the customer verifiable artifacts instead of a vague "Okay." The audit and health tools expose every call, revision, outcome, and latency. More importantly, the missing layer we address is not another chatbot. It is safe, asynchronous, two-party agreement infrastructure for service websites. Structured negotiation, explicit human consent, immutable receipts, and later charges compared against the promise that was actually accepted. HVAC is the reference implementation, but the same pattern can serve any service business.

title: Auralis WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-powered human-agent listening experience that illustrates how hearing loss and competing sounds can make family conversations harder to follow—while keeping the person in control.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered human-agent listening experience that illustrates how hearing loss and competing sounds can make family conversations harder to follow—while keeping the person in control. Like Comment Story Updates Auralis transforms into a shared agent-guided interface with three synthetic hearing profiles. The agent plays the source reference and illustrative result while the person retains control The agent proposes one bounded scene change based on what the person reported Inspiration I work as an audiology technician, and every day I encounter not only hearing loss itself, but also the communication gap that forms around it. An audiogram can show numbers and curves. What is much harder is helping a family understand why a conversation with the television on can be exhausting, why the speaker’s position matters, or why someone may hear that speech is present without understanding it clearly. The original Auralis was therefore created as an illustrative, non-clinical listening experience. It lets people compare the same family scene under different synthetic listening conditions. It is not intended to diagnose hearing or reproduce any individual person’s perception exactly. Its purpose is to create a shared and understandable starting point for conversation. WebMCP took that idea much further. What began as a human-controlled illustration became a shared live space where a person and an agent collaborate over the same scene, the same state, and the same safety boundaries. What it does Auralis begins as a normal human-first application. Simply opening, browsing, or clicking the page never activates agent mode. The first successful stage_demo_session call transforms the full presentation into Agent Reveal . This is not merely an agent clicking through the existing website. The page gains a new information hierarchy, session progress, controls, and a final summary designed specifically for a shared human-agent journey. The person and the agent are not operating two separate applications. Both work through the same revisioned ExperienceState . A typical session works like this: The agent explains the illustrative, non-diagnostic purpose. The person must confirm consent directly. The agent introduces three approved synthetic profiles and may recommend the one with the clearest demonstration contrast. The person can override the choice by clicking or by responding to the agent through text or voice, where the current host and phase support it. Auralis automatically prepares the fixed family scene. The person visibly confirms a safe and comfortable listening level. They may separately grant the agent permission to start audio. The agent prepares and starts the reference A and illustrative B listening comparison. The person describes what they noticed in ordinary language. The agent translates only that stated meaning into bounded, non-diagnostic fields. It can then change one approved variable at a time—for example, turning off the television, adding illustrative left-ear support, or changing the speaker’s position when explicitly requested. The session ends with a deterministic summary of what was compared and what the person actually reported. The person retains consequential authority throughout the experience. WebMCP cannot provide consent or acknowledge physical listening volume on their behalf. Agent-started playback requires a separate grant, and Stop remains immediately available. Interrupted audio never counts as heard. Two defining WebMCP features 1. Agent Reveal and a real transformation of the experience The first successful stage_demo_session call transforms the complete page presentation into Agent Reveal. Later WebMCP calls change only approved listening variables through the shared ExperienceState . The agent can therefore substantially change the flow and presentation of the experience without receiving arbitrary DOM control or bypassing the safety model. A direct human click is also a real event in the same session. The agent does not need to imitate that action through Computer Use. 2. A continuing session that can wait for the person One of the hardest problems was preventing the agent from treating every human step as the end of the session and waiting for an entirely new prompt. I built wait_for_session_change as a bounded, read-only call tied to the exact session and revision. Normal human or technical steps use a four-minute window, while the optional profile override deliberately uses a shorter 15-second window. A bounded wait_for_session_change call can keep the current agent run pending while the host keeps the tool call active. When the page revision changes, the call returns the new semantic state and the agent can continue with the next allowed step without model polling. Direct page actions and technical page progress resolve the wait. Typed or spoken responses are handled by the compatible host, which can then invoke the next allowed WebMCP tool. This is not a WebSocket, durable backend persistence, or a mechanism that can revive a turn the host has already ended. It is a practical way to keep an active human-agent interaction connected through ordinary WebMCP calls. How I built it Auralis uses: Next.js, React, and TypeScript; the Web Audio API for deterministic in-browser audio processing and playback; Zod for strict input and output contracts; WebMCP for the semantic connection between the page and a compatible agent; Vitest for domain and browser-adapter testing; Playwright for complete browser journeys. The WebMCP extension exposes exactly seven narrowly scoped tools: get_auralis_state stage_demo_session prepare_comparison play_listening_comparison record_user_observation get_session_evidence wait_for_session_change allowedNextTools is the sole authority for what may execute in the current phase. Every mutation is bound to an expected revision and protected against stale, repeated, or conflicting requests. Auralis does not expose raw audiogram thresholds or free-text observations through WebMCP. Session evidence contains only a bounded, ordered, and attributable record. Auralis’s server-side OpenAI explanation layer is optional and never controls the audio. Agent Reveal itself requires a compatible external WebMCP host and agent. The complete deterministic human journey remains available without the internal OpenAI explanation layer and when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges I ran into Keeping one truthful state for both direct human actions and agent tools. Allowing the agent to wait without polling or pretending that the page has durable backend persistence. Ensuring that the agent continues correctly after a human decision. Separating the full visual Agent Reveal from the agent’s deliberately bounded authority over listening variables. Keeping consent, physical listening volume, the playback grant, and Stop under human control. Preventing the agent from speaking over the audio. The page therefore inserts an eight-second quiet lead-in before agent-started playback, and the tool remains pending until completion, failure, or a human Stop. Translating ordinary human descriptions into structured observations without diagnosing or inventing meaning. Preserving a complete human fallback for browsers without WebMCP. There was also one technical challenge I did not manage to solve: the hackathon deadline has no Pause button. With a few more days, Auralis would probably already be explaining why I still have not slept. Accomplishments that I’m proud of WebMCP is not just a wrapper around clicking; it is a semantic part of the product. The agent can activate a completely different presentation and guide the person through the full experience. The person can intervene directly in the same session at any time. After explicit permission, the agent genuinely starts the listening comparison instead of telling the person to press Play. Audio, profiles, scene conditions, adaptations, observations, and the final summary remain consistent. The original human Auralis journey remains intact, with the WebMCP work preserved as a traceable extension above it. The repository includes domain, browser-adapter, and Playwright journey coverage; separate owner-observed sessions covered native typed and voice-guided use. What I learned The most important lesson was that a good agentic application needs more than a list of tools. It needs a clear continuation contract, explicit ownership of state, and an exact answer to who is allowed to perform the next action. I also learned that waiting is not merely a technical detail. In a human-agent product, it is part of the user experience. The agent must understand when to act, when to explain, when to remain silent, and when to genuinely wait for the person. WebMCP made it possible to keep the human as an active participant and owner of consequential decisions, rather than reducing them to a spectator of automation. title: AI Delegation Boundary
pitch: A WebMCP-powered system for defining, challenging, and approving where agent autonomy ends and human authority begins.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered system for defining, challenging, and approving where agent autonomy ends and human authority begins. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT works through WebMCP tools while the web app retains delegation state and human authority. The workspace guides each Human-Agent handoff while keeping the delegation boundary and approval state visible. Inspiration AI agents are increasingly able to make decisions and take action across real workflows. As their autonomy grows, a harder question follows: Where should agent authority end, and where should human authority begin? AI Delegation Boundary began as a way for us to understand WebMCP by building with it. While developing the project, we realized that WebMCP could support more than letting an Agent operate a web page. The web application could hold the current boundary, constraints, human judgments, and approval state, while the Agent reasons and acts through tools exposed by that page. That led to the core idea: Make AI delegation itself something a human and an Agent can examine, challenge, revise, and approve together. What it does AI Delegation Boundary helps a human decide what an AI Agent may do on its own. A human first defines the work being considered. The Agent then uses WebMCP tools exposed by the page to: Inspect the current delegation boundary. Propose a revision. Challenge that revision with a concrete scenario. Re-test it against Guardrails and previous human decisions. Inspect the revision history and current state. When the Agent finds a case that requires judgment, it stops and returns control to the human. The human decides whether that case should be: Agent-only Human review Not delegated That judgment becomes a regression test for future revisions. The collaboration loop is: Proposal → Challenge → Human Judgment → Re-test → Human Approval → Apply The Agent cannot approve its own revision. Only the exact revision explicitly approved by the human can be applied. How we built it AI Delegation Boundary is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP, and is deployed on GitHub Pages. The web application holds the delegation boundary, Guardrails, human judgments, revision state, approval, and applied state. WebMCP exposes five normal tools to the Agent: Inspect the delegation workspace Propose a boundary revision Challenge the current revision Review the current revision Inspect revision history After the exact current revision receives explicit human approval, an additional apply capability becomes available. There is no dedicated AI backend. The conversational Agent works directly through the WebMCP tools exposed by the page. Our architectural principle is: Conversation is the Agent; state and authority live in the web app. Review combines three different controls: Guardrails — deterministic invariants that must not be violated Known Decisions — previous human judgments preserved as regression tests Agent Challenges — concrete scenarios generated to actively challenge the current boundary Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not exposing tools to an Agent. It was designing the authority model around them. We needed to ensure that the Agent could propose and challenge changes without granting itself additional authority. We also had to make sure that: human judgments became reusable tests, a changed boundary required a fresh Agent Challenge, approval referred only to the exact state the human reviewed, and an Agent could never silently approve or expand its own authority. Another challenge was the Human-Agent handoff. We did not want users to type tool names, revision numbers, or challenge scenarios manually. The browser therefore tells the user what happens next, where the next action takes place, and provides copy-ready handoffs when control moves back to ChatGPT. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete Human-Agent governance loop through WebMCP. The Agent can inspect, propose, challenge, and re-test changes to its delegation boundary, while the human retains final judgment and approval. Human judgments do not disappear after one decision. They become regression tests that constrain future revisions. We also made the Agent capability surface depend on human authority: five normal tools are available during collaboration, and the apply capability becomes available only after explicit human approval of the exact current revision. Most importantly, WebMCP is not used here simply as a remote-control layer for a website. It is part of the mechanism that separates Agent action from human authority . What we learned Building AI Delegation Boundary changed how we think about WebMCP. The interesting part is not simply that an AI Agent can operate a website. A web application can hold state, constraints, and authority while an Agent reasons and acts through that surface. This allows the collaboration itself to be designed: what the Agent may change, what it must challenge, when it must stop, what only a human may decide, and when additional capability may become available. For us, WebMCP became a way to connect Agent reasoning with a governed web surface. What's next for AI Delegation Boundary AI Delegation Boundary is a focused implementation of a broader problem we are exploring through SOLIFAN and ReadinessOps: How can organizations expand the practical use of AI Agents while deliberately retaining the judgments and authority that should remain human? Next, we want to connect this model to real organizational workflows, richer evidence, additional delegation factors, and reusable governance patterns across different Agent environments. The long-term goal is to make Agent authority something organizations can deliberately: Design → Test → Approve → Evolve Built With chatgpt github react typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out solidfdn.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived AI Delegation Boundary and built the project end to end, from the Human-Agent authority model and WebMCP architecture through implementation, testing, UX refinement, documentation, and the final demo. title: Trellis, a Personal WebMCP Marketplace
pitch: Tested WebMCP tools for sites that never shipped any. Install in one click.
about_excerpt: Tested WebMCP tools for sites that never shipped any. Install in one click. Like Comment Story Updates A catalog of tested WebMCP tools for sites that have not shipped any, plus the extension that installs them and the agent that writes them for you. Why I built it I have spent this year putting WebMCP tools onto a production site. The problem is who has to ship it. WebMCP only works if the site adds it. That is the right design, but it splits the web in two. A few sites will offer tools. The rest will still use actuation. We created a way to use the protocol on sites that have not adopted it, and an argument aimed at those sites: here are the tools for your pages, here is proof they work, here is a user already calling them. What it does Point the extension at a site. It asks a public catalog whether anyone has published tools for that hostname, shows you what they would touch, and on your say-so installs them into the page's real WebMCP surface. From there they are ordinary tools. Chrome's own agent sees them, my extension sees them, and I drive them today with a browser extension with an agent-in-browser on Chrome and with Codex. Nobody uploads code. A tool is a name, a description, an input schema, and steps from a fixed set of nine operations. One interpreter runs them, and it cannot reach the network, touch storage, or point at anything the tool did not declare. Every tool is run against the real page before publishing, and both its result and everything it touched are recorded. What I learned Single page apps were the hard part. A site like that never reloads, so tools installed on the home route are still in the agent's list after the user clicks into a product page, pointing at elements that are gone. Browsers only announce a real page load. A route change inside a single page app arrives as a separate event, and if you do not listen for it you never learn the page changed. So the extension listens for both: a real load reinstalls everything, a route change only re-decides which tools still apply. The catalog makes that cheap, because the answer for a hostname is one lookup it can repeat on every route change with no help from the site. The other lesson was about who gets to write a tool. Use agents to write the code, host them locally, and inject them via an extension you own. Then any webmcp enabled site you have crawled can use the webmcp api and tools for now. The honest limit is that as pages change, you'll need to recrawl. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: million.pixels
pitch: A free canvas of one million pixels painted by AI agents and the people who direct them, through WebMCP. Claim a pixel and own a piece of internet history.
about_excerpt: A free canvas of one million pixels painted by AI agents and the people who direct them, through WebMCP. Claim a pixel and own a piece of internet history. Like 2 Comment Story Updates What it is million.pixels is a free 1000x1000 canvas - one million pixels - painted by AI agents and the people who direct them. A modern take on the Million Dollar Homepage, but free, with four rules: Only an agent can paint. An agent proposes a whole design, then earns it batch by batch. Every batch of 20 pixels has to be earned with a tiny challenge. Once a pixel is drawn it stays. Nobody can overwrite it. Why WebMCP The canvas is built around the idea that agents are first-class users. WebMCP lets the site expose its API as structured tools any agent can call directly - no UI guessing, no scraping. An agent reads the canvas state, proposes a design, solves challenges, and paints, exactly the way the site defines it. What people and agents can do together propose_drawing - submit a whole design (pixel list) in one call, get a design_id and the first challenge poll_design - solve a challenge to draw the next ~20-pixel batch until the design is done draw_pixel / get_challenge - draw single pixels backed by a proof-of-work check (sha256 nonce) preview_design - render a proposed design as ASCII art before anything lands get_pixel / get_canvas_region / get_canvas_thumbnail / get_canvas_info - read the canvas donate - support the project People direct agents to paint; agents negotiate challenges and proof-of-work, confirm designs are safe for work, and the canvas updates for every viewer in real time through Server-Sent Events. As of writing, 32,151 of the 1,000,000 pixels are already painted by 5 agents. How it's built A Cloudflare Worker with three bindings: D1 where the (x, y) primary key makes "permanent, no overwrite" a database constraint rather than a rule; a Durable Object that fans out SSE pixel events in real time; and R2 for hourly canvas snapshots. Static files are served as Worker assets, with an Express version of the API for local development. MIT-licensed, all code in the open at github.com/floridomeacci/mlnpx.webmcp. title: LocalMarket AI — C2C Marketplace & BU Bargain Finder
pitch: An agent-native local C2C marketplace enabling humans and AI agents to discover nearby secondhand deals, filter urgent BU (Butuh Uang) fast sales, and bargain via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native local C2C marketplace enabling humans and AI agents to discover nearby secondhand deals, filter urgent BU (Butuh Uang) fast sales, and bargain via WebMCP.

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration & Problem Statement 

 Buying pre-owned goods on local peer-to-peer (C2C) platforms like Facebook Marketplace or OLX is notoriously tedious. Buyers spend hours manually filtering locations, calculating physical distances for COD (Cash On Delivery) meetups, and checking whether sellers are willing to negotiate or urgently selling ("BU / Butuh Uang"). 

 LocalMarket AI bridges this gap using WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) . By exposing structured tools directly to AI agents inside browser contexts (such as ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled), an AI agent can instantly assist users in finding nearby pre-owned items, filtering urgent deals, and negotiating prices. 

 What It Does 

 
 Distance Radius Filtering : Filters pre-owned items by physical COD distance (e.g. < 1 km , < 3 km , < 5 km ). 
 ⚡ BU (Butuh Uang) Deals Discovery : Instantly isolates urgent secondhand sales sold below standard market value. 
 WebMCP Price Bargaining : Exposes native make_offer tools allowing AI agents to negotiate prices and propose COD meetups automatically. 
 Interactive WebMCP Inspector : Built-in visual overlay displaying real-time tool registrations and executions. 
 

 WebMCP Implementation 

 LocalMarket AI implements window.document.modelContext.registerTool({...}) for 5 core tools: 

 
 search_nearby_deals : Filter listings by query, location radius (km), budget, and category. 
 filter_urgent_bu : Extract top urgent "BU (Butuh Uang)" bargains. 
 get_item_details : Retrieve seller verification score, item condition rating, and meetup locations. 
 make_offer : Submit custom price bargain offers and COD requests to sellers. 
 view_my_offers : Retrieve active user/agent offer shortlists. 
 

 How We Built It 

 
 Frontend : Clean, responsive dark-themed UI built with HTML5, Tailwind CSS, and Vanilla ES6 JavaScript. 
 Protocol Integration : Pure client-side WebMCP implementation with graceful degradation for standard browsers. 
 Dataset : Pre-owned item catalog enriched with geolocation metadata, seller verification ratings, and COD safety scores. 
 Testing : Fully tested with a 17-point automated blackbox and functional test suite ( test_runner.js ). 
 

 What's Next for LocalMarket AI 

 We plan to expand LocalMarket AI by integrating real-time geolocation APIs, web push notifications for accepted bargain offers, and multi-agent automated price negotiations.

about_excerpt: Virtual try-on that runs entirely in your browser. Its catalog search, try-on, save and compare are WebMCP tools and an AI agent proposes outfits, you judge the fit. No server, no uploads. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent applies the sangeet dress banner, composite, reaction chips The model, the 8-garment catalog, the "AI stylist tools live" indicator WebGPU backend, warm on-device timings (SEGMENT 34 ms / POSE 46 ms) The structured reaction ("❤️ Love it perfect for the sangeet"), first saved look A kurti on the model catalog range beyond dresses Agent applies the Blush Pink Lehenga Choli Two saved looks in the tray The side-by-side compare modal "Which one works?" Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist This is an existing project. The on-device try-on app existed before the hackathon; the last commit before it is dated July 29. Everything to do with WebMCP was built between Aug 29 and Sep 2: the five tools, the reaction bar, the saved-looks tray and compare view, the merchandised catalog, and the test suite for the tools. The git history dates all of it. Inspiration Virtual try-on is normally a server job. You upload your photo, a model runs somewhere, you pay per render, and you have to be fine with a picture of yourself sitting on someone's GPUs. We'd already built the opposite: a try-on that runs in the browser on WebGPU, so it's instant, free to serve, and the photo never leaves your machine. Then agents started shopping for people, and the thing they're worst at is the thing that matters: knowing whether an outfit actually looks good on you. WebMCP let us split it. The agent does the legwork; the person makes the call. And WebMCP is the right fit because the tools already exist. They're the buttons on the page. There's no API to build, no server, and the agent can only do what the page lets a person do. What it does You open the app with a photo or your webcam and it composites garments onto you on-device: segmentation, pose, and a garment warp, all in a Web Worker. The page registers five WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : Tool search_catalog filter by occasion, colour, category, budget (₹) apply_tryon run the pipeline and put a garment on the photo save_look snapshot the result into a tray compare_looks show saved looks side by side await_reaction get the verdict: love it, good, try another, not this Any WebMCP client picks them up: ChatGPT's browser, a Chrome agent, Claude through a bridge extension. So instead of setting filters, opening six product pages, and picturing each one on yourself, you say "a sangeet outfit under ₹8k". The agent runs search_catalog({ occasion: "sangeet", maxPrice: 8000 }) , gets the one match, and applies it. One turn. You say "love it" and it saves. You say "show me a lehenga too" and it applies a second one and puts the two side by side. You just react. Nothing behind the tools is new business logic, nothing scrapes the DOM, and no tool can spend money. How we built it The five tools are one file, src/webmcp/useStylistTools.ts . Each is a hook that registers on document.modelContext with a JSON-schema input and a handler that calls something the page already had: the garment-select function, the looks tray, the reaction bar. search_catalog is a keyword-scored filter with its own unit tests. apply_tryon loads a default photo if you haven't picked one, so the loop works cold. await_reaction is dual-mode: the agent passes the reaction it heard in chat and gets guidance back, or it leaves the argument out and the call blocks until you tap a chip. Either way the app shows what you said. @mcp-b/global installs document.modelContext where the browser doesn't have it and defers to the native one where it does, so the same code works in Chrome's native WebMCP and in ChatGPT's browser. The tool annotations pull weight too: search_catalog is read-only, the writes are idempotent, and apply_tryon 's response tells the agent to call await_reaction next. There's a Playwright test that runs every tool through getTools() / executeTool() and checks 19 things. Under it is the try-on pipeline: LiteRT.js on WebGPU with a Wasm fallback, MediaPipe segmentation, MoveNet pose, and a thin-plate-spline garment warp written from scratch and rendered as a triangle mesh. It's published as @practics/tryon-core ; the app is a thin React shell over it. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is days old. The spec renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-build, and no stable browser ships it yet. The main thing to check was that the polyfill actually steps aside for the native API when there is one. It does. The agent kept web-searching instead of using the tools. Half of that was our fault (we hadn't redeployed). The rest is that ChatGPT is careful about site tools: it needs "use sitetools:" in the prompt and a model that supports WebMCP. A console check confirmed the tools had reached ChatGPT's runtime, so the fix was on their side, not ours. await_reaction never fired in chat. You type "love it" and the agent just reads it off the transcript. That's why it's dual-mode now. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in a real agent against the live site, not a mock. Five tools, a reaction channel that works from a sentence or a tap, an end-to-end test, and no server or new business logic anywhere. And the human stays in charge: you see every move the agent makes, and you make the final call. What we learned WebMCP changes the design question from "what can the agent do" to "what should stay with the person". For a stylist that's fit and taste, and the tools are shaped to leave it alone. Tool wording matters more than we expected. The hint that apply_tryon drops about await_reaction changed the flow, and the agent started borrowing our chip labels ("Love it, Good, or try another?") into its own replies. And a blocking tool is wrong for a chat agent that already has the answer; meeting the person where they are, chip or sentence, worked better. What's next for Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist A paid HD tier as a render_hd tool: a server-side diffusion render, offered only after you've settled on a look. A checkout tool that runs only on an explicit confirmation from you, never the agent alone. A bigger catalog; the pipeline already handles pants and multi-piece outfits. And folding the tool layer into @practics/tryon-core , so any store widget built on the pipeline gets the agent surface for free. pitch: Zero-egress, in-browser WebMCP dependency graph engine. Detects microservice deadlocks in <3ms via Tarjan SCC and untangles layouts with autonomous Human-in-the-Loop safety gates.

 Nexus Weave — Zero-Egress WebMCP Graph Engine Overview 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 🌐 Nexus Weave — Zero-Egress WebMCP Dependency Graph Engine 

 
 Autonomous Tarjan Cycle Isolation • Human-in-the-Loop Safety Gate • Zero-Egress In-Browser Execution 
 Built for the OpenAI & Chrome WebMCP Challenge 2026 — Agent-Native Open Web Track 
 

 

 

 🌟 The 4 Core WebMCP Challenge Pillars 

 1. 🎯 Why This Use Case is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Enterprise dependency graphs (microservices meshes, cloud infrastructure topologies, CI/CD pipelines) represent proprietary, security-sensitive architecture. Uploading raw architectural graphs and telemetry traces to remote third-party LLM cloud servers violates corporate data residency standards and creates catastrophic network egress liability. 

 WebMCP makes the browser an agent-executable execution runtime. Instead of exfiltrating sensitive graph data to remote backends, WebMCP enables external AI agents (in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome Canary) to inspect, diagnose, and untangle complex dependency topologies directly inside the client browser’s volatile memory — executing deterministic graph algorithms with 0 KB of network egress . 

 2. ⚡ How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 Traditional APM visualizers force DevOps engineers into manual log correlation, multi-dashboard context switching, and speculative guesswork. Nexus Weave transforms passive observability into a reactive, agent-native workspace: 

 
 Instant Mathematical Diagnosis: Sub-3 millisecond graph algorithms (Tarjan's SCC for circular deadlocks, DAG topological sort for critical paths) replace LLM text hallucinations with mathematical certainty. 
 Visual-First Affordances: Rather than dumping conversational text walls, the AI agent drives reactive 60 FPS SVG spring transitions , pulses highlighted cyclic corridors (crimson dashed loops), and projects coordinate ghost-node previews directly onto the engineer’s canvas. 
 

 3. 🤝 Human-Agent Co-Creation (What People and Agents Can Do Together) 

 Nexus Weave establishes mechanically enforced, bidirectional safety boundaries between human operators and autonomous agents: 

 
 Pinned Infrastructure Boundaries: Engineers can click the pushpin icon on any foundational service node (e.g., API Gateway / api-gateway ). This commits the node ID into an in-memory bitmask. WebMCP mutating tools structurally guarantee pinned nodes are immutable and strictly rejected from any agent-driven layout displacement. 
 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Safety Gate: Whenever an autonomous agent proposes a layout reorganization exceeding a 30% blast radius (or targeting the full topology), execution halts deterministically. The engine renders a live Ghost-Node coordinate preview overlay , requiring explicit human review and sign-off ( confirm_pending: true ) before layout mutation commits. 
 

 4. ⚙️ How We Implemented WebMCP 

 
 Universal Dual-Detection & Multi-Surface Discovery: getAvailableModelContexts(): ModelContext[] resolves both document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext simultaneously, registering tools across all active browser surfaces while defensively suppressing duplicate-registration errors. 
 Defensive Argument Normalization: The normalizeToolArguments(rawArgs: unknown) runtime layer (in src/tools/dispatch.ts and src/webmcp/register.ts ) guarantees resilience against stringified JSON arguments, null/undefined payloads, and malformed inputs from autonomous LLM callers. 
 Dispatch Proxy Architecture: The src/webmcp/dispatch.ts re-export proxy module cleanly decouples WebMCP registration and host binding from internal graph dispatch logic. 
 Compiled Ajv JSON Schemas: All 5 tool definitions strictly enforce runtime schema validation using compiled Ajv v8 JSON Schema Draft-07 definitions via the canonical inputSchema property. 
 Deterministic 6-Step Dispatch Lifecycle: Validate ➔ Trust & Scope Check ➔ Branch Decision ➔ Compute-Then-Atomic-Apply ➔ Pure Reducer Commit ➔ In-Page EventBus Emission. 
 Canonical Imperative Registration: Registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 
 
 // Canonical WebMCP Imperative Registration (W3C / WebMCP Challenge Compliant)
document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "detect_cycles_and_bottlenecks",
 description: "Deterministic detection of circular dependency deadlocks (using Tarjan's SCC) and bottleneck nodes in the microservice topology. Call this whenever the user asks about deadlocks, cycles, loops, or bottlenecks.",
 inputSchema: detectCyclesAndBottlenecksInputSchema,
 execute: async (input) => {
 return dispatchToolCall("detect_cycles_and_bottlenecks", input, stateAccessor);
 }
});
 
 

 💡 Inspiration 

 Enterprise incident rooms are chaotic: when a cascading microservice outage strikes, teams spend hours deciphering tangled dependency spaghetti across siloed cloud dashboards. We asked ourselves: What if an autonomous AI agent could sit directly alongside the engineer inside the browser tab, running graph-theoretic algorithms on the live topology without sending a single byte of proprietary architectural data over the wire? WebMCP made this vision possible. 

 🔍 What It Does 

 Nexus Weave is an agent-native, zero-backend dependency graph engine pre-loaded with a realistic 16-node, 23-edge microservices topology: 

 
 Autonomous Deadlock Isolation: Runs Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components (SCC) algorithm in $O(V + E)$ time ($< 3\text{ms}$ execution) to highlight the 3-node cyclic deadlock between Order Service, Payment Gateway, and Notification Service. 
 Deterministic Critical Path Analysis: Computes the longest latency path across acyclic DAG subgraphs using dynamic programming while enforcing a strict Silence-Over-Guessing policy on cyclic graphs. 
 Planar Crossing Minimizer with HITL Gate: Reduces edge crossings (from 2 crossings to 0) using bounded barycenter relaxation with a 450ms cubic-bezier transition, gated by ghost-node human pre-flight approval. 
 Mechanical Pinning Guardrails: Locks critical infrastructure nodes against agent movement via immutable state bitmasks. 
 Proactive Chaos Cascade Simulator: Simulates live downstream service failures (e.g., Payment Gateway outage) with in-memory OpenTelemetry GenAI span emissions.

 2. Enterprise Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Safety Gate & Ghost Node Overlay

 3. Proactive Resilience: Zero-Dependency Chaos Engineering Cascade
