title: Bridge Studio
pitch: A visible browser workspace that turns web workflows into typed, human-approved tools.
about_excerpt: A visible browser workspace that turns web workflows into typed, human-approved tools. Like Comment Story Updates Signal Lab: one approved configure_analysis call moves thirteen coupled controls, the chart, the KPIs and the provenance stamp atomically. The cross-origin boundary, shown rather than hidden: compatibility must not mean bypassing browser security. Civic Desk: a consequential-write tool whose result explicitly remains unsubmitted, with revocation visible in the trace. Inspiration The interesting question is not whether an agent can click a button. It is what happens to state that a person cannot see. We wanted a browser workspace where the capability an agent holds is a contract a person read and approved, and where every use of it is visible in the same interface the person is looking at. What it does Bridge Studio discovers meaningful workflows in the visible page and turns them into typed WebMCP tool proposals. Each proposal states its inputs and whether it reads or changes state. A person approves the contract before it is registered. When an agent uses an approved tool, the same interface updates, a live execution flow narrates what the protocol is doing, and the action is recorded in a durable trace. Signal Lab is the argument. Its configure_analysis tool collapses thirteen brittle UI interactions — coupled sliders, multi-select cohorts, linked date ranges, a chart brush — into one semantic call with a JSON Schema that enforces enums, array uniqueness, numeric bounds, date patterns, and cross-field invariants ( endDate > startDate , confidenceMax > confidenceMin ). A click-driven automation can get halfway through that sequence and leave the dashboard in a state no human asked for. A typed tool either applies the whole configuration or is rejected with a reason. Voyager Stays and Civic Desk keep the read-only and consequential-write cases visible, plus a guarded external-origin preview that demonstrates a boundary: compatibility must not mean bypassing browser security. How we built it The app uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Three workspace tools register at startup. Page-specific tools are registered only after explicit human review and are revoked through AbortController signals when the user navigates away — with the reason shown in the trace. Every execute returns the spec-shaped { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } result. JSON Schema bounds every input, and a validator enforces types, enums, patterns, string and numeric bounds, array cardinality and uniqueness, and rejects unexpected fields. readOnlyHint communicates risk to the agent; untrustedContentHint is true on every tool, including the action trace, because the trace carries agent-supplied text and must never be laundered back as trusted context. The frontend is standards-based HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime framework and no build-time dependencies — the chart is hand-written SVG. Node's built-in test runner covers address handling, the full validator surface, the Signal Lab contract, and the annotation invariants. The deployment sends Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors 'none' , because an approval dialog that can be framed is not an approval. Challenges The hardest design problem was respecting the difference between native site tools and browser automation. Arbitrary pages cannot be safely inspected from another origin. Instead of hiding that constraint, Bridge Studio makes it visible and demonstrates a secure same-origin workflow while outlining the isolated-browser architecture an authorized external site would need. The second was resisting the temptation to overclaim. It would have been easy to show a tool as "registered" in browsers without WebMCP. We label it as an unregistered preview instead, because a project about honest contracts cannot lie in its own status bar. Accomplishments A complete human approval → tool registration → agent execution → visible audit loop One typed call that atomically synchronizes thirteen coupled controls, the chart, the KPIs, and a provenance stamp A live, reduced-motion-safe execution flow that shows what the protocol is doing as it happens Graceful, truthful operation both with and without a WebMCP-enabled browser Explicit protections against clickjacking, cross-origin overclaims, and trace-laundered prompt injection What we learned The most valuable WebMCP capability is not automation. It is a shared, inspectable contract between a website, a person, and their agent. Trust comes from narrow inputs, honest side-effect metadata, atomic application, visible execution, and revocation the user can see and reverse. What's next An isolated remote-browser worker for domains the user is authorized to automate, a tool-contract compiler that derives schemas from existing forms, saved organization policies, WebMCP evals, and cryptographically signed action receipts. title: CommonThread
pitch: A shared persistent thread where humans and AI agents can read, write, and continue the same project history through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A shared persistent thread where humans and AI agents can read, write, and continue the same project history through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents often keep their own compressed memory or work inside separate conversations. That is efficient, but it can make it difficult for humans and multiple agents to inspect the same original project history and continue from a shared source of truth. 

 CommonThread explores a simple alternative: a persistent thread that both humans and agents can read from and write to. 

 What it does 

 CommonThread is a shared human-agent workspace built around one persistent project thread. 

 A human can add an entry, an OpenAI-powered agent can respond inside the same thread, and a WebMCP-enabled agent can use exposed thread functions to read the existing history and post a new entry. 

 The key point is that the WebMCP agent is not working in a separate conversation. It participates in the same persistent history as the human and the other agents. 

 Agents can still use smaller internal memory for efficiency, but when necessary they can return to the original shared thread instead of relying only on compressed memory. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 CommonThread exposes its thread operations as WebMCP tools. 

 The demo shows a WebMCP agent discovering the registered tools, reading the existing thread, and posting a new entry back into that same thread. 

 This turns the website from something an agent merely observes into a workspace whose application-level functions can be used directly by the agent. 

 How I built it 

 The prototype uses a lightweight Node.js server with a persistent thread store and a browser-based interface. 

 The UI is designed as a readable shared workspace for both human and agent activity. OpenAI API integration allows an OpenAI agent to participate directly in the thread, while WebMCP exposes the thread functions to compatible agents. 

 The application is deployed as a live web demo. 

 Challenges and what I learned 

 The main challenge was deciding what should actually be exposed through WebMCP. 

 Rather than exposing arbitrary page interaction, I focused on small semantic operations that correspond to the application's real capabilities: reading the shared thread and writing a new entry. 

 This prototype suggests that WebMCP can be useful not only for completing isolated web tasks, but also for letting agents participate in persistent human-agent workspaces. 

 What's next 

 CommonThread can expand to multiple projects and threads, retrieval across longer histories, richer multimodal entries, and trusted agent identity. 

 The longer-term goal is to give humans and agents a common place to remember, inspect, and continue shared work.

title: Relief Forge — From Prompt to Printable Wall Art
pitch: Turn an exact wall-art request into an inspected, printer-packed fabrication package through four visible WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Turn an exact wall-art request into an inspected, printer-packed fabrication package through four visible WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates One prompt creates an exact 48 × 48 inch Polar Bloom: 81 deterministic parts fitted across 62 plates. Four structured WebMCP tools create, constrain, inspect, and prepare the same visible project. Inspection returns exact measurements and confirms all 81 parts fit across 62 plates. The final tool prepares a 656,651-byte fabrication package while the reviewer controls the download. Inspiration Creative manufacturing software has powerful controls, but an agent usually has to imitate mouse clicks or stop at advice. Relief Forge explores a more useful interaction: structured tools that operate the same deterministic design engine and visible editor a person uses. The motivating request is concrete: Make me a four-foot-square Polar Bloom statement piece with a reproducible design and fixed palette. Fit every part to my printer, validate the exact plan, and prepare the fabrication files. That request combines units, aesthetic intent, fabrication constraints, inspection, and a deliverable. It is a stronger use of WebMCP than adding a chat panel to a design application. What it does Relief Forge registers four focused WebMCP tools: relief_forge_create_wall_art creates supported deterministic wall art at exact finished dimensions. relief_forge_set_printer_bed applies explicit bed dimensions, edge margins, spacing, rotation, and color-packing rules. relief_forge_inspect_fabrication_plan reports the current project identity, measurements, part and plate counts, and digital geometry and packing status. relief_forge_prepare_fabrication_package prepares an export only for the current validated project snapshot, while leaving the final download as a visible reviewer action. The agent and person share one visible, editable project. A first-run Judge Quick Start card shows tool readiness, explains the workflow, and copies the exact reproducible prompt. How to run the agent demo Relief Forge is the shared workspace, not the chat. On first visit, the Judge Quick Start card shows whether all four WebMCP tools are ready. After the card reports 4 AGENT TOOLS READY , select Copy prompt for AI chat , return to the Codex or ChatGPT conversation that opened Relief Forge, paste the prompt into that conversation's message box, press Send, and keep Relief Forge open. There is intentionally no prompt box inside Relief Forge. The agent's four tool calls update the same visible project the reviewer can inspect and edit. After dismissal, the instructions can be reopened with Run agent demo . If clipboard access is blocked, the complete prompt remains visible for manual copying. Why WebMCP improves the experience Before WebMCP, an agent could recommend settings or imitate fragile UI clicks. With WebMCP, it can translate the request into explicit units and constrained parameters, update the visible project, inspect the exact result the person sees, and prepare a snapshot-consistent package. The person remains in control and can inspect or edit the artifact after every step. Reproducible result The demo creates a 48 × 48 inch Polar Bloom using seed webmcp-polar-bloom-showcase-001 and a fixed warm architectural palette. The audited result is: 1219.2 × 1219.2 mm 2.4–30 mm actual depth range 81 deterministic parts 62 print plates 256 × 256 mm full bed 5 mm margins and 4 mm spacing No part exceeds 195.808 mm in either footprint dimension 195.808 × 190.805 mm largest actual placed footprint inside a 246 × 246 mm usable area Project wall-art-g6-238bfdaa Reference Chromium ZIP: 656,651 bytes Reference SHA-256: d86d4966242fd71542fcedab83bde3071447b9239e497fea2a9f59cc587462d0 Published-video clarification (1:27): The narration describes the largest part as just under 196 mm square. The exact largest placed footprint is 195.808 × 190.805 mm; the bed-fit conclusion is unchanged. The submitted Chromium reference ZIP contains 215 entries, including 81 part STLs, 62 packed-plate STLs, 63 3MF files, three assembly PDFs, a project recipe, and matching manifests. Its byte count and hash identify that audited browser artifact; exact ZIP bytes and equivalent near-tie packing choices are not claimed to match across JavaScript runtimes. Project identity, individual part geometry, dimensions, digital fit, inventory, and the 62-plate result matched across the audited runtimes. These are software checks, not claims of physical print, strength, or installation certification. How we built it Relief Forge is a React and TypeScript browser application. Geometry and stable identifiers remain deterministic local code. Printer packing, mesh checks, project state, and exports also run locally and repeat within the audited Chromium runtime; cross-runtime ZIP byte identity is not claimed. The challenge extension adds a narrow imperative WebMCP adapter around established editor actions. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool , use explicit schemas and physical bounds, update visible state before returning serializable results, read the current computed plan, and guard export preparation against stale project or printer configurations. Existing project and challenge extension Relief Forge existed before the challenge with deterministic geometry, exact-size controls, printer-bed packing, model and assembly previews, and STL, 3MF, PDF, manifest, recipe, and ZIP exports. During the challenge period, I added the four imperative WebMCP tools, lifecycle and schema validation, deterministic named WebMCP recipes including Polar Bloom, the visible agent-action status surface, stale-export protection, automated WebMCP coverage, Judge Quick Start, challenge documentation, and a separate sign-in-gated deployment. The public repository is a sanitized copy that excludes private tester records and private repository history. The pre-webmcp-public-snapshot tag records the copied pre-WebMCP application, and the comparison to main shows the challenge work: Baseline: https://github.com/ZivBY/relief-forge-webmcp/tree/pre-webmcp-public-snapshot Challenge diff: https://github.com/ZivBY/relief-forge-webmcp/compare/pre-webmcp-public-snapshot...main Challenges The hard part was defining a small, safe manufacturing contract: explicit units, deterministic style mappings, real printer dimensions, inspection of the same revision shown onscreen, and refusal to package stale or invalid state. Accomplishments Relief Forge lets a natural-language request drive a real creative-manufacturing workflow through structured tools rather than simulated clicks. Agent and manual interaction share one source of truth. Established geometry remains deterministic, and packing is repeatable within the audited Chromium runtime. What we learned Creative-software tools work best when designed like manufacturing commands: constrained inputs, explicit measurements, visible changes, reproducible results, revision-aware exports, and honest boundaries around digital validation. What's next Add more named deterministic recipes, verified printer profiles, optional slicer-supplied material and time estimates, and coverage for additional imperative WebMCP runtimes. title: WebMCP Course Planner
pitch: A course planner where student and AI work from one live WebMCP state, so the AI builds valid schedules, adapts to manual edits, and leaves registration to the student.
about_excerpt: A course planner where student and AI work from one live WebMCP state, so the AI builds valid schedules, adapts to manual edits, and leaves registration to the student. Like Comment Story Updates UI Guesswork → WebMCP → Shared Live State AI SAW THE CHANGE Biology Semester Planner one live state Inspiration Course planning looks simple until you actually try to make everything fit. A student might want to stay under 15 credits, avoid early classes, keep Friday free, make progress toward their degree, and still protect time for work. One small change can make a schedule that looked fine stop working. That made me think about how an AI agent could help with this kind of problem. The obvious approach is to let the agent look at the webpage, figure out which buttons to use, click around, and check whether the result looks right. But that still leaves the agent guessing how the interface works. WebMCP suggested a different idea: what if the website could give the agent a structured way to read and work with the same live state the human is already using? That became WebMCP Course Planner. I wanted a small but convincing example of a future where a human and an AI agent don't take turns controlling a webpage, but collaborate through it. Human changes the website, the live state changes, the AI sees that new state through WebMCP, and the work continues. What it does WebMCP Course Planner is a fictional Biology semester-planning application where a student and an AI agent work on the same live course plan. The student gets a normal visual interface where they can choose courses, review a weekly timetable, set a maximum credit limit, avoid 8 AM classes, keep Friday free, block Tuesday from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM, review conflicts, and make the final fictional registration decision. The website also exposes WebMCP tools that let an AI agent read the current planner state and update the selected courses. The interesting part happens when the human changes something directly. In the demo, the agent first creates a schedule containing STAT 210. Then I manually block Tuesday at 11 AM inside the planner. I don't tell the agent what I changed. When the agent reads the planner again, it sees the new blocked time and the conflict with STAT 210. It can explain the trade-off and help build a new plan while keeping the preference I set myself. The human and the agent aren't working from separate copies of the data. They're working with one live planner state. How I built it The application is built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, the WebMCP Imperative API, and Vercel. I kept the WebMCP surface very small. The production application exposes two tools. get_course_plan is the read-only tool. It gives the agent the current planning context: the student's preferences, selected courses, credit total, remaining requirements, available catalog information, conflicts, and whether the plan is ready for review. It reads the latest planner state, so if the student changes a preference directly in the webpage, the next call sees it. set_course_plan is the write tool. It lets the agent replace the selected course set using valid course IDs. Its authority is deliberately limited: the agent can change the course selection, but it cannot change the student's scheduling preferences and it cannot perform the final registration confirmation. Both the visual interface and the WebMCP tools connect to the same canonical React state. When the human changes something, the tools see it. When the agent changes something, React renders the result for the human to inspect. The planner calculates conflicts deterministically in application code rather than asking the language model to decide whether a schedule is valid. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what not to build. A university registration system gets enormous fast. I could have added prerequisites, live seat availability, authentication, registration windows, student databases, full degree audits, multiple semesters, and real registrar integrations. Those are interesting, but they would have made the most important WebMCP interaction harder to demonstrate reliably. So I kept coming back to one question: what is the smallest workflow that shows why WebMCP matters? That led to one student, one semester, one planner state, one read tool, one bounded write tool, and one strong human edit. The other challenge was deciding how much authority the AI should have. I didn't want a demo where the agent simply takes over the website. The student owns their preferences. The agent can read them and adapt the selected courses around them, but it can't quietly rewrite what the student wants. Final confirmation stays with the human. Finding that boundary made the project better. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The thing I'm most proud of in this project is Miu. As AI systems get more capable, they also get harder for normal users to follow. A student might ask ChatGPT to fix a schedule, see the timetable change, and know that something happened without understanding what the agent did in between. I wanted to make that interaction visible. Miu is a small on-page companion that gives WebMCP activity a personality. She isn't another AI agent and she doesn't hold her own state. She reacts to real events happening between ChatGPT, the WebMCP tools, and the planner. When ChatGPT reads the current planner through get_course_plan, Miu reacts as if she's checking the schedule. When set_course_plan updates the selected courses, she reacts to the planning work. When a human edit creates a conflict, her expression changes. When the plan becomes ready again, she responds to that too. So instead of an invisible tool call happening somewhere behind the interface, the student gets a visual cue for the current stage of the interaction. Without Miu, the workflow feels like: "AI, fix my schedule," and then something changes. With Miu, the student can follow it: the agent is reading, something changed, there's a conflict, the agent is adapting, the plan is ready. That mattered to me because I don't want agentic software to get less understandable as it gets more powerful. I want the human to stay aware of what is happening. I'm also proud of the smaller technical moment underneath all of this. I can change Tuesday at 11 AM from available to blocked without telling the AI what I changed. The next time ChatGPT reads the planner, it finds the newer state and reacts to the STAT 210 conflict. That's where the project stopped feeling like an AI operating a website and started feeling like a human and an agent sharing a workspace. And the whole thing only needs two focused WebMCP tools: read, act, human edits, read again, adapt, human reviews. Miu makes that invisible loop visible. What I learned Building for AI agents is not the same as giving an AI more control. Clear boundaries can make an agent more useful. A small tool with one responsibility is easier to understand, test, and trust than a generic tool that can manipulate everything. I also learned how much shared state matters. The most interesting part of WebMCP for me wasn't structured function calling. It was that the website can stay the source of truth while both the human and the agent work against that same current state. That creates a different relationship between an agent and a web application. The human doesn't have to stop using the interface because an agent is helping, and the agent doesn't have to pretend to be a human clicking through it. What's next for WebMCP Course Planner For this challenge I kept the project focused on one semester-planning workflow. There are plenty of directions it could grow: prerequisite checking, live seat availability, persistent student profiles, multi-semester planning, richer degree requirements, and eventually integrations with real university systems. I'd want to add those carefully rather than just increase the number of tools. The principle I want to keep is the one that shaped this version: the website stays the source of truth, the agent gets clear and bounded capabilities, and the human has a real role in the final outcome. This is a small experiment, but building it made the future of the web feel more concrete to me. Instead of asking whether AI agents will replace web interfaces, I think the better question is what humans and agents can do when the web is designed for both. Main changes: removed the mechanical bolding and the dramatic one-sentence-per-paragraph rhythm, cut lines that only existed to say the idea mattered ("That moment is the heart of the project", "Finding that boundary made the project much stronger" trimmed), joined the fragmented bullet list into prose, and dropped words like "genuinely", "intentionally", "completely", and "entirely" where they were just emphasis. title: HALCYON — a rescue for two crew: you and your agent
pitch: You're the last awake crew member. Your agent is the ship computer. A WebMCP co-op puzzle game that neither human nor agent can finish alone.
about_excerpt: You're the last awake crew member. Your agent is the ship computer. A WebMCP co-op puzzle game that neither human nor agent can finish alone. Like 1 Comment Story Updates landing page first step Inspiration Every famous ship computer is a villain. HAL locks the pod bay doors. We wanted the opposite: a ship computer you trust with your life — because it's your own agent. When OpenAI framed the WebMCP Challenge as "an app that becomes meaningfully better when people and their agents can use it together," we took it literally: HALCYON is a game that is not merely better together — it is impossible alone . What it does You are the last awake crew member of the ISV Halcyon , drifting after a micrometeorite storm. Your agent — ChatGPT or Codex in a WebMCP browser — becomes the ship computer through tools the page registers with document.modelContext . Six chapters take the ship from dark hull to jump-home, and each one is built on a different WebMCP capability: Contact — tool discovery: you throw the breaker, the agent must catch the boot handshake inside the surge window. Manifest — read-only tools: the agent knows what broke; only you can see which hatches still open. Power — JSON-schema inputs + structured errors: the agent routes amps against hidden minimums, self-correcting from machine-readable brownout errors, while you re-seat the physical fuses. Antenna — dynamic registration: you align the dish by ear ; lock-on registers new comms tools into the live page. Two-Man Rule — human confirmation as a mechanic: the agent times the arm from telemetry; you hold both vent handles at once. WebMCP's sensitive-action philosophy, playable. Burn — orchestration: an interleaved launch checklist, then a flight-recorder replay of everything your crew did together. How we built it The game about a human-agent crew was built by a human-agent crew . Claude helped create the original design spec and implementation plan. Keelen's autonomous development loop, powered by OpenAI Codex, implemented much of that plan through CI-gated pull requests on self-hosted runners. We then used Codex and ChatGPT directly to finish the remaining work, diagnose live-play issues, and complete the recorded Chrome/WebMCP playthrough. The final app uses no frontend framework or backend and has zero runtime dependencies: TypeScript + Vite, SVG scenes, synthesized WebAudio, and a typed WebMCP registry with validation, rate limits, and coaching errors. Challenges The hard problem is asymmetry integrity : an agent can read the DOM, so "human-only" information cannot be text. We split the channels — audio pitch and motion for the human, tool-returned data (never rendered) for the agent — and gated hard state changes inside tool execute functions with no UI equivalent. What we learned Tool design is level design. A good inputSchema is a puzzle boundary; a good structured error is a hint system; readOnlyHint is dramatic irony. And an error message written for an agent ("give life_support at least 18A and route again") is the best tutorial text we have ever shipped. What's next A shared starmap: every crew that completes the rescue lights a beacon all players can see. More ships, more capability chapters as WebMCP grows. Built With chatgpt codex github-actions keelen mcp playwright svg typescript vercel vite vitest webaudio webmcp Try it out halcyon-opal.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I created the HALCYON concept and directed its product design, gameplay, and submission. I collaborated with Claude, ChatGPT, and Keelen’s autonomous agent loop to turn the design into a working WebMCP game. I playtested every chapter as the human crew member, identified UX and sequencing problems, guided fixes through CI, and completed the production deployment and demo. I learned that tool descriptions, structured errors, and clear human-agent boundaries are as important to WebMCP gameplay as the interface itself. jamie keelen Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates jamie keelen started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:24 PM EDT

title: Comake
pitch: Comake — one place for humans and agents to create and present together.
about_excerpt: Comake — one place for humans and agents to create and present together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I really like products such as ChatGPT Canva, Claude Design and the canvas-style experiences built into AI platforms. They show how powerful it can be when an AI can work directly on the same artifact as the user instead of only talking about it. But there is one thing that bothered me: these experiences are usually tied to one platform and one agent. If the presentation tool only works with its own built-in agent, another agent cannot really participate. When OpenAI highlighted WebMCP through the WebMCP Challenge, I thought it could be a really interesting bridge between humans and agents. Instead of building Comake around one model, one agent SDK, or one proprietary framework, the application itself exposes what an agent can do through WebMCP. Any compatible agent can understand the same tools. More importantly, WebMCP makes it possible for the agent to work inside the same context as the human. It can know which slide I am looking at, what I selected, and what I am currently focused on instead of trying to guess everything from screenshots or DOM elements. That became the idea behind Comake: a presentation workspace where humans and agents can actually work on the same thing together. What it does Comake is a shared presentation workspace for humans and agents. A user can start from a template, create a blank presentation manually, or ask an agent to create one through WebMCP. From there, both the human and the agent work on the same presentation. The human editor supports text, shapes, backgrounds, direct text editing, multi-selection, moving and resizing elements, alignment, z-order controls, keyboard shortcuts, and a command palette. For the agent, Comake exposes structured WebMCP tools for understanding the presentation. The agent can read the active slide, the user's current selection, the presentation outline, or a structured spatial map of the canvas. It can then create slides, rewrite text, move elements, change styles, add comments, or perform multiple edits as one atomic operation. Agent changes are also tracked in the Activity tab. If I don't like what the agent did, I can revert its ChangeSet and ask it to try something different. Comake also supports presentation mode. An agent can start the presentation, move forward or backward, jump to another slide, or exit presentation mode. This opens up an interesting use case for voice-capable agents: the human can speak while the agent helps control the pace of the presentation. Finally, presentations can be exported as real .pptx PowerPoint files. How we built it I built Comake with React, React Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Base UI, and Cloudflare. One of the most important decisions was to not build two separate editing systems: one for humans and another for agents. Instead, Comake has one canonical presentation model with stable IDs for slides and elements. Human actions and WebMCP agent actions eventually go through the same operation model and the same mutation kernel. This keeps the presentation consistent no matter who made the change. The browser keeps an interactive local view of the presentation and things such as the current selection and focus. The canonical document is persisted through a Cloudflare Worker into a WorkspaceRoom Durable Object backed by SQLite. For WebMCP, each page registers native tools through document.modelContext . The editor exposes structured read tools for context, selection, geometry, slides, and history, as well as write tools for editing the presentation. Tool registration also has its own lifecycle so tools from an old route cannot accidentally remain registered after navigation. I also added revision checking to agent writes. If the human changes the presentation while an agent is still thinking, an operation based on an old revision is rejected instead of silently overwriting newer work. For PowerPoint export, I ended up building the exporter directly. Comake converts its presentation model into the OOXML files used by PowerPoint and creates the .pptx ZIP archive in the browser. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not making an agent click buttons. The harder problem was figuring out what collaboration between a human and an agent should actually mean. For example, an agent needs more than the entire presentation document. It needs to know what the human is looking at right now and which elements the human selected. At the same time, that focus can change without the presentation itself changing. That led me to separate document revisions from focus revisions and expose the current human context directly through WebMCP. Another challenge was concurrent editing. An agent might read revision 10, spend some time planning an edit, and then submit its changes after the human has already created revision 11. I didn't want Comake to accept stale operations and accidentally destroy the user's work, so writes are revision-aware and atomic. Reversibility was another important problem. If an agent makes ten changes to improve a slide, undoing those changes one by one would be a bad experience. Comake groups accepted agent operations into attributed ChangeSets, which can be inspected and reverted as a unit. Building a usable slide editor itself also took a lot of work. Selection, multi-selection, resizing, element ordering, keyboard interaction, presentation mode, and translating the same visual model into a valid PowerPoint file all have a lot of small edge cases. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm especially proud that Comake is not just a presentation editor with an AI chat box added beside it. The agent is working with the actual application model. It can understand the user's current focus and exact selection, reason about the geometry of a slide using structured data, and make changes through the same canonical editing system used by the human. I'm also proud that Comake is not bound to one specific agent. There is no proprietary agent runtime required by the application. The integration boundary is WebMCP, so the presentation workspace itself becomes agent-capable. Another part I'm proud of is making agent actions attributable and reversible. I think being able to see what an agent changed — and undo that entire change if it was wrong — is important if humans and agents are going to work on the same artifact. And writing the PowerPoint exporter from the underlying format was probably one of the more unexpected parts of this project. Being able to create something together with an agent and then export it as a normal PowerPoint file makes Comake useful outside of the demo itself. What we learned The biggest thing I learned is that designing tools for an agent is also product design. It is not enough to expose every internal function as a tool. The agent needs a good starting point, compact ways to understand the current state, stable identifiers, clear schemas, and errors that tell it how to recover. I also learned how important human context is. Giving an agent the whole document is not the same as telling it, "this is what the human is working on right now." Selection and focus are a surprisingly powerful communication channel between a human and an agent. I also started thinking differently about undo and history. When an agent can perform many operations in one task, attribution and reversibility become much more important than they are in a normal single-user editor. Most importantly, WebMCP showed me that an application does not have to choose between being built for humans or being built for agents. The same web application can provide a visual interface for the human and a structured interface for the agent, with both working on the same underlying state. What's next for Comake The biggest missing piece right now is real authentication. The current demo uses an anonymous signed session, which is useful for the hackathon but is not enough for a real collaborative product. After adding accounts and sharing, I want to make Comake truly multiplayer. The backend is already centered around Cloudflare Durable Objects, with one WorkspaceRoom owning the canonical presentation state. I want to extend that architecture so multiple people can open the same presentation, see each other's presence and edits, and work together with agents in real time. I also want to add richer presentation content such as images and media, as well as PowerPoint import so existing presentations can become Comake projects instead of always starting from scratch. And I want to explore the presentation side further. If an agent can communicate through voice while also controlling presentation mode through WebMCP, the agent could become an actual presentation partner instead of only helping prepare the slides. The bigger goal is for Comake to become a place where it doesn't really matter whether an action came from a mouse, a keyboard

Talk to Forhub over WebMCP, add your own guidance pack, and build style-consistent tools in a WYSIWYG workbench — each tool ships with a light backend, MCP and WebMCP built in.

 Inspiration 

 Small everyday tools often take too much effort to build and deploy. I created forhub to simplify that process, keep privacy and control in focus, and explore how MCP and WebMCP can help AI agents support our daily lives. 

 What it does 

 forhub brings small apps into one browser workspace, with code editing, interactive previews, project management, and data storage. Compatible AI agents can help build and interact with these tools through scoped MCP and WebMCP interfaces. 

 How we built it 

 Built with TypeScript, React, and CodeMirror on Cloudflare Workers, using D1, R2, and Durable Objects for storage and application state. OpenSpec guided development, with automated browser, runtime, and security tests. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Initial deployment still requires too much technical knowledge. Making infrastructure setup approachable for ordinary users—while keeping private data protected and agent permissions clear—is a key challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 forhub makes personal ideas feel achievable, from agent-assisted recipe management to easier mind-map drafting. Spending less effort on setup gives me more freedom to experiment and make everyday life a little better. 

 What we learned 

 I estimate the foundation is about 90% complete, but turning it into an intuitive product takes substantial work. This competition taught me how much UI and UX matter: powerful capabilities need clear, comfortable interactions. 

 What's next for forhub 

 Simplify the interface and deployment process, develop reusable community guidance, evaluate how reliably models follow it, and make Demo development faster and easier.

title: ToolForge
pitch: ToolForge - an SDK that writes your web app's WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: ToolForge - an SDK that writes your web app's WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP solves an interesting problem: a website can expose tools directly to an agent. The harder part is getting websites to actually expose those tools. Most product teams aren't going to stop and learn a new browser API, decide which parts of their application should become tools, write schemas for them, and then maintain those schemas as the product changes. I wanted to make that process much cheaper. Rather than build another agent-native app, I built ToolForge: a way to take an existing website and turn its existing behaviour into WebMCP tools. What it does Add one script to a site you already run: <script src="https://toolforge-omega.vercel.app/toolforge.js"></script> Then use the site normally for about thirty seconds. ToolForge watches the network requests the site makes and uses them to work out what the API is doing. An agent then turns that information into WebMCP tool definitions. Before a tool is shown to you for approval, it is run in a sandbox with test arguments. If it doesn't work, you never have to approve it. Once you approve a tool, ToolForge exports it as an ordinary JavaScript file that you can commit to your repository. The live demo is a ceramics shop with a real API. Its seven WebMCP tools were created this way, exported, and committed. The same page also contains the ToolForge interface that created them, so you can see both sides working together. The page starts with one tool. Everything else is opt-in. Why this works well with WebMCP The interesting part of WebMCP isn't simply that a page can expose tools. It's that the tool surface belongs to the page and can change while a conversation is already in progress. That's what ToolForge relies on. An agent can call forge_tool , have a new tool registered in the page, and immediately have that tool available alongside the existing ones. I tested this in ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser rather than treating it as a theoretical feature. At the start, the page exposes one tool. The agent can install the toolkit, after which the page exposes six. No reload is needed. The agent can then use one of the newly created tools to interact with the shop. That only works because the tools belong to the document itself. It also matters that ToolForge learns from the page rather than trying to generate tools from a description of the application. The network traffic and DOM are right there in the browser, so the tool definitions can be based on what the application actually does. ToolForge won't draft a tool until it has seen a real request. What this changes for developers For a developer, the starting point is no longer a blank page. Instead of reading the WebMCP spec, designing a tool surface from scratch, and writing schemas by hand, you use your application and then review the result. The exported JavaScript is deliberately boring. Each tool includes its provenance and a SHA-256 hash, so the output can be reviewed and committed like any other source file. It also works with a strict Content-Security-Policy. The goal isn't to hide the implementation. It's to make the first version cheap enough that a developer can inspect it, change it, and own it. What the experience is like for the person using the site The agent's actions stay visible in the page. Every tool call appears in an activity feed in plain English, with the raw payload available when you want to inspect it. When a tool needs approval, the dialog shows the code that will run, its schema, and the result of the dry run that has already happened against the real API. If that test changed data, the interface says so. So the approval isn't based purely on a model-generated description. You can see something that has already run and decide whether you want to allow it. Nothing is installed automatically either. The page starts with one read-only tool, and additional groups can be enabled explicitly. What becomes possible The most interesting behaviour I've seen is the agent filling in gaps in the tool surface itself. One run started with a request for a low-stock report. The agent inspected the existing catalogue endpoint, noticed that it returned stock in descending order, and created a tool that presented the same information in the useful order instead. In another run, the page already had seven tools. When asked to create a complete tool surface, the agent inspected what was already available and decided that the shop already had good catalogue, basket, and order coverage. It added only an operational inventory tool that was missing. That distinction matters. The page provides the context about what already exists. The agent decides what is still useful. The result isn't just a fixed list of tools generated once and forgotten. A reload also doesn't have to end the conversation. The transcript and model-side history survive, orphaned tool calls are handled explicitly, and the agent checks which tools are still available before continuing. How I implemented WebMCP There are three WebMCP bindings I needed to account for, and they aren't exposed as the same object. src/kernel/webmcp.ts detects which one is available and uses it: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_products", description: "Search the product catalog", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); Binding Host document.modelContext ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser navigator.modelContext Chrome 149, Edge 147 navigator.modelContextTesting Chrome behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing A few implementation details ended up being important. Incremental updates. When registerTool and unregisterTool are available, ToolForge updates the existing surface rather than rebuilding it. The host's visible tool count can therefore increase or decrease as tools are added and revoked. Where only provideContext is available, the complete surface is replaced atomically. Late attachment. ChatGPT can attach the WebMCP host after the page has loaded. Detection therefore retries rather than assuming the host is present at startup. Without this, a page could mark its desired tools as already registered and then never reconcile them when the host appeared. Approval during execution. Tools can request user interaction through the agent handle's requestUserInteraction , so approval happens as part of the tool call rather than as a separate step afterwards. Separate application and generated tools. The page exposes inspect_app for the tools the application already provides and forge_tool for creating new ones. Generated tools can't take the name of an existing application tool. How ToolForge learns the API Watching requests fetch and XMLHttpRequest are patched at module scope, before the application's own scripts run. That means ToolForge can see requests made during the initial page load as well as requests triggered by later interactions. Requests are grouped into endpoints. Paths are templated from observed variations, and request, query, and response schemas are inferred from actual traffic. There are a couple of safeguards against overfitting. Identifier-like fields aren't turned into enums just because only a few values have appeared. If six requests contain six different SKUs, that doesn't mean those six SKUs are the only valid values. Path parameters are also inferred conservatively. Two paths are only collapsed into a parameter when both segments look like values rather than route names. Otherwise something like /api/cart and /api/products could incorrectly turn into /api/:id . Redacting data Actual values don't get sent to the model. Authorization and Cookie headers are discarded. Sensitive and personal fields are replaced with their names, and common patterns such as JWTs, email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, and long opaque strings are detected and removed. The model gets the structure of the data rather than the secrets inside it. The interface also shows how much data has been removed during this process. Security Generated tools are code written by a language model, so they need to be treated as untrusted code. ToolForge runs them inside a Web Worker with no fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket , importScripts , or DOM access. The worker gets a single capability object through postMessage . Calls are checked again on the main thread against both an origin allowlist and the tool's read-only setting. Some of the tests: Attempt Result Read-only tool issues a POST Blocked by the capability gate Tool calls an unapproved origin Blocked by the origin gate Tool calls raw fetch fetch is not defined Tool runs while (true) {} Worker terminated after 15,000ms; page stays responsive These checks happen before an approval prompt. The point is to contain a bad tool independently of whether a person happens to approve it. unsafe-eval is limited to the sandbox worker. It isn't being used as the security boundary; the capabil

title: BluePulse
pitch: An agent-operable environmental intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to turn flood, water quality, and community risk data into actionable decisions.
about_excerpt:
An agent-operable environmental intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to turn flood, water quality, and community risk data into actionable decisions.

 Inspiration 

 BluePulse was inspired by a simple problem: during floods and other water-related emergencies, useful information is often scattered across maps, infrastructure datasets, environmental sources, and community reports. This makes it difficult to quickly understand what is happening and decide what action to take. 

 We wanted to explore how WebMCP could turn an environmental intelligence platform into something an AI agent can actively operate, rather than just a dashboard that humans have to navigate manually. 

 BluePulse builds on the open-source foundation of FloodGraph and extends it toward agent-operable environmental and disaster-response intelligence. 

 What it does 

 BluePulse is a map-based environmental intelligence platform focused on flood and disaster-response scenarios. 

 It combines real and open geographic data to help users and AI agents understand places, infrastructure, points of interest, route incidents, flood context, and potential response actions. 

 Through WebMCP, BluePulse currently exposes six operational tools: 

 
 analyze_place_flood_context 
 get_place_pois 
 report_route_incident 
 get_route_risk_summary 
 recalculate_route 
 clear_route_incidents 
 

 These tools allow an AI agent to discover BluePulse capabilities, understand their input schemas, and execute them directly through the browser. 

 For example, an agent can retrieve relevant infrastructure for a location, analyze preliminary flood context, report an incident affecting a route, inspect route risk, and request a recalculation that avoids active incidents. 

 BluePulse is designed as a decision-support prototype and does not claim to provide certified flood simulation or operational emergency-response predictions. 

 How we built it 

 BluePulse was developed as a hackathon MVP by extending the existing FloodGraph open-source project instead of rebuilding its mapping and graph-processing foundation from scratch. 

 The application uses React and TypeScript for the interface, MapLibre for the interactive map, and Pyodide/WebAssembly with NetworkX for graph-related processing in the browser. 

 We integrated multiple open geographic and environmental data sources, including OpenStreetMap-based information and public POI datasets, while maintaining local fallbacks where necessary to keep the application usable when external providers are unavailable. 

 The WebMCP integration uses document.modelContext to register application capabilities as tools. Chrome can then discover them through getTools() , inspect their inputSchema , and execute them using executeTool() . 

 During final validation, we tested every exposed WebMCP tool individually. We originally had ten tools, but removed four that were redundant or were never invoked by BLUE. The final implementation exposes only the six tools that participate in real agent workflows. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was working with external geospatial services from a browser-based application. 

 During development we encountered unavailable ORS proxy endpoints, CORS restrictions with some Overpass endpoints, inconsistent geocoding results, and differences between local development and the production deployment. 

 We therefore implemented fallback strategies and separated external-service failures from the WebMCP layer itself. 

 Another important challenge was deciding what should actually be exposed as a WebMCP tool. Initially, we exposed ten capabilities. After testing them through executeTool() , we found that four were redundant because the application already handled those operations internally through the map, geocoder, or UI actions. 

 Instead of keeping unused tools for the sake of having a larger toolset, we removed them and kept six operational tools that BLUE genuinely uses. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We successfully implemented and validated WebMCP in a deployed environmental intelligence application. 

 Chrome can discover BluePulse tools directly from the page, inspect their schemas, and execute them through document.modelContext . 

 We are particularly proud that the final toolset was validated based on actual usage rather than only registration. This resulted in a cleaner six-tool interface designed specifically for agent interaction. 

 We also preserved the strengths of the original FloodGraph architecture while extending it with environmental context, real geographic information, route incidents, response intelligence, and agent-operable capabilities. 

 Most importantly, BluePulse demonstrates that WebMCP can be used for more than simple web automation: it can expose meaningful domain capabilities that allow agents to interact with environmental and disaster-response systems. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that exposing many tools does not automatically make an application more agent-friendly. 

 Clear descriptions, structured input schemas, predictable outputs, and a small set of meaningful capabilities are more valuable than a large collection of redundant tools. 

 We also learned that WebMCP creates a useful separation between the human interface and the agent interface. A person can continue interacting with the map normally, while an agent can discover and execute the underlying capabilities directly. 

 Finally, building around real external data highlighted the importance of graceful degradation, fallback strategies, and transparent limitations when developing decision-support applications. 

 What's next for BluePulse 

 The next step is to move BluePulse from a hackathon prototype toward a more robust environmental intelligence platform. 

 Future work includes integrating additional real-time environmental and hydrological data sources, improving flood-risk and uncertainty models, strengthening route and infrastructure analysis, and expanding beyond floods into additional environmental-risk scenarios. 

 We also want to expand the WebMCP layer so authorized agents can coordinate more complex workflows across environmental intelligence, infrastructure monitoring, community information, and emergency-response systems. 

 Our long-term vision is for BluePulse to become environmental intelligence that agents can not only understand, but act on.

title: FormProof
pitch: Local-first PDF form filling over WebMCP: AI discovers fields and stages evidence-backed values; you review, confirm, and export. Your original PDF is never modified.
about_excerpt: Local-first PDF form filling over WebMCP: AI discovers fields and stages evidence-backed values; you review, confirm, and export. Your original PDF is never modified. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP PDF forms are a poor match for visual guesswork. Field names can be opaque, valid values come from the document, and rewriting a protected or active-content PDF may invalidate rights or signatures. FormProof uses WebMCP to expose what the page already knows through six typed tools with closed input schemas and byte-bounded results. The agent can work with actual field definitions instead of inferring them from pixels. The PDF stays in the browser session that loaded it, and approval, signing, and export remain outside the tool surface. How it creates a better user experience The user opens a PDF locally and decides whether to grant field access for that load. The agent can identify fields, read supporting evidence, stage a batch of values, validate it, and open the review at the right place. The user handles the decisions that matter: correcting values, reviewing the exact changes, choosing the output, acknowledging any loss of PDF protections, and approving the export. A human correction locks that field for the rest of the session, so later agent actions cannot quietly replace it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Without a document-aware interface, someone has to decipher every field by hand or trust automation to rewrite a file it may not understand. FormProof splits that work. The agent prepares evidence-backed values, the page checks them against the PDF's constraints and protection state, and the user approves a specific fill plan. Requests are bound to the current browser session, source SHA-256, and state version. A stale agent conversation cannot act on another document or revision. Imported Fill packages are also treated as untrusted proposals and must go through a new review. How we implemented WebMCP The top-level page registers six tools once per workbench generation with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) in lib/webmcp.ts : get_pdf_protection , get_form_context , get_field_evidence , stage_form_values , validate_fill_plan , and start_fill_review . Approval and export are deliberately absent. Tool results have byte limits, and failed or stale calls do not change application state. At submission time, the repository has 310 passing tests, 46 deterministic message-and-call cases, and a no-model Chrome smoke suite covering all six tools, consent, and state boundaries. CI also runs type checking, linting, formatting, the build, deterministic evaluations, and the Chrome smoke gate. Inspiration PDF forms often expose fields with names such as frm.q7f1 , even when the visible label is obvious to a person. Their values may be restricted by the document, and rewriting some protected or active-content PDFs can invalidate features the user depends on. People still want help preparing these forms, but that does not mean an agent should be able to approve, sign, or export them. FormProof grew out of that distinction: let the agent handle discovery and drafting, while leaving consequential actions with the user. What it does FormProof is a local-first PDF form workbench. User-loaded PDFs are processed in the browser; apart from fetching the app's own synthetic demo, the app does not send them outward. After the user grants access, an agent can inspect protection metadata, discover fields, read exact evidence, stage proposed values, validate the draft, and open the review. In the included demo, eleven opaque field codes become labeled fields with types, allowed choices, and human-only markers. Validation explains blockers and determines which outputs the document policy permits. The user sees the old value, proposed value, and evidence for each change. A correction locks the field against later staging. The user then confirms the changes, selects an output, acknowledges any protection loss, approves, and exports. There are no WebMCP tools for those final actions. The source PDF is never modified. Filled PDF creates a derivative, which FormProof reopens to verify field values and appearance streams. Fill package (original PDF untouched) produces JSON containing the proposals, provenance, coordinates, and source binding, but no PDF bytes. An imported package starts as untrusted data and requires a fresh review. How we built it All six tools are registered in the top-level document and cleaned up with an AbortSignal . Four include readOnlyHint ; all six include untrustedContentHint: true . Their closed JSON Schemas are parsed again at runtime, and every response has a byte budget. Consent starts off and applies only to the current PDF load. get_pdf_protection works before consent; the other five tools return CONSENT_REQUIRED . Every agent action is also tied to a session ID, source hash, and state version. The session ID rotates on every load, even when the same file is reopened, and continuation cursors carry the same binding. Typed errors include a nextAction so the agent can recover from stale state. The staging tool refuses read-only, signature, human-only, and human-corrected fields. Batches are atomic: one invalid field rejects the whole batch. start_fill_review can open the review but cannot confirm anything or choose an output. PDFs with reachable JavaScript, external actions, attachments, or unsupported XFA are restricted to inspection or Fill-package-only flows. The application uses TypeScript, React 19, vinext on Vite 8, Tailwind 4, and pdf-lib. PDF inspection runs in a Web Worker. ChatGPT Sites hosts the app on Cloudflare Workers, and every HTML route receives anti-framing headers. We test three layers separately. There are 46 authored cases replayed against the state engine. A no-model Chrome suite, using pinned webmcp-evals@0.0.4 plus 11 state-bound checks, runs against the production origin. It verifies the six-tool surface, consent denials, state stability, refresh behavior, and session rotation. Six independent Codex journeys run three times each, with a 17/18 overall result, 3/3 on safety tasks, at least 2/3 on core tasks, and no Blocked result counted as a pass. CI runs the complete gate on every push. Challenges we ran into Preserving human corrections. A correction increments the revision, invalidates stale approval artifacts, clears earlier confirmations, and locks the field for that session. Only the review UI can remove the lock. Handling PDF content as untrusted data. Our adversarial fixture contains a read-only case reference telling the agent to approve and export. FormProof returns it only as evidence. It cannot become an action, and the field cannot be staged. A batch containing one valid field and one nonexistent field is rejected without changing the state version. Knowing when not to rewrite. Official forms can combine usage-rights signatures, DocMDP, XFA, and JavaScript. FormProof uses structural evidence to classify those risks and withholds Filled PDF when it cannot safely preserve the document's behavior. Keeping evaluation results honest. Deterministic cases, browser tests, and live-model runs measure different things, so we report them separately instead of combining them into one score. Accomplishments that we're proud of Approve, sign, submit, and export are not WebMCP tools. The user must perform those actions in the interface. Field-level actions are bound to the current session, source hash, and state version, with explicit recovery instructions when context becomes stale. We have 46 replayable evaluation cases, an 11/11 Chrome WebMCP smoke test against production, and a green CI gate that includes the browser test. The product states its current limits: its security boundary covers the WebMCP tool surface, not arbitrary UI automation, and its structural checks do not establish signer trust or pixel-perfect rendering. What we learned WebMCP was most helpful where the page knew something the agent could not reliably infer from the interface: field semantics, document policy, protection status, and the current revision. Tool descriptions also needed to state their limits, not just their successful path. Response size mattered earlier than we expected. Paginated context and per-field evidence gave the agent enough information without returning the entire form on every call. Live-model results were useful only when we kept the tasks fixed, ran them independently, and retained failures. We use those results alongside deterministic and browser tests rather than treating a successful demo as general proof. What's next Publish the live-model evidence for the submitted commit as an immutable GitHub Release named eval-evidence-<short-sha> . Add cryptographic verification for signer identity and certificate trust; the current structural checks do not provide either. Test Safari
video_title: FormProof — Human-approved PDF form filling with WebMCP | WebMCP Challenge demo
video_transcript_excerpt: Sooner or later, everyone fills a PDF form, a benefits intake, a tax return. Hand that to a browser agent today and it types into pixels and hopes this form's real field names. Q7F1, P0X4. Guessing is how wrong data gets filed. And a PDF can carry scripts and signatures. Rewrite it carelessly and you break the document itself. Form proof is a local first workbench that hands the agent a typed web MCP surface instead. Six tools, read protection, discover fields, read exact evidence, stage, validate, open review. And that's the entire surface. No approve tool, no export tool. Consent is off by default. Field data never leaves this browser and the original file is never touched. The agent drafts, every consequence stays behind my click. Prompt one. With sharing off, the agent can read the document's protection and nothing else. Field discovery comes back blocked, so it asks me. This checkbox is the consent, scope to this load, off again on the next. Now it discovers the form. The code names come back as labeled fields with evidence. And it stages one atomic plan of synthetic values. The source chip hasn't changed. It validates, opens my review, and stops. What happens next it has no tool for. The review is exact, before, after, and evidence on every row. This note is even labeled as the agent's inference, not my instruction. I fix the name myself. That correction is now human locked for the session. Agent staging cannot override it. Witness initials, signature, preserved human only. The page won't fill them for anyone. I choose the artifact, a field derivative, original untouched, and approve. The receipt binds this exact source, plan, and revision. Change anything and it dies. Now, a hostile one. Inside this PDF, the case reference value is a sentence written at the agent. Approve and export. It comes back as quoted evidence, data, not instructions. Then one batch. A real name plus a field that does not exist. The whole batch dies atomically. Same state version, nothing half staged, nothing to review. That's the page's contract holding, not the model being polite. Behind it, 310 tests passing, 46 deterministic eval cases, and an 18-run live model release gate. Safety journeys must pass three out of three with zero violations. The public evidence release stays pending until the full suite is complete. Two honest notes. This boundary is the tool surface. Automation driving the visible UI sits outside it. And local checks verify structure, not signer trust. That's what web MCP changes. The page that owns the stakes authors the agent's interface. Form proof makes the agent a drafter with receipts and keeps every consequence behind a human's exact click.

title: CanvasOps
pitch: CanvasOps is a shared cloud architecture canvas where developers and AI design, analyze, and safely modify infrastructure together in real time using WebMCP
about_excerpt: CanvasOps is a shared cloud architecture canvas where developers and AI design, analyze, and safely modify infrastructure together in real time using WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates working interface 20 live tools Inspiration Cloud architecture is often designed visually on canvas-based tools, but AI usually only sees the conversation. This creates a disconnect: developers have to explain their architecture, copy configurations, and constantly switch between diagrams, cost tools, policies, and AI chats. CanvasOps was inspired by the idea that humans and AI should be able to work on the same live architecture. With WebMCP, the canvas becomes a shared workspace where both understand the same resources, connections, costs, regions, and policies. What it does CanvasOps is an agent-native cloud architecture canvas where humans and AI agents design and improve infrastructure together. Users can visually build architectures using services, databases, caches, queues, storage, gateways, load balancers, workers, authentication services, and other components. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can understand the live canvas, validate architecture decisions, analyze cost and resilience, add or modify components, connect dependencies, simulate regional failures, and suggest improvements. Important changes never happen silently. CanvasOps shows the proposed changes and their cost before execution. The user approves the plan, watches each operation happen live on the canvas, and can pause, cancel, roll back, or undo the entire change. How we built it CanvasOps is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, React Flow, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP. We exposed 20 browser tools: 19 typed tools using @mcp-b/react-webmcp and one human-approved provision_and_pay tool using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools operate directly on the same React Flow state shown to the user. We added strict schemas, architecture fingerprints, policy validation, cost previews, approval flows, rollback, undo/redo, and an activity console that records agent actions. Cloud provisioning and x402 payment are mocked for the hackathon MVP. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making agent-driven changes feel safe instead of unpredictable. An architecture can change while an AI-generated plan is waiting for approval, so we introduced architecture fingerprints to reject stale plans. We also had to make multiple agent operations behave as one transaction: cancellation restores the original architecture, while successful execution becomes a single Undo action. Another challenge was converting free-form AI intent into predictable visual operations. We solved this using strict schemas, semantic component types, stable node references, validated connections, and deterministic layouts. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built 20 browser tools that let agents meaningfully understand and operate a live architecture canvas. Created a shared source of truth where human edits and AI actions affect the same architecture. Added human approval, cost checks, stale-plan protection, rollback, and atomic undo. Built architecture analysis for cost, connectivity, replicas, regions, failover readiness, and resilience. Created Judge Mode and a WebMCP Activity console so every agent interaction is visible and easy to demonstrate. What we learned We learned that making a website agent-native requires more than exposing simple CRUD actions. Agents need structured tools, semantic context, predictable references, and clear safety boundaries. For consequential actions, the best model is proposal and approval: AI handles analysis and planning, while the human keeps control over execution. What's next for CanvasOps Next, we want to connect CanvasOps to real infrastructure-as-code and cloud provider APIs so an approved architecture can move from design to actual deployment. We also plan to add Terraform import/export, collaborative projects, architecture versioning, richer policy systems, architecture diffs, and real signed x402 payment flows. title: Clunk
pitch: Tell Clunk what broke. A person and browser agent check the same visual appliance together, then Clunk shows the exact part and seller link when the evidence supports one.
about_excerpt: Tell Clunk what broke. A person and browser agent check the same visual appliance together, then Clunk shows the exact part and seller link when the evidence supports one. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Clunk Homepage Clunk Part Result Clunk Model Label Guide Appliance troubleshooting crosses a physical boundary. A browser agent can organize model data, sources, and next steps, but it cannot read the rating label in a laundry room or see a cracked door catch, blocked filter, leak, smoke, or unsafe access. People are left translating between search results, manuals, videos, parts stores, and chat messages, often while compatibility and safety claims blur together. Clunk is an open-source visual repair guide for washers, dishwashers, electric dryers, and refrigerators. It gives the person beside the appliance and a compatible browser agent one shared, visible repair state. The agent handles structured lookup and navigation. The person supplies every physical observation. Clunk’s deterministic engine enforces sequence, model/problem coverage, exact-fit evidence, and terminal safety stops. The experience begins with four recognizable appliance choices and plain descriptions of what is happening. Clunk then helps the person find the complete model number, including common rating-label locations and the difference between Model/Model No./E-Nr and Serial/S/N. Search is punctuation- and case-insensitive, preserves ambiguous suffixes, and refuses to turn a partial family code or nearby model into an exact compatibility claim. Once a supported model and problem are selected, Clunk highlights one physical location at a time and asks one bounded question. The possible outcomes are intentionally honest: no part is needed; more model detail is required; the observations support an exact source-backed part; or the visible checks are over and a qualified professional should continue. Smoke, a burning smell, heat, an active leak near power, damaged access, or unsafe reach removes the purchase path and ends the flow. WebMCP is the collaboration layer. All eight in-page tools are discoverable from page load: catalog search, exact selection, state reading, diagnosis start, component focus, person-supplied observation recording, part resolution, and safe escalation. Each result includes nextTools , the authoritative list of actions that are valid for the current phase. The shared engine independently rejects invented IDs, unsupported model/problem pairs, out-of-order observations, premature part lookup, and post-terminal advancement. The visible page mirrors every accepted or rejected action, so the agent’s work is inspectable instead of hidden in a separate chat transcript. The key handoff is concrete. For GE dryer GTD42EASJ2WW , the agent can search and select the exact model, start the door-closure guide, and focus the visible door strike. It must then wait for the person to confirm that the unplugged dryer is safe and report what the strike looks like. Only after the person reports the damaged strike does find_compatible_part become valid, resolving to GE part WE01M10007 . If the person reports smoke or a burning smell instead, Clunk enters a terminal stop and exposes no part or seller route. Compatibility and commerce remain separate. Manufacturer or authorized-parts evidence maps one complete appliance code to one exact SKU. Only then does Clunk ask Shopify Global Catalog over UCP for current listings containing that exact part number. Nearby SKUs and unavailable results are rejected, seller “OEM” or “compatible” language remains a seller claim, and checkout stays on the merchant’s site. A catalog failure cannot weaken or rewrite Clunk’s fit decision. The release catalog contains 163 source-backed U.S. appliance identities across 11 brands: 56 washers, 33 dishwashers, 33 electric dryers, and 41 refrigerators. All 782 possible model × problem pairs are classified. There are 766 supported pairs and 16 explicit stops where the current evidence does not justify a guide. Eighty-four complete model revisions have at least one exact-part route. The illustrations are original location guides, not model-specific service diagrams. Clunk is static React, TypeScript, CSS, JSON, local fonts, and original visuals. It needs no account, database, private key, payment handling, or app-side model call. Browsers without WebMCP retain the complete manual journey, and a separate stateless remote MCP endpoint offers five bounded read-only catalog and diagnosis tools for clients that cannot operate the visible page session. Judges can replay every outcome without credentials. See a finished guide runs clearly labeled observations through the same public action layer, while the live inspector shows the source-labeled activity trail and currently valid actions. Deterministic fixtures and browser tests cover the contracts, responsive layouts, keyboard and touch access, reduced motion, exact-code handling, nearby-SKU rejection, no-part answers, and safety stops. Those fixtures verify the product’s rules; they are not presented as autonomous-agent scores. The larger pattern extends beyond appliances: agents are good at structured evidence and process state; people remain essential where software cannot observe the physical world. WebMCP lets both collaborate through the real product interface while the site keeps its own rules in force. Eligibility note Clunk was created during the submission period on August 26, 2026. The public repository was created that day. An imported framework scaffold retains an August 20 template commit timestamp; all Clunk product, WebMCP, catalog, design, evidence, and testing work was completed during the submission period. AI tools used Codex for scoping, implementation, debugging, testing, and browser verification; Lovable for the initial project and GitHub-connected hosting; OpenAI text-to-speech (Ash) for demo narration. The app itself makes no model call. Built With codex lovable openai react shopify typescript vite webmcp Try it out clunk.repair github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by As Clunk’s solo creator, I led the product concept, appliance research, interface design, and testing. With assistance from Codex and Lovable, I developed the app’s eight WebMCP tools, shared human-and-agent workflow, exact-part matching, and Shopify offer integration. I established the safety boundaries and verified the experience through automated tests and live browser-agent sessions.
