title: Floortris
pitch: WebMCP agents turn dimensioned sketches into rule-checked 2D and 3D rooms, while people compare proposals and control every final change.
about_excerpt: WebMCP agents turn dimensioned sketches into rule-checked 2D and 3D rooms, while people compare proposals and control every final change. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I started Floortris late in the challenge with a practical question: why can an AI describe a room layout but struggle to work directly with the room planner already open in front of it? Before implementing WebMCP, I was surprised by how difficult it was for an AI agent to use the website reliably. It had to interpret controls visually, infer the state of the room and hope that each interaction had worked. Even when the result looked reasonable, the agent could miss important details such as door swings, walking routes, furniture orientation or the measurements of items someone already owned. I wanted to explore a better approach: a room planner designed from the beginning for a person and an agent to use together. The agent should understand the same measured room shown on screen, work under the same rules and produce a visible proposal—while the person retains control of every final change. What it does Floortris is a local-first room planner for people and agents. A person can enter a measured room, add doors and windows, record furniture they already own, lock its dimensions or position and edit the layout directly. An agent can use 16 native WebMCP tools to inspect the same document, construct a separate Proposal, arrange furniture, change finishes and check the resulting layout. The agent works in Proposal , while the accepted room remains in Yours . It does not switch the person’s view or apply its own work. Apply, room-input confirmation, discard, unlock and view switching remain human-only actions. Floortris checks more than whether two rectangles overlap. Its shared rule engine evaluates: door swings and open door leaves; hard and preferred walking clearances; routes between entrances and activity zones; TV positioning and seating relationships; coffee-table gaps; usable bed sides; storage and window access; linked desks and chair pull zones; radiators and wall-mounted objects; measured curtains, blinds and lighting fixtures. An agent can recreate rectilinear rooms with alcoves, recesses, nooks and L-shaped outlines from dimensioned information. The same measured outline is then used by the 2D board, 3D scene, collision rules, ceiling checks, walking routes and placement search. Agents can also create measured custom furniture inside a Proposal, including genuine connected L- and U-shaped sectionals. These use a closed, validated geometry format instead of arbitrary code or remote 3D assets. They remain subject to the same placement rules and human approval boundary as catalogue furniture. Why WebMCP The floor plan itself is the product. A hidden API response or a paragraph describing where furniture should go is not enough—the measurements, furniture, warnings and proposed changes need to remain visible and reviewable. Floortris registers 16 native tools through document.modelContext . These include generateRoom , getRoomState , createProposal , createCustomFurniture , placeFurniture , updateFurniture , findPlacements , setAppearance and checkLayout . These tools give the agent structured access to the same room state and rule engine used by the visible interface. Instead of guessing what a button does or interpreting the page from pixels, the agent can request exact measurements, submit a revision-bound change and receive structured feedback explaining whether the layout is healthy. WebMCP made the agent much more reliable, but I deliberately avoided giving it complete authority. It can perform substantial spatial work, but its result remains a Proposal until a person reviews and applies it. How I built it Floortris is built with TypeScript, React, Next.js on the vinext runtime, Three.js, Vite and Cloudflare Workers. At its centre is a shared rule engine operating on a measured 20 cm grid. Human controls and WebMCP commands pass through the same document store and validation logic. This prevents the visible room and the agent’s representation from developing different versions of spatial truth. Each WebMCP tool has a strict JSON Schema, explicit metadata, revision checks and abort-aware execution. Placement searches are bounded, and candidates are ranked by functional quality rather than simply returning the first coordinate without a collision. I also added seven difficult benchmark rooms, three checked planning strategies, static accommodation-provider packs, advisory accessibility planning packs, a local evaluation dashboard, furniture-schedule exports, printable move-in sheets and server-free share links carried in the URL fragment. Room, evaluation and share data is not sent to an application data backend. Share data only leaves the device when the person explicitly shares the generated URL. A Cloudflare Worker serves the client application; there is no application database or remote LLM service. Challenges I faced The hardest technical challenge was maintaining one spatial truth across every part of the application. A custom cut-out in an L-shaped room could not simply be hidden in the 2D view. It also had to be absent from collision cells, walking routes, ceiling placement, search candidates and the 3D shell. Custom sectional furniture created a similar problem: an L- or U-shaped sofa needed to behave as one connected object without treating its empty internal area as occupied floor space. Furniture rules were more relational than I initially expected. Whether a coffee table works depends on the sofa’s true facing edge and measured gap. Whether a desk works depends on its chair and pull zone. Whether shelving is correctly placed depends on which edge is actually its back—not merely whether some part of its bounding box touches a wall. I also encountered problems with door clearances, TVs appearing behind doors, shelving facing the wrong direction, disappearing 2D labels and stuttering 3D shadows. Fixing these required the rule engine and renderers to use explicit geometry rather than visual assumptions. Another challenge was protecting human work while an agent was operating. Proposal branches, revision-bound commands, immutable snapshots and exact-revision review checks prevent a delayed agent action from silently overwriting a newer human edit. What I learned I was most surprised by how difficult it was for an AI agent to use the website before I implemented the WebMCP tools. A page that feels obvious to a person can still be ambiguous to an agent when its capabilities and state are only communicated visually. That changed how I think about building websites. In future projects, I want to consider agent-native compatibility from the beginning rather than treating it as something added afterwards. As the world becomes increasingly reliant on AI, websites should expose clear, structured and constrained capabilities that allow agents to help without taking control away from people. I also learned that useful agentic interfaces need visible state, explicit authority and reversible proposals—not simply more tools. Geometry needs to be centralised as well. Once the 2D plan, 3D scene, placement search and validation engine all used the same measurements, complex room shapes and custom furniture became much easier to support correctly. I am proudest of how quickly I produced a working prototype despite starting late, while documenting the development publicly on TikTok at the same time. Building in public forced me to explain each problem clearly and showed how quickly an initial prototype could develop into a much more capable agent-native application. Floortris ultimately became more than a furniture visualiser. It became an experiment in how people and agents can share one visible, rule-checked document while the person retains ownership of the final decision. title: StudyTree
pitch: Play a learning game with an AI that can talk but can't cheat. A human and a voice agent alternate turns growing a knowledge tree, and the agent moves only through WebMCP tool calls.
about_excerpt: Play a learning game with an AI that can talk but can't cheat. A human and a voice agent alternate turns growing a knowledge tree, and the agent moves only through WebMCP tool calls. Like Comment Story Updates GamePlay chatgpt image gen inspiration Inspiration I'm a lifelong learner, and I've always loved the idea of studying new topics with tech. Over the last few years I've tried just about every way there is to learn with AI. The seed for this project goes back further than the challenge. Years ago I bought the domain studytree.ai (I'm a bit of a domain freak) and it's been rattling around in my head ever since. The original concept was a way to organize your ChatGPT history: a folder system with interconnected nodes so you could go back and actually study what you'd learned in conversation. The problem was keeping that data in sync, so I could never make it seamless. (err proprietary systems) So I pivoted toward a pure studying tool, but I never quite knew what it wanted to be. I even tried wiring in backend MCP servers to prototype it. It wasn't until WebMCP came out that I saw the real unlock: the agent could live inside the page and act through tools the page exposes, no backend required. That's what turned a vague study tool into a game you play with an AI. I mean I had experimented with somewhat of a complex node system here https://app.studytree.ai but I never was truly satisfied. What it does StudyTree is a turn-based learning game on a shared canvas. A human and an AI agent take turns building a knowledge tree around a single learning question. The human clicks and types. The agent can only change the board by calling registered tools. Voice is the agent's controller. Node types: 🌱 Root (the learning question) · 💡 Concept · 📚 Resource · ⚡ Skill · ❓ Gap Moves: Plant, Branch, Prune, Mark Gap, Mark Clear, and a human-only Undo of the agent's last move. Rules: 10 moves total, alternating turns. Win with 5+ nodes and zero gaps remaining when the moves run out. Lose if gaps are still open. The game works through two agent surfaces, and both go through the same six tools: WebMCP an in-browser agent (like ChatGPT's built-in browser) calls tools registered on document.modelContext . ElevenLabs voice an on-canvas voice panel connects to a public ElevenLabs agent that invokes the same moves as client tools. get_board is read-only and free; the other five are the legal moves. Tool arguments accept a node's label as well as its id, so a voice agent can say "branch from First Principles" instead of spelling out n3 . How I built it The build was almost entirely agent-driven, in stages: Voice dump. I started by talking the idea out loud with a Grok voice bot and let it spit the concept back to me. Cloud agent scaffold. That spec went into a Cursor Cloud agent, which spun up the first version. I pulled it down and tested it on a local port inside the Codex browser. Refinement. I brought in Claude Opus 5 to refine the architecture and tighten the tool layer. Redesign. When Claude 5.1 dropped yesterday, I had it re-evaluate the whole design. I pulled visual references from Cosmos for inspiration and had it pick apart the game mechanics. That's where it evolved from "a tree you build" into a real turn-based pairing between human and agent. Stack: Vite · React 19 · TypeScript · React Flow (canvas) · Zustand (state) Architecture: there is exactly one implementation of each move, in the Zustand store. Three entry points reach it: human buttons ──┐ WebMCP tools ──┼──→ applyMove() ──→ store action ──→ React re-render voice tools ──┘ Neither agent surface can touch the DOM or skip a rule, because both call the identical store actions the human's buttons call. Adding a move means adding it once in moves.ts , and both surfaces pick it up. WebMCP registration is feature-detected, so nothing breaks in browsers without it, and the ElevenLabs SDK is code-split so the board is interactive before the voice stack loads. Challenges I ran into Getting the agent to take its turn on its own. Right now the agent moves when you prompt it. I want true back-and-forth: I make a move, and the agent immediately responds without me nudging it. I don't think I've solved this yet. My current thinking is a polling or event loop that watches get_board and triggers the agent when the turn flips. Keeping the agent honest. The agent needed real agency without being able to cheat. Routing every move through the same applyMove dispatcher the human uses, and giving the human an undo, was how I solved that. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Two completely different agent surfaces (WebMCP and ElevenLabs voice) driving one shared rule set, with zero duplicated game logic. No API keys, no backend, fully static deploy. The whole thing runs in the browser. A concept I've been circling for years finally has a shape I can actually play. What I learned WebMCP is far more powerful than I expected. Exposing a handful of well-defined tools on the page is enough to turn a static app into something an agent can genuinely collaborate in. The Codex browser is going to change how people use the internet. Once the general public starts adopting agent-driven browsers, the interactions are going to get profound. Voice-first, agent-first workflows (talk the idea out, let cloud agents scaffold it, iterate with frontier models) are a real way to build now, not a gimmick. What's next for StudyTree Autonomous turn-taking. Finish the polling/event system so the agent moves the instant the human does. Real back-and-forth, no prompting. Fold it into StudyTree. Finished trees persist as study maps, resource nodes become live links, and the 10-move game becomes the on-ramp to a longer learning session. This is the studytree.ai vision I've been sitting on, finally with a front door. Classroom mode. Make this fun for younger students: a whole class builds one tree together with the agent as a co-player, taking turns to plant concepts, spot gaps, and fill them. The game format already has the ingredients (a shared board, clear turns, a win condition) to turn "what do we know about this topic?" into something kids actually want to play. title: Agent Riff
pitch: Agent Riff turns your browser agent into a musical partner. Play a phrase, and it listens through WebMCP and riffs back for a live human and AI music jam.
about_excerpt: Agent Riff turns your browser agent into a musical partner. Play a phrase, and it listens through WebMCP and riffs back for a live human and AI music jam. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Riff — Play a Musical Idea Together Live Musical Conversation in the webpage Human Plays the First Phrase Agent Responds with Its Own Phrase Life in Tech is already complicated, so many tools and frameworks to learn each day and tons of stress to deal with. So why not add more stress to your life when you find out your agent is better than you at playing music!! Inspiration for this Project Most AI music tools work in roughly the same way: you describe what you want, wait for the model, and receive a finished piece of music. We wanted to try somethingball that felt more collaborative. Instead of asking an AI to make music for us, we asked a different question: could a browser agent actually play music with us? That idea became Agent Riff , a musical call-and-response experience between a person and their browser agent. The person plays a short phrase, the agent receives the notes and timing through WebMCP, and then responds with a phrase of its own. The goal was not to create another song generator. We wanted the agent to feel like a second musician who listens before deciding what to play. What it does Agent Riff is a playable browser instrument built for live human and AI collaboration. A person can play notes using a mouse, touchscreen, or the keys on their computer keyboard. The application captures the performance as structured musical events, including the notes, timing, tempo, key, scale, instrument, register, and density. The browser agent can then: Join the current session Analyze the latest human phrase Choose a complementary instrument and register Perform a precisely timed response Wait for the person to play another phrase Change the shared tempo, key, or scale when requested Perform longer musical sets efficiently Agent Riff does not use the microphone or record the user's audio. The agent receives the musical information already created inside the application. This gives it accurate notes and timing without asking it to interpret sound or guess what happened from a screenshot. Human and agent performances appear in a shared live score. Each completed phrase is also saved as a clickable card. A person can replay their own phrase, replay the agent's response, or play both simultaneously to hear how well they work together. The agent can remain available for up to ten minutes between turns. This means the person can continue playing without repeatedly returning to the chat and typing "listen again." If they want to stop sooner, they can release the agent directly from the interface. How we built it Agent Riff is built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. All instrument sounds are synthesized directly in the browser using the Web Audio API. There are no recorded samples, user accounts, external music services, or runtime dependencies. A person can open the page and begin playing immediately. The application exposes seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : riff_join_session riff_get_session_state riff_listen riff_wait_for_human_phrase riff_perform_phrase riff_perform_set riff_set_compass These tools give the agent musical abilities rather than generic browser controls. For example, the agent does not need to find individual piano keys on the screen and click them at the correct moment. It can call riff_listen to receive an analysis of the recent performance, then call riff_perform_phrase with the notes, durations, timing offsets, instrument, and velocity of its response. The performance tool supports sequential notes, rests, chords, overlapping notes, and exact beat-relative timing. For speed, the agent can use a compact score format instead of sending a large object for every note. The waiting tool keeps the call-and-response session active. When the person finishes another phrase, the tool returns both the new notes and the analysis needed for the next response. This lets the agent perform directly without making an additional listening call. We also created riff_perform_set for requests involving complete songs or multiple sections. It can schedule several public-domain or custom pieces in one call, reducing repeated model and browser round trips. Every tool uses a bounded JSON Schema, and all inputs are validated again during execution. The project also includes automated tests for musical analysis, input constraints, WebMCP registration, tool behavior, cleanup, and the production deployment artifact. Challenges The first version technically worked, but it did not feel much like a live musical interaction. The agent would inspect the session, analyze the notes, think about its response, call another tool, play a very short phrase, and then return to the chat. The delay between turns was long enough that it was easy to forget what had just been played. We reduced that delay by combining related information. The waiting tool now returns the completed phrase together with its musical analysis and a suggested response shape. We also added compact score notation so a complete response can be sent in one efficient tool call. Response quality created another tradeoff. Faster models replied more quickly, but their musical answers were often only a few notes long or sounded like random keyboard input. More capable models produced better phrases, but took longer to respond. We improved this by giving the agent clearer musical guidance. Normal responses are encouraged to develop across roughly 12 to 16 notes, with an echo of the human idea, a variation, and a resolution. Dense human phrases receive shorter or more spacious answers so the agent does not overcrowd the music. We also had to account for ChatGPT's side-by-side browser layout. A design that looked good in a full browser window became extremely tall and difficult to use when the browser occupied only half the screen. We redesigned the responsive layout so the instrument, score, activity, agent status, and copied prompt remain accessible in that narrower configuration. Long waits created a separate usability problem. People needed a clear way to tell whether the agent was still present and how to stop it. We added visible agent status, a bounded waiting period, and a release button that ends the current wait and cancels queued agent playback. Finally, browser audio has its own restrictions. Audio must begin from a user interaction, and keyboard input should not interfere with focused form controls. We had to balance reliable instrument input with normal keyboard and accessibility behavior. What we learned The biggest lesson was that a good agent experience depends just as much on tool design as it does on the model. When an agent receives vague page content and generic browser controls, it spends much of its effort figuring out how to operate the interface. When it receives focused tools with compact, structured context, it can spend that effort making a better creative decision. We also learned that fewer tool calls do not necessarily mean less capable tools. Combining the right information at the right moment made the experience faster while giving the agent more useful musical context. WebMCP was a natural fit for Agent Riff because the important information is difficult to communicate through pixels alone. A screenshot can show a piano, but it cannot reliably describe the exact notes, timing, density, and musical direction of the phrase that was just played. With WebMCP, the website becomes more than an interface the agent operates. It becomes a shared creative space where a person and an agent can listen, respond, and build something together. title: human-agent-collab
pitch: AI-powered robotics procurement where agents research and recommend, while humans stay in control.
about_excerpt:
AI-powered robotics procurement where agents research and recommend, while humans stay in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore what the web looks like when AI agents are treated as first-class users. 

 Robotics procurement felt like the perfect use case. Choosing cameras, LiDAR, compute, sensors, and power systems involves a lot of searching, comparing, budgeting, and repetitive decision-making. 

 Our idea was simple: let the AI handle the research and recommendations, while keeping the human in control of the final decision. 

 That became Human-Agent Robotics Procurement 

 What it does 

 Human-Agent Robotics Procurement lets an AI agent work directly with a robotics procurement workspace through WebMCP. 

 The agent can search equipment, compare products, calculate budgets, and generate complete configurations. Instead of simply returning a list of products, it can reason about the project and propose different configurations based on priorities such as cost or performance. 

 The human remains in control. Recommendations are presented for review, and consequential project changes require explicit human approval. 

 The agent proposes. The human decides. 

 How we built it 

 We built the application with React Native, Expo, TypeScript, and Zustand, with WebMCP providing the agent-facing interface. 

 We exposed six structured tools through document.modelContext for product search, comparison, budgeting, project updates, optimization, and human approval. 

 The application maintains shared project, activity, and approval state, allowing the human UI and AI agent to work with the same underlying workspace. 

 A key part of the implementation was separating recommendation from mutation. The optimization agent can generate configurations without changing the project. Only an explicit human approval can turn a recommendation into an actual project change 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out how to integrate WebMCP into an existing Expo application while keeping browser-specific functionality separate from the native application. 

 We also had to carefully design the boundary between agent autonomy and human control. 

 It was tempting to let the agent automatically apply its recommendations, but that would remove an important part of the procurement decision. We instead designed a workflow where the agent can do the time-consuming work independently, while the human remains the final authority. 

 Making the agent's actions visible was another challenge, so we added activity tracking to show users what the agent is doing and when human input is required 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that we transformed a normal procurement interface into an agent-ready web application. 

 The agent can discover and use structured capabilities directly from the page instead of trying to understand the application by interpreting the UI. 

 We successfully implemented six WebMCP tools and connected them to the same application state used by the human interface. 

 We're especially proud of the approval workflow. The agent can search, analyze, optimize, and recommend independently, but it cannot silently make consequential changes. 

 That creates a practical model for human-agent collaboration: 

 AI handles the work. Humans retain the authority 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building for AI agents requires thinking beyond traditional UI design. 

 A human sees buttons, screens, and menus. An agent needs clearly defined capabilities, inputs, outputs, and consequences. 

 WebMCP gave us a way to expose those capabilities directly to the agent. 

 We also learned that meaningful agent autonomy doesn't require removing humans from the process. In many real-world workflows, the best experience may be an agent that can do most of the research and reasoning while keeping humans responsible for important decisions 

 What's next for human-agent-collab 

 We're excited to take the project from a prototype into a more complete autonomous procurement system. 

 Next, we want to connect the workspace to real supplier catalogs, live pricing, inventory, quotations, and delivery information. We also want to introduce multiple specialized agents that can handle supplier discovery, technical compatibility, cost optimization, and negotiation. 

 The long-term vision is a procurement workspace where AI agents can take on increasingly complex work across the entire purchasing process, while humans remain in control of approvals and high-impact decisions. 

 Human-Agent-Collab is our exploration of what procurement could look like when humans and AI agents work in the same workspace not as separate systems, but as collaborators

title: Handrail WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP server that gives AI agents safe, reliable access to web workflows
about_excerpt: A WebMCP server that gives AI agents safe, reliable access to web workflows Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents should eventually help streamline day-to-day store operations, but a tool should never become a way to circumvent orders, refunds, price adjustments, etc., without restraint. With Handrail I aim to add more control by allowing the agent to investigate orders and propose actions that the merchant can ultimately approve and execute. What it does Handrail is a browser based store operations console. Agents can search orders, customers, policies, inventory, shipping, products, and sales data using WebMCP tools. When the agent needs to perform an action like issue a refund or cancel an order, the agent cannot mutate the data. Handrail does validation and creates a parameter approved ticket. The merchant approves the action in the application and only then can the agent execute the same parameters. The guided demo shows the refund for an order ORD-1042 and shows validation failures and request protections against requests that are mismatched or replayed. How I built it Handrail was built using Vite to speed up development and deployed as purely a browser based React application. Handrail also provides a fallback interface when WebMCP tools are not available as it registers 14 WebMCP tools. The safety flow is implemented in the application logic: agent suggestion → approval → exact parameter match → one time execution → confirmation All demo data is held in memory, so it can be safely reset without a backend or payment integration. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was still making the approval step more meaningful than just a confirmation must be checked. An approval should be for the actual amount, the actual order and the actual operation, not a statement like an agent is going to “do this later”. I dealt with this by freezing the canonical parameters for each ticket, validating them again at the time of ticket execution, preventing ticket replay, enforcing expiry, and recording both successful actions and denials in an activity log. What I learned Executable actions and audit receipts make sense between reaching out and approval. The executive semantics of an actual execution are very important when it comes to safe agent tooling, and this is more important than having a label like “read-only” or “write” on that action. title: The Cartographer's Cabinet
pitch: Build worlds together. Explore how they work. Tell their stories.
about_excerpt: Build worlds together. Explore how they work. Tell their stories. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration It started with a palace. A real, historical palace. Or, more precisely, with trying to understand how it actually worked. I wasn’t satisfied with simply finding the dining room or the library on a floor plan — especially because some of the things I wanted to understand were not visible on plans at all. I wanted to know what life in a residence like that looked like, and how the entire space was designed around it. How rooms were positioned in relation to the cardinal directions to make use of daylight, and where a pantry should be placed if it was actually meant to stay cool. How far a serving dish had to travel before it reached the table, and how the movement of guests, residents and servants was kept separate. How architecture itself created privacy, hierarchy and boundaries of access. Over time, those questions turned into a project of my own fictional residence. I started designing the plan together with an AI agent — and it was a difficult, but surprisingly productive collaboration. Codex developed the generator while I inspected and adjusted the generated model in Blender. Together, we analysed sources, discussed possible solutions and iterated on the layout. The problem was that every change, even a small one, meant another code edit, another generation, another render, another review and another explanation of what still needed fixing. My sketches and descriptions were not always as clear to the agent as I thought they were. It became increasingly frustrating that we couldn’t simply work on one shared project — something that would be understandable and editable for both of us. And then WebMCP appeared. Who it's for We built the Cabinet first with writers, game masters and worldbuilders in mind, but the underlying idea is deliberately broader. A fictional palace, a game map, a room layout or a treasure hunt for children may be very different projects, but they all involve thinking through a space, deciding what matters about it and turning those decisions into something visible and editable. The Cabinet brings maps, spatial rules, story information, notes and collaboration with an agent into one working environment. Its aim is simple: to help people build worlds that remain coherent as they grow, and stories that fit the worlds in which they take place. What it does The Cartographer’s Cabinet is a spatial worldbuilding studio for designing places, describing how they work and turning them into stories. It can be used entirely by a human author, but through WebMCP an AI agent can sit beside them as a second cartographer at the table — and, on the narrative side of the same project, as a co-author. A project can begin at almost any scale: a world, a region, a town, an estate, a building, a floor or a single room. These places remain connected in one hierarchy. The author or agent can move from a map of an entire realm to a town within it, then enter an estate, open one of its buildings and continue down to an individual room with its furniture and objects. Adding detail does not divide the world into unrelated maps. In Drawing mode , the physical world takes shape. The user or agent can create terrain, roads and paths, boundaries, buildings, walls, rooms, doors, windows, stairs, furnishings and other objects. The editor can therefore support both broad maps and detailed architectural plans while preserving the relationships between them. In Story mode , the same project captures the information that makes those places part of a living world. The author can create characters and groups, assign ownership, define access and keys, describe relationships, add custom properties, establish zones and record authorial intentions or design constraints. Scenarios represent different moments or possible versions of events, lenses reveal selected information, and the writer’s notebook keeps ideas, scenes and longer passages beside the world to which they belong. WebMCP gives the agent practical access to this workspace. It can inspect the project, create its hierarchy, draw maps, construct and furnish buildings, organise their surroundings and establish the initial Story layer. The human can review that work, change it directly and let the agent continue from the edited version without rebuilding the entire context in conversation. The Cabinet can also examine parts of the world rather than merely store them. Route planning can consider geometry, doors, access rules, keys and character knowledge. Scenarios make it possible to test different circumstances without destroying the base version. The author and agent can therefore ask whether a planned sequence of events actually works inside the world they have built. Because geography, architecture, objects, characters, relationships, rules and intentions remain connected, the project becomes a structured memory for the agent. It can return to the world itself instead of relying only on what still fits in the conversation. The result is a living model of a place or world: something a person can draw, understand and write from alone, or develop together with a second cartographer and co-author at the same table. How we built it We built The Cartographer’s Cabinet as a browser-based application using Next.js, React and TypeScript . Maps are rendered as interactive SVG, giving us precise control over geometry while keeping visible elements selectable, editable and connected to their underlying data. The project is represented as a structured world rather than a canvas of unrelated shapes. Its domain model covers nested places, irregular regions, paths, walls, openings, rooms, furnishings and transitions between levels. Geometry operations combine our own TypeScript code with JSTS . Changes pass through a transaction system before they are committed. This validates operations, keeps related edits together as a single undoable action and prevents a partially applied change from leaving the project in an inconsistent state. Drawing and Story data belong to the same project structure. The writer’s notebook uses Lexical for editing while storing portable Markdown. Projects are kept locally in the browser with IndexedDB and Dexie , validated using Zod , and can be imported or exported as versioned JSON. Immutable snapshots and revision-aware persistence help protect data as edits and asynchronous operations overlap. WebMCP sits directly on top of this domain model. The page registers structured tools that allow an agent to inspect the editor context, navigate the hierarchy, read project data, create and modify objects, manage Story information, calculate routes, create checkpoints and apply larger batches of related changes. Agent actions pass through the same validation and transaction system as edits made through the interface. This keeps their results visible, reviewable and undoable by the human author. Performance-sensitive operations are separated from the interface where necessary. Route calculations run in a Web Worker , while reusable spatial data is cached to avoid repeating work when the relevant parts of the project have not changed. We developed and tested the Cabinet through both the interface and WebMCP, using the full Residence of the Silver Lindens demonstration project alongside smaller focused cases. Our verification pipeline includes linting, TypeScript checks, dead-code and architecture-boundary checks, more than 1,500 Vitest tests , a production build, live browser sessions and additional release checks. The application is exported as a static site and hosted on Cloudflare Pages . It requires no account or application server, and project content remains in the user’s browser unless they deliberately export and share it. Challenges we ran into The greatest challenge was keeping the spatial editor, Story layer, human interface and WebMCP connected to one coherent model. Agent actions had to remain valid, editable and undoable through the ordinary interface instead of creating a separate version of the project behind the scenes. Geometry became increasingly demanding as the editor grew beyond simple shapes. Irregular regions, paths with changing widths, walls, openings and transitions between floors all needed to work together. A door had to be both a visible object and a real opening in a wall. Stairs had to connect the correct levels. Route planning had to understand physical geometry alongside access rules, keys and character knowledge. Scale exposed problems that small examples did not reveal. Operations that were effortless on a simple map could freeze the interface on a complete estate. Route searches produced too many possible connections, large saves interrupted editing, and asynchronous work could finish after the project on which it began had already changed. Solving these problems required changes to both computation and persistence rather than merely hiding the
video_title: The Cartographer’s Cabinet — Building Worlds with AI and WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: Let's start by rebuilding part of an existing project together. I selected the footman's room. The problem is simple. It's meant to be lived in, but it has no window. The agent can read my current selection as context and highlight its own suggestions on the map. It's first solution fixed the daylight problem, but I wasn't satisfied with the result. I wanted a larger rearrangement, so I started it myself by adding new walls and changing the doors. I left the more tedious part to the agent, updating room names, functions, properties, access rules, and furnishings. While finishing the redesign, it caught something I had missed. The new footman's room had inherited guest access from the area it was divided from. The agent corrected it to keep the story data consistent. Finally, I asked it to compare the new layout with the earlier version. We saved the original as a checkpoint and displayed it as a tracing overlay, making the changes easy to see. This was only a small redesign, so the differences are subtle. Now, let's step outside and look at the whole estate. We can expand that, too. The agent was asked to add a farmstead to the existing estate without disrupting the formal gardens. And here it is. The green area that used to occupy this part of the estate has been reorganized into a working farmstead. The agent noticed that the road connection had not been completed correctly, so it added the missing section. It did not stop at the building footprints. The interiors were planned as well, and we can open them and look inside. I accidentally deleted the road the agent had just added, so I simply asked it to rebuild it. Now, let's see what happens when we give the agent a blank project and a design brief. It can create a new project on its own. The previous map remains saved and isn't lost. We can return to it at any time. The agent has access to the same creative tools as the human author. It can shape terrain, add bodies of water and roads, design buildings and rooms, place objects, and much more. It can name every place it creates and give it meaning within the world. You don't have to treat the agent's version as final. You can change it yourself at any point, or you can simply draw a rough sketch on the dedicated sketch layer and ask the agent to turn your idea into the actual project, exactly as I'm doing here. The agent followed my sketch quite closely, but the project still isn't quite where I want it. The location boundaries have become slightly inconsistent, so I'll simply ask the agent to fix them. And done. Our estate now has its stables. Now, let's look at the other side of the coin, literally. Click the red wax seal at the top of the page and the cabinet switches into story mode. Here the focus shifts from building the world to developing what happens inside it. Characters, rules, scenarios, and story ideas all live here. The agent can work with them alongside you. Story mode is a little less spectacular on screen, so I'll keep this part short, but don't let that fool you. This is where much of the world-building knowledge and logic lives. For this demo, I asked the agent to create a small fictional cast for our new estate and set up a scenario. A guest wants to reach the stable secretly at night. Scenarios can temporarily change the conditions of the world, and the agent can check whether an idea actually works within established rules. In this case, it quickly found a problem. The stables are locked at night, so our guest cannot get inside without waking the person responsible for them. Instead of ignoring that fact, the agent suggested story solutions that preserve the established world. Lenses let us reveal selected information directly on the map. Here the agent highlights all service areas of the estate. Roots can be checked for a specific character under specific conditions. The same journey may be possible for someone with the right access or keys, and impossible for an uninvited guest.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. With a passion for thoughtful, over-engineered UX flows. Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Luca Gugliemi started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:26 AM EDT

title: Schedule-Rank-WebMCP-Adapter
pitch: A reusable WebMCP adapter that normalizes contractor availability and ranks it by scheduling-evidence reliability.
about_excerpt:
A reusable WebMCP adapter that normalizes contractor availability and ranks it by scheduling-evidence reliability.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Contractor scheduling data is fragmented. One provider exposes explicit slots, another has business hours and calendar events, and another only has workforce information. Agents need a consistent way to find suitable appointments without pretending that every availability answer is equally reliable. 

 What it does 

 Schedule-Rank-WebMCP-Adapter gives service-provider websites a shared WebMCP scheduling interface. An agent can discover a provider's services and service areas, request available times, and make an appointment request through predictable tools. 

 The adapter also assigns an evidence tier to availability: 

 
 CONFIRMED — explicit bookable slots 
 DERIVED — calculated from business hours and existing appointments 
 INFERRED — based on partial structured data such as workforce schedules 
 UNCERTAIN — based primarily on formatted free text 
 UNAVAILABLE — insufficient scheduling evidence 
 

 The tier measures the reliability of the scheduling evidence, not the quality or reputation of the contractor. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Scheduling is an action-oriented workflow. Visual page scraping forces agents to reinterpret every provider website and can hide the difference between a real slot and a plausible time. WebMCP lets each page expose structured, typed capabilities directly. 

 This creates a better experience for both people and agents: customers can compare relevant providers without repeatedly searching and filling forms, while businesses can keep their existing scheduling backend and expose only the capabilities they already support. 

 How it works 

 The shared JavaScript scheduler registers three tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 get_business_services 
 find_times_for_appointment 
 book_appointment 
 

 Provider-specific adapters supply their own backend data and functions. The shared layer normalizes those different representations and classifies their evidence strength. Three hosted examples demonstrate explicit-slot, calendar-derived, and workforce-inferred scheduling systems. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 An agent can discover which providers offer the requested service, discard providers outside the customer's postcode, query suitable times, and explain the evidence behind each result. The person retains control over the final provider and appointment choice, particularly before a booking action. 

 Testing 

 The three public provider demos were tested in ChatGPT's Codex in-app browser. Each registered all three WebMCP tools with valid JSON Schemas and no console errors. get_business_services was invoked successfully for every provider and returned provider-specific services, service areas, and timezone information. 

 Additional demos: 

 
 https://tomishninja.github.io/MCPDemos/sparkys-electrical/ 
 https://tomishninja.github.io/MCPDemos/rapid-plumbing/ 
 

 Built with Codex 

 Codex assisted with JavaScript development, provider examples, documentation, debugging tool registration and schema problems, live WebMCP browser verification, and preparing the hackathon materials. 

 Limitations 

 This is a prototype using demonstration provider data rather than live contractor systems. Availability confidence is deterministic and based on exposed scheduling capabilities. Production-grade holds, release, revalidation, idempotency, and externally sourced contractor reputation remain future work.

title: Inkframe — An Agent-Native Motion Studio
pitch: Compose editable short-form videos with a browser agent: plan scenes, review every change, manage media, and explicitly approve a local MP4 export through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Compose editable short-form videos with a browser agent: plan scenes, review every change, manage media, and explicitly approve a local MP4 export through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inkframe keeps the agent’s proposed edit visible and editable in the same browser timeline. Inspiration Video editors are built for people who can see what is selected, infer whether a drag worked, and recover from an accidental click. A browser agent faces a different problem: it sees controls and pixels, while the project itself is structured state—clips, timing, text, audio, transitions, and export rules. Inkframe explores a better collaboration model. The person defines the creative direction. The agent works through the editor’s real capabilities, and the person reviews every consequential change. What it does Inkframe is an agent-native motion studio for short-form video. It creates editable 9:16 and 16:9 timelines with video, images, captions, audio, and transitions. In the demo, an agent plans a 16-second Vietnam travel Reel, finds matching Pexels footage and licensed Freesound audio, imports those assets into the browser, composes four scenes, adds captions and transitions, validates the result, and reports the required attribution. The finished work remains an ordinary editable timeline rather than a black-box generated file. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Inkframe expose named, typed editor tools instead of asking an agent to imitate a person clicking through the UI. The agent can inspect the project, search stock footage, plan a storyboard without changing anything, compose an approved plan, validate the timeline, inspect attribution, and request local export. The key control point is approval. A storyboard plan returns a one-use token bound to that exact plan. Composition requires the token and explicit confirmation, so a later mutation cannot silently reuse an earlier approval. Export and destructive actions are confirmed too. How we built it Inkframe is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Its reducer-backed editor session keeps separate 9:16 and 16:9 timelines. WebMCP tools are registered through the browser’s model context with strict Zod schemas and JSON Schema inputs. Elah renders the composition in a browser worker and MediaBunny encodes the MP4 locally. Pexels, Jamendo, and Freesound imports retain provider, creator, source, license, and required-credit metadata. Projects and media stay in browser storage; Inkframe does not upload the source media or rendered video to a render server. Challenges we ran into The main design challenge was making the agent capable without making it authoritative. An early lesson was that atomically exposing every editor action is not enough: the agent also needs a safe workflow. We added capability discovery, preview-first storyboards, content-bound approval tokens, isolated variants, bounded tool output, timeline validation, visual QA, attribution reporting, cancellation, and local export verification. We also had to make tools read current editor state at call time, rather than stale state captured when the page mounted. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when tools express product intent rather than DOM mechanics. A browser agent becomes more reliable when it can reason about a project’s actual state and report what changed. The best outcome is collaborative: people direct taste, make approvals, and retain control; agents handle the structured, repeatable editing operations. What's next We want to make visual review and comparison faster, give creators more reusable motion templates, and continue refining agent workflows that are easy to inspect, approve, and undo. The underlying editor predates this challenge. The WebMCP tool surface, approval workflow, live state bridge, validation, attribution, and judge flow were added during the challenge period. title: RescueRelay
pitch: Live nonprofit data in. An agent prepares the food-rescue handoff. People decide.
about_excerpt: Live nonprofit data in. An agent prepares the food-rescue handoff. People decide. Like Comment Story Updates What it does RescueRelay is a two-sided coordination workspace for time-sensitive surplus food. A donor or browser agent records one structured offer, checks it against three New York City nonprofit profiles, and prepares a reviewable handoff. Live IRS-derived organization and filing records come from ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, while sourced food-intake guidance explains every eligibility result. Agents can prepare work, but they cannot cross the consequential boundaries: only a visible donor control can send the simulated handoff, and only a visible recipient control can confirm the response. Why WebMCP RescueRelay exposes five narrow, schema-defined WebMCP tools: create_surplus_offer, find_eligible_partners, prepare_reservation, get_pending_offer, and prepare_response. They let a compatible browser agent structure facts, run deterministic checks, retrieve the current handoff, and prepare the next safe action without guessing how to operate the page. The human UI and WebMCP handlers share one typed action contract. Sending and final confirmation are deliberately absent from the tool surface. Live data and transparency The app fetches current legal identity and filing records for three allowlisted organizations from ProPublica's IRS-derived Nonprofit Explorer API. Published food-intake guidance is mapped into deterministic, reason-coded pilot rules. The UI distinguishes live records, sourced policy mappings, donor-declared facts, and simulated state. Limitations The handoff is simulated and no charity is contacted. Live public records do not represent current food demand or capacity. The public demo uses browser-local workflow state; Convex is included as the path to shared realtime persistence. title: DevSmith
pitch: DevSmith forge ideas into software with AI-powered project planning.
about_excerpt:
DevSmith forge ideas into software with AI-powered project planning.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project roadmap generation 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Settings and Ollama model selection when using local 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AI assistant 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Upload files section in AI Assistant 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project roadmap generation 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Settings and Ollama model selection when using local 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AI assistant 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Upload files section in AI Assistant 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project roadmap generation 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 From AI Assistant to AI Teammate 

 Inspiration 

 As developers, we use a lot of different tools to build software: an AI assistant for questions and code generation, a task manager for planning, a code editor for implementation, and documentation for figuring out how everything fits together. 

 I wanted to build something that brought the planning and AI development workflow into one place . 

 That idea became DevSmith . 

 DevSmith lets a developer create a project, generate an AI-powered roadmap of milestones and tasks, and then use an in-context AI assistant to ask questions, generate code, explain code, and fix problems. 

 But while building it, I realized there was another interesting problem: 

 AI agents can interact with websites, but interacting with a website through the UI isn't the same as understanding the application's actual capabilities. 

 An agent shouldn't have to guess which button creates a project or determine whether a status badge means "Planning" or "In Progress" from a screenshot. 

 That's where WebMCP became the most important part of DevSmith. 

 

 What I Built 

 DevSmith is a local-first AI development workspace designed to be usable by both developers and AI agents . 

 The workflow is simple: 

 Idea → Project → Roadmap → Tasks → Development 

 A developer can start with an idea and use AI to turn it into a structured development plan. 

 For example: 

 
 "Create a project for a habit tracker API and plan it out." 
 

 With WebMCP, an AI agent can perform that workflow using DevSmith's actual capabilities: 
 create_project
 ↓
generate_roadmap
 ↓
get_roadmap
 ↓
create_task
 
 DevSmith currently exposes tools including: 

 
 list_projects 
 create_project 
 get_project 
 generate_roadmap 
 get_roadmap 
 create_task 
 update_task 
 ask_devsmith_assistant 
 

 Instead of an agent trying to navigate the DOM, it can call a structured tool with a defined schema. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "generate_roadmap" , 
 description : 
 "Generate an AI roadmap (milestones and tasks) for a project." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 projectId : { type : "string" } , 
 model : { type : "string" } , 
 } , 
 required : [ "projectId" ] , 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const res = await fetch ( 
 ` / api / projects / $ { input . projectId } / roadmap / generate` , 
 { 
 method : "POST" , 
 headers : { 
 "Content-Type" : "application/json" , 
 } , 
 body : JSON . stringify ( { 
 model : input . model ? ? "default" , 
 } ) , 
 } 
 ) ; 

 return res . json ( ) ; 
 } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 This means the agent interacts with the capability rather than the visual representation of the capability. 

 

 Why WebMCP Matters 

 Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with DevSmith would essentially have to behave like a human using a browser: 
 Agent
 ↓
UI
 ↓
DOM / Screenshots
 ↓
Guess what to click
 ↓
Application
 
 With WebMCP: 
 Agent
 ↓
WebMCP
 ↓
Structured Tool
 ↓
DevSmith API
 ↓
Database / AI
 
 This makes the interaction more reliable and meaningful. 

 For example, instead of: 

 
 "Find the Generate Roadmap button and click it." 
 

 the agent can perform: 
 generate_roadmap({
 projectId: "...",
 model: "..."
})
 
 The agent doesn't need to know where the button is. 

 It needs to know what capability it wants to use . 

 That is the part of WebMCP that I found most interesting. 

 

 How I Built It 

 DevSmith is built with: 

 
 React + TypeScript + Vite for the frontend 
 Tailwind CSS for the UI 
 Express + TypeScript for the backend 
 SQLite + better-sqlite3 for local project data 
 Ollama for local AI models 
 WebMCP for agent interaction 
 

 The application is designed to run locally with Ollama. 

 The local architecture looks like: 
 ┌──────────────────┐
│ DevSmith UI │
└────────┬─────────┘
 │
 ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│ Express Backend │
└───────┬──────────┘
 │
 ┌────┴─────┐
 ▼ ▼
SQLite Ollama
 │
 ▼
 Local LLM
 
 For the WebMCP integration, DevSmith exposes its important application actions as tools. 

 The tools communicate with the same backend functionality used by the application itself. 

 I also created a cloud LLM fallback for the deployed version so that someone visiting the live demo doesn't need to install Ollama or download a local model. 

 This allowed me to keep the local-first architecture while still making the project accessible to judges. 

 

 What I Learned 

 The biggest lesson I learned was that adding AI to an application and designing an application for AI agents are two different things . 

 Initially, I was mostly thinking about AI as an assistant: 
 User → AI → Response
 
 WebMCP made me start thinking about AI as an actor that can interact with the application: 
 User
 ↓
AI Agent
 ↓
WebMCP
 ↓
Application capabilities
 
 That changed how I thought about application architecture. 

 I had to think about: 

 
 What capabilities should an agent have? 
 What information does an agent need? 
 What should each tool's schema look like? 
 Which actions should be separate tools? 
 What information should a tool return? 
 How can agents modify application data safely? 
 

 I learned that a good agent interface isn't just a collection of API endpoints. 

 The tools need to represent meaningful actions that make sense to an agent. 

 I also learned more about integrating local LLMs into a full-stack application and designing the application so it can support both local and hosted AI providers. 

 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was making WebMCP more than just a checkbox feature. 

 It would have been easy to expose one simple tool and say that DevSmith supports WebMCP. 

 Instead, I wanted the tools to represent actual development workflows. 

 That meant connecting: 
 AI Agent
 ↓
WebMCP Tool
 ↓
Backend API
 ↓
SQLite / AI
 
 Another challenge was balancing the local-first philosophy with the need for an accessible live demo. 

 Locally, DevSmith uses Ollama: 
 DevSmith → Ollama → Local Model
 
 But requiring every judge to install Ollama and download a model would create unnecessary friction. 

 So I implemented a hosted LLM fallback: 
 DevSmith → Cloud LLM
 
 The result is an application that can be fully local for developers who want privacy, while still being easy for someone to test through the live deployment. 

 I also had to work through the normal challenges of building a full-stack application while integrating a relatively new agent interaction model: connecting frontend and backend state, generating useful AI roadmaps, managing tasks and milestones, handling different LLM providers, and making the WebMCP tools work with the existing application. 

 

 What's Next 

 DevSmith is currently focused on project planning and AI-assisted development, but I see WebMCP as the foundation for much more. 

 Future possibilities include: 

 
 GitHub repository integration 
 Codebase-aware AI assistance 
 Git operations through agents 
 Automated task implementation 
 Pull request generation 
 Local code indexing 
 Automated testing and debugging 
 Agent-driven roadmap updates 
 Specialized development agents 
 

 The long-term goal is not to replace the developer. 

 It's to create an AI teammate that understands the project, the roadmap, the tasks, and the tools available to build it . 

 DevSmith started as an AI-powered development workspace. 

 With WebMCP, it became something more interesting: 

 a development workspace that an AI agent can actually operate. 

 

 
 Built With 

 agents css developer express.js generative javascript llm local ollama react sqlite tailwind tools typescript vite webmcp 
 

 
 Try it out

title: ThreatWeaver
pitch: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates simulate_attack — attacker and STRIDE threat edges on the live graph Eight document.modelContext tools discovered in ChatGPT apply_security_patch (patchType: waf, target: api-gateway-1) — WAF inline on the shared ThreatWeaver canvas, verified in the activity log. Inspiration Threat modeling usually lives in a spreadsheet or a chat reply that says “add a WAF.” You still redraw the system by hand. I joined the WebMCP Challenge because architecture work is spatial: if an agent is going to help, it should operate the same live graph the human is looking at—not guess from a screenshot or a text memo. I evaluated a few directions (generic architecture canvases, workflow builders) and chose a narrow B2B technical niche: security-by-design cloud diagrams where the agent can read topology, simulate STRIDE findings, and patch the canvas in place. What it does ThreatWeaver is a security-by-design architecture canvas for cloud systems. The page loads an insecure 3-tier starter: Internet → Web Server → API Gateway → Backend → Database + Object Storage. The human can drag components onto the canvas, toggle public / encrypted / rate-limit flags, or ask the agent to add and connect nodes. The agent uses eight WebMCP site tools on the open page. A typical flow: get_architecture_state → simulate_attack on api-gateway-1 (denial of service) and database-1 (information disclosure), which draws an Attacker node, animated red threat edges, and STRIDE badges → apply_security_patch to insert a WAF in front of the gateway, encrypt the database, and remove public access → get_threat_report for what is still open vs secured vs misconfigured. Every tool call is recorded in the activity log so the human can audit what the agent did. Live demo: https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ This is a graph visualizer and mutator with deterministic tool handlers. The LLM reasons about STRIDE; the app applies consistent canvas changes. It is not a production vulnerability scanner or pentest tool. How we built it Stack: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, xyflow, Zustand, Tailwind CSS v4. Frontend only—no backend MCP server. WebMCP: Eight tools register with await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) in client/src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . Each tool has JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , a title, and readOnlyHint where appropriate. Cleanup uses AbortSignal on unmount. Agent-facing data: Read tools return semantic kind values ( apigateway , database , waf , …) and stable ids like api-gateway-1 , not React Flow internals such as architectureNode . Write path: Tool handlers mutate a Zustand store; React Flow re-renders. The WAF patch inserts a real WAF node and rewires incoming data edges to the target gateway—not just a badge on the card. Deploy: Static Vite build on Vercel; Root Directory is client/ . Scope: New project built during the submission period, not a pre-existing product extended with a thin WebMCP layer. Challenges we ran into Discovering the real WebMCP path: Site tools appear in ChatGPT desktop on Work or Codex with models like Terra / Terra Light. The Chat tab and Luna do not expose site tools the same way. The in-page badge “WebMCP ready · 8 tools” only means tools registered—it does not mean an agent has called them yet. Keeping the agent on the page: The agent sometimes tried to open GitHub or leave the live URL. Tighter prompts (“Stay on this page. Use site tools only.”) were required for reliable demos. Separating reasoning from mutations: STRIDE narrative belongs to the LLM; canvas changes must be deterministic. Each write tool has explicit validation and predictable graph effects so the UI always matches what the tool contract promises. From thin PoC to demo-ready product: An early version was too shallow. I refactored toward an insecure starter graph, topology-changing patches, and an activity log so judges could see tool leverage, not just chat text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single-canvas red-team / blue-team story: attack paths appear on the graph, then WAF insertion, encryption, and private access clear the relevant threat edges—visible in one session and in the demo video. Eight non-trivial tools with clear read vs write roles and schema descriptions agents can follow. WAF mitigation that mutates topology (node + edge rewire), matching what architects expect from “put a WAF in front of the gateway.” Shipping frontend-only on document.modelContext without standing up a separate MCP server. What we learned WebMCP leverage comes from tools against live application state , not from describing UI in chat. Agent APIs should expose stable semantic ids and kinds, not framework implementation details. await registerTool and AbortSignal matter for correct registration and teardown. For this hackathon, the demo video and written description are what help a submission land—show the canvas move when tools fire, not only the agent’s prose. What's next for ThreatWeaver Richer component library and optional import hints from IaC snippets (still scoped as design-time, not auto-deploy). Sharper in-page guidance for agents (copy-ready prompts, clearer misconfiguration rules in get_threat_report ). Shareable threat-report exports for review sessions. Out of scope for the MVP: claiming enterprise SecOps scanning, multiplayer collaboration, or real infrastructure apply from the canvas. Built With javascript react react-flow tailwindcss typescript vercel vite webmcp zustand Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo submission. I owned the product direction, scope, and final delivery for ThreatWeaver. What I did: - Chose the ThreatWeaver concept (security-by-design architecture canvas with agent red/blue team on a shared graph) and locked scope: frontend-only WebMCP, eight tools, insecure starter graph, no backend MCP server. - Defined the WebMCP tool contract (read vs write tools, semantic node kinds, JSON Schema, simulate_attack / apply_security_patch behavior including WAF topology changes). - Directed implementation and refactors after an early thin PoC—toward demo-ready behavior: activity log, inspector payloads, threat report, and judge-friendly sample prompts. - Tested WebMCP end-to-end with ChatGPT desktop (Work/Codex, Terra Light) and Chrome (WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector). - Deployed the static app to Vercel ( https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ ), recorded the demo video, and prepared Devpost/README submission materials.
